episodes.title: AMBOSS Resident Training
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture introduces the AMBOSS Knowledge Plus platform as a comprehensive digital medical library and clinical decision support tool for family medicine residents. It emphasizes that the platform extends beyond a question bank, offering over 1,400 constantly updated articles covering diseases, symptoms, health maintenance, and procedures. The talk demonstrates how residents can quickly find evidence-based answers within 90 seconds using the mobile app, including pocket guides, flow charts, drug monographs, and procedure checklists. Key features include peer-reviewed content, integration with NEJM question banks, and tools for value-based care, such as tiered diagnostic recommendations and red flag identification.
key_points: AMBOSS Knowledge Plus is a digital medical library covering family medicine, internal medicine, pediatrics, and emergency medicine, updated weekly based on guidelines and impactful studies.
The platform is designed to help residents find clinical answers within 90 seconds, with 90% of users reporting success in that timeframe.
Articles are categorized into diseases, symptoms, health maintenance, and procedures, all accessible on a laptop, tablet, or phone, with most features available offline.
Pocket guides collapse key information for common conditions, including checklists for history, exam, diagnostics, and initial management, emphasizing value-based care.
Symptom-based articles guide workup of unspecified conditions, starting with red flags, clinical evaluation, and differential diagnosis broken down by features.
Drug database includes full monographs with dosing and renal/hepatic adjustments, accessible offline.
Over 200 flow charts and 2,000 radiographs with interactive overlays are available to support imaging interpretation and management algorithms.
Procedure articles provide step-by-step techniques, landmarks, illustrations, and checklists to refresh memory before procedures like paracentesis.
Acute management checklists allow sequential tracking of evidence-based steps, useful for handoffs and staff discussions.
Content is peer-reviewed by physicians, not generated by large language models, reducing risk of hallucinations.
Integration with NEJM Knowledge Plus question banks allows seamless linking from library articles to relevant questions.
Calculators (e.g., Ranson, APACHE) are embedded and can save results to clipboard for dictation.

episodes.title: Antenatal Testing - Dr. Bea Abraham
episodes.speaker: Unknown

episodes.title: Dr. Brad Beasley on Podiatry, Diabetic Foot Care, Pearls
episodes.speaker: Brad Beasley
episodes.abstract: Dr. Brad Beasley, a podiatrist (DPM), presents an interactive lecture on diabetic foot care for family medicine residents. He emphasizes the high morbidity of diabetic foot ulcers, the critical role of neuropathy in wound formation, and the often-missed diagnosis of Charcot neuroarthropathy. Practical advice includes checking shoe fit as a simple intervention, recognizing that diabetics may not mount a typical infectious response, and stressing strict non-weight-bearing for Charcot. The talk aims to provide immediately actionable clinical pearls for the office setting.
key_points: DPMs (Doctors of Podiatric Medicine) complete a medical-school-based curriculum with early specialization in lower extremity care, followed by a 3-year residency.
Diabetic foot ulcers have high morbidity and mortality, often worse than many cancers, yet receive less attention.
Neuropathy is the primary contributor to diabetic foot wounds, as it masks pain from injury.
Charcot neuroarthropathy presents as a swollen, red, painless foot in a neuropathic diabetic; it is frequently missed and requires immediate offloading.
X-ray showing bone fragmentation or dislocation is key for diagnosing Charcot; MRI may help differentiate from osteomyelitis.
In diabetics with infection, white blood cell count and left shift may not be elevated due to impaired cellular response.
Over 90% of adults wear the wrong shoe size; shoes should allow about half an inch of space beyond the longest toe.
Simple shoe-fit correction can resolve forefoot pain, nail thickening, and skin issues in neuropathic patients.
Diabetics should remove shoes and socks at every visit, even for non-foot complaints, to facilitate early detection of pathology.
Charcot neuroarthropathy progression takes 6-9 months; strict non-weight-bearing for at least 3 months is critical to prevent foot collapse.
Foot infection is the number one reason a diabetic is hospitalized.
An A1c below 8 is a threshold to reduce lower extremity complications.

episodes.title: Behavioral Med
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the complexities of mental health referrals in a family medicine setting. The speaker explains that finding a therapist is more like finding a primary care doctor or dentist than referring to a specialist. Key resources include a SharePoint list of referral options at IHI, but the speaker emphasizes starting with the patient's insurance list. The St. John referral system is described, noting that referrals often lack clinical details and that mental health providers typically offer 6-8 sessions of 30 minutes each. Practical advice includes walking referrals back to the counseling office for faster processing and using co-counseling appointments for underinsured patients.
key_points: Mental health referrals map more like finding a primary care doctor or dentist than referring to a specialist like a urologist.
The IHI SharePoint list of referral options is organized by license and includes yellow-highlighted entries for providers whose status is unconfirmed.
Patients with insurance should start by checking their insurance company's provider list, then cross-reference with other sources.
SoonerCare (Medicaid) provides excellent mental health benefits for children under 21, but finding adult providers who accept it is difficult.
St. John's referral system sends names to a licensed clinical social worker, but referral notes are not included; the office must dig into records to determine reason for referral and insurance.
St. John mental health providers typically offer 6-8 sessions of 30 minutes each, with limited availability for 60-minute or extended sessions.
Walking a referral back to the counseling office with a demographic sheet and referral sheet can speed up processing by 2-3 weeks compared to the standard email list.
Co-counseling appointments are available for underinsured patients at $20 per session, with a resident observing; these are not for physicians or alumni.
Initial appointment cost at the counseling office is approximately $300, with follow-up appointments around $155 per hour.
The counseling office does not accept SoonerCare for patients over 21 due to administrative barriers with small practices.
LPC, LMFT, LCSW, and LADC represent different training emphases, but the license does not guarantee competence; clinical experience matters.
Insurance coverage for couples therapy is limited in Oklahoma; one partner must be the identified patient for billing.

episodes.title: Cardiovascular Risk& Reduction
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers cardiovascular risk reduction, a core primary care topic. It emphasizes that heart disease is the leading cause of death in the US and that half of all heart attacks are caused by five modifiable risk factors: smoking, cholesterol, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes. The talk focuses on lipid screening guidelines, statin therapy as the cornerstone of risk reduction, and the use of the ASCVD risk calculator to guide treatment decisions. Key teaching points include when to screen for familial hypercholesterolemia, how to monitor statin therapy, and how to manage common side effects like myalgias.
key_points: Half of all heart attacks are caused by five modifiable risk factors: smoking, cholesterol, obesity, hypertension, and diabetes.
USPSTF recommends lipid screening starting at age 11 for familial hypercholesterolemia, then every 5 years from age 40 to 75 for those without risk factors.
Non-fasting lipid panels are acceptable unless triglycerides are over 400, which requires a fasting sample to calculate LDL.
The Dutch Lipid Clinic Network criteria can diagnose familial hypercholesterolemia with a score >8, even without genetic testing.
ASCVD risk score <10%: lifestyle modifications; 10-20%: moderate-dose statin; >20%: high-dose statin.
After starting a statin, recheck lipids at 6-12 weeks, then annually; routine monitoring of LFTs and CK is not indicated.
Statins reduce LDL by 30-50% depending on dose; atorvastatin 10 mg gives ~30% reduction, 20 mg gives ~45% reduction.
Common statin side effects include myalgias (7-20%), elevated LFTs, and a small increase in diabetes risk, but cardiovascular benefits far outweigh these risks.
For statin-associated myalgias, options include switching to a less intense statin (e.g., pravastatin), reducing dose, or using every-other-day dosing.
Non-statin alternatives like ezetimibe provide only ~17% LDL reduction and are best used as add-on therapy, not primary treatment.
Lipoprotein(a) and high-sensitivity CRP are emerging risk factors not captured in the standard ASCVD risk calculator.
Smoking cessation with pharmacotherapy (e.g., varenicline, bupropion, NRT) significantly improves quit rates compared to advice alone.

episodes.title: Care for the un-homed with Dr. Carroll
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Carroll discusses caring for unhoused patients, emphasizing that homelessness has diverse causes including transient bad luck, mental illness, addiction, personality disorders, and low intellectual ability. He stresses meeting patients where they are, removing barriers to care, and building trust through listening. Practical strategies include simplifying medication regimens, using long-acting insulin when patients refuse multiple daily injections, and leveraging community resources like Family and Children's Services, Tulsa Housing Authority, and the Mental Health Association. He also highlights frustrations with unhelpful agencies and the importance of persistence and flexibility in managing this population.
key_points: Homelessness is heterogeneous: transient bad luck, chronic mental illness, addiction, personality disorders, low IQ, and voluntary lifestyle choices are all common.
Meeting patients where they are and building trust through listening is more effective than imposing standard medical recommendations.
Simplify medication regimens when possible (e.g., long-acting insulin alone instead of basal-bolus) to improve adherence.
Many homeless patients have Medicaid but cannot navigate the system; they need maximal hand-holding for appointments, pharmacy, and labs.
Writing a simple note that a patient 'cannot work' can help them qualify for food stamps and other benefits.
APS (Adult Protective Services) is often unhelpful and can make problems worse.
Tulsa Housing Authority and Mental Health Association can help house disabled patients; substance abuse alone is a more challenging route.
Public urination can result in a sexual offender designation in Tulsa County, creating major housing barriers.
Family and Children's Services and Women in Recovery are key mental health and addiction resources for homeless patients.
The Tulsa Healthcare Coverage Project partners with OU to screen homeless individuals for Medicaid eligibility.
Use nurse case managers to coordinate transportation and medication security for unhoused patients.
Practice nonjudgmental care and detach from personal frustration when patients do not follow advice.

episodes.title: COPD - Dr. Matt Haney
episodes.speaker: Unknown
key_points: Inhaler devices have specific mechanisms: Diskus requires opening cap and pulling tab; Respimat twists to load one dose; Ellipta has a counter that shows remaining doses.
Clicking an inhaler multiple times does not deliver extra doses—it wastes medication; patients must take separate breaths for each dose.
Dry powder inhalers are suitable for most patients, but those who cannot coordinate or take a deep breath may benefit from a Respimat.
ICS-containing inhalers (e.g., Symbicort, Advair) reduce exacerbations but increase pneumonia risk; de-escalate ICS if patient is stable.
Always rinse mouth after using ICS inhalers to prevent oral thrush.
LABA/LAMA combinations (Anoro, Stiolto, Breo) are first-line for many patients; each uses a different device (Ellipta, Respimat).
Trelegy (once daily) and Breztri (twice daily) are triple therapies; prefer Trelegy if insurance covers it.
Screen all COPD patients for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency at least once per WHO recommendation.
Long-term oxygen therapy reduces mortality when resting SpO2 <88% or PaO2 <55 mmHg; target SpO2 ≥90%.
For exacerbations despite triple therapy, consider Daliresp (if severe COPD with chronic bronchitis and ≥1 exacerbation/year) or azithromycin (if not currently smoking).
Assess COPD control by asking about symptoms (e.g., dyspnea on level ground) and exacerbation frequency.
For patients with group B COPD (symptoms but few exacerbations), optimize LAMA therapy.

episodes.title: COVID Update, Vaccines, Antibody Tests - Dr. Gerald Miller, PhD
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Gerald Miller provides an update on COVID-19, vaccines, and antibody testing. He describes the SARS-CoV-2 virus structure, focusing on the spike protein's role in infection. The lecture covers vaccine platforms (mRNA and adenovirus vector), how they generate both antibody and T-cell immunity, and the importance of memory cells. He also discusses infectious periods, variants of concern, and the clinical relevance of antibody durability and breakthrough infections.
key_points: The spike protein S1 contains the receptor binding domain that attaches to ACE2; S2 mediates membrane fusion.
Antibodies block infection by neutralizing the virus and promoting opsonization; T cells terminate infection by killing infected cells.
mRNA vaccines (Pfizer, Moderna) use lipid nanoparticles to deliver mRNA encoding the spike protein; J&J uses a nonreplicating adenovirus vector with DNA that produces mRNA for the spike protein.
Because the spike antigen is produced inside the cell, mRNA and adenovirus vaccines generate both antibody and cell-mediated immunity.
Memory B and T cells are stored in lymphatic tissues and provide a rapid anamnestic response upon reexposure, typically within 3-4 days.
Infectious period begins 2-3 days before symptom onset and lasts about 8-10 days based on viral culture data.
Variants of concern (Alpha, Beta, Delta) show increased transmissibility, virulence, or immune escape; no variant has yet rendered spike protein unreactive to vaccine-induced antibodies.
IgG antibody testing can be used to assess response to vaccine or infection, but not for acute diagnosis.
Breakthrough infections in vaccinated patients are often mild or asymptomatic due to rapid memory cell response.
Novavax (protein subunit vaccine) primarily generates antibody response with minimal T-cell immunity.
Natural infection generates antibodies and T cells against many viral epitopes; vaccines generate a more limited response focused on the spike protein.
Vaccine-induced antibodies decline ~40% per month (half-life ~1.5 months); infection-induced antibodies decline ~4% per month (half-life ~6-7 months).

episodes.title: Dr. Cyr on Headaches 6/25/26
episodes.speaker: Cyr
episodes.abstract: This lecture, delivered by Dr. Cyr, covers the clinical distinction of migraine from other headache types, emphasizing the POUND mnemonic (Pulsatile quality, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea/vomiting, Disabling intensity) for diagnosis. Practical management strategies include headache diaries (with an app called Migraine Buddy), early use of NSAIDs or triptans, and a stepped approach to rescue therapy. The speaker also highlights the risk of medication overuse and shares a personal experience with monthly injectable preventive therapy (Ajovy) to illustrate the value of prophylaxis.
key_points: Migraine is a recurring headache lasting 4–72 hours, typically unilateral, moderate-to-severe, aggravated by routine activity, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia.
The POUND mnemonic (Pulsatile, One-day duration, Unilateral, Nausea/vomiting, Disabling) helps increase diagnostic probability for migraine.

Key history questions include triggers (sleep, caffeine, missed meals, weather), red-flag symptoms (Snoop mnemonic: Systemic, Neurologic, Older age >50, Onset sudden, Pattern change), and what the patient has tried at home.
Headache diaries, especially using a free app like Migraine Buddy, help identify triggers and track medication response; they are a recommended tool for patients.
First-line rescue therapy includes acetaminophen, NSAIDs (e.g., naproxen), and aspirin; triptans are more effective when combined with naproxen.
Triptans should be taken early at headache onset; increasing the dose of the same triptan does not generally improve efficacy—if one fails, try a different triptan.
Medication overuse headache is a common pitfall: limit triptan use to <10 days per month to avoid rebound headaches.
Preventive therapy (e.g., monthly injectable anti-CGRP like Ajovy) can dramatically reduce migraine frequency, as illustrated by the speaker’s personal improvement after six months.
Non-pharmacologic measures (dark room, rest, ice/heat packs, hydration) are important adjuncts and should be reinforced with patients.
Recognizing prodromal features (e.g., yawning, fatigue, neck pain) can help patients initiate treatment earlier and potentially reduce attack severity.
Medication overuse limits: analgesics ≤3 days/week, triptans ≤2 days/week or 8 days/month.
Indications for prophylaxis: frequent headaches, medication overuse, interference with daily activities, patient preference.

episodes.title: Dianne Hughes on WIR
episodes.speaker: Dianne Hughes
episodes.abstract: The Women in Recovery (WIR) program provides intensive day treatment for women with substance use disorders and legal system involvement. Residents may encounter these patients presenting with somatic complaints that are often manifestations of psychological withdrawal, anxiety, or avoidance behaviors rather than organic disease. Key clinical pearls include recognizing that ADHD-like symptoms may be due to dopamine depletion, that weekly patterns of stomach pain may correlate with anxiety-provoking programming, and that establishing a medical home and continuity is crucial. The program uses an abstinence-based model with occasional suboxone use and emphasizes teaching self-soothing and coping skills.
key_points: WIR is a structured, three-phase day treatment program for women who are deeply entrenched in the legal system and often have no other treatment options.
Patients in early recovery (Phase 1) present with heightened pain sensation and exaggerated somatic complaints due to psychological withdrawal and lack of coping skills.
Somatic symptoms such as headaches and stomachaches frequently stem from anxiety about court reports, peer presentations, or other program requirements.
Avoidance behaviors are common; patients may request unnecessary medical record reviews or other 'side quests' to escape uncomfortable programming.
ADHD-like symptoms in early recovery are often due to dopamine depletion from substance abstinence, not true ADHD.
The program is abstinence-based but allows suboxone for patients who started it in jail, with careful monitoring.
Patients often have never learned basic self-soothing or how to manage minor symptoms, leading to overreporting and urgent visits.
Establishing a consistent medical home and teaching patients to use it appropriately is a key goal of the program.
The average patient is 34 years old with about 16 years of addiction, and many have experienced trauma and developmental delays.
Sexual abstinence is expected in the program, and UTIs and STDs are common presenting complaints.
Medication noncompliance in this population often stems from resource hoarding, bartering, and mistrust of providers.
Many over-the-counter and prescription medications cause false positives on urine drug screens, including Zofran, phenergan, decongestants, labetalol, dextromethorphan, and Wellbutrin.

episodes.title: Discernment & Perspective
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture explores the unique perspectives and responsibilities of Christian physicians, emphasizing that healing extends beyond physical ailments to encompass spiritual and emotional dimensions. It challenges the modern tendency to separate the spiritual from the physical, drawing on biblical narratives and ancient perspectives to argue for an integrated view of reality. The skin horse's wisdom from *The Velveteen Rabbit* is used to illustrate how becoming 'real' through love and suffering mirrors the physician's journey. Practical implications include recognizing divine appointments with patients and treating the whole person as an inseparable biopsychosocial-spiritual being.
key_points: Alleviation of suffering is not the physician's only or primary goal; healing includes spiritual and emotional restoration.
Modern medicine often creates barriers to whole-person care due to productivity pressures and compartmentalization.
Physicians have unique access to patients' hearts, serving as a launchpad for spiritual and emotional healing beyond physical care.
All healing ultimately comes from God, though it may be mediated through various means including medicine, prayer, diet, and physical therapy.
The Christian worldview embraces an integrated reality where the spiritual and physical are not separate, contrasting with Cartesian dualism.
Biblical narratives show no conceptual distinction between physical, spiritual, and emotional illness; they are interconnected.
Treating the whole person means attending to mind, body, and spirit as an indivisible whole, not as separate parts.
Science provides an important but limited slice of reality; it cannot address spiritual or metaphysical questions.
Ancient and some contemporary cultures do not separate supernatural from natural, viewing illness and healing holistically.
Becoming ‘real’ as a physician involves enduring hardship and love, leading to a deeper, more authentic practice.
Whole-person care requires seeing patients as integrated beings—physical, social, relational, and spiritual—not merely biological organisms.
Biblical shalom implies completeness, peace, and harmony with self, God, and creation, which should inform the physician's approach.

episodes.title: Dr. Abdo on Common Acute Vestibular Syndromes
episodes.speaker: Abdo
episodes.abstract: Dr. Abdo defines acute vestibular syndrome (AVS) as sudden continuous vertigo lasting 24 hours with nausea, head motion intolerance, and imbalance, most commonly due to vestibular neuritis or posterior circulation stroke. He distinguishes vertigo (false sense of motion) from dizziness and explains nystagmus types, including physiologic gaze-evoked nystagmus, pathologic primary gaze nystagmus, and direction-changing nystagmus (central cause or drug toxicity). He emphasizes history taking: timing and triggers are more reliable than symptom description, and medications like phenytoin can cause vestibular side effects due to zero-order kinetics. He reviews BPPV diagnosis with the Dix-Hallpike test, noting that a positive test requires upward torsional nystagmus (not just dizziness) and proper neck extension, and presents a case of phenytoin toxicity mimicking central vertigo.
key_points: Acute vestibular syndrome is defined by sudden continuous vertigo ≥24 hours with nausea, head motion intolerance, and imbalance.
Only 10% of dizziness complaints qualify as AVS; main causes are vestibular neuritis and posterior circulation stroke.
Vertigo is a false sense of motion; if head movement does not worsen symptoms, it is not vertigo.
Nystagmus is named by the fast phase; physiologic end-gaze nystagmus (2-3 beats) is normal.
Primary gaze nystagmus indicates vestibular system dysfunction; direction-changing nystagmus suggests central cause (stroke, drugs, intoxication).
History: symptom description is unreliable; focus on timing (onset, duration, periodicity) and triggers.
Episodic vertigo: BPPV (<1 min), TIA (2-15 min), vestibular migraine/Meniere's (hours).
Constant vertigo: evaluate for vestibular neuritis vs stroke.
BPPV diagnosis: Dix-Hallpike test with neck extension; positive = delayed upward torsional nystagmus that abates.
Phenytoin has zero-order kinetics; doubling dose can cause toxicity (level 6 to 30).
Medication history: ototoxic drugs (gentamicin) cause bilateral vestibular loss (imbalance without nystagmus); antiepileptics can cause central nystagmus.
A positive Dix-Hallpike test requires a delay of 15–30 seconds before nystagmus onset, with rotary nystagmus that abates; if absent, the patient does not have BPPV.

episodes.title: Dr. Acker on Shoulder Disorders & Examination
episodes.speaker: Acker
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers acute and chronic shoulder disorders, including traumatic and non-traumatic causes. Dr. Acker introduces a diagnostic algorithm starting with X-ray for traumatic injuries and evaluating intrinsic vs extrinsic soft tissue problems for non-traumatic cases. Key conditions discussed include AC joint separations (graded I–VI with specific management recommendations), shoulder dislocations (anterior most common with a reduction technique), and biceps tendon ruptures. The talk emphasizes the importance of considering extrinsic causes of shoulder pain such as cervical radiculopathy, MI, and hepatobiliary disease, and provides actionable examination and treatment strategies.
key_points: Use a diagnostic algorithm: for traumatic shoulder pain, obtain X-ray; if negative, evaluate for intrinsic soft tissue injury.
Intrinsic shoulder problems include glenohumeral joint disorders (rotator cuff, impingement, adhesive capsulitis) and extra-articular issues (biceps tendinopathy, AC arthritis).
Extrinsic causes of shoulder pain include cervical radiculopathy, MI, pancreatitis, hepatobiliary disease, splenic injury, lung pathology, and herpes zoster.
AC joint separation types I–VI: types I and II are managed conservatively; type III may need surgery based on patient activity; types IV–VI require urgent orthopedic referral.
For type II AC injury, the AC ligament is torn but the coracoclavicular ligament is intact; palpation reveals tenderness over the AC joint and coracoid.
Anterior shoulder dislocation is most common; reduction can be attempted with thumb pressure on the scapular spine and gentle inferior traction on the forearm.
Biceps tendon rupture presents with a sudden ‘pop,’ pain, ecchymosis, and a characteristic arm deformity; MRI is needed to guide management.
The triad of tests for rotator cuff pathology has ~98% sensitivity when all three are positive; in older patients, two of three may suffice for diagnosis.
Painless passive glenohumeral motion suggests an extrinsic cause of shoulder pain rather than intrinsic joint pathology.
Shoulder dislocations require urgent reduction or orthopedic referral; posterior and inferior dislocations are more difficult to diagnose on exam.
Key bony landmarks to palpate include the sternoclavicular joint, AC joint (with its characteristic divot), acromion, greater tuberosity, and coracoid process.
The AC joint is located at the tip of the clavicle and can be injected at a depth of only 0.5–1 cm.

episodes.title: Dr. Amanda Nichols on Sleep Deprivation
episodes.speaker: Amanda Nichols
episodes.abstract: This lecture addresses the importance of avoiding sleep deprivation for both patient safety and resident well-being. It reviews the history of work hour restrictions following the Libby Zion case and presents evidence that sleep deprivation impairs clinical performance, increases error rates, and contributes to burnout. The talk also explores the cultural barriers that lead residents to 'power through' exhaustion rather than using available resources, and provides practical strategies for alertness management including sleep hygiene and judicious caffeine use.
key_points: Sleep deprivation is linked to car accidents, impaired decision-making, reduced learning ability, and compromised patient safety.
The ACGME work hour restrictions originated from the Libby Zion case and were adopted nationally in 2003.
Clinical performance declines by 1.5 standard deviations in sleep-deprived physicians, with increased errors in tasks like reading EKGs and performing procedures.
50% of residents experience burnout during training, and sleep deprivation is a contributing factor.
There is a cultural tendency to celebrate sleep deprivation and to 'power through' exhaustion rather than seek help, leading to underutilization of support services like taxi/Uber programs.
Signs of sleep deprivation include decreased vigilance, memory impairment, cognitive dysfunction, mood changes, and gross motor performance decline, but there is no standardized assessment.
Good sleep hygiene includes maintaining a regular bedtime, using the bedroom only for sleep, avoiding screens before bed, and keeping the room cool, dark, and quiet.
Caffeine should be used as a medicine—avoided before sleep and after naps, and consumed when most fatigued—rather than as a routine beverage.
Residents must account for moonlighting and charting time within work hour restrictions, and prioritize sleep over additional shifts.
Individual responses to sleep loss vary; factors like pregnancy, children, and life stressors affect tolerance and recovery.

episodes.title: Dr. Amell on Opioid Stewardship 5/14/26
episodes.speaker: Amell
episodes.abstract: Dr. Amell reviews the history of harmful opioid use, including the iatrogenic prescription opioid pandemic, and discusses inpatient opioid stewardship standards. He distinguishes between complex prescription opioid dependence (CPOD) and opioid use disorder (OUD), emphasizing that buprenorphine is a safer treatment for both. The lecture covers the advantages of oral over IV opioids, the rationale for switching to buprenorphine, and its unique pharmacology including partial agonism and ceiling effect.
key_points: The prescription opioid pandemic resulted in nearly 200,000 deaths from prescribed opioids, making it the largest iatrogenic mortality blunder in history.
Complex prescription opioid dependence (CPOD) differs from opioid use disorder (OUD) in that doctors are the 'drug dealers' for CPOD, and it is more common when opioids are started by prescription.
Inpatient exposure to opioids is associated with about 10% of patients becoming 'stuck on opioids' after 2015, regardless of the cause of pain.
IV Dilaudid is twice as strong as IV heroin and carries higher risks of nausea, vomiting, hypotension, hypoxemia, delirium, and pruritus compared to oral or subq administration.
Oral opioids provide smoother pharmacokinetics and can be dosed as effectively as IV for pain control without the spiky peaks and troughs.
Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with high affinity for mu-opioid receptors, allowing it to displace full agonists like oxycodone and fentanyl.
Buprenorphine has a ceiling effect at higher doses, reducing the risk of respiratory depression and abuse potential.
Buprenorphine is not renally cleared, making it safer in patients with renal impairment or dehydration.
The Yale opioid stewardship standard achieved an 81% reduction in IV opioid usage without worsening pain scores.
Physicians must guide decisions when risks outweigh benefits, rather than offering false choices in opioid prescribing.
Buprenorphine is sublingual, allowing administration even when patients are NPO or vomiting, and has lower diversion risk than oral Dilaudid.
One milligram of buprenorphine is roughly equivalent to 20 mg of OxyContin; caution is needed in opioid-naive patients.

episodes.title: Dr. Anne Hogan on Hearing Loss 3/12/26
episodes.speaker: Anne Hogan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Anne Hogan, an audiologist with Ascension ENT, presents a family-medicine oriented lecture on hearing loss. She covers the types of hearing loss (conductive, sensorineural, mixed, and auditory processing disorder), risk factors including genetics, noise exposure, diabetes, and ototoxic medications, and basic audiogram interpretation. The talk emphasizes interprofessional collaboration and provides practical tips for recognizing when to refer patients to audiology or ENT.
key_points: The speech banana on an audiogram shows the frequency and loudness range of common speech sounds; patients with moderate-to-severe hearing loss miss most speech sounds without amplification.
Conductive hearing loss involves outer or middle ear pathology preventing sound from reaching the cochlea; sensorineural loss involves the cochlea or auditory nerve.
Age-related hearing loss has a genetic component; if a patient's parent had hearing loss starting in their 60s, begin screening the patient 10 years earlier.
The cochlea is extremely sensitive to blood flow changes; diabetes, hypertension, and smoking all increase risk of sensorineural hearing loss.
Ototoxic medications (e.g., cisplatin, carboplatin, IV antibiotics) can cause hearing loss; monitoring during treatment allows dose adjustments to protect hearing.
Pediatric ear canals are smaller, acting as Helmholtz resonators that amplify sound at the eardrum, making loud noises more painful for children.
Scarred eardrums (tympanosclerosis) do not cause hearing loss; cholesteatomas, however, can cause conductive loss and require otologic evaluation.
Recurrent conductive hearing loss in childhood is a risk factor for auditory processing disorder because inconsistent auditory signals disrupt neural pathway development during language years.
Tympanometry is a quick, objective test of eardrum mobility; a flat line indicates no movement (e.g., middle ear effusion), while a peaked mountain indicates normal function.
Bone conduction testing differentiates sensorineural from conductive hearing loss: if bone thresholds are normal but air thresholds are elevated, the loss is conductive.
Oklahoma does not require a hearing screening before a child starts school.
Jackie Sethin Scholl pushed through 1990s legislation requiring private insurance to pay for pediatric hearing aids in Oklahoma.

episodes.title: Dr. Anne Hogan on Vertigo 3/12/26
episodes.speaker: Anne Hogan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Anne Hogan discusses the assessment and treatment of dizziness and vertigo, emphasizing that dizziness is a broad symptom while vertigo is the sensation of motion when none exists. She highlights the importance of the vestibular system, including the otolith organs and semicircular canals, and the four-legged stool of balance: visual, vestibular, proprioceptive, and central nervous systems. Key assessments include hearing tests, VNG, VEMPs, and head impulse testing, with attention to patient anxiety during calorics. Risk factors for falls include hearing loss, age, and gender, with up to 50% of older audiology patients reporting a fall.
key_points: Vertigo is defined as a sense of motion when there is none, distinct from dizziness which is an umbrella term.
The vestibular system includes otolith organs (linear acceleration) and semicircular canals (angular acceleration), working in push-pull pairs.
Balance relies on a four-legged stool: visual, vestibular, proprioceptive systems, and central nervous system (motor planning and cerebellum).
The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) stabilizes gaze during head movement; the vestibulospinal reflex (VSR) stabilizes posture.
Hearing loss of 20 dB or greater confers a three-fold increased risk of falls; any hearing loss over mild increases fall risk.
Falls are the leading cause of accidental death in adults 65+, with women at twice the risk of men due to higher fracture rates from osteoporosis.
VNG includes assessment of saccades, smooth pursuit, gaze testing, Dix-Hallpike positioning, and calorics; anxiety reduction improves patient experience.
VEMPs (cVEMP and oVEMP) assess saccule and utricle function, respectively; oVEMP can be abnormal in active BPPV due to otoconia detachment.
Head impulse testing detects acute semicircular canal dysfunction; with chronic dysfunction, compensatory saccades may appear.
Non-modifiable fall risk factors include age over 85 (1 in 2 fall annually) and female gender; white non-Hispanic older adults have higher fall rates than Black or Hispanic counterparts.
The ECOG is not part of the diagnostic criteria for Meniere's disease per the Barany Society; diagnosis relies on fluctuating hearing loss, roaring tinnitus, and episodic vertigo.
Constant dizziness is not otologic because the ear acts as an accelerometer; persistent symptoms suggest a central cause.

episodes.title: Dr. B Howard on RA & Lupus 10/23/25
episodes.speaker: B Howard
episodes.abstract: This segment of a residency lecture on rheumatoid arthritis and lupus opens by distinguishing acute from chronic pain and introducing centralized pain as the dominant mechanism of chronic musculoskeletal complaints. Dr. Howard then focuses on fibromyalgia—one of the most common causes of chronic widespread pain—and traces its evolving diagnostic criteria from 1990 tender points to the 2011/2016 widespread pain index and symptom severity scale. He emphasizes that fibromyalgia is not a discrete disease but a spectrum of polysymptomatic distress, and he reviews standardized history-taking and mechanism-based medication selection. The talk sets up RA and lupus as inflammatory, peripheral nociceptive conditions to be considered alongside fibromyalgia in the differential.
key_points: Chronic pain is defined as lasting more than 3 months; most chronic pain is centralized, arising from the brain and spinal cord rather than peripheral tissue damage.
Fibromyalgia, RA, and lupus are the usual suspects for chronic widespread pain; fibromyalgia is common (~1.5% of US adults, 9:1 female predominance).
Fibromyalgia criteria have evolved from the 1990 tender point exam to the 2011/2016 WPI + SS scale; tender point exam is no longer required.
Fibromyalgia can be diagnosed with WPI ≥7 and SS ≥5, or WPI 4–6 plus SS ≥9.
Fibromyalgia symptoms must be present for at least 3 months, and widespread pain must involve at least 4 of 5 body regions.
All humans fall somewhere on a 0–31 polysymptomatic distress scale; fibromyalgia represents the upper end of this common symptom pool.
PHQ-15 >10 or polysymptomatic distress score >12 identifies patients who cluster with fibromyalgia-positive diagnoses.
Mechanism-based treatment: NSAIDs/opioids for peripheral nociceptive pain, TCAs/SNRIs for both central and peripheral, gabapentinoids/cannabinoids for central pain.
There is ongoing controversy about whether central sensitization is causal; Wolfe cautions against over-medicalizing fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia frequently coexists with RA and lupus and can amplify symptoms of those conditions.
Prevalence: fibromyalgia 3.4%, RA ~2%, SLE ~0.5% in US women.
RA is a symmetric inflammatory peripheral polyarthritis; hallmark is morning stiffness >1 hour.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Foot & Ankle Basics 9/4/25
episodes.speaker: Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft presents a practical guide to common foot and ankle conditions for primary care. The lecture covers Morton's neuroma, plantar fasciitis, hammertoes, bunions, and posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (PTTD), emphasizing office-based diagnosis and management. Key teaching points include the anatomy-based explanation for the common location of Morton's neuroma, the importance of differentiating plantar fasciitis from Achilles tendinitis, and the critical need for early recognition of PTTD to avoid irreversible flatfoot deformity. The talk also highlights injection risks, such as fat pad atrophy with plantar fascia injections, and conservative treatment strategies including footwear modification and stretching.
key_points: Morton's neuroma is a sensory nerve swelling most common between the third and fourth digits due to movement of adjacent metatarsal heads; the fourth and fifth digits share a common bone attachment, restricting motion and causing nerve impingement.
Diagnosis of Morton's neuroma is clinical: splaying of toes, decreased sensation along the nerve distribution, and pain elicited by squeezing between digits; no imaging is needed.

First-line treatment for Morton's neuroma is proper footwear (wide toe box, low heels); Crocs can help by splaying toes. Cortisone injection shrinks the nerve; surgical excision is definitive if conservative care fails, with residual numbness but no motor deficit.
Plantar fasciitis pain is worst on the first step in the morning and localized to the calcaneal origin; however, Achilles tendinitis can present identically and must be considered.
A heel spur on X-ray is a result of chronic inflammation and calcium deposition, not the cause of pain.
Corticosteroid injection for plantar fasciitis is very painful and risks fat pad atrophy, causing long-term pain with every step; avoid injecting into the fat pad.
First-line therapy for plantar fasciitis includes NSAIDs, heel drops (dropping heel off a stair for 30 seconds, 10 times/day), and night splints.
Hammertoes and bunions only require treatment when they cause symptoms like skin breakdown, which risks infection; management includes padding, wide-toe-box shoes, and corn pads.

Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (PTTD) is an acquired flatfoot from chronic inflammation and tendon degeneration; early diagnosis is critical because flexible deformities can be reversed with arch supports, but rigid deformities require surgery.
The 'too many toes sign' is a diagnostic clue for PTTD: when standing behind the patient, the lateral toes are visible from behind due to hindfoot valgus and forefoot abduction.
Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (PTTD) presents with medial foot pain, inability to rise on one foot, and active arch collapse after age 50; differentiate from congenital flat feet.
PTTD treatment includes arch support, physical therapy targeting tibialis posterior, and OMT; rigid arches that cause pain with support require podiatry referral.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Head & Neck in Urgent Care Setting
episodes.speaker: Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft presents two urgent care cases: an elderly woman with a fall and subdural hemorrhage, and a young woman with anaphylaxis. Key teaching points include recognizing elevated BNP as a marker for intracranial hemorrhage, appropriate management of subdural hematoma (avoid hyperventilation/mannitol, maintain normotension and isotonic fluids with sodium >135, arrange transfer), and the diagnostic criteria and treatment of anaphylaxis (IM epinephrine, repeat dosing every 5 minutes, prepare for intubation). The lecture also emphasizes not treating based on labs alone and the importance of effective communication with nursing staff.
key_points: Elevated BNP can be a marker for intracranial hemorrhage, not just heart failure.
In elderly patients with fall and altered mental status, consider subdural hemorrhage even if symptoms are stable.
For chronic subdural hematoma, avoid hyperventilation and mannitol; they are not indicated.
Manage blood pressure and maintain isotonic fluids with sodium above 135 in subdural hemorrhage.
Before transferring a patient with subdural hemorrhage, obtain acceptance from the receiving neurosurgical facility.
Epinephrine for anaphylaxis must be given intramuscularly, not subcutaneously.
In anaphylaxis, epinephrine can be repeated every 5 minutes; after two doses without improvement, prepare for intubation and ICU transfer.
Diagnostic criteria for anaphylaxis: two of three – skin involvement, respiratory compromise, or hypotension/GI symptoms.
Do not leave the patient alone during anaphylaxis; stay in the room and be ready for airway management.
Always verify lab results with clinical picture; do not treat based solely on abnormal labs (e.g., BNP, elevated white count).
Anaphylaxis: give epinephrine every 5 minutes as needed, up to three doses; start an epinephrine drip if third dose is required.
After second epinephrine dose, consider nebulized albuterol and IV steroids; Benadryl is also indicated.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Hematuria Evaluation
episodes.speaker: Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft's lecture on hematuria evaluation emphasizes the importance of risk stratification for malignancy, particularly bladder cancer, based on the American Urologic Association guidelines. He covers the two types of hematuria (gross and microscopic), proper detection methods (dipstick confirmed by microscopy), and key risk factors such as smoking, age, male sex, and occupational exposures. The talk details initial workup including history, physical exam (DRE, abdominal, CV tenderness), labs, and imaging (low-dose CT for thin patients, standard for obese). He stresses that anticoagulation or known medical renal disease does not obviate the need for urologic evaluation, and warns against anchoring on UTI in women without follow-up. Risk stratification into low, intermediate, and high categories guides referral decisions, especially in rural settings.
key_points: Microscopy is the gold standard for confirming hematuria; dipstick can have false positives from myoglobin, hemoglobin, semen, alkaline pH, or cleaning agents.

Risk factors for malignancy include smoking (>10 pack-years), age >35, male sex, history of gross hematuria, persistent microscopic hematuria, prior pelvic radiation, certain chemotherapies, occupational exposure to dyes/rubbers/petrochemicals, and chronic indwelling foreign bodies.
Reassuring symptoms that suggest benign causes include transient flank pain, recent exercise, dysuria, vaginal discharge, and BPH symptoms.
Initial evaluation includes a detailed history, physical exam (DRE, abdominal, CV tenderness, testicular exam), blood pressure, creatinine, and urinalysis with culture.
Anticoagulation does not explain hematuria; patients on anticoagulants with unexplained hematuria require the same urologic workup.
Even if medical renal disease is present, patients should be referred to both nephrology and urology to avoid missing a lower tract malignancy.
Imaging for suspected stones: low-dose CT for BMI <30, standard-dose CT for obese patients; ultrasound is an alternative.
Low-risk patients (3-10 RBC/HPF, women <60 or men <40, never smoked or <10 pack-years, no other risk factors) can be followed without urology referral.
Intermediate-risk patients (11-25 RBC/HPF, or persistent low-risk findings, women >60, men 40-59, 10-30 pack-years, or any one risk factor) warrant urology consultation.
About 50% of women with bladder cancer are initially treated for UTI; persistent or atypical symptoms require further workup rather than repeated antibiotic courses.
AUA guidelines stratify hematuria risk into low, intermediate, and high, with specific referral and imaging recommendations.
Patients over 60 with any hematuria should be referred to urology, regardless of BPH.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Rural ER Medicine
episodes.speaker: Bancroft
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bancroft provides a practical overview for family medicine residents preparing to work in rural ER settings, emphasizing both administrative know-how and clinical preparedness. He covers the financial realities of 1099 independent contractor work, including quarterly tax payments, deductions for mileage, meals, and educational supplies, and the value of forming a PLLC or working with a CPA. Clinically, he discusses bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) settings, rapid sequence intubation (RSI) using ketamine and succinylcholine, and the importance of having procedure checklists, a bougie, and a consultant on speed dial. Throughout, he encourages residents to embrace hard work as part of professional growth and to keep a log of all expenses and miles.
key_points: 1099 contractors must pay self-employment tax (additional 15% for Medicare/Social Security) and may owe quarterly estimated taxes or face IRS fines and interest. Setting aside 20% (5% state, 15% federal) of each 1099 paycheck is a simple strategy.
Mileage can be deducted at a fixed IRS rate (e.g., 65¢/mile), and per diem meal deductions for travel shifts: ~$50 first/last day, ~$60 full days.
Educational supplies (books, UpToDate subscriptions, CME travel/hotel, scrubs, stethoscopes, shears) are deductible business expenses.
Creating a Professional Limited Liability Company (PLLC) can provide tax benefits (home office, computer, car) but does NOT shield personal assets from malpractice liability.

For BiPAP initiation in acute respiratory failure: start IPAP 12, EPAP 5, FiO2 100%, inspiratory time 1 second. Adjust EPAP upward for pulmonary edema (e.g., EPAP 8) and watch for mask seal at IPAP >16.
If a BiPAP patient is tachypneic, consider reducing inspiratory time (e.g., to 0.5 sec) to avoid stacking breaths and dyssynchrony.
Minute ventilation (respiratory rate × tidal volume) from BiPAP can be used to guide initial ventilator settings after intubation.
Rapid sequence intubation (RSI): ketamine 1-2 mg/kg plus succinylcholine 1.5 mg/kg is a common and effective combination; always have a bougie and glidescope ready as backup.
Maintain a personal 'crash' algorithm for difficult airway; reach out to a trusted colleague by phone/text to review your intubation plan before proceeding when possible.
Document all shifts, miles, and expenses in a logbook or app (like QuickBooks) to streamline deductions and CPA handoff.
Bougie use for difficult airway: feel vibration over tracheal rings to confirm placement.
RSI technique: minimize bag-masking; use BiPAP until patient fades, then remove and intubate.

episodes.title: Dr. Bancroft on Sore Throat, Rhinitis, & Sinusitis
episodes.speaker: Bancroft
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the diagnosis and management of allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, and pharyngitis. Key points include proper use of intranasal glucocorticoids, antibiotic stewardship for sinusitis (10-day rule), and recognition of serious complications. The importance of differentiating viral from bacterial causes and avoiding unnecessary antibiotics is emphasized. Special attention is given to high-risk patients and appropriate treatment escalation.
key_points: Allergic rhinitis is IgE-mediated; nonallergic rhinitis is triggered by irritants like smoke or cold air.
First-line treatment for allergic rhinitis is intranasal fluticasone (Flonase) with proper technique (no inhalation needed).
For sinusitis, antibiotics are indicated only after 10 days of symptoms without improvement; exam findings alone are not sufficient.
Avoid macrolides (e.g., Z-Pak) for sinusitis due to poor efficacy.
High-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (2 g twice daily) is used for severe cases or risk factors (age >65, recent hospitalization, antibiotics in past month, immunocompromised, diabetes, CAD).
Montelukast carries a black box warning for neuropsychiatric events; use only in patients with asthma or when other treatments fail.
In pharyngitis, consider gonorrhea and chlamydia testing in patients with high-risk sexual behavior (MSM, oral sex).
Exam findings for allergic rhinitis include a transverse nasal crease and bluish turbinates.
Recurrent sinusitis requires 10 symptom-free days; if symptoms recur within 5 days of treatment, it is considered the same infection.
Complications of sinusitis (orbital cellulitis, osteomyelitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis) require imaging: CT for bone, MRI for soft tissue.
Use Centor criteria to determine who needs testing for strep throat; do not test if criteria are not met.
A negative rapid antigen test is reliable; do not routinely send a culture unless the patient is high risk.

episodes.title: Dr. Beasley on Diabetic Foot Disease
episodes.speaker: Beasley
episodes.abstract: Dr. Beasley provides a practical overview of diabetic foot disease for family medicine residents. He covers the three main high-risk foot types (PAD, neuropathy, and diabetes) and emphasizes that diabetes causes systemic issues including immunosuppression. He discusses Charcot neuroarthropathy as a frequently missed diagnosis in patients with unilateral swelling and no pain, and highlights the importance of early surgical intervention for septic joints. The talk concludes with actionable pearls for patient education and shoe fitting.
key_points: Capillary refill delay and absent pedal pulses warrant noninvasive vascular testing like ABI.
When neuropathy is idiopathic, consider lumbar spine pathology (bulging disc) as a cause.
Diabetic patients may not mount a septic response despite having abscess or septic joint; urgent surgical drainage is required.
Charcot foot presents with unilateral swelling, redness, and no pain history; obtain an X-ray even if no remembered injury.
Mortality rises significantly after major lower extremity amputations; preserve the foot whenever possible.
Risk of lower extremity complications decreases when A1c is below 8%.
Cotton socks are outdated; recommend synthetic wicking socks (e.g., SmartWool, Thorlo, Darn Tough).
Patients should inspect their feet daily using a mirror or phone camera if they cannot bend down.
Feet grow about half a size every 10-15 years due to gravity; many patients wear shoes too small.
Check shoe fit by removing the insole and stepping on it: toes should be within one thumb's width of the end and not spill over the sides.
Checking shoe fit is a high-yield preventive measure; half of surgeries may be avoided by identifying improperly fitting shoes.
Diabetic feet should be inspected daily, moisturized to maintain skin elasticity, and never left barefoot due to risk of injury.

episodes.title: Dr. Bhakta on Acute GI Concerns
episodes.speaker: Bhakta
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bhakta discusses acute GI concerns, emphasizing the importance of proper triage for upper GI bleeds, pancreatitis, and obstructive uropathy. He highlights that ICU admission is driven by nursing ratios and monitoring capabilities rather than different medications, and stresses the need for early enteral feeding in pancreatitis to reduce bacterial translocation. The lecture also covers diagnostic pearls such as checking triglycerides in first-time pancreatitis and recognizing pneumatosis intestinalis as a surgical emergency, while underscoring the importance of honest communication with patients and families about poor prognoses.
key_points: For upper GI bleeds, especially with cirrhosis or varices history, request ICU admission due to higher monitoring and rapid response capability.
ICU vs floor care differs primarily in nurse-to-patient ratios (1:2 vs 1:6) and speed of lab/imaging, not in available medications.
In pancreatitis, early enteral feeding protects the mucosal barrier and reduces bacterial translocation; if no improvement in 48-72 hours, evaluate for abdominal compartment syndrome.
For first-time pancreatitis, always check a lipid panel to rule out hypertriglyceridemia, which can be treated with high-dose insulin or plasmapheresis.
In obstructive uropathy with hydronephrosis and sepsis, urgent urology consultation is needed; stent placement can trigger rapid deterioration from endotoxin release.
Pneumatosis intestinalis on CT indicates bowel ischemia; start heparin drip and call surgery, and be honest with the patient and family about the grim prognosis.
For small bowel obstruction without peritonitis, patients do not need ICU but require surgical consultation and possibly NG tube.
In patients with DNR/DNI status and deteriorating condition, consider comfort-focused care rather than ICU transfer, as ICU offers no different medications.
Always ask about NSAID use, prior GI bleeds, peptic ulcer, and H. pylori history in patients with upper GI bleeding to assess perforation risk.
Red Gatorade can mimic hematemesis; always verify the nature of emesis before escalating care.
In cirrhotic patients with ascites, multiple paracenteses increase the risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP).
CT finding of gas in the scrotum (suggestive of Fournier's gangrene) in a patient with abdominal pain is a surgical emergency requiring immediate surgical consultation and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

episodes.title: Dr. Bhakta on Distress in Adults
episodes.speaker: Bhakta
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the recognition and management of respiratory distress in adults, emphasizing clinical assessment over isolated numbers. Key cases include asthma exacerbation, DKA with compensatory tachypnea, CHF with pulmonary edema, and tension pneumothorax. The speaker reviews oxygen delivery devices, ABG interpretation, and contraindications to BiPAP. Practical pearls include not suppressing compensatory tachypnea, using accessory muscle use as a key sign, and recognizing that a patient's report of being tired of breathing is an indication for ventilation.
key_points: Respiratory rate >30 is concerning; accessory muscle use is a key indicator of distress.
In DKA, tachypnea is compensatory; do not slow it down.
For asthma exacerbation, start with albuterol and reassess before escalating.
In CHF with fluid overload, step up Lasix dose; expect a creatinine bump.
Tension pneumothorax is diagnosed by midline shift, widened rib spaces, and depressed diaphragm; treat with needle decompression.
ABG interpretation: first determine acidotic or alkalotic, then check CO2 and bicarb; use chemistry bicarb not calculated ABG bicarb.
Oxygen delivery: nasal cannula max 6 L/min (~40%), simple mask 5-10 L/min (35-55%), non-rebreather up to 15 L/min (60-95%).
BiPAP contraindications: GCS <7, vomiting, facial trauma, cardiac arrest (absolute); anxiety and inability to protect airway (relative).
Defibrillators can be identified by a coil on the lead; all defibrillators can pace.
A patient saying they are tired of breathing is a strong indication for intubation regardless of numbers.
On BiPAP, FiO2 and EPAP improve oxygenation; the IPAP-EPAP difference determines tidal volume and CO2 clearance.
For a patient with pH 7.2, pCO2 80, O2 50, increase FiO2 and respiratory rate first.

episodes.title: Dr. Bhakta on Rapids, ICU Criteria 8/27/26
episodes.speaker: Bhakta
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bhakta provides a practical guide for residents on managing rapid responses and deciding between floor vs ICU care. He stresses the importance of seeing the patient first, assessing ABCs, and using specific criteria to differentiate ventricular tachycardia from supraventricular tachycardia. Key pearls include how to manage hypotension in ESRD patients, when to use electricity for unstable rhythms, and the need for clear, direct goals-of-care discussions at a fifth-grade level. The talk also covers oxygen escalation, code status separation, and taking ownership of patients.
key_points: During a rapid response, look at the patient first for appearance and distress before gathering vitals or details.
Major ICU indications include need for ventilator, vasopressors, or higher nurse-to-patient ratio (e.g., 1:2 or 1:1).
For hypotension in ESRD, consider recent hemodialysis; give fluids if volume-depleted, albumin only if albumin <3 g/dL, and midodrine can be tested but stopped if ineffective.
Tele-nurses are trained to call any wide-complex tachycardia V-tach; you must decide using criteria (absence of normal bundle branch, notching sign, etc.).
Unstable patients (passing out, slumped) require immediate electrical cardioversion regardless of underlying rhythm.
For stable atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, beta blockers are first-line; refractory cases seldom need ICU transfer and EP consultants often agree.
Code status and advance directives should be discussed in clinic early, readdressed on every admission and daily rounds; DNR and DNI are separate orders.
Communicate prognosis and goals of care directly at a fifth-grade education level, avoiding sugarcoating or false hope.
Take ownership of patients by making nurses face you, not the attending, and start decision-making early in residency.
Oxygen escalation to heated high flow, BiPAP, or ventilator typically requires a step-down unit or ICU.
Directly communicate poor prognosis to patients to prevent false hope about curative treatment.
Use specific mortality statistics (e.g., 97% mortality) to convey the severity of an injury or illness.

episodes.title: Dr. Bothwell on Anemia of Pregnancy
episodes.speaker: Bothwell
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers anemia of pregnancy, distinguishing physiologic dilutional anemia from pathologic causes. Iron deficiency anemia is the most common pathologic anemia, diagnosed by ferritin less than 30 ng/mL. Management includes oral iron every other day to optimize absorption, with IV iron reserved for severe cases or intolerance after the first trimester. The lecture also reviews macrocytic anemia due to folate deficiency and hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease, emphasizing preconception counseling and management adjustments during pregnancy.
key_points: Physiologic anemia results from plasma volume increasing 40-50% while RBC mass increases only 15-30%, causing a dilutional drop in hemoglobin.
Iron deficiency anemia is confirmed by ferritin <30 ng/mL; it is the most common pathologic anemia in pregnancy.
Risk factors for iron deficiency include short interpregnancy interval, teenage pregnancy, vegetarian diet, and medications that impair absorption (e.g., antacids).
Oral iron should be given every other day (not daily) because hepcidin blocks absorption for 24 hours after a dose.
IV iron is safe after the first trimester (starting at 13 weeks) and can achieve higher hemoglobin levels at delivery with fewer GI side effects; avoid iron dextran due to benzoyl alcohol.
USPSTF finds insufficient evidence for routine screening, but ACOG/CDC recommend CBC at first visit and again at 24-28 weeks.
Folate deficiency is the most common cause of macrocytic anemia in pregnancy; treat with 1 mg folic acid daily.
In sickle cell disease, hydroxyurea is teratogenic and must be stopped before pregnancy; increase folate to 4 mg daily and manage pain crises with analgesia and oxygen.
Screen for hemoglobinopathies with CBC and hemoglobin electrophoresis in patients of African, Southeast Asian, or Mediterranean descent.
Acetaminophen can rarely cause drug-induced hemolytic anemia in pregnancy.
No consensus exists on HELLP syndrome criteria; the Tennessee classification is considered more specific than ACOG criteria.
Tennessee HELLP criteria include haptoglobin less than 25, hemoglobin less than 8, bilirubin greater than 1.2, and schistocytes on peripheral blood smear.

episodes.title: Dr. Bothwell on Breastfeeding
episodes.speaker: Bothwell
episodes.abstract: Dr. Bothwell presents a comprehensive lecture on breastfeeding for family-medicine residents, covering counseling techniques, latch mechanics, and evidence-based benefits for both infant and mother. She reviews common barriers, complications such as mastitis and engorgement, and management strategies including positioning, antibiotics, and supportive care. The talk emphasizes the importance of continued breastfeeding support and practical resources for clinicians.
key_points: Breastfeeding reduces infant risk of asthma, obesity, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, ear/respiratory infections, SIDS, and necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants.
Maternal benefits include decreased risk of ovarian, breast, and endometrial cancers, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, plus enhanced postpartum weight loss and lactational amenorrhea.
Human milk provides IgA, lactase, lysozymes, and amino acids that support infant gut health, immunity, and neurobehavioral development.
Analgesic effect of breastfeeding during painful procedures may be mediated by higher cortisol levels, as shown in a 66-infant study.
Only 25.4% of U.S. infants are exclusively breastfed at 6 months; 45% of mothers report early undesired weaning, often due to pain, poor latch, or work-related barriers.
Good latch technique: baby's nose opposite nipple, wide mouth, chin touching breast, more areola visible above upper lip, no pain beyond initial attachment.
Mastitis treatment includes continued breastfeeding, warm compresses, and first-line antibiotics such as cephalexin; bilateral mastitis warrants checking baby's mouth for streptococcal infection.
Breast abscess complicating mastitis is often MRSA and requires surgical drainage.
Low milk supply should be objectively assessed by wet diaper count (≥8/day), weight checks (15-30 g/day gain after day 4, <10% loss at week 1, return to birth weight by 10-14 days).
Supportive resources: lactation consultants, employer pumping accommodations per Oklahoma law (2021), and video tutorials for latch technique.
Engorgement usually occurs postpartum day three to five, later in C-section moms by 24-48 hours due to increased stress.
Risk factors for engorgement include extended labor with IV fluids, baby sleeping through the night, and first-time mothers.

episodes.title: Dr. Bothwell on Effects of Vitamin D Supplementation and Pregnancy Outcomes: Pre-Eclampsia
episodes.speaker: Bothwell
episodes.abstract: This journal club presentation discusses a double-blind randomized controlled trial examining the effect of vitamin D supplementation (50,000 IU every two weeks) versus placebo on recurrent preeclampsia in pregnant women with a history of preeclampsia. The study found a statistically significant reduction in preeclampsia incidence in the intervention group (p=0.036). The discussion covers background on preeclampsia risk factors and vitamin D deficiency prevalence, study methodology, results, and limitations including lack of control for other supplements and generalizability to Iranian women. Current guidelines from ACOG and USPSTF do not recommend routine screening or supplementation, but meta-analyses suggest a potential benefit of vitamin D in reducing preeclampsia risk.
key_points: Preeclampsia complicates 8% of pregnancies and accounts for 25% of maternal deaths.
Vitamin D deficiency prevalence ranges from 18% to 84% depending on the country.
The study was a double-blind RCT with 70 women in the intervention group and 72 in the control group.
Intervention: vitamin D 50,000 IU every two weeks (equivalent to ~3,500 IU daily) vs placebo.
Inclusion required a history of preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy and normal baseline vitamin D levels.
The intervention group had a significantly lower probability of recurrent preeclampsia (p=0.036).
No side effects were reported from the vitamin D supplementation.
ACOG does not recommend routine screening for vitamin D deficiency in pregnancy.
USPSTF states insufficient evidence to recommend for or against vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy.
Meta-analyses of RCTs and observational studies suggest vitamin D supplementation may decrease preeclampsia risk.

episodes.title: Dr. Brad Hardy on Contracts, Coding, and Resident Financial Basics
episodes.speaker: Brad Hardy
episodes.abstract: Dr. Brad Hardy presents a high-level overview of financial literacy for family medicine residents, covering student loan management, disability insurance, term life insurance, Roth accounts, contract evaluation, and how physicians get paid. He emphasizes that medical training does not teach financial skills and residents must become the CFO of their own family. The talk highlights the importance of understanding loan repayment options, the need for individual disability insurance before diagnosis, and the value of ongoing financial education through books and podcasts like The White Coat Investor.
key_points: Physicians must become financially literate as a second job; clinical expertise alone does not guarantee financial success.
Student loans accrue interest during training; residents should avoid unnecessary borrowing and understand compounding.
Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) is a valuable option for those planning to work at not-for-profit hospitals, but refinancing locks you out of that opportunity.
Disability insurance should be purchased during residency before any medical diagnoses occur, as rates are cheaper and you are still insurable.
Individual disability policies are portable and preferable to group policies, which are tied to employment.
Women should seek unisex disability policies because sex-based underwriting can lead to higher premiums.
A physician’s greatest asset is their education and earning potential; disability coverage protects that asset.
Term life insurance is recommended for residents with families, as it is inexpensive and provides crucial protection.
Residents should read foundational finance books such as 'Personal Finance for Dummies,' 'The Bogleheads' Guide to Investing,' and William Bernstein's free book.
Financial advisors from companies like Northwestern Mutual or Edward Jones are often salespeople; residents should seek independent advice from fee-only planners.
Term life insurance is preferable to whole life for most residents; invest separately rather than mixing investing with insurance.
Whole life insurance's first-year premium often goes to the broker; it's a poor investment, especially at this career stage.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Abnormal Uterine Bleeding, Chronic Anovulation, and PCOS
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses abnormal uterine bleeding, focusing on chronic anovulation from PCOS and insulin resistance. The lecture covers diagnostic criteria for PCOS (2 of 3: irregular menses, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, elevated free testosterone), the pathophysiology of the menstrual cycle and hormonal feedback, and the strong association between PCOS and insulin resistance (20-80% of women). Management strategies include progesterone withdrawal to prevent endometrial cancer, birth control pills to increase SHBG and reduce free testosterone, spironolactone for hirsutism, and metformin for insulin resistance to restore ovulation. The talk emphasizes practical diagnostic and treatment approaches for family physicians.
key_points: Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized as organic (pathologic) or functional (including chronic anovulation from PCOS and insulin resistance).
PCOS diagnosis requires 2 of 3: irregular menstrual periods, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (specific request for follicle count <1 cm), and elevated free or total testosterone.
In the normal cycle, low estrogen triggers FSH, which converts androgen to estrogen; a rapid estrogen rise causes LH surge and ovulation; progesterone then stops endometrial proliferation.
In PCOS, there is a block in androgen-to-estrogen conversion, leading to low FSH, no LH surge, and chronic anovulation with high androgens.
Androgens decrease sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), magnifying free testosterone and causing hirsutism.
Insulin resistance is present in 20-80% of PCOS patients; testing fasting glucose/insulin ratio (normal >5) helps stratify severity and guides treatment.
Women with PCOS and amenorrhea must have uterine evacuation (withdrawal bleed) at least 2-3 times per year to prevent endometrial cancer.
Birth control pills provide 3-5 times normal estrogen levels, increasing SHBG and lowering free testosterone to slow hirsutism progression.
Metformin treatment for insulin resistance can normalize insulin, lower testosterone, and restore ovulation within 2-3 months.
Spironolactone prevents conversion of vellus hairs to terminal hairs but cannot reverse existing terminal hairs (require laser or electrolysis).

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews abnormal uterine bleeding, focusing on physiologic dysfunctional uterine bleeding. It covers normal menstrual cycle parameters, definitions of abnormal bleeding patterns, and the hormonal regulation of the menstrual cycle. The speaker discusses clinical scenarios including menarche, perimenopause, and polycystic ovary syndrome, emphasizing history-taking and treatment strategies.
key_points: Normal menstrual interval is 21-35 days, duration 5-7 days.
Quantify bleeding by asking number of pads/tampons used on the heaviest day.
When taking a bleeding history, establish the patient's normal cycle off birth control.
After menarche, allow up to 2 years for cycles to regulate before evaluating for chronic anovulation.
Perimenopause onset is defined by irregular periods, not hot flashes; mean age 45, duration 2-8 years.
In PCOS, high testosterone reduces SHBG; treatment with high-estrogen birth control pills increases SHBG and reduces hirsutism.
A rapid rise in estrogen triggers an LH surge, which triggers ovulation.
Progesterone withdrawal causes menstruation; exogenous progestin withdrawal can also induce bleeding.
Women over 60 with any bleeding should be evaluated for endometrial cancer.
Combined oral contraceptives treat both dysmenorrhea and perimenopausal irregular bleeding by thinning the endometrium.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Adnexal Masses
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture, delivered by Dr. Calvert, covers the clinical evaluation and management of six common adnexal mass presentations. Through case-based teaching, the speaker emphasizes the importance of taking a thorough sexual and menstrual history, linking symptoms such as dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and pelvic fullness to specific diagnoses like endometriosis, hemorrhagic ovarian cyst, hydrosalpinx, and tubo-ovarian abscess. Ultrasound interpretation is highlighted, with particular attention to the 'ground glass' appearance of endometriomas. The lecture also reinforces the role of the pelvic exam, fertility counseling, and clinical reasoning to narrow the differential before imaging.
key_points: Assess sexual history (age at first intercourse, lifetime partners) to identify risk for STDs and PID.
Sudden severe pelvic pain that migrates from left to right suggests intraperitoneal fluid from a ruptured hemorrhagic cyst.
Endometrioma appears on ultrasound as a cystic ovarian structure with homogeneous 'ground glass' internal echoes.
Dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and infertility together strongly suggest endometriosis with possible endometrioma.
Cervical purulent discharge indicates gonorrhea or chlamydia infection, which can ascend to cause adnexal abscess.
Hydrosalpinx is a dilated, fluid-filled fallopian tube often resulting from prior PID and appears hypoechoic on ultrasound.
Regular menstrual periods imply ovulation; timing intercourse daily from day 5-15 may decrease sperm count and fertility.
Pelvic exam should include bimanual palpation if the examiner is skilled; limited uterine mobility suggests adhesions from prior infection or endometriosis.
Asymptomatic patients with history of STDs still warrant a pelvic exam because many infections (e.g., chlamydia) are asymptomatic.
Hemorrhagic ovarian cysts are common; most can be managed observationally if the patient is stable and pain controlled.
Complex ovarian cysts with septations and solid components should be considered ovarian cancer until proven otherwise.
Most women with ovarian cancer are symptomatic at the time of diagnosis.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Cervical Vaginal Infection
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers common vaginal infections, focusing on differentiating physiologic discharge from pathologic conditions using wet prep, pH, and microscopy. It details bacterial vaginosis (Amsel criteria, treatment with metronidazole), atrophic vaginitis (parabasal cells, estrogen therapy), and candidiasis (hyphae, fluconazole dosing, and resistant Candida glabrata requiring ibrexafungerp). Management strategies include addressing pH, estrogen levels, and recurrence prevention. The talk emphasizes actionable diagnostic and treatment pearls for family medicine residents.
key_points: Physiologic leukorrhea has clear discharge, pH 4, negative whiff test, no clue cells; management is supportive with hygiene and cotton underwear.
Bacterial vaginosis requires 3 of 4 Amsel criteria: thin white discharge, pH >4.5, fishy odor with KOH, >20% clue cells.
Oral metronidazole is more effective than vaginal gel (≈60% efficacy) for bacterial vaginosis.
Recurrent bacterial vaginosis can be managed with patient-initiated short-course metronidazole at first symptom or vaginal pH buffers.
Atrophic vaginitis shows parabasal cells, elevated pH, inflammation; treat with vaginal estrogen, tapering to once-weekly maintenance.
Candidiasis diagnosis requires hyphae on wet prep; treatment is fluconazole 150 mg every 3 days for 3 doses (9 days coverage).
Candida glabrata is resistant to azoles; confirm with NAAT and treat with ibrexafungerp (Brexafemme) 300 mg two doses 12 hours apart.
Recurrent candidiasis: induction with fluconazole every 3 days then weekly for 6 months.
Factors raising vaginal pH include douching, menstrual blood, low estrogen, antibiotics, and semen; condoms and vaginal buffers help.
Speculum size selection: ask number of vaginal births and patient size; use larger speculum for larger patients.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Chronic Anovulation & PCOS
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Calvert covers the physiology of the menstrual cycle and the four physiologic categories of chronic anovulation: post-menarchal (up to two years), perimenopause (four to seven years), polycystic ovary syndrome, and insulin resistance. Key concepts include the roles of estrogen and progesterone in the proliferative and secretory phases, the necessity of an LH surge for ovulation, and the use of endometrial biopsy and progesterone withdrawal testing to assess ovulatory status. Clinical evaluation of abnormal uterine bleeding requires establishing the patient's normal cycle interval, duration, and amount. Practical pearls address starting combination oral contraceptives, recognizing perimenopause, and the importance of asking about stress in secondary amenorrhea.
key_points: Chronic anovulation has four physiologic categories: post-menarchal (up to 2 years), perimenopause (4-7 years), PCOS, and insulin resistance.
The menstrual cycle includes proliferative (estrogen-driven), secretory (progesterone-driven), and menstruation (progesterone withdrawal) phases.
Ovulation requires an LH surge triggered by a rapid rise in estrogen; without it, the endometrium remains proliferative.
Endometrial biopsy in the luteal phase can confirm anovulation if proliferative endometrium is found.
Progesterone withdrawal test (giving progesterone then withdrawing it) can assess if a woman will menstruate.
When evaluating abnormal uterine bleeding, first establish the patient's normal cycle interval, duration, and amount.
Starting combination birth control pills on the first day of menses ensures efficacy; starting after day 3 may fail.
Perimenopause is defined by a change in menstrual pattern, not hot flushes; average menopause age is 52, with 95% by age 54.
Persistent menstruation after age 55, especially in obese women, raises concern for endometrial hyperplasia.
Combination OCPs treat both irregular bleeding and dysmenorrhea by thinning the endometrium and reducing prostaglandins.
Stress is a common cause of hypothalamic amenorrhea; always ask about recent stressors in secondary amenorrhea.
