Chronic anovulation leads to a lack of estrogen feedback, which the hypothalamus-pituitary axis does not recognize, resembling a car out of gas.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Exam Pathology 5/7/26
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert reviews vulvar anatomy and normal variants, then teaches systematic lesion description using location, color, texture, and morphology. The lecture covers common benign findings (ectopic sebaceous glands, epidermal inclusion cysts, angiokeratomas, lentigo) and distinguishes them from concerning lesions like melanoma and HPV warts. Lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are discussed in detail, emphasizing diagnostic features (silver sheen, atrophy, fusion, oral involvement) and management differences. The session stresses the importance of palpation to assess firmness and the need for biopsy of suspicious pigmented or firm lesions.
key_points: Use anatomic landmarks (mons, clitoral hood, urethra, labia majora/minora, fourchette, perineum) and clock-face orientation to precisely document vulvar lesions.
Normal labia minora vary widely in size, symmetry, and pigmentation; symmetric variants are normal and require only reassurance.
Palpation is essential: HPV warts are hard and firm, while normal papillae and skin tags are soft; firmness raises concern for malignancy.
Ectopic sebaceous glands appear as small, raised, yellow-white spots on labia minora; they are benign and cannot be removed without excision.
Epidermal inclusion cysts are firm, filled with exfoliated skin, and cannot be drained; definitive treatment requires excision of the cyst wall.
Angiokeratomas are common, benign, black-to-red pinpoint papules often clustered on labia majora (or scrotum in males); reassurance is the main management.
Lichen sclerosus presents with pale, atrophic, thin skin with a silver sheen, often with labial fusion; it causes intense itching and requires high-potency topical steroids.
Lichen sclerosus increases skin cancer risk; patients need vulvar exams every six months to monitor for firm, raised lesions that may burrow deep.
Lichen planus features tender, eroded areas without significant lichenification; look for oral lacy white plaques (Wickham striae) to aid diagnosis.
Herpes simplex shows grouped vesicles in various stages (clear, purulent, scabbed) simultaneously; folliculitis is centered on hair follicles and not grouped.
Melanoma warning signs: irregular borders, multiple colors (black, blue, red, white), raised areas; any suspicious pigmented lesion warrants biopsy and referral.
Postmenopausal atrophy can cause itching, but lichen sclerosus is distinguished by silver sheen, fusion, and lack of response to standard itch treatments.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Exam & Pathology 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert provides an interactive lecture on female vulvar examination and common pathologies encountered in family medicine. The talk covers benign conditions such as urethral caruncle, Bartholin cyst, and Gartner duct cyst, as well as premalignant and malignant lesions including vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) and vulvar cancer. Emphasis is placed on the importance of thorough physical examination, palpation to detect subtle changes in texture, and a low threshold for biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain. Clinical pearls include recognizing painless syphilitic chancres, distinguishing infected from noninfected Bartholin cysts, and avoiding reliance on emergency department evaluations for vaginal complaints without performing a pelvic exam.
key_points: Urethral caruncle is a common benign lesion in older women that presents with blood on the tissue; typically no treatment is needed, but symptomatic lesions can be removed by suture ligation of the stalk.
Bartholin cysts: infected cysts present with severe pain and require incision and drainage with a word catheter; noninfected cysts with clear fluid may be associated with cancer and warrant biopsy.
Vaginal dysplasia (VIN) can be very subtle, appearing as a pale or red color change with palpable thickness; always palpate and biopsy any suspicious area.
Lichen sclerosus lacks distinct margination, which helps differentiate it from VIN.
Syphilis chancres are characteristically painless—asking about pain can help distinguish from other ulcerative lesions.
Gartner duct cysts are often identified in newborns by family physicians; they usually require no intervention unless complicated by infection or obstructing delivery.
Urethral diverticulum is confirmed by MRI; it presents as a cystic structure near the urethra and may require surgical management.
Always perform a pelvic exam for vaginal complaints; relying on emergency department assessments may lead to missed diagnoses, as illustrated by a case of advanced VIN.
When uncertain about a vulvar lesion, perform a punch or shave biopsy—it is minor surgery and provides definitive diagnosis.
Palpation of lesions is critical: warts feel soft and mushy, while dysplastic or malignant areas feel thick, firm, or have depth.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Examination Pathology 9/4/25
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert's lecture reviews vulvar anatomy and pathology, emphasizing normal variants and common conditions. The talk covers descriptive terminology for lesions, distinguishing benign findings like Fordyce spots and epidermoid cysts from concerning lesions such as melanoma and herpes simplex. Key conditions discussed include lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, Paget disease, yeast infection, folliculitis, and herpes simplex, with clinical pearls on diagnosis and management. The importance of palpation, biopsy for changing lesions, and trusting clinical judgment over lab tests is stressed throughout.
key_points: Labia majora have hair follicles; labia minora do not.
Bartholin glands open in the labia minora, not the mons pubis or inguinal area.
Fordyce spots (ectopic sebaceous glands) are very common, yellow, raised, and hard; they are normal variants requiring reassurance.
Epidermoid cysts are common, filled with epithelial cells, and often require only reassurance; patients should avoid picking at them.
Vulvar melanoma presents with raised, irregular borders, multiple colors, and change in growth; biopsy is indicated for any suspicious lesion.
Lichen sclerosus typically presents with itching, hypopigmentation, a silver sheen, and agglutination of the labia; it can cause urinary stream issues.
Lichen planus causes pain (not itch) and erythema; always check the oral mucosa for characteristic findings.
Herpes simplex presents with grouped vesicles, pustules, and erosions at different stages; a prodrome (tingling, pain, itch) is almost always present.
Primary herpes infection is systemic and severe; secondary recurrences are milder and localized to the same dermatome.
Trust clinical judgment over negative microscopy when classic yeast infection features (satellite lesions, mirror imaging) are present.
Palpation helps distinguish vesicles (soft, fluid-filled) from Fordyce spots (hard) and warts (hard, irregular).
Biopsy any pigmented or changing lesion with asymmetry, irregular borders, or color variation.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Examination & Pathology
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert reviews female vulva anatomy and common pathologies using case-based images. Key conditions include herpes simplex virus with its classic vesicular stages, benign cysts (Skene's, Gartner, Bartholin), urethral caruncle and diverticulum, and vulvar neoplasia. Emphasis on physical exam techniques such as palpation for urethral diverticulum and the painless chancre test for syphilis. Management pearls include leaving asymptomatic cysts alone, using word catheter for first Bartholin abscess, and performing biopsy for any suspicious discolored or indurated lesion.
key_points: Herpes simplex virus presents with painful vesicles in different stages (clear to purulent) over several days.
Urethral caruncle is common in older women and should be left alone unless symptomatic.
Skene's gland cysts are benign blocked glands; only intervene if problematic, using incision and drainage or catheter placement.
Gartner duct cysts are embryologic remnants along the vagina; avoid surgery due to risk of extending to the kidney.
Urethral diverticulum can be detected by palpating the anterior vaginal wall and milking the urethra.
Bartholin gland abscess: first episode managed with word catheter; recurrent may require marsupialization.
Vulvar neoplasia: look for red, white, or black discoloration and palpate for underlying induration; biopsy any suspicious lesion.
Syphilis chancre is painless; test by touching the center with a wooden Q-tip – no pain indicates chancre.
Always perform a thorough vulvar exam; failure to examine can miss serious pathology like advanced cancer.
Biopsy of vulvar lesions can be done with punch or colposcopy forceps; a small sample is sufficient as dysplasia is superficial.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Female Vulva Examination Pathology 11/6/25
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert leads a family medicine residency lecture on vulvar examination pathology, reviewing both normal variants and abnormal findings. The session covers ectopic sebaceous glands, epidermal cysts, angiokeratomas, genital warts, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, yeast infection, folliculitis, HSV, urethral caruncles, Skene's gland cysts, and Gartner duct cysts. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing benign conditions from malignant ones, using history and physical exam clues, and knowing when to biopsy.
key_points: Ectopic sebaceous glands are normal, found on non-hairy vulvar skin, and often mistaken for lesions by patients.
Epidermal cysts are benign, filled with epithelial cells, and require complete excision if removal is desired.
Angiokeratomas are benign capillary lesions that appear as raised, shiny papules, often multiple, and can be confused with melanoma.
Genital warts (HPV) appear as hard, flesh-colored lesions; in the vagina they may be soft and require palpation to detect.
Lichen sclerosus presents with pale, atrophic, shiny mucosa, agglutination, and sheen; it can be treated but requires months of therapy.
Lichen planus is distinguished from lichen sclerosus by purple plaques and oral involvement (white web-like lesions, geographic tongue).
Yeast infections present with fiery red, irregular borders and satellite lesions; treatment is typically antifungal.
Folliculitis is common after shaving; differentiate from HSV by asking about pain, ulceration, and sexual history.
HSV lesions appear as grouped vesicles at different stages (vesicles, ulcers, scabs) and are painful.
Urethral caruncles are benign polyps in older women that may bleed; Skene's gland cysts and Gartner duct cysts are benign and usually require no intervention.
Cervical prolapse is identified when the cervix is at or beyond the hymenal ring.
When in doubt about a vulvar lesion, perform a full-thickness punch biopsy to confirm diagnosis.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on GYN Adnexal Mass
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses the approach to adnexal masses, distinguishing functional (physiologic) cysts from neoplastic or infectious pathology. He emphasizes the importance of ultrasound timing relative to the menstrual cycle and the key distinction between simple and complex cysts. The lecture covers normal ovarian size, bimanual examination technique, and illustrative cases of follicular cysts, hemorrhagic cysts, and tubo-ovarian abscess.
key_points: Adnexal masses are classified as functional, organic, or neoplastic (benign or malignant).
Functional cysts (follicular, corpus luteum) are cyclic and benign; ultrasound timing relative to menses helps confirm this.
Multiple small cysts on ultrasound in reproductive-age women are often normal follicles, not pathology.
Normal ovarian volume is ≤20 cc in reproductive age and ≤10 cc in postmenopausal women; a palpable ovary in a postmenopausal woman is abnormal.
A simple cyst on ultrasound is very low risk; a complex cyst requires further evaluation for possible malignancy.
Bimanual exam: use vaginal fingers to bring the uterus anteriorly; inability to feel the fundus suggests retroversion/retroflexion.
If the uterus does not move freely on bimanual exam, consider adhesions or pathology.
Fullness in the adnexa (not a discrete mass) is abnormal and warrants imaging.
Hemorrhagic cysts appear with a ground-glass appearance on ultrasound and typically resolve spontaneously.
Tubo-ovarian abscess presents with localized and systemic symptoms, and ultrasound shows a debris-filled complex mass adjacent to the ovary.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on GYN Inservice Review 10/2/25
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert reviews GYN in-service exam questions with residents, emphasizing efficient question interpretation, key clinical concepts in reproductive endocrinology, and practical management strategies. Coverage includes interpreting androgen levels in PCOS, understanding IUD mechanisms beyond copper/hormones, recognizing hypothalamic amenorrhea triggers, and using progesterone withdrawal for chronic anovulation. The lecture also addresses dysmenorrhea treatment escalation, endometriosis diagnosis, breast pain evaluation, and fibroid management options.
key_points: In patients with normal menses but high androgen, focus on conditions like PCOS; need 2 of 3 criteria for PCOS: irregular periods, polycystic ovaries, elevated testosterone.
IUDs primarily work by causing inflammation; copper adds ~5% efficacy by killing sperm, progestin adds ~5% by thinning endometrium.
For right lower quadrant pain, differential includes appendicitis, ovarian torsion, ectopic pregnancy, and pelvic inflammatory disease.
Two first-line guidelines for initial cervical cancer screening at age 21-29: HPV testing with reflex cytology, or conventional cytology.
Male pattern baldness in females is driven by androgens (testosterone); frontal scalp thinning is characteristic of female pattern hair loss.
Hypothalamic amenorrhea is common in stress, ICU patients, burn patients, and severe illness.
Kegel exercises are a recurring board exam topic and should be routinely counseled for pelvic floor support.
New guideline for hematuria workup: age threshold for cystoscopy is 50 (changed from 45 in 2022).
Severe dysmenorrhea may not respond to naproxen; consider combined oral contraceptives to thin endometrium and reduce prostaglandins.
Chronic anovulation requires evaluation for both PCOS and insulin resistance; treat the primary driver first.
Patients with chronic anovulation need at least 2 withdrawal bleeds per year to prevent endometrial hyperplasia; use medroxyprogesterone acetate 10 mg x 5 days → withdrawal bleed.
Submucosal fibroids cause heavy menstrual bleeding; intramural and subserosal typically do not.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Hormonal Contraception 3/5/26
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert's lecture covers hormonal contraception methods including IUDs, implants, patches, rings, and birth control pills. He emphasizes the importance of starting combination pills on the first day of the cycle, especially with low-dose formulations. He discusses mechanisms of action, effectiveness rates, and practical prescribing tips such as managing breakthrough bleeding and the superiority of monophasic pills. The talk also addresses weight considerations for patches and the need for strict adherence with progestin-only pills.
key_points: Start combination birth control pills on the first day of the menstrual cycle to ensure efficacy, particularly with low-dose estrogen formulations.
Progestin-only pills require strict same-time daily dosing; missing even one pill necessitates backup contraception.
IUDs work primarily via local inflammation; copper IUDs are effective immediately, while Mirena may take one to two cycles.
The contraceptive patch is less effective in women with BMI >30 and should be avoided in this population.
Monophasic pills are preferred over multiphasic pills because side effects such as breakthrough bleeding are easier to manage.
Breakthrough bleeding on monophasic pills can be managed by adjusting estrogen and progestin based on the timing of spotting.
Long-acting reversible contraception (IUDs, implants) is the most effective form of contraception.
Multiphasic pills were developed primarily for marketing purposes, not clinical superiority.
Vaginal ring and contraceptive patch have lower estrogen doses because they avoid first-pass hepatic metabolism.
Continuous birth control pills (e.g., three months) can be used to treat severe menorrhagia and dysmenorrhea.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Hormonal Contraception 4/9/26
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert discusses the physiology of hormonal contraception, emphasizing the importance of starting low-dose pills on the first day of menses to suppress FSH and prevent follicle formation. He categorizes estrogen into high (50 mcg), low (35 mcg), and very low (15-25 mcg) groups, and progestins into three groups based on progestin and androgen strength. Using a simplified 3x3 matrix, he advises selecting pills by estrogen/progestin profile rather than brand name, and applies this framework to clinical scenarios including acne, dysmenorrhea, breakthrough bleeding, and heavy menstrual bleeding. He also provides practical guidance on managing breakthrough bleeding by timing in the cycle and on tapering high-dose estrogen for acute heavy bleeding.
key_points: Low-dose birth control pills (15-25 mcg ethinyl estradiol) must be started on the first day of menses to suppress FSH and prevent follicle formation; starting even three days late may allow FSH triggering.
Estrogens in pills are ethinyl estradiol and mestranol; mestranol is converted to ethinyl estradiol at a ratio of 50 mcg mestranol to 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol.

Progestins vary by progestin strength and androgenicity: norgestrel/levonorgestrel are strong progestin and strong androgen (acne risk); desogestrel/norgestimate are strong progestin and weak androgen; others are weak progestin and moderate androgen.
Monophasic pills are preferred because they simplify management—only one estrogen and one progestin dose per cycle, avoiding multiple combinations.
For patients with acne, choose a low-androgen progestin (group 2 or 3) and avoid levonorgestrel/norgestrel.
For dysmenorrhea or menorrhagia, select a strong progestin (group 1 or 2) to thin the endometrium and reduce prostaglandins.

Breakthrough bleeding in the first half of the cycle suggests low estrogen or high progestin; management is to increase estrogen or decrease progestin. In the second half, decrease estrogen or increase progestin.
Always recheck blood pressure and assess tolerance at three months after starting pills; do not adjust for spotting earlier as it often resolves.
In women over 40, use low-dose estrogen (group B or C) to minimize hypertension risk; in younger women (15-25), use 35 mcg estrogen for reliability.

For acute heavy bleeding, use high-dose estrogen (50 mcg) three times daily for three days, then taper to twice daily for three days, then once daily; continue pills without withdrawal for 3-6 months to allow anemia recovery.
Smoking plus age over 35 is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception; patients must stop smoking to use pills.
All combined hormonal contraceptives are equally effective; choose based on side effect profile and patient characteristics, not brand claims.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Menopause
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert's lecture covers the gynecologic exam in menopausal women, including proper speculum and bimanual technique, anatomy of the uterus and ovaries, and the evaluation and management of vaginal atrophy. He emphasizes understanding pelvic anatomy to improve exam accuracy and discusses the natural history of vasomotor symptoms, the role of hormone therapy, and a stepwise protocol for treating vaginal atrophy with topical estradiol.
key_points: The Bartholin glands are located near the introitus, not the clitoris, and should not be palpable normally.
When placing a speculum, aim for the posterior fornix to entrap the cervix between the blades.
The uterus is suspended by the broad ligament and should move freely in all directions; restricted movement suggests adhesions or pathology.
Ovaries are palpable about 60% of the time; if felt, they should slide like a marble between the fingers and be mobile.
A retroverted or retroflexed uterus may require a rectovaginal exam to palpate the fundus, especially before endometrial biopsy.
Vasomotor symptoms resolve spontaneously in about 80% of women over time, even without treatment.
Hormone replacement therapy is not indicated for perimenopausal symptoms; birth control pills are used instead to control ovarian function.
Vaginal atrophy is the most common cause of postcoital spotting in menopausal women, accounting for about 80% of cases.
Topical estradiol (not conjugated estrogen) is preferred for treating vaginal atrophy; treatment requires months of gradual dose reduction.
The goal of atrophy treatment is to normalize the vaginal epithelium using the lowest effective maintenance dose, typically 1 gram once or twice weekly.
Topical estrogen for atrophic vaginitis requires consistent use over weeks to months for full healing, not just symptom relief.
Patients may worsen if estrogen is stopped too soon or dose is reduced too quickly.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Pap Smears Colposcopy 8/6/26
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert's lecture covers proper Pap smear technique, emphasizing the need to collect cells from the squamocolumnar junction and transformation zone, which are high-risk areas for cervical cancer. He reviews the anatomy of the cervix, tools (broom, cytobrush, spatula), and the liquid-based cytology process. The talk then transitions to vocabulary for abnormal uterine bleeding and the basics of the menstrual endocrine cycle.
key_points: The squamocolumnar junction is the border between squamous cells (pink) and columnar cells (dark red) of the cervix.
The transformation zone, between the old and new squamocolumnar junctions, is the highest risk area for cervical cancer.
To maximize Pap smear accuracy, sample cells from the squamocolumnar junction and transformation zone.
In prepubertal or menopausal women, the squamocolumnar junction may be inside the os; use a cytobrush inserted fully and rotated more than once.
Large ectropion (e.g., pregnancy, birth control pills) requires using the broom like a paintbrush to sample the visible junction.
Liquid-based cytology removes red cells, allowing Pap smears even during light menstruation.
In liquid-based cytology, a computer screens 100% of slides; 5% are reviewed by a tech, and of those, 5% by a pathologist.
Abnormal uterine bleeding is classified as dysfunctional (physiologic: menarche, perimenopause, chronic anovulation) or organic (polyps, fibroids, cancer).
Normal menstrual interval is 21–35 days, duration 5–7 days; amount is variable and assessed by pad/tampon use on heaviest day.
The menstrual cycle: estrogen rise triggers LH surge causing ovulation; progesterone fall triggers menstruation.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Pelvic Pain Cases 2/9/26
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert presents several cases of pelvic pain, emphasizing the differentiation between cyclic and chronic pain patterns. The lecture covers endometriosis, adenomyosis, interstitial cystitis, and Bartholin gland cysts, highlighting key diagnostic features and management strategies. Specific attention is given to the pathophysiology of endometriosis, including cyclic pain from ectopic endometrial tissue and chronic pain from adhesions. The talk also reviews treatment options such as oral contraceptives, surgical interventions like marsupialization, and the use of a Word catheter for recurrent Bartholin cysts.
key_points: Pelvic pain can be classified as cyclic or chronic, with endometriosis causing both types due to endometrial implants and resulting scar tissue.
Adenomyosis involves endometrial tissue within the myometrium, leading to a boggy, enlarged uterus and cyclic pain including dyspareunia, dyschezia, and urinary frequency.
Interstitial cystitis presents with pain on bladder filling and relief with emptying; urine cultures are often negative, and it may be autoimmune.
Bartholin gland cysts are fluctuant masses located posterolateral to the vaginal introitus; treatment requires creating a new opening to prevent recurrence.
For recurrent Bartholin cysts, a Word catheter should be kept in place for at least 7-10 days; suturing it to the skin can help maintain position.
Marsupialization for Bartholin cysts involves suturing the cyst lining to the external skin with absorbable sutures to maintain patency.
Mittelschmerz is mid-cycle ovulatory pain that alternates sides, lasts minutes to hours, and is managed by suppressing ovulation with oral contraceptives.
Abdominal wall pain can be differentiated from intra-abdominal pain by having the patient raise both legs and head off the table, which isolates the abdominal muscles.
Endometriosis management in early stages may include oral contraceptives to suppress endometrial growth and reduce pain.
Adenomyosis treatment options include oral contraceptives, Depo-Provera, or hysterectomy as a last resort; IUDs and GnRH agonists are less effective.

episodes.title: Dr. Calvert on Pelvic Pain
episodes.speaker: Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Calvert presents a systematic approach to evaluating pelvic pain using eight key history questions. Through multiple case examples, he illustrates the differential diagnosis of chronic and acute pelvic pain, including endometriosis, adenomyosis, interstitial cystitis, abdominal wall pain, Bartholin cyst, mittelschmerz, ectopic pregnancy, and hemorrhagic corpus luteum cyst. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing primary from secondary dysmenorrhea, using physical exam maneuvers such as the one-finger test for abdominal wall pain, and recognizing red flags like bilateral shoulder pain indicating hemoperitoneum. The lecture provides actionable guidance on diagnosis and initial management, including the use of oral contraceptives for mittelschmerz and Word catheter or marsupialization for Bartholin cyst abscess.
key_points: Use eight questions for pelvic pain history: location, quality, frequency, duration, aggravating factors, relieving factors, change over time, and radiation.
Secondary dysmenorrhea develops after a period of painless cycles and suggests underlying pathology such as endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Endometriosis diagnosis is confirmed by laparoscopy; physical exam may reveal nodularity in the posterior cul-de-sac.
Adenomyosis can often be diagnosed by history and physical exam (boggy, tender uterus) without imaging in 95% of cases.
Interstitial cystitis is frequently associated with endometriosis and irritable bowel syndrome; consider it when suprapubic pain worsens with bladder filling.
Abdominal wall pain is identified by the one-finger test and Carnett's sign (pain increases with tensing abdominal muscles).
First Bartholin cyst abscess is treated with Word catheter; recurrent abscess requires marsupialization.
Mittelschmerz (mid-cycle ovulation pain) can be managed with oral contraceptives; if persistent, consider continuous OCPs.
In acute pelvic pain, always rule out ectopic pregnancy with a pregnancy test.
Bilateral shoulder pain with inspiration (Kehr's sign) indicates diaphragmatic irritation from intra-abdominal blood, as in ruptured ectopic or hemorrhagic cyst.

episodes.title: Dr. Catherine Hodge on Neonatal Unit Setup
episodes.speaker: Catherine Hodge
episodes.abstract: Dr. Catherine Hodge describes her experience opening a neonatal unit in a rural mission hospital in Malawi. Initially, sick newborns were not treated due to lack of trained staff and equipment. She overcame challenges by securing a separate room, dedicated nursing staff, and building homemade hot cots. Key interventions included kangaroo mother care, simple CPAP using a bottle of water, and use of burettes for IV fluids. The main diagnoses are neonatal sepsis, prematurity, asphyxia, and low birth weight, with presumptive treatment due to limited diagnostics.
key_points: Separate neonatal unit and dedicated nursing staff are essential for effective care.
Hospital administration support is critical for funding and staffing.
Homemade hot cots using plywood and heating bulbs can provide warmth for preterm infants.
CPAP can be constructed with a bottle of water and tubing; start at 5 cm H2O for preterm babies.
Kangaroo mother care (skin-to-skin) ensures perfect thermoregulation regardless of prematurity.
Presumptive diagnosis of neonatal sepsis is common due to lack of blood cultures; CRP can help reduce inappropriate antibiotic use.
Burettes allow safe IV fluid administration in small volumes (50-80 mL) to prevent fluid overload.
Oxygen concentrators are preferred over cylinders for reliability and safety.
Needs assessment may underestimate demand once care becomes available.
Protocols must be adapted to locally available medicines and equipment.
Prematurity is the leading cause of infant mortality; contributing factors include maternal malaria, malnutrition, HIV, and dehydration.
Without ability to measure CRP, all babies born before 34 weeks are treated presumptively for neonatal sepsis per WHO guidelines.

episodes.title: Dr. Christine Liu on Gender Affirming Care
episodes.speaker: Christine Liu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Christine Liu discusses the complexities of gender affirming care, emphasizing the need to weigh risks and benefits. She reviews the evolution of gender dysphoria as a diagnosis, the lack of clear genetic cause, and the importance of early psychological counseling. She contrasts the traditional binary paradigm with the current fluid model and highlights the controversy and lack of robust data supporting medical interventions. The talk aims to equip physicians to navigate these challenging clinical situations.
key_points: Gender dysphoria replaced gender identity disorder in the DSM, shifting from a disorder to a dysphoria.
No genetic cause has been identified; it is considered a psychological disorder of unclear origin.
Early counseling for children with gender dysphoria is critical to address underlying psychological issues.
There is data both supporting and opposing medical treatments; systematic reviews are needed.
The traditional paradigm aligns biological sex, cultural affirmation, and personal identity.
The current paradigm shift allows personal identity to define gender, overriding biology.
Risks of gender affirming care include medical and mental health risks.
Benefit-risk ratio must be considered for any treatment.
Many studies exist (over 10,000) but quality varies.
A plastic surgery chair resigned due to pressure to perform gender surgery, citing lack of evidence.
The paradigm shift from reality-based to perception-based gender identity drives current gender affirming care.
The five principles of medical ethics (autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, justice) guide decision-making in gender affirming care.

episodes.title: Dr. Christopher Abdo on Approach to Lower Extremity Weakness 2.19.26
episodes.speaker: Christopher Abdo
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Christopher Abdo provides a systematic approach to evaluating lower extremity weakness, emphasizing localization along the neuraxis using motor, sensory, and reflex findings. Key pathways discussed include the corticospinal tract, posterior column, and anterolateral system. The MRC scale for muscle strength, reflex grading, and the Babinski sign are reviewed with clinical pearls. Two cases illustrate localization: a cervical myelopathy from C5-C6 compression and an acute leg weakness scenario. The lecture stresses the importance of precise localization to guide appropriate imaging and avoid unnecessary tests.
key_points: Weakness must be distinguished from fatigue; weakness is an actual loss of muscle strength.
Localize the lesion along the neuraxis using motor, sensory, and reflex findings.
Upper motor neuron lesions cause increased tone and reflexes; lower motor neuron lesions cause atrophy, fasciculations, decreased tone and reflexes.
Acute CNS injury (stroke, spinal shock) may initially present with areflexia and flaccidity.
Three main sensory pathways: corticospinal (motor), posterior column (vibration/proprioception), anterolateral (pain/temperature).
MRC scale: 5/5 full strength, 4/5 against some resistance, 3/5 against gravity only, 2/5 with gravity, 1/5 trace, 0 none.
Reflex grading: 0 absent (pathologic), 1-3 normal if symmetric; asymmetry or sustained clonus is abnormal.
Babinski sign is always pathologic in adults.
Crossed sensory findings (e.g., pinprick loss on one side, vibration loss on other) strongly suggest spinal cord lesion.
Localization guides imaging; avoid whole neuraxis MRI due to time, cost, and patient tolerance.
ACA strokes can present with unilateral lower extremity weakness without sensory loss, distinguishing them from lumbar spine or spinal cord pathology.
Spinal cord infarction often occurs in the thoracic region (T8-L2) due to the artery of Adamkiewicz; anterior cord syndrome preserves vibration and proprioception.

episodes.title: Dr. Comninellis on Tropical Fever 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Comninellis
episodes.abstract: Dr. Comninellis delivers a practical lecture on evaluating acute febrile illness in low-resource tropical settings. Using case-based role play, he emphasizes that epidemiology—specifically the patient's geographic location—is the most critical diagnostic clue. He demonstrates how to use simple tools like the tourniquet test for dengue and a fever evaluation grid based on duration, malaria test, and CBC. The talk covers key exam findings (palatal Koplik spots, rose spots, posterior cervical adenopathy) and provides guidance on when empiric therapy is justified.
key_points: The most important diagnostic step in tropical fever is determining the patient's geographic location and local disease epidemiology.
Measles can present with palatal Koplik spots before the classic skin rash appears.
The tourniquet test (blood pressure cuff inflated above diastolic, below systolic) is a specific bedside test for dengue fever when petechiae develop.
Typhoid fever causes rose spots (erythematous lesions on the chest) from systemic septic emboli.
Posterior cervical adenopathy (scrofula) is the most common extrapulmonary presentation of tuberculosis, especially in children.
Fever of unknown origin in a resource-limited setting can often be managed by scheduling follow-up; most cases resolve spontaneously.
Empiric antibiotics are justified for unstable vital signs, septic shock, very young or elderly patients, or suspected meningitis when LP is unavailable.
Rapid diagnostic tests (e.g., for malaria, HIV, typhoid) have become affordable ($1/test) and provide objective data in low-resource settings.
Eosinophilia in a prolonged febrile patient (>2 weeks) strongly suggests a parasitic etiology such as schistosomiasis or filariasis.
The dengue mosquito (Aedes aegypti) bites during the day and breeds in standing water, unlike the Anopheles mosquito that transmits malaria.
Schistosomiasis can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer by invading the liver's collecting system.
Diagnosis is made via iodine stain of urine or stool to identify ova, requiring no advanced laboratory.

episodes.title: Dr. Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.2 8/28/25
episodes.speaker: Crouch
episodes.abstract: Dr. Crouch shares his experience as a supervising physician at an HIV clinic in Papua New Guinea, which serves as a referral center for 500,000 people and provides free ART. He reviews key HIV epidemiology, including transmission risks for health workers, the importance of using person-centered language like 'person living with HIV' over stigmatizing labels, and the clinical presentation of acute HIV infection as a mono-like illness. The talk emphasizes social determinants of health, the low transmission risk from needlestick injuries when managed with prompt ART, and the diagnostic testing timeline. He frames HIV as a manageable chronic illness and stresses that physicians are uniquely positioned to advocate for vulnerable patients.
key_points: Person-centered language like 'person living with HIV' reduces stigma, but clinicians must balance terminology with direct patient care.

In the US, HIV disproportionately affects African American men who have sex with men, while globally it is predominantly heterosexual with slightly more females due to transmission biology and testing bias from antenatal clinics.
Poverty, incarceration, and poor access to healthcare are major social determinants that increase both HIV acquisition risk and worsen disease outcomes.
A hollow-bore hypodermic needlestick carries a 0.1-0.2% HIV transmission risk; prompt post-exposure ART reduces that to near zero.
The most common route of HIV acquisition in healthcare workers is sexual, not occupational needlesticks, which can lead to misattribution if staff do not report exposures.
Acute HIV infection typically presents 2-4 weeks after exposure as a flu-like illness with rash, often confused with infectious mononucleosis.
HIV RNA amplification tests become positive as early as 7 days post-infection, preceding antibody-based tests.
HIV has become a chronic illness with effective treatment, changing the paradigm from fatal disease to manageable condition.
Antenatal HIV prevalence data, at 1-2% in the speaker's province, is used as a surrogate for general population prevalence worldwide.
Physicians are uniquely positioned to advocate for patients with HIV, as poverty and social circumstances often predict both acquisition and difficulty coping with the disease.
HIV antibody tests become positive about two weeks after infection, creating a 'window period' where early testing may be negative.
Screening tests are designed to favor false positives over false negatives to avoid missing cases, requiring confirmatory testing.

episodes.title: Dr. Cunningham on Osteoarthritis of the Knee 5/21/26
episodes.speaker: Cunningham
episodes.abstract: Dr. Cunningham presents a clinical overview of osteoarthritis of the knee, beginning with the Kellgren-Lawrence grading scale for severity and emphasizing that running does not worsen arthritis for average runners. First-line management includes exercise, weight loss (every pound lost reduces four pounds of force on the knee), and medications such as acetaminophen and NSAIDs. Injection therapies are discussed in detail: corticosteroid injections (limit three per year due to chondrotoxicity), viscosupplementation (ultrasound-guided, non-chondrotoxic, superior to placebo), and orthobiologics like PRP (one injection, non-weight-bearing for a week, $1,200 out-of-pocket). Emerging options include cryoneurolysis (freezing nerves for pain control, lasts ~90 days) and shockwave therapy. Throughout, the speaker stresses the importance of exercise and strengthening to support all interventions.
key_points: Kellgren-Lawrence grades 0-4 define severity; most research focuses on grades 2-3, not stage 4.
Running does not worsen arthritis for most patients; inactivity is more harmful than activity.
Weight loss significantly reduces knee load: each pound lost equals four pounds off the knee.
First-line pharmacotherapy: acetaminophen and NSAIDs (with caution for comorbidities).
Corticosteroid injections: limit to three per calendar year (every 4 months) due to chondrotoxicity from steroid and anesthetic.
Viscosupplementation provides superior relief to placebo and corticosteroids, is not chondrotoxic, and should be injected under ultrasound guidance.
PRP (leukocyte-poor, single injection) can provide years of relief but does not reverse arthritis; cost is ~$1,200 and not covered by insurance.
Bone marrow aspirate and adipose tissue ('stem cell' treatments) are not proven to regenerate cartilage; adipose preferred in older patients.
Cryoneurolysis freezes sensory nerves to the knee for pain control, lasting ~90 days; effective for patients who cannot undergo surgery.
All injections should be coupled with an exercise program to strengthen the quadriceps, hamstrings, and calves.
Ultrasound-guided knee injection: identify the joint line in the longitudinal plane first, then rotate perpendicular to enter the joint space.
The infralateral approach targets the soft spot between the femoral condyle, tibial plateau, and patellar tendon.

episodes.title: Dr. Dolin on Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease & Asthma
episodes.speaker: Dolin
key_points: Pulmonary rehabilitation improves FEV1 and lung function as much as starting another pharmaceutical, and breaks the deconditioning spiral in COPD.
Oxygen therapy criteria include resting or ambulatory desaturation below 88%, and a DLCO of 30% or less is a good rule of thumb for needing supplemental oxygen.
Triple therapy is indicated for patients with frequent or severe exacerbations.
Roflumilast (Daliresp) can cause GI side effects (nausea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhea); starting at half dose for 1-2 weeks then increasing may improve tolerability.
Regular ICS use increases pneumonia risk (evidence level A); consider discontinuing ICS during hospitalization for COPD exacerbation with pneumonia.
Initiate ICS for COPD when: >2 moderate exacerbations/year, eosinophilia >300 cells/mcL, history of asthma, or FEV1 30-50% predicted.
All new pulmonary patients should be tested for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency because treatment differs (enzyme replacement therapy).
For COPD exacerbations, IV steroid dosing of 80 mg methylprednisolone every 8 hours is reasonable; undertreatment may prolong the episode.
Dr. Dolin's preferred COPD action plan steroid taper: prednisone 40 mg x3 days, then 30 mg x3, 20 mg x3, 10 mg x3, then stop.
At hospital discharge, ensure patients can actually obtain prescribed inhalers due to high cost; verify what they are taking vs. what is ordered.
For stable COPD, obtain yearly PFTs; for asthma, follow every 3 months until exacerbations are controlled and rescue use is ≤1-2 times/month.
Long-term macrolides are used infrequently; preferred antibiotics in COPD action plans include doxycycline or azithromycin.

episodes.title: Dr. Dolin on Obstructive Sleep Apnea
episodes.speaker: Dolin
episodes.abstract: Dr. Dolin presents a practical guide to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) screening, diagnosis, and management. She reviews the STOP-Bang questionnaire and Epworth Sleepiness Scale for initial evaluation, discusses home-based versus in-lab polysomnography, and emphasizes the importance of insurance documentation and Medicare scoring rules. The talk also covers treatment initiation with CPAP, including mask selection, humidification, and follow-up to ensure compliance and equipment coverage.
key_points: STOP-Bang includes snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, high blood pressure, BMI >35, age >50, neck circumference >17/16 inches, and male sex.
Epworth Sleepiness Scale score >10 indicates excessive daytime sleepiness and is used to decide treatment.
For AHI <15 and asymptomatic patients, treatment may not be necessary; reassurance is appropriate.
Home sleep test uses a thermistor for airflow, a plethysmography belt for effort, and oximetry.
In-lab polysomnography adds EEG, EKG, and EMG for eye, chin, and leg movements, allowing detailed sleep staging.
Medicare uses a 4% desaturation rule for hypopnea scoring; a 3% rule may require a repeat study.
Split-night study is performed if >20 events/hour occur in the first two hours; at least four hours of treatment are needed for a CPAP prescription.
Zolpidem 5 mg can be given as a sleep aid for the lab study.
Heated tubing is recommended to prevent rainout; adjust humidity and temperature to manage dry mouth.
A chin strap helps mouth breathers using a nasal mask to prevent air leak and dryness.
Insurance requires CPAP usage >70% of nights for >4 hours to cover therapy and supplies.
Prescribe a pressure range (e.g., 10–13 cmH₂O) instead of a single pressure to allow for weight changes, mask differences, and positional variation.

episodes.title: Dr. Duininck on Controversies in Medicine 8/27/26
episodes.speaker: Duininck
episodes.abstract: The speaker challenges residents to think critically rather than follow protocols mechanically, highlighting the prevalence of defensive medicine driven by fear of litigation. He emphasizes building trust through empathy and listening, especially with non-compliant patients, and uses the COVID-19 pandemic and vaccine mandate to illustrate the importance of questioning authority and making personal, well-reasoned decisions. The talk aims to encourage residents to wrestle with hard questions and prioritize patient care over self-protection.
key_points: Thinking is different from memorizing and following protocols; true clinical reasoning goes beyond checklists.
Defensive medicine (CYA) leads to unnecessary tests and scans, such as CT for every abdominal pain or repeat brain imaging for altered mental status.
Patients come because they are unhealthy and want to be healthy; understanding their fears is key to building trust.
Men often avoid doctors due to fear; use analogies like checking truck oil to encourage preventive care.
Non-compliance often reflects distrust or fear, not defiance; respond with empathy, not anger.
Trust is built by listening, affirming concerns, and showing empathy even when the concern seems irrational.
The COVID-19 pandemic tested willingness to care for patients despite uncertainty; our team stepped up.
The vaccine mandate raised questions about medical authority and personal conviction; it's important to think through such decisions.
Avoid copying and pasting differentials from templates; that takes thinking out of the diagnostic process.
Asking hard questions and challenging conventional thought is necessary to be a good doctor.
COVID-19 vaccines were initially promoted to prevent transmission, but later evidence showed they primarily reduce severe disease in at-risk individuals.
No documented cases of healthcare workers transmitting COVID-19 to patients were found in the speaker's health system during the first 18 months of the pandemic.

episodes.title: Dr. Duininck on Leadership
episodes.speaker: Duininck
episodes.abstract: Dr. Duininck delivers a lecture on biblical leadership to family medicine residents transitioning into senior roles. He emphasizes that physicians are inherently leaders and must develop character qualities like integrity, humility, and servant-heartedness. The talk explores the tension between organizational hierarchy and equality in the body of Christ, urging residents to discover their God-given identity rather than imitating others. He concludes by encouraging personal reflection on one's unique purpose and the need to submit natural personality traits to Christ's lordship for effective leadership.
key_points: Physicians are thrust into leadership roles whether they intend it or not, in clinic, family, and community.
Biblical leadership differs from cultural or business models; it is rooted in character and service.
Key leadership qualities identified by residents include integrity, honesty, decisiveness, humility, servant-heartedness, and being grounded in faith.
Organizational hierarchy and authority are biblical concepts (e.g., the centurion's understanding of authority) and do not contradict equality of value.
Residents should not try to copy other leaders but must discover and develop their own God-given identity and strengths.
Natural personality traits (e.g., temper, sensitivity, steadiness) must be submitted to Christ and refined, not used as excuses.
Less than 5% of people ever discover their true identity, which comes from God, not from family, titles, or personality tests.
Knowing one's identity provides purpose, meaning, and fearlessness, as modeled by Jesus.
Leadership influence should be used for good—to promote integrity, honesty, and godly character in others.
The lecture calls for intentional solitude and prayer to ask God: 'Who do you say I am?'
Leadership requires knowing your identity; fear and self-promotion stem from not knowing who you are.
Jesus never lived for people's approval but for the Father's, modeling confident, servant leadership.

episodes.title: Dr. Dunn on Addiction Med
episodes.speaker: Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn, board-certified in psychiatry and addiction medicine, discusses medication for opioid use disorder (OUD), framing addiction as a chronic brain disease similar to hypertension or diabetes. She reviews the three FDA-approved medications—methadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist), and naltrexone (antagonist)—and their mechanisms of action. Strong emphasis is placed on medication for opioid use disorder (MOUD) as the gold standard treatment, highlighting its ability to reduce mortality, prevent overdose, and improve functioning, while also addressing stigma and the biology of addiction.
key_points: Addiction is a chronic brain disease affecting reward, motivation, memory, and related circuitry, with cycles of relapse and remission.
The opioid epidemic has progressed through four waves: prescription opioids, heroin, fentanyl, and now psychostimulant-opioid mixtures.
Only 20-30% of people with OUD remain abstinent at 12 months without medication treatment, making MOUD the gold standard.
Methadone is a full mu-opioid agonist available only through federally regulated opioid treatment programs (OTPs).
Buprenorphine is a partial agonist that caps receptor activation, reducing overdose risk and blocking the effects of other opioids.
Naltrexone is an antagonist that fully blocks mu-opioid receptors and is available in oral and injectable forms.
The DATA waiver (X-waiver) for buprenorphine prescribing has been eliminated; only a DEA license is needed.
Return to use is common and should be managed like other chronic diseases—patients should be retained in treatment, not dismissed.
Mortality ratio for opioid use disorder drops from 6-fold to below 2-fold with access to medication treatment.
Harm reduction strategies, like seat belts and helmets, are routine in medicine and should be applied to addiction care without stigma.
Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid receptor agonist with high affinity, which displaces full agonists and can cause precipitated withdrawal if given too early.
Higher buprenorphine doses (e.g., 16-24 mg) are associated with better retention and more opioid-free urines; 8 mg is the minimum to block most receptors.

episodes.title: Dr. Dunn speaks on Depression
episodes.speaker: Dunn speaks
key_points: Genetic testing for depression primarily assesses metabolism (tolerability), not efficacy, and is often not standard of care.
GI side effects from SSRIs are due to serotonin receptors in the GI tract and are not indicative of therapeutic effect.
Sexual side effects (anorgasmia) typically emerge at higher doses and can be managed with dose reduction or augmentation (e.g., bupropion).
Black box warning for SSRIs in adolescents: increased suicidal ideation, not behavior; must discuss with patients.
Optimize dosing of a single agent before switching; aim for remission (PHQ-9 <5) rather than just response.
Mirtazapine is more activating at higher doses; lower doses are more sedating.
Trazodone at antidepressant doses (300-400 mg) is poorly tolerated; it is primarily used for sleep at low doses.
Do not combine an SSRI and SNRI due to risk of serotonin syndrome.
Second-generation antipsychotics for augmentation require a 6-12 week trial before assessing efficacy.
Lithium reduces suicide risk but can be toxic in overdose; consider for augmentation in refractory cases.
Light therapy can induce hypomania; patients must have eyes open (retinal mechanism).
Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH high-normal) may be worth treating in depression; targeting TSH closer to 1 may improve response.

episodes.title: Dr. Engstrom on ACS
episodes.speaker: Engstrom
episodes.abstract: Dr. Engstrom discusses acute coronary syndrome (ACS), emphasizing the urgency of timely diagnosis and intervention to prevent myocardial damage. He reviews typical and atypical presentations, noting that about one in five patients, especially women, diabetics, the elderly, and non-white individuals, may not have classic symptoms. The lecture highlights the limitations of current STEMI criteria, citing evidence that 25-40% of occlusive myocardial infarctions are missed, and introduces the emerging paradigm of occlusive versus non-occlusive MI. Engstrom stresses the importance of clinical context and patient appearance over EKG findings alone, urging clinicians to act when a patient looks bad even if the EKG is subtle.
key_points: ACS includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI, representing a spectrum of coronary occlusion and myocardial injury.
Time is myocardium; delays in EKG review or action increase morbidity and mortality.
Classic ACS presentation: elderly, exertional left-sided chest pressure radiating to left jaw/shoulder/arm with diaphoresis and nausea.
Atypical presentations are common in women, diabetics, the elderly, and non-white patients; up to 1 in 5 lack typical symptoms.
Patients who look acutely ill (diaphoretic, distressed) warrant high suspicion regardless of EKG findings.
Positive likelihood ratios for ACS include known CAD (2.0), pain radiating to both arms (2.6), and high-risk HEART score (7-10).
Unstable angina is a clinical diagnosis of new or worsening chest pain in patients with known CAD, often without EKG or troponin changes.
NSTEMI involves elevated troponin with new/worsening chest pain; type 1 is occlusive, type 2 is demand ischemia.
STEMI criteria: ≥2 mm ST elevation in V2-V3 for men >40, ≥1.5 mm for women, ≥1 mm in other leads; benign early repolarization is a common mimic in young men.
25-40% of occlusive MIs are missed by strict STEMI criteria; subtle findings like inferior ST elevation with aVL depression or hyperacute T waves may indicate occlusion.
New bifascicular block in the right clinical context can signal an occlusive MI.
Hyperacute T waves are tall, symmetric, and disproportionate to QRS amplitude, often from local potassium release by infarcted myocytes.

episodes.title: Dr. Engstrom on Approach to Undifferentiated Shock
episodes.speaker: Engstrom
episodes.abstract: In this lecture, Dr. Engstrom presents a rapid approach to undifferentiated shock, covering the four main categories: cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive, and hypovolemic. He uses clinical cases to illustrate key features and management strategies, including the use of ultrasound, IV access, fluids, and vasopressors. Emphasis is placed on early recognition of shock type, timely antibiotics in septic shock, and appropriate use of intraosseous access when IV access is difficult. The lecture also includes specific pearls on the MAP goal of 65 and the importance of blood in hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: Shock is defined as lack of perfusion to critical organs, not necessarily low blood pressure; cardiogenic shock can present with high blood pressure.
The four types of shock are cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive, and hypovolemic.
Obstructive shock includes cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, aortic stenosis, and air embolism.
For massive PE with obstructive shock, systemic thrombolytics are indicated; for stable right heart strain, consider catheter-directed thrombolysis.
In hemorrhagic shock, give blood not just saline – fluids do not carry oxygen.
Septic shock is the most common cause of distributive shock; mortality increases by 35% per hour without antibiotics.
In distributive shock, consider sepsis, anaphylaxis, adrenal crisis, neurogenic shock, and toxicologic causes.

Initial approach: assess IV access (two large-bore IVs or IO), determine shock type (ultrasound for IVC, tamponade, pneumothorax, free fluid), start fluids, and start vasopressors early if no response.
MAP goal of 65 mmHg is used to perfuse critical organs; a MAP below 60 leads to hypoperfusion.
Intraosseous access (humeral preferred over tibial) can be used for fluids and vasopressors if IV access is not available.
In undifferentiated shock, delaying vasopressors while waiting for fluid response can lead to acute kidney injury from underperfusion.
Some patients live at low MAPs without appearing sick; vasopressors can be deferred in such cases.

episodes.title: Dr. Engstrom on ER Q&A 9/23/26
episodes.speaker: Engstrom
episodes.abstract: Dr. Engstrom emphasizes the importance of asking nuanced clinical questions throughout residency training, using open evidence to understand reasoning behind medical decisions. He discusses disposition planning for common presentations like seizures, stroke mimics, chest pain, and syncope, focusing on expected clinical trajectory and available interventions. The lecture covers practical diagnostic techniques including Carnett's test for abdominal wall pain and distinguishing piriformis syndrome from sacroiliitis. He also addresses the challenge of dizziness evaluation and the value of giving patients a clear plan even when a definitive diagnosis is not reached.
key_points: Residents should ask nuanced questions about clinical reasoning, not just lookupable facts, especially early in training when knowledge gaps are expected.
Disposition decisions hinge on whether the patient's clinical trajectory is expected to improve or worsen over the next hours to days.
For seizures, breakthrough seizures on medication or multiple seizures in short succession warrant admission; single seizure from missed meds can often go home.
ABCD2 score helps risk-stratify TIA; high-risk patients should be admitted or started on aspirin and statin if they refuse admission.
New neurologic deficits require stroke workup; same deficits as prior hemiplegic migraines may not need repeat imaging if established.
Chest pain disposition depends on stable vs unstable angina; HEART score guides admission for rule-out if risk >2% in 30 days.
Carnett's test (pain worse with abdominal flexion) suggests abdominal wall pathology rather than visceral origin.
Piriformis syndrome presents with lateral buttock pain radiating down leg; responds to stretching and NSAIDs.
Sacroiliitis presents with pain directly over SI joint; treat with NSAIDs or Cox-2 inhibitors.
Fifty percent of patients change their description of dizziness (vertigo vs lightheadedness) when asked again an hour later.
When no clear diagnosis is reached, giving patients a concrete next-step plan improves satisfaction and disposition.
Open evidence can be used to quickly identify three emergencies to rule out for any presentation.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Antibiotics
episodes.speaker: Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer provides a practical, clinically oriented review of antibiotic selection for common infections, emphasizing a three-question framework: spectrum (does the antibiotic cover the likely organism?), pharmacology (does it reach the infection site?), and patient factors (renal function, drug interactions). He teaches residents to interpret susceptibility reports by antibiotic class rather than individual drugs, enabling lateral switches or de-escalation. Key bacterial exceptions—Enterococcus (cephalosporins have zero activity), Pseudomonas (limited drug options), and Enterobacter (resistant to early-generation cephalosporins)—are highlighted as critical knowledge gaps that can lead to treatment failure. The talk stresses using resources like the Sanford Guide and calling the lab for additional susceptibilities when standard panels are incomplete.
key_points: Ask three questions before choosing an antibiotic: does it cover the organism (spectrum), does it reach the infection site (pharmacology), and are there patient factors (renal dosing, interactions)?
Susceptibility reports list antibiotic classes, not individual drugs; susceptibility to one drug in a class (e.g., cefazolin) implies susceptibility to others in that class (e.g., cephalexin).
Lab panels are alphabetical, not arranged by spectrum or generation; clinicians must mentally reorder by class to avoid confusion.
Enterococcus faecalis is universally resistant to cephalosporins; never use a cephalosporin for enterococcal infections even if the report appears susceptible.

Pseudomonas has a limited set of effective antibiotics (ceftazidime, cefepime, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem); memorize these for empiric coverage when risk factors exist.
Enterobacter cloacae and Serratia are typically resistant to penicillins and first- through third-generation cephalosporins; cefepime or a carbapenem is often needed.
The lab only tests antibiotics known to have activity against the isolated organism; if a drug is not listed, it is almost certainly ineffective (e.g., amoxicillin not tested for Pseudomonas).
When a culture shows an unexpected organism (e.g., Enterobacter), consult a reference like the Sanford Guide before susceptibilities return to avoid continuing a wrong empiric antibiotic.
For pyelonephritis, nitrofurantoin (Macrobid) is ineffective because it does not achieve adequate renal parenchymal concentration; use it only for cystitis.
Oral vancomycin has no systemic absorption; use it only for C. difficile colitis, not for skin or soft tissue infections.
When culture results show enterococcus, immediately switch from cephalosporin to amoxicillin, ampicillin, or vancomycin because cephalosporins are ineffective against enterococcus.
Automatic ID consults are indicated for endocarditis, osteomyelitis, Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, staph empyema, and staph pneumonia.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Induction of Labor 4/9/26
episodes.speaker: Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer's lecture on induction of labor covers indications for medical and elective induction, cervical ripening, and management of latent and active labor. He reviews the ARRIVE trial and its impact, noting that while elective induction at 39 weeks was associated with lower cesarean rates in the trial, post-ARRIVE data did not show a significant reduction. He emphasizes patient-centered counseling, especially for nulliparous women, and highlights the importance of distinguishing between primiparous and multiparous patients. Key guidelines from ACOG and the use of the committee opinion on timing of delivery are discussed.
key_points: Medical indications for induction include preeclampsia, diabetes, fetal growth restriction, and postterm pregnancy; elective inductions should not be performed before 39 weeks.
The ARRIVE trial showed a 16% reduction in cesarean delivery with elective induction at 39 weeks, but post-ARRIVE data did not replicate this benefit despite a 42% increase in elective inductions.
ACOG's 2025 update recommends counseling patients on risks and benefits of induction at ≥39 weeks but does not mandate induction.
Cervical ripening and management of latent/active labor differ between primiparous and multiparous patients; multips with a proven pelvis are easier to induce.
Patient-centered care is critical: induction can be a prolonged, exhausting process, and shared decision-making should include realistic expectations.
The ACOG committee opinion on medically indicated late-term and early-term deliveries is available on SharePoint and guides timing for conditions like placenta previa and FGR.
Gestational hypertension is treated similarly to preeclampsia with severe features (delivery at 37 weeks) due to high risk of progression, unlike chronic hypertension.
Umbilical artery Doppler findings (e.g., reversed diastolic flow) are urgent indicators for delivery in fetal growth restriction.
For scheduled medically indicated inductions, the week window (e.g., 38 0/7 to 38 6/7) allows flexibility; urgent conditions require same-day admission.
Elective induction in nulliparous women requires careful counseling about potential difficulty and the impact of a failed induction on future obstetric history.
Oral misoprostol 25 mcg is considered a weak induction agent.
Combining a Foley balloon with Pitocin is more effective than oral misoprostol alone.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Knee Injuries
episodes.speaker: Ganzer
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews knee anatomy, biomechanics, physical exam, and common knee injuries for family medicine residents. The speaker emphasizes how understanding biomechanics helps diagnose which structures are injured and notes that history and physical exam can be 93% as accurate as MRI. Key injuries covered include ACL tears (most common, often noncontact), PCL injuries (dashboard mechanism), and meniscal tears. The talk includes practical exam techniques like the Lachman test and pivot shift test, and highlights that rapid effusion within two hours suggests ACL tear or fracture, while gradual effusion suggests meniscal injury.
key_points: The knee is a complex joint with bones, ligaments, menisci, cartilage, bursa, and a large joint capsule; the fibula is not part of the knee joint.
The four main ligaments are ACL, PCL, MCL, and LCL; cruciate ligaments cross each other and control anterior/posterior translation and rotation.
The knee functions as a four-bar linkage mechanism where ligaments are taut in tension and slack when brought together.
History and physical exam can be 93% as accurate as MRI for diagnosing knee injuries.
Rapid effusion within two hours suggests ACL tear or intraarticular fracture; gradual effusion over a day suggests meniscal tear.
ACL is the most common ligament injury (50% of ligamentous injuries), with 70% occurring in noncontact situations, more common in females due to larger Q angle.
The Lachman test (knee flexed 20 degrees, pull tibia anteriorly) evaluates ACL; guarding in acute setting may limit its utility.
The pivot shift test (internal rotation, valgus stress, flexion from extension) can catch ACL instability even when patient guards.
PCL injury is uncommon (3% of ligamentous injuries), often from dashboard injury or fall onto a flexed knee with foot plantar flexed.
Examine the unaffected knee first to establish baseline before examining the injured knee.
The posterior drawer test assesses PCL integrity; a posterior sag sign indicates PCL injury.
Quadriceps active test uses the patient's own quadriceps to reduce a posteriorly sagging tibia, confirming PCL rupture.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Outpatient Management of Kidney Disease
episodes.speaker: Ganzer
key_points: CKD staging uses both GFR and albuminuria; high albuminuria with normal GFR still indicates high risk of progression to ESRD.
Initial evaluation includes A1c, urine albumin-creatinine ratio, lipid panel, renal ultrasound, serum electrolytes, urinalysis, and urine microscopy.
For CKD with hypertension or diabetes, use ACE/ARB and titrate to maximally tolerated dose for renal protection, monitoring potassium (hold if >5.5) and GFR (discontinue if drop >30%).
Finerenone (a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist) reduces sustained GFR decline and risk of ESRD in stage 3-4 CKD.
Lifestyle interventions: plant-based diet, protein 0.6-0.8 g/kg/day for stage 3-4, 150 min/week moderate exercise, resistance training to prevent sarcopenia, and tobacco cessation.
Statins are recommended for cardiovascular risk reduction in CKD regardless of kidney protection.
In CKD with diabetes, target A1c 6.5-8% depending on life situation and use SGLT2 inhibitors and metformin.

Refer to nephrology for hematuria, hereditary kidney disease, approaching ESRD, nephrotic syndrome, rapidly progressive disease, severe electrolyte abnormalities, structural abnormalities, or uncontrolled hypertension.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer on Prenatal Screening for Chromosomal Abnormalities of the Fetus 9/4/25
episodes.speaker: Ganzer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ganzer's lecture covers prenatal screening for fetal chromosomal abnormalities, including aneuploidy and copy number variants. He reviews historical screening methods such as first-trimester nuchal translucency and second-trimester quad screen (AFP quad), noting their limited sensitivity (70-80%). The lecture emphasizes the modern shift to cell-free DNA (NIPS) testing, which offers higher sensitivity and specificity but does not screen for neural tube defects. Dr. Ganzer also discusses common ultrasound markers (e.g., thickened nuchal fold, echogenic intracardiac foci) and the importance of sensitive counseling to avoid unnecessary patient anxiety.
key_points: Aneuploidy (extra or missing chromosome) risk increases with maternal age due to nondisjunction in meiosis I, but most Down syndrome births occur in younger women because they have more pregnancies overall.
Copy number variants (microdeletions/duplications) are independent of maternal age and occur in approximately 0.4% of pregnancies, making them more common than aneuploidy in women over 36.
Cell-free DNA (NIPS) is a highly sensitive screening test derived from placental DNA fragments in maternal blood; it does not evaluate for neural tube defects.
The quad screen (AFP tetra) remains useful for detecting neural tube defects in addition to trisomy 21 and 18, though its sensitivity is only 75-80%.
First-trimester screening (nuchal translucency + PAPP-A + beta-hCG) has ~70% sensitivity and is time-dependent (12-13 weeks).

Ultrasound markers such as thickened nuchal fold (>3.5 mm), echogenic bowel, and intracardiac echogenic foci can be associated with aneuploidy but often have benign explanations and require specialist referral.
Resolved ultrasound findings (e.g., pyelectasis) should not be carried forward in the medical record to avoid patient confusion and anxiety.
Screening test accuracy depends on the skill of the ultrasonographer obtaining the measurements.
Counseling for abnormal screening results must be done with sensitivity, as the information is highly anxiety-provoking for pregnant patients.
Integrated and sequential screening protocols combine first- and second-trimester tests to improve accuracy, but single-time-point screening is now more common.
Cell-free DNA screening analyzes fetal DNA fragments in maternal circulation starting at 9-10 weeks and can be done at any point in pregnancy.
Unlike quad screening, cell-free DNA does not rely on hormone levels that vary with gestational age.

episodes.title: Dr. Ganzer Overviews Gestational Diabetes
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) management in a family medicine residency context. The speaker reviews terminology (GDM A1 vs A2), screening timing (24-28 weeks routine, earlier for high-risk patients), and the importance of tight glycemic control linked to the HAPO trial. Preconception counseling for pregestational diabetes is emphasized due to teratogenic risks of hyperglycemia, and the lecture provides practical pearls on using metformin safely in pregnancy and interpreting glucosuria. The California Sweet Success program and perinatology.com are cited as key resources.
key_points: GDM A1 is diet-controlled; GDM A2 requires medication (insulin or oral agents).
Preconception counseling is critical for type 2 diabetics because hyperglycemia in the first 8 weeks is teratogenic (cardiac anomalies, spontaneous abortion).
Routine GDM screening is at 24-28 weeks; earlier screening (16-20 weeks) is for high-risk patients (BMI >25, first-degree relative with diabetes, prior GDM).
A1c is not useful in pregnancy due to physiologic anemia and dynamic glucose changes; a glucose challenge test is preferred.
The HAPO study showed a continuous linear relationship between maternal hyperglycemia and adverse outcomes (LGA, neonatal hypoglycemia, cesarean delivery).
Metformin is safe in the first trimester and throughout pregnancy for PCOS, prediabetes, or type 2 diabetes; GLP-1s and SGLT2s are avoided due to fetal toxicity concerns.
Glucosuria alone is not diagnostic; it can reflect diet or normal pregnancy changes; consistent 3+ glucose warrants further workup.
After delivery of a true GDM patient, insulin can be abruptly stopped because the placenta—the source of insulin resistance—is gone; check postpartum to rule out overt diabetes.
Preconception A1c <6% is associated with low risk of major malformations; risk increases linearly with higher A1c levels.
The California Sweet Success program improved maternal outcomes; its PDF is still accessible via perinatology.com.
One-step screening for GDM diagnoses twice as many patients but does not improve maternal or neonatal outcomes and increases neonatal hypoglycemia; two-step screening is recommended by ACOG and ADA.
Lifestyle modification (diet, exercise) is first-line management; if not controlled after two weeks, initiate pharmacotherapy.

episodes.title: Dr. Gerald C. Miller on Syphilis Testing Tools and Interpretation of Results
episodes.speaker: Gerald C. Miller
key_points: Order syphilis antibody screen; the lab will reflex to RPR and TPPA if needed.
Index values 1-9 are weak positives; further testing with TPPA is required.
Index >9 is highly likely true positive and does not need TPPA confirmation.
TPPA is reliable in non-pregnant individuals but has a high false-positive rate in pregnant women (15/18 false positives in a recent series).
Once a patient is treponemal antibody positive, never order another treponemal test; use only RPR to monitor for reinfection.
Serofast is defined as RPR titer that decreases to 1:2 and remains stable; no further treatment is needed.
False negatives can occur from testing too soon (within 2-3 weeks of exposure), steroid use, or HIV with CD4 <200.
False positives are common in pregnancy, dialysis, IV drug use, and autoimmune diseases.
Always read the footnote on syphilis lab reports; it may indicate false-positive or inconclusive results.
Clinical history is paramount; if results are discordant, challenge the lab and discuss with the pathologist.

episodes.title: Dr. Gerald C Miller on Syphilis Testing Tools and Interpretation of Results
episodes.speaker: Gerald C Miller
episodes.abstract: Dr. Gerald C Miller emphasizes that the clinician's history is the gold standard for syphilis diagnosis, not laboratory tests. He explains the natural history of syphilis, including incubation periods, chancre characteristics, and the one-third progression to late disease. The lecture covers RPR (nontreponemal) and treponemal antibody testing, false positive/negative rates, the serofast phenomenon, and the reverse screening algorithm. He stresses interpreting all lab results in the context of clinical history and encourages clinicians to challenge discordant results.
key_points: The clinician's history is the gold standard for syphilis diagnosis; lab results must be interpreted in that context.
Only 4-8 spirochetes can cause infection; incubation ranges from 10 to 90 days depending on inoculum size.
The chancre is painless, heals in 2-6 weeks, and may be absent in some patients.
Two-thirds of untreated patients spontaneously resolve; one-third progress to late syphilis over 5-30 years.
RPR has an 11% false positive rate; titers of 1:4 or greater have 98% specificity.
False positive RPRs occur in autoimmune disease, pregnancy, IV drug use, and various infections.
The serofast phenomenon: treated patients may have persistent low titers (1:1-1:4) that do not clear with further treatment.
25% of late-stage syphilis patients lose RPR reactivity, making serologic monitoring impossible.
The reverse algorithm uses treponemal antibody screening first; if reactive and RPR nonreactive, a second treponemal test is needed.
Treatment success is defined by a fourfold drop in RPR titer over 3-6 months, with seroreversion by 12 months.
In congenital syphilis, RPR is the test of choice on the newborn; treponemal antibody crosses the placenta and persists for life.
Immunocompromised patients (HIV, steroids) may have low or negative RPR titers despite active infection.

episodes.title: Dr. Glaser on Medical Advocacy 6/11/26
episodes.speaker: Glaser
episodes.abstract: Dr. Glaser presents a talk on medical advocacy from a Christian perspective, aimed at family medicine residents. She defines advocacy as promoting the interests of patients and communities through social, economic, and political changes, and emphasizes the importance of identifying one's unique qualifications, passions, and barriers to engagement. Using her own journey and the 2018 AAFP policy shift on medical aid in dying as a catalyst, she provides practical steps for advocacy including prayer, seeking counsel, and developing actionable plans. The talk integrates scriptural foundations such as the seven acts of mercy and Micah 6:8, encouraging residents to uphold human dignity and advocate for life-affirming care at all levels of healthcare.
key_points: Advocacy is a core competency in medical education, integrated into ACGME professionalism and systems-based practice.
Physician advocacy includes promoting social, economic, educational, and political changes that reduce suffering and improve well-being.
Christian physicians are called to affirm the inherent dignity of every person, advocate for the marginalized, and uphold Christ-centered values of justice and mercy.
The AAFP changed its stance from opposing medical aid in dying to neutral in 2018, which spurred a call to action for life-affirming physicians.
Effective advocacy requires identifying a specific problem, understanding its scope, and joining existing efforts rather than working in isolation.
Barriers to advocacy include fear of negative publicity, time constraints, lack of training, and the perception that advocacy is ineffective.
Practical first steps for advocacy include prayer, seeking wise counsel, identifying personal passions, and avoiding analysis paralysis.
Advocacy occurs in multiple settings: healthcare systems, medical societies, community organizations, and public policy at local, state, and national levels.
Scriptural foundations for advocacy include Proverbs 31:8–9, Micah 6:8, and Matthew 25 (the seven acts of mercy).
The goal of medicine is to restore wholeness and respect human dignity, not merely to treat biological specimens.
Physicians should testify on bills and resolutions when adequately trained or called.
Authoring a resolution in a medical society can lead to policy change, as demonstrated by the Right of Conscience resolution.

episodes.title: Dr. Greer on Anxiety & Depression 5/7/26
episodes.speaker: Greer
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greer's lecture covers pharmacological management of anxiety and depression, focusing on SSRIs as first-line therapy. He discusses specific SSRIs including escitalopram, sertraline, citalopram, fluoxetine, and paroxetine, highlighting their unique side effects, indications, and dosing considerations. He then reviews SNRIs (venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine) as second-line options, noting withdrawal symptoms and cross-titration strategies. Finally, he covers bupropion for atypical depression and buspirone for anxiety, emphasizing the importance of screening for bipolar disorder before prescribing bupropion.
key_points: SSRIs are first-line for anxiety and depression; escitalopram and sertraline are common initial choices.
