Each SSRI has unique side effects: citalopram prolongs QT interval at 40 mg, escitalopram causes headaches, sertraline is first-line in pregnancy, fluoxetine is useful for PMDD, and paroxetine has the worst side effect profile but may work for refractory anxiety.
Start SSRIs at low doses and titrate slowly (e.g., quarter-dose for 1-2 weeks) to improve tolerability.
SNRIs (venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, duloxetine) are second-line after two SSRI failures; they have significant withdrawal symptoms with missed doses.
Avoid combining SSRIs and SNRIs due to serotonin excess risk.
Bupropion is useful for atypical depression and smoking cessation but can trigger mania in bipolar disorder; screen for bipolar before starting.
Buspirone is effective for some anxiety but must be taken on a scheduled basis, not as needed (PRN).
Cross-titration with fluoxetine (due to its long half-life) can help discontinue SNRIs more smoothly.
Start buspirone at 7.5 mg twice daily (half of a 15 mg tablet) for one week, then increase to 15 mg twice daily; maximum 30 mg twice daily is sometimes needed.
Buspirone often has an all-or-nothing effect—either it works well for anxiety or it does nothing.
Atypical antipsychotics (e.g., aripiprazole, quetiapine, brexpiprazole) are used as augmentation after SSRI/SNRI failure, not as first-line monotherapy.
Quetiapine (Seroquel) dosing for insomnia starts at 25 mg, can increase to 50–100 mg; higher doses (up to 800 mg) are for severe cases best managed by psychiatry.

episodes.title: Dr. Greta Warta on Valve Diseases 11/6/25
episodes.speaker: Greta Warta
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greta Warta, an Ascension cardiologist, presents a lecture on aortic valve stenosis for family medicine residents, focusing on outpatient evaluation and management. She covers the causes, pathophysiology, symptoms, and physical exam findings of aortic stenosis, with emphasis on echocardiographic interpretation including gradient, valve area, and LV function. Management strategies include surveillance intervals based on severity, cautious blood pressure control, and timely referral for valve replacement. The talk also addresses bicuspid valve considerations, TAVR advances, and clinical pearls such as the disappearing murmur of low-flow stenosis and the importance of listening for murmurs at every visit.
key_points: Aortic stenosis is the most common valvular disorder in older adults (over 80), also seen in patients with bicuspid aortic valves (fifth or sixth decade).
Echo findings: initially preserved/hyperdynamic EF, concentric LV hypertrophy; a normal EF with severe AS indicates the heart is weakening.
Symptoms of severe AS include syncope, dizziness, angina, and dyspnea; symptoms are absent in mild to moderate disease.
Physical exam: harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur, soft or absent S2, tardus pulse, and possible S4 gallop with LVH.
Grading severity uses aortic valve area (<1.0 cm² severe), mean gradient, and leaflet calcification; correlation with clinical context is essential.
Asymptomatic surveillance: mild AS echo every 3-5 years, moderate every 1-2 years, severe every 6-12 months.
Referral indications: symptomatic severe AS, severe AS even if asymptomatic, new murmur in older adult, and pre-operative evaluation if murmur present.
Blood pressure control in AS must be cautious: avoid aggressive diuresis and overly tight BP targets (e.g., keep systolic around 130-140, not 120).
Bicuspid valve patients require monitoring of the thoracic aorta for dilation (surgical threshold 4.5 cm vs 5 cm for others).
Any diastolic murmur is pathologic and warrants referral to cardiology; TAVR is now an option for intermediate and low-risk patients.

Endocarditis prophylaxis: Dr. Warta uses old guidelines (2 g amoxicillin) for severe AS before dental procedures, despite current guidelines limiting prophylaxis to prosthetic valves or prior endocarditis.
Left ventricular thrombus can form in the setting of methamphetamine-induced cardiomyopathy due to stasis and poor contractility.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on 1st TM Pregnancy
episodes.speaker: Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greuel presents a lecture on first-trimester pregnancy loss management, focusing on the two core questions: determining if the pregnancy is live and ensuring appropriate follow-up. He reviews the three management options (expectant, medical with misoprostol, and surgical D&C), highlights the importance of a one-week follow-up until resolution, and provides practical counseling tips using tables from AAFP articles. The talk also covers ultrasound interpretation, including gestational sac measurements, yolk sac appearance, and the discriminatory zone for beta-hCG, along with patient education on warning signs that require emergency care.
key_points: The two critical questions in miscarriage management are whether the pregnancy is live and ensuring adequate follow-up; the ball is often dropped on follow-up.
Expectant management success rates: about 25% pass within 1 week of diagnosis, and an additional 27% by week 2, then gains slow.
Medical management with misoprostol alone is 84% effective by day 8; adding mifepristone increases to 88%.
For medical management, instruct patients to place 4 misoprostol 200 mcg tablets vaginally, lie down for 30 minutes, expect bleeding/cramping in 2-4 hours lasting 3-5 hours.
ER precautions: bleeding >2 pads per hour for 2 hours, fever >101°F, chills, foul discharge, anemia symptoms, or uncontrolled pain.
Rh-negative patients should receive Rhogam (class C evidence but low risk to prevent alloimmunization).
A CBC is recommended at baseline for all miscarriage patients.
On transvaginal ultrasound, a yolk sac (like a Cheerio) should be seen by end of 6 weeks; by 7 weeks a fetus with heartbeat should be visible.
Beta-hCG doubling time: expect 1.5× rise in 48 hours, 2× in 72 hours, but only reliable up to about 9 weeks gestation.
A gestational sac mean diameter >25 mm without a fetal pole defines anembryonic gestation (blighted ovum).
A positive pregnancy test with no clear intrauterine pregnancy is diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
Free fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac on ultrasound suggests a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on Management of Fetal Malpresentation in the Third Trimester 8/13/26
episodes.speaker: Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greuel reviews the management of fetal malpresentation in the third trimester, focusing on breech presentation. He outlines the use of Leopold's maneuvers for clinical assessment, the importance of ultrasound confirmation by 36 weeks, and shared decision-making regarding external cephalic version (ECV). He discusses contraindications, counseling strategies, and practical steps for offering ECV as a safe option to reduce cesarean rates.
key_points: Perform Leopold's maneuvers routinely on all third-trimester patients to detect malpresentation.
Ultrasound confirmation of presentation should be documented by the 36-week visit; offering it at GBS screening is practical.
Approximately 3-4% of term pregnancies are breech; about 1/3 of primary cesareans are related to malpresentation.
Complete (frank) breech is most common; footling breech has the highest risk of cord prolapse.
ECV is optimally offered at 37 weeks; success expectations should be set around 50%.
Absolute contraindications to ECV include placenta previa, non-reassuring fetal status, severe preeclampsia, ruptured membranes, and multiple gestation.
Terbutaline is used for uterine relaxation; RhoGAM given if Rh negative; anesthesia is typically not used.
Complication rate requiring immediate cesarean is about 1%; post-success spontaneous reversion occurs in ~3% of cases.
Counseling should be tailored to the patient's gestational age and readiness, including prayer and handouts.
If ECV fails or is not appropriate, plan for scheduled cesarean delivery near term.
Perform Leopold's maneuvers and document at 35-36 weeks for suspected malpresentation; confirm with ultrasound.
Terbutaline should be given at least 15 minutes before ECV for tocolysis.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on Miscarriage & Treatment 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greuel lectures on managing early pregnancy loss (miscarriage) in family medicine, emphasizing the importance of timing, communication, and psychosocial-spiritual care. He compares the encounter to a trauma scene, where patients are in shock and cannot make major decisions. He reviews definitions, ultrasound criteria, HCG trends, and three management options: expectant, medical (misoprostol), and surgical (uterine aspiration/D&C). He stresses respecting patient preferences, providing follow-up, and avoiding myths, while ensuring safety and ruling out ectopic pregnancy.
key_points: Nearly 1 in 4 women experience early pregnancy loss (4-13 weeks gestation).
50% of miscarriages are caused by chromosomal anomalies; routine exams (pap, transvaginal ultrasound, bimanual) do not cause miscarriage.
Transvaginal ultrasound is the most reliable diagnostic tool; the discriminatory zone for a gestational sac is around 2000 mIU/mL beta-hCG.
Expectant management (wait and see) is up to 90% effective for incomplete abortion but less effective for anembryonic gestation or embryonic demise.
Misoprostol makes the process quicker and more predictable but may be more traumatic for patients with anxiety or poor support systems.
Mental health outcomes are significantly better when patient preferences are respected; all three management options are essentially equally safe.
Follow-up should occur weekly until resolution; an 80% drop in HCG or ultrasound documentation of a collapsed endometrial stripe is diagnostic of completed miscarriage.
Do not let the sunset on an ectopic pregnancy that cannot be ruled out; patients with pain and unknown location need same-day evaluation.
Color flow Doppler can help differentiate retained products of conception (blood flow) from blood clot (no flow).
Patients can switch from expectant to medical or surgical management at any time if needed.
Expectant management success rates plateau after 2-3 weeks; most patients who will pass tissue do so within 14 days.
Misoprostol alone is 67% successful within 2 days and 84% within a week; adding mifepristone increases success to 89%.

episodes.title: Dr. Greuel on Transvaginal Ultrasounds 12/4/25
episodes.speaker: Greuel
episodes.abstract: Dr. Greuel's lecture covers the practical use of transvaginal ultrasound in a family medicine setting, including patient communication, proper setup, and scanning technique. Key topics include distinguishing true gestational sacs from pseudosacs using the double decidual sign, measuring mean sac diameter and crown-rump length, and recognizing ectopic pregnancy with free fluid in the cul-de-sac. The talk emphasizes systematic scanning to avoid missing twins or adnexal pathology, and provides guidance on when to repeat studies or refer for formal ultrasound.
key_points: Obtain informed consent by explaining the procedure, including the use of a condom-covered probe and the possibility of needing a formal ultrasound later.
Perform transvaginal ultrasound with an empty bladder; the probe is inserted along the posterior vaginal wall and advanced slowly while looking for the uterus.
Orient the probe with the marker to the patient's right (your left) for transverse views; the left side of the screen corresponds to the patient's anterior.
Systematically scan the uterus from side to side in both longitudinal and transverse planes to avoid missing twins, heterotopic pregnancy, or ovarian cysts.
A true gestational sac is rounded or elliptical in two planes, eccentric to the endometrial stripe, and shows a double decidual sign; a pseudogestational sac lacks these features.
Mean sac diameter is calculated from three orthogonal measurements; crown-rump length is the average of three measurements from the top of the head to the bottom of the buttocks.
If no fetal pole is seen at 6 weeks, consider anembryonic gestation (blighted ovum) and repeat ultrasound in one week with ectopic precautions.
Switch from crown-rump length to Hadlock fetal biometry at 14 weeks gestation.
Free fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac raises concern for ruptured ectopic pregnancy or infection, especially when no intrauterine pregnancy is seen.
Pregnancy of undetermined location should be treated as ectopic until an intrauterine gestational sac is definitively identified.
Absence of a yolk sac by the end of 6 weeks is abnormal.
No cardiac activity by the middle of the 6th week is a concerning finding.

episodes.title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro Exam
episodes.speaker: Hadwen
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hadwen reviews the NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS) and tendon reflex techniques for hospital-based exams. He emphasizes the importance of standardized scoring to ensure inter-rater reliability, noting that a change of 3 or more points is clinically significant. Key teaching points include proper administration of level-of-consciousness questions (month and age), avoiding pantomime for command-following, and using binocular visual field testing to detect homonymous hemianopia. The talk also covers motor exam timing (10 seconds for arms, 5 seconds for legs) and scoring nuances for facial palsy and drift.
key_points: NIHSS has high inter-rater reliability; a change of 3 or more points warrants head imaging or rapid response.
For level of consciousness, ask only two standardized questions: month and age (not orientation to place).
When testing ability to follow commands, tell the patient to make a fist and close eyes—do not pantomime or place your fingers in their hand.
For visual fields, test binocularly with fists held 2–2.5 feet away; flash fingers in upper and lower quadrants.
Extraocular movements are tested with horizontal gaze only; inability to cross midline scores 2 points.
Arms are held for 10 seconds, legs for 5 seconds; score 0 if no drift, 4 if no movement at all.
Facial palsy is scored by inspecting the nasolabial fold at rest and asking the patient to smile; lower-face weakness is typical for hemispheric stroke.
A score of 4 or more on initial NIHSS is considered disabling and may qualify for tPA.
Use MDCalc or a reference card to ensure accurate scoring, even experienced stroke neurologists do this.
Always perform NIHSS for any acute change in mental status, not just suspected stroke.
Motor testing should capture the patient's best effort by encouraging them during arm and leg holds.
Arm drift is assessed for 10 seconds, leg drift for 5 seconds, with the examiner helping position the leg initially.

episodes.title: Dr. Hadwen on Neuro ITE Prep 9/26/25
episodes.speaker: Hadwen
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hadwen reviews peripheral nerve injuries and headache red flags for ITE preparation. The talk covers radial nerve palsy from Saturday night palsy, meralgia paresthetica from compression, and peroneal nerve injury from weight loss. Key hand muscle tests for median, ulnar, and radial nerves are demonstrated. The SNOOP mnemonic for secondary headache red flags is emphasized, along with cluster headache management using oxygen and prophylaxis.
key_points: Radial nerve injury at the spiral groove causes wrist drop and sensory loss on the dorsal forearm and hand; it usually resolves in weeks.
Meralgia paresthetica presents with burning/numbness on the anterolateral thigh without weakness; common in larger men with tight belts or weight gain.
Peroneal nerve injury at the fibular head causes foot drop; differentiate from L5 radiculopathy by testing ankle eversion (weak in radiculopathy, spared in peroneal injury).
Rapid weight loss, including from GLP-1 agonists, predisposes to peroneal nerve compression due to loss of protective fat pad.
For foot drop, prescribe a stiff ankle brace to prevent tripping; recovery may be incomplete if nerve is severely stunned.
Cluster headache is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia with unilateral severe pain and autonomic features; acute treatment includes high-flow oxygen.
Cluster headache prophylaxis includes verapamil, topiramate, and lithium; lithium is reserved due to toxicity.
The SNOOP mnemonic identifies red flags for secondary headache: Systemic symptoms, Neurologic signs, Onset thunderclap, Older age >50, and Prior headache change or positional triggers.
A new or different headache in a migraineur warrants serious evaluation for secondary causes like tumor or idiopathic intracranial hypertension.
Thunderclap headache (peak within 1 minute) requires immediate ER evaluation for subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Headache in pregnancy with hypertension should raise concern for preeclampsia; assess for worsening with Valsalva.
Pulsatile tinnitus, especially unilateral with headache, warrants evaluation for aneurysm with CT CTA through temporal bone.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney- CHF
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney provides a focused overview of outpatient heart failure diagnosis and management. He emphasizes heart failure as a clinical syndrome requiring both structural/functional impairment and symptoms, not just lab values. The lecture contrasts NYHA functional classification (which can improve) with ACC/AHA staging (which is fixed), and details the evidence-based GDMT pillars for HFrEF: ARNI, beta-blockers, spironolactone, and SGLT2 inhibitors. He stresses the importance of identifying the underlying cause (ischemia, hypertension, valvular disease) and using BNP as one piece of the diagnostic picture, not a standalone test.
key_points: Heart failure is a clinical syndrome defined by structural or functional cardiac impairment plus symptoms; elevated filling pressures are central.
NYHA class is a functional classification that can change (I=asymptomatic, IV=symptoms at rest); ACC/AHA staging is fixed (A=at risk, D=advanced).

Common causes of heart failure include ischemic heart disease, hypertension, and valvular disease; consider zebras like rheumatologic conditions, tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy, or peripartum cardiomyopathy.
BNP >400 is consistent with CHF, <100 makes CHF unlikely; it is only a piece of the picture and should not be used alone or trended routinely.
High-sensitivity symptoms: dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, weight gain. High-specificity findings: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea, JVD, and IVC >2.1 cm with <50% collapse.
Echocardiogram is essential for diagnosis. HFrEF = EF ≤40%; HFmrEF = EF 41-49%; HFpEF = EF ≥50%.
Initial workup should include iron panel, TSH, urinalysis, EKG, chest X-ray, and echo; consider stress test if ischemic etiology is suspected.
GDMT for HFrEF: start an ARNI (or ACE/ARB if cost prohibitive) plus a beta-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, or metoprolol succinate) as first-line therapy.
Add spironolactone if still symptomatic after ARNI and beta-blocker, unless contraindicated by renal function or hyperkalemia.
SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) reduce hospitalizations and CV mortality; no diabetes requirement for initiation.

GDMT for HFrEF consists of four drug classes: ARNI/ACE/ARB, beta blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), spironolactone, and SGLT2 inhibitor, and all four reduce hospitalizations and mortality.
Start with an ARNI if possible, titrate to moderate dose, then add and titrate a beta blocker to target, then return to further titrate the ARNI.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney on Epidemiology
episodes.speaker: Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney discusses the epidemiology of heart failure, noting that prevalence is rising while incidence declines due to guideline-directed medical therapy. He reviews common causes (hypertension, ischemic heart disease, valvular disease) and emphasizes distinguishing NYHA functional classification (which can change) from ACC/AHA staging (which is fixed). Diagnosis relies on BNP ( >400 specific, <100 rules out), exam findings (JVD, laterally displaced PMI, IVC collapse), and initial workup including CBC, chem14, iron panel, EKG, chest X-ray, and echo. Treatment centers on four pillars of GDMT: ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), beta blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate), and alternatives like hydralazine/isosorbide dinitrate.
key_points: Prevalence of heart failure is increasing but incidence is decreasing due to GDMT.
Top causes to investigate: hypertension, ischemic heart disease, and valvular heart disease.
NYHA functional class can improve or worsen; ACC/AHA stage is permanent once reached.
BNP >400 pg/mL is specific for CHF; <100 pg/mL effectively rules it out.
JVD and laterally displaced PMI are highly specific exam findings for volume overload.
Initial workup for suspected CHF includes CBC, chem14, iron panel, EKG, chest X-ray, and echocardiogram.
HFrEF is defined as ejection fraction ≤40% with symptoms; HFmrEF is EF 41-49%.
Four pillars of GDMT: ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan), beta blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor (implied but not detailed).
Switching from ACE inhibitor to ARNI requires a 36-hour washout to avoid angioedema; no washout needed from ARB.
Only three beta blockers are proven in HFrEF: bisoprolol, carvedilol, and metoprolol succinate.
Start all four pillars of GDMT for HFrEF: ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2i.
Do not start a beta-blocker during an acute exacerbation if cardiac output is low; wait until the patient is stable near discharge.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney on I-Pass and Senior Addendum
episodes.speaker: Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney presents a lecture on I-PASS structured patient handoffs and the senior addendum, emphasizing the importance of accurate and efficient sign-outs to reduce medical errors and adverse events. She reviews common pitfalls such as excessive information, copy-pasted assessments, and mismatched handoff content for day versus night coverage. The lecture also covers the I-PASS framework—illness severity, patient summary, action list, situational awareness and contingency planning, and synthesis by the receiver—and evidence that standardized handoffs decrease error rates by 23%.
key_points: Omission of critical information occurs in 2 out of 3 handoff errors, per Johns Hopkins data.
Inefficient handoffs contribute to duty-hour violations and delays in patient care.
Standardized handoff programs (e.g., I-PASS) reduced medical errors by 23% and adverse events by 30% (NEJM 2014).
Handoff content should differ based on audience: overnight coverage needs contingency plans, not daytime updates.
Too much information can be as harmful as too little; chronic problems not being actively managed should be omitted.
The I-PASS framework includes: illness severity (stable/watcher/unstable), patient summary, action list, situational awareness/if-then plans, and synthesis by the receiver.
Copy-pasted assessment plans often obscure relevant active problems and are not helpful for the covering team.
Active problem management details (e.g., IV vs PO diuretics for heart failure) are critical for rapid-response preparation.
Handoffs should be written for the covering person, not as a future reminder for oneself.
Synthesis/repeat-back should be very brief to avoid wasting time.

episodes.title: Dr. Haney on Vaccine Hesitancy
episodes.speaker: Haney
episodes.abstract: Dr. Haney discusses vaccine hesitancy, defining it as a state of indecision or uncertainty about vaccination before a decision is made to act. He explores reasons for increasing hesitancy, including the pandemic, decreased trust in authority, political polarization, and social media misinformation. The lecture emphasizes the importance of understanding vaccine safety processes, using an evidence-based approach to counsel patients, and recognizing the global health impact of declining vaccination rates, particularly with measles resurgence. He shares a personal story to illustrate why vaccination matters and advocates for good-faith discussions that separate vaccine advocacy from other personal beliefs.
key_points: Vaccine hesitancy is distinct from outright refusal and represents a state of indecision or uncertainty before a decision is made.
87.5% of surveyed clinicians encounter vaccine-hesitant patients, yet only 8% feel definitely confident discussing immunizations.
Hesitancy is increasing due to the pandemic, decreased trust in authority, political polarization, and changes in the digital landscape.
Measles serves as a sentinel vaccine-preventable disease; US cases rose from near elimination to over 121 cases in the current year.
Many measles hospitalizations are for isolation rather than severe illness, an important distinction for good-faith discussions.
The Wakefield paper falsely linking MMR to autism and the rise of Google are cited as historical triggers for misinformation.
Thimerosal was removed from most vaccines despite lack of evidence of harm, a concession to public concern.
Personal stories (e.g., a patient who died from COVID-19) can be more effective than any single counseling strategy.
Good-faith discussions require not jumping to conclusions and maintaining reasonable, objective dialogue.
Vaccine advocacy can be separated from other personal beliefs (e.g., political, religious, dietary) to avoid conflating issues.
The first vaccine (1796) used material from smallpox pustules and left scars, but successfully eradicated smallpox.
Common vaccine concerns include autism, thimerosal, aluminum, fetal cells, necessity, and autonomy; aluminum exposure from breastfeeding exceeds that from vaccines.

episodes.title: Dr. Hannah Howard on Biopsies
episodes.speaker: Hannah Howard
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hannah Howard discusses the two main types of biopsies (shave and punch) and when to use each, emphasizing that shave biopsies are preferred for most lesions including melanoma because they provide the full lesion for pathology. She covers common skin cancers (basal cell, squamous cell, melanoma) and benign lesions, along with practical tips for biopsy technique, documentation, and communication with pathologists. The lecture also includes treatment pearls for warts, molluscum, infantile hemangiomas, and acne, as well as guidance on when to refer for Mohs surgery.
key_points: Shave biopsies are preferred for most skin lesions, including suspected melanoma, because they allow the pathologist to see the entire lesion.
Punch biopsies are indicated for rashes and conditions where deeper dermal pathology is needed.
Important biopsy tips: mark before numbing, send all tissue to pathology, provide a differential diagnosis, and take photos.
Common skin cancers: basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and melanoma; SCC causes more deaths than melanoma due to higher prevalence.
Mohs surgery is for high-risk skin cancers; the AUC app helps determine appropriateness.
Benign lesions include cherry angioma, pyogenic granuloma, seborrheic keratosis, milia, sebaceous hyperplasia, dermatofibroma, solar lentigo, idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, and skin tags.
Warts require multiple treatments; liquid nitrogen typically takes three sessions; consider Gardasil vaccine and topical 5-FU/salicylic acid compound.
Molluscum contagiosum usually self-resolves in 1-2 years; the boat sign indicates impending resolution.
Infantile hemangiomas: refer if >5 lesions, on cosmetically sensitive areas, or >4 cm; treat with topical timolol or oral propranolol.
Acne treatment: start tretinoin 0.025% with slow titration, use benzoyl peroxide 4% face/10% trunk, limit antibiotics (doxycycline) to ≤3 months.
Spironolactone is effective for hormonal acne in women; typical starting dose is 100 mg daily, taken with food in the evening to minimize blood pressure drop.
Isotretinoin requires monthly pregnancy tests for females; newer evidence shows weaker correlation with IBD and depression than previously thought.

episodes.title: Dr. Hannah Youmans on Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy
episodes.speaker: Hannah Youmans
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hannah Youmans presents a comprehensive overview of hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, covering definitions, pathophysiology, clinical features, and management for both inpatient and outpatient settings. She emphasizes the importance of elevated blood pressure as a prerequisite for diagnosis, distinguishes between gestational hypertension, preeclampsia with and without severe features, eclampsia, and HELLP syndrome, and discusses long-term cardiovascular risks for affected women. The lecture includes practical guidance on diagnostic criteria, laboratory evaluation, and treatment thresholds, with a focus on actionable clinical decision-making for family medicine residents.
key_points: Gestational hypertension is defined as systolic BP ≥140 or diastolic ≥90 after 20 weeks gestation.
Preeclampsia without severe features requires gestational hypertension plus proteinuria (≥300 mg/24h or protein/creatinine ratio ≥0.3).

Preeclampsia with severe features is defined by end-organ damage, including severe-range BP (≥160/110), thrombocytopenia, transaminitis, renal impairment, intractable headache, or visual disturbances; proteinuria is no longer required.
Eclampsia is new-onset tonic-clonic seizures in the setting of preeclampsia, but can present without classic preeclampsia features.

HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) may be on the spectrum of pregnancy-induced hypertension, with diagnostic criteria including LDH >600, AST/ALT >2x upper limit of normal, and platelets <100,000.
Prophylactic aspirin 81 mg started at 12-18 weeks reduces preeclampsia risk by improving placental vascular development.
Antihypertensive therapy is indicated only for severe-range blood pressures (≥160/110) in pregnancy; mild-moderate hypertension is managed with monitoring.
Delivery is recommended at 38 weeks for gestational hypertension or preeclampsia without severe features, as placental function declines after this point.
Magnesium sulfate is the first-line agent for seizure prophylaxis in preeclampsia with severe features and for eclampsia treatment.
Long-term cardiovascular risk is increased in women with a history of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, warranting ongoing postpartum monitoring.

episodes.title: Dr. Harris on Polycythemia Vera
episodes.speaker: Harris
episodes.abstract: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by overproduction of myeloid cells, particularly red blood cells, leading to elevated red cell mass. It is often found incidentally on routine labs, but common symptoms include fatigue, insomnia, difficulty concentrating, aquagenic pruritus, and erythromelalgia. Diagnosis requires elevated hemoglobin/hematocrit (male >16.5/≥49%, female >16/≥48%), JAK2 V617F mutation (98% of cases), low erythropoietin level, and bone marrow biopsy showing trilineage proliferation. Treatment focuses on reducing thrombotic risk: therapeutic phlebotomy to maintain hematocrit <45%, low-dose aspirin for prophylaxis, and cytoreductive therapy (hydroxyurea, interferon-α, or busulfan) for high-risk patients (age >60 or prior thrombosis).
key_points: PV is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with elevated red blood cell mass; median age at diagnosis is 60, more common in males.
Untreated median survival is 18 months; with treatment, median survival extends to 13 years.
Most common symptoms are fatigue, insomnia, and difficulty concentrating; aquagenic pruritus (worse with warm water) and erythromelalgia (burning pain with erythema) are characteristic.

Diagnosis requires elevated Hb/Hct (male >16.5/≥49%, female >16/≥48%), JAK2 V617F mutation, low erythropoietin, and bone marrow biopsy showing trilineage proliferation with pleomorphic megakaryocytes.
Secondary causes of erythrocytosis (e.g., cardiopulmonary disease, high altitude, smoking, renal disease, sleep apnea, testosterone use) must be ruled out first.
Therapeutic phlebotomy goal is hematocrit <45% (both sexes); one unit (500 mL) reduces Hct by ~3 percentage points; avoid iron supplementation.
Low-dose aspirin (40–100 mg/day) is recommended for thrombosis prophylaxis; twice-daily dosing may be considered for symptomatic patients or those with cardiovascular risk factors.

Cytoreductive therapy is indicated for high-risk patients (age >60 or prior thrombosis) and may be considered for low-risk patients with uncontrolled symptoms, rising leukocytes/platelets, progressive splenomegaly, or phlebotomy intolerance.
Hydroxyurea (15 mg/kg/day initially, goal platelet count 100–400 × 10⁹/L) is first-line; it takes 3–5 days to work, and dose adjustments should be no more than once weekly.
Interferon-α is preferred in pregnancy but poorly tolerated; busulfan is reserved for patients >60 who fail hydroxyurea and interferon due to risk of leukemia and other toxicities.
Elevated hemoglobin requires systematic exclusion of secondary causes before diagnosing polycythemia vera.
JAK2 mutation testing is a key confirmatory test for polycythemia vera.

episodes.title: Dr. Hermann on Adult Wellness
episodes.speaker: Hermann
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hermann discusses adult wellness visits, emphasizing that while there is limited evidence that wellness visits decrease mortality, they provide an opportunity to build patient relationships and focus on preventive care. He covers billing nuances, such as when to add a modifier for acute issues during a wellness visit, and outlines his three-part approach: screening questions, physical exam, and preventive labs/orders. Key screening topics include tobacco, alcohol, depression, diet, exercise, and social determinants, while the physical exam is tailored but typically includes heart, lungs, ears, and skin checks. Preventive orders follow USPSTF guidelines, such as diabetes screening for adults 35-70 with BMI >25, lipid panels for ages 40-75, and colon cancer screening starting at age 45.
key_points: Wellness visits are primarily for building relationships and preventive care, not proven to decrease mortality directly.
Billing for a wellness visit plus an acute problem (with modifier 25) increases RVUs but may lead to patient dissatisfaction if unexpected copays arise.
For Medicare patients, a wellness visit can often be added to a sick visit using a questionnaire, avoiding extra charges.
Screening questions should cover tobacco, alcohol, depression (PHQ-2/9), diet, exercise, social determinants (housing, income), and violence.
Review and update medical, surgical, family, and social history at each wellness visit, verifying medications and allergies.
Physical exam varies by clinician but typically includes heart, lungs, ears, eyes, skin, and lower extremity assessment; extensive neuro or abdominal exams are not routine unless indicated.
For older adults, pay attention to skin for suspicious growths and assess gait or mobility.

Preventive orders should follow USPSTF guidelines: diabetes screening (A1C or fasting glucose) for ages 35-70 with BMI >25, lipid panel for ages 40-75 every 5 years, and colon cancer screening starting at age 45.
Hepatitis C testing is recommended for all adults aged 18-79, and bone density (DEXA) screening for women over 65.
CBC is not routinely recommended for asymptomatic adults; labs should be guided by risk factors and guidelines.
Lung cancer screening: age 50-80, 20 pack-year history, current smoker or quit within 15 years, annually.
Colon cancer screening: USPSTF grade A for ages 50-75, grade B for ages 45-75.

episodes.title: Dr. Herrmann on Liver Disease for Primary Care 4/23/26
episodes.speaker: Herrmann
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the outpatient approach to elevated liver enzymes, focusing on differential diagnosis and management of common causes. The speaker uses a case of a 41-year-old man with mildly elevated AST and ALT to illustrate workup, including repeat labs, ultrasound, and hepatitis panel. Key tools like the FIB-4 score for fibrosis risk stratification and lifestyle interventions, especially weight loss, are emphasized. The talk also reviews pharmacologic options for fatty liver disease, including GLP-1 agonists and the newer agent resmetirom.
key_points: Fatty liver disease (MASLD) is the most common cause of elevated transaminases, affecting 20-30% of the population and 70% of obese patients.
For mildly elevated LFTs, initial management includes repeat labs in 3-6 months and counseling on lifestyle changes, particularly weight loss.
If LFTs remain elevated, obtain an ultrasound to assess for steatosis and a hepatitis panel to rule out chronic viral hepatitis.
Elevated ferritin is most often due to inflammation from fatty liver disease; to evaluate for hemochromatosis, order a full iron panel with percent saturation.
The FIB-4 score (using age, AST, ALT, and platelets) is a validated tool to rule out advanced fibrosis; a score <1.3 indicates low risk.
5% body weight loss yields a 30% reduction in hepatic steatosis; 10% weight loss leads to a 76% reduction, effectively curing steatosis in most patients.
GLP-1 agonists (e.g., Wegovy) are now FDA-approved for NASH and can be prescribed, though insurance coverage remains a common barrier.
Resmetirom is the only FDA-approved medication specifically for fibrosis due to fatty liver disease, but it is expensive and often requires liver biopsy for insurance approval.
In patients with type 2 diabetes and fatty liver, prefer medications that do not increase insulin (e.g., pioglitazone, GLP-1s, SGLT2s) over insulin or sulfonylureas.
Severe transaminitis (AST/ALT >1000) is most commonly due to ischemic liver injury, acute viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury (e.g., Tylenol overdose), or biliary obstruction.
Use phosphatidylethanol (PEth) to objectively quantify alcohol intake over 3 weeks; levels <20 nondrinker, 20-50 occasional, >500 heavy drinker.
Naltrexone is first-line for alcohol use disorder; common side effect is GI upset.

episodes.title: Dr. Herrmann on Outpatient Management
episodes.speaker: Herrmann
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Herrmann focuses on outpatient management of hypertension. It covers the importance of blood pressure control, definitions of hypertension stages, diagnostic criteria including ambulatory monitoring, and lifestyle modifications such as the DASH diet. The talk also reviews first-line pharmacologic classes (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide diuretics, long-acting calcium channel blockers) and provides practical algorithms for choosing therapy based on comorbidities, race, and blood pressure level.
key_points: Every 20 mmHg systolic increase over 115 doubles the risk of heart attack or stroke.
Diagnosis of hypertension requires ambulatory home monitoring averaging >130/80 or at least three elevated office readings.
Lifestyle modifications including weight loss, DASH diet, sodium reduction (<1500 mg/day), potassium increase, aerobic exercise, and alcohol moderation can lower BP by 3–11 points.
First-line antihypertensive classes are ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazide diuretics, and long-acting calcium channel blockers.
For African American patients, thiazide diuretics or CCBs are preferred first-line agents.
In patients with diabetes or CKD, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is recommended for kidney protection.
For systolic BP >160 mmHg, consider starting combination therapy (e.g., amlodipine/benazepril).
Home blood pressure monitoring should be done once daily, with follow-up in two weeks.
Before starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, check baseline creatinine and potassium.
Staging hypertension uses the higher of systolic or diastolic values to determine the stage.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are first-line for heart failure, CKD, diabetes, and post-MI; ARBs have fewer side effects like cough.
Expected creatinine bump <0.3 mg/dL after starting ACE/ARB is benign; >0.3 or persistent rise warrants further evaluation.

episodes.title: Dr. Hershberger on Antepartum Fetal Surveillance 6/4/26
episodes.speaker: Hershberger
episodes.abstract: This lecture on antepartum fetal surveillance covers its purpose to prevent stillbirth by detecting fetal hypoxia, the main modalities (nonstress test, biophysical profile, modified BPP, contraction stress test, umbilical artery Doppler), and the indications and timing for high-risk pregnancies. The speaker reviews criteria for test interpretation, such as NST reactivity requiring 15 bpm accelerations for 15 seconds within 20 minutes, and BPP scoring with each component graded 2 or 0. Common indications discussed include chronic hypertension on medication, pregestational or medication-controlled gestational diabetes, fetal growth restriction, and advanced maternal age, with most surveillance starting at 32 weeks. Case examples reinforce when to initiate testing and highlight pitfalls such as not testing stable maternal conditions.
key_points: Antepartum fetal surveillance aims to identify fetuses at risk for stillbirth by detecting hypoxia/acidosis.
The nonstress test (NST) requires accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes for reactivity; for fetuses <32 weeks, a lower threshold applies.
Biophysical profile (BPP) scores five components (fetal breathing, movement, tone, amniotic fluid, NST) each 2 if normal, 0 if abnormal; total 8-10 is reassuring, 6 is equivocal, <6 is abnormal.
Modified BPP combines a reactive NST with a normal amniotic fluid index (≥5 cm) and is less resource-intensive.
Umbilical artery Doppler is essential for fetal growth restriction; absent or reverse end-diastolic flow indicates severe hypoxia and requires urgent management.
Indications for surveillance include chronic hypertension on medication, pregestational or medication-controlled gestational diabetes (GDM A2), and fetal growth restriction.
Surveillance generally starts at 32 weeks for most high-risk conditions, but earlier for severe disease or abnormal Doppler findings.
For diet-controlled gestational diabetes (GDM A1), advanced maternal age (≥40), and stable cardiac/pulmonary/seizure disorders, routine surveillance is not clearly recommended.
Decreased fetal movement warrants a single workup with NST/BPP; if reassuring, serial testing is not needed.
Postterm pregnancy (≥41 weeks) should prompt consideration of surveillance and induction.
Antepartum fetal surveillance should start at 32 weeks for most high-risk conditions.
Conditions requiring surveillance include hypertension, gestational diabetes, and fetal growth restriction.

episodes.title: Dr. Hershberger on Post Partum Care
episodes.speaker: Hershberger
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers comprehensive postpartum care, emphasizing the transition from pregnancy to parenthood. Key topics include screening for postpartum depression using the Edinburgh scale, breastfeeding guidance and contraception counseling, management of chronic conditions like gestational diabetes and hypertension, and health maintenance such as vaccinations and Pap smears. The speaker highlights the importance of ongoing, tailored follow-up visits and connecting patients with resources like lactation consultants and WIC.
key_points: Screen for postpartum depression using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale; a score of 10 or more or a positive answer to question 10 (suicidal ideation) warrants further evaluation.

Breastfeeding guidance includes encouraging on-demand feeding at least 8-12 times per day; lactation amenorrhea can provide contraception only if exclusively breastfeeding, intervals ≤4-6 hours, baby <6 months, and no return of menses.
Short interpregnancy interval is defined as <18 months between pregnancies; avoid pregnancy within 6 months due to risks of preterm labor, low birth weight, and maternal stress.
Progestin-only contraceptives can be started at 6 weeks postpartum; combination contraceptives should be delayed until at least 3 weeks due to thromboembolism risk.
Postpartum bleeding should decrease over time; persistent or worsening bleeding at 6 weeks requires evaluation for retained products, endometritis, or laceration.
Gestational hypertension, preeclampsia, and gestational diabetes increase long-term cardiovascular risk; follow up with glucose tolerance testing at 6 weeks and annual blood pressure checks.
For women with stillbirth or miscarriage, provide follow-up care due to higher rates of PTSD and need for support.
Ensure rubella nonimmune patients receive MMR postpartum; offer influenza and RSV vaccines as indicated.
Use resources like LactMed (NIH) for medication safety during breastfeeding.
Postpartum care is an ongoing process; aim for a visit within the first 3 weeks, then comprehensive care at 2 and 6 weeks, tailored to individual needs.

episodes.title: Dr. Hildebrand on Arthritis
episodes.speaker: Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hildebrand presents a systematic approach to diagnosing and managing rheumatoid arthritis (RA) in a family medicine setting, emphasizing the use of ACR criteria rather than memorization. She reviews key history features (morning stiffness >6 weeks, small joint involvement), physical exam findings (synovitis, boggy joints), and appropriate lab testing (RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP) while cautioning against indiscriminate ANA ordering. Treatment initiation with methotrexate, including baseline screening and dose titration based on ESR, is discussed, along with the importance of referral to rheumatology. The lecture also briefly touches on lupus and the value of clinical reasoning over exhaustive testing.
key_points: RA diagnosis requires symptoms lasting at least six weeks, with morning stiffness and small joint involvement as key triggers.
Use the ACR 2010 criteria (joint involvement, serology, acute phase reactants, duration) to systematically classify RA; a score ≥6 indicates definite RA.
Physical exam should assess for synovitis (warm, boggy, tender joints) and compare to unaffected joints; absence of synovitis makes RA less likely.
Order RF, anti-CCP, ESR, and CRP; avoid ordering ANA unless lupus is specifically suspected due to high false-positive rates.
High-positive RF and anti-CCP (e.g., >3x upper limit) are strongly supportive of RA.
Before starting methotrexate, screen for TB, HIV, hepatitis B/C, and check baseline liver and renal function.
Start methotrexate at a low dose and titrate every 2-4 weeks based on ESR response; disease activity is reassessed at 3 months.
If rheumatology access is delayed, initiate methotrexate and refer concurrently; steroids can be used for symptom relief while waiting.
Psoriatic arthritis should be considered if nail pitting or distal joint involvement is present; fibromyalgia is a diagnosis of exclusion.
Lupus can present with pleuritic chest pain, rash, photosensitivity, and low complement; use SLICC criteria if suspected.
Fatigue workup should include CBC, TSH, and a comprehensive metabolic panel (chem 14).
Small joint pain (DIP, PIP, MCP) with fatigue can be a presenting symptom of autoimmune disease.

episodes.title: Dr. Hildebrand on DKA/HHS 10/23/25
episodes.speaker: Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hildebrand's lecture on DKA and HHS presents two cases to illustrate the differences between these hyperglycemic emergencies. She reviews updated 2024 diagnostic criteria, including a lower glucose threshold for DKA, and emphasizes the importance of identifying underlying precipitating causes such as infection or medication nonadherence. The lecture highlights pitfalls in using urine ketones to monitor resolution, as acetoacetate persists longer, and stresses that fluid resuscitation is the mainstay of treatment.
key_points: DKA develops over hours to days, while HHS evolves over days to weeks due to residual insulin secretion.
HHS criteria: plasma glucose ≥600 mg/dL, serum osmolality ≥300 mOsm/kg, pH >7.3, bicarbonate ≥15, and no significant ketonemia.
Updated 2024 DKA criteria: glucose ≥200 mg/dL, beta-hydroxybutyrate ≥3 mmol/L or urine ketones ≥2+, and metabolic acidosis.
Euglycemic DKA (glucose <250 mg/dL) can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors, pregnancy, or prolonged vomiting.
Urine dipsticks detect acetoacetate, not beta-hydroxybutyrate; therefore, negative urine ketones do not rule out early DKA, and positive results persist after resolution.
The most common precipitating factors are infection, medication nonadherence (especially insulin omission), and steroids.
IV fluids are the cornerstone of initial management for both DKA and HHS, with insulin therapy initiated after volume repletion.
Always search for an underlying cause such as infection, medication nonadherence, or social determinants of health.
DKA resolution requires plasma ketones to be gone and pH normalized (via venous blood gas or bicarbonate).
HHS resolution requires normalized osmolality, glucose <250 mg/dL, and normal urine output.
Anion gap is not reliable for DKA resolution due to hyperchloremic acidosis from normal saline.
ICU admission is often necessary for DKA/HHS due to frequent vital sign monitoring and insulin drip requirements.

episodes.title: Dr. Hildebrand on Osteoporosis
episodes.speaker: Hildebrand
episodes.abstract: Dr. Hildebrand's lecture on osteoporosis covers diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. She emphasizes that bisphosphonates are first-line therapy for primary osteoporosis, with a typical treatment duration of five years. Nonpharmacologic management includes balance training (e.g., tai chi) and spine-loading exercises using a weighted vest. She reviews second-line agents such as raloxifen, teriparatide, and denosumab, highlighting their indications and limitations. Key safety considerations include monitoring for osteonecrosis of the jaw, especially with prolonged bisphosphonate use, and ensuring proper medication timing for Synthroid and bisphosphonates.
key_points: Bisphosphonates are first-line for primary osteoporosis; treat for 5 years.
Avoid daily bisphosphonate dosing due to GI side effects.
Nonpharmacologic treatment should include spine-loading (weighted vest) and balance training (tai chi).
Synthroid must be taken on empty stomach, wait 1 hour before other meds; bisphosphonate also on empty stomach, wait 1 hour.
Raloxifen only reduces vertebral fractures, not nonvertebral; may be considered in select patients.
Calcitonin can help with pain in acute compression fractures.
Teriparatide is anabolic, approved for severe osteoporosis, men, or failed bisphosphonate.
Denosumab (Prolia) is a subcutaneous injection every 6 months; check calcium before administration.
For dental procedures, if on bisphosphonate >4 years, consider stopping for 2 months.
Osteonecrosis of the jaw risk increases with prolonged bisphosphonate use (>4 years) and dental procedures.
Screen women age 65 and older with DEXA (USPSTF Grade B); for men, no consensus — USPSTF recommends against, but AACE suggests age 70.

DEXA screening in postmenopausal women under 65 is appropriate if additional risk factors (e.g., prior fragility fracture, prolonged glucocorticoid use, rheumatoid arthritis, smoking, low BMI) are present.

episodes.title: Dr. Hoslinger on Spiritual Resiliency
episodes.speaker: Hoslinger
episodes.abstract: Dr. Brian Holsinger, a family medicine missionary in Northeast China, discusses spiritual resiliency for healthcare professionals, focusing on cumulative stress, moral injury, and the postures of the heart. He emphasizes the importance of recognizing stress recovery, processing moral injury through lament and confession, and grounding identity in being with God rather than performing for God. The talk integrates personal stories, biblical references, and concepts from a medical retreat to offer practical strategies for sustaining spiritual health in demanding clinical and cross-cultural contexts.
key_points: Cumulative stress occurs when stressors arrive faster than recovery, leading to chronic physiologic responses and increased risk of anxiety, depression, and suicide.

Moral injury arises from committing, witnessing, or failing to prevent acts that violate deeply held values, and it is distinct from PTSD in that its primary emotions are guilt and shame rather than fear.
Moral injury is inevitable in medicine and cross-cultural work; recognizing it and processing it intentionally is essential to prevent spiritual deconstruction.
Strategies for moral injury include lament, sharing burdens with empathetic peers, confessing and receiving forgiveness, and seeking redemption through new strategies.
Spiritual resiliency requires knowing both who you are (a child of God) and whose you are (belonging to Jesus), which anchors identity amidst challenges.
The postures of the heart—under God, over God, from God, for God, and with God—shape how one relates to God and finds significance.
A 'with God' posture, as exemplified by John 15:4-5 and 2 Corinthians 6:16, prioritizes relationship over rules, gifts, or service.
Grace-based living contrasts with works-based living, where significance is derived from performance rather than from God's unconditional love.
External expressions of faith, such as good works and spiritual disciplines, should flow from an internal passionate love for Jesus, not empty ritual.
Community and shared storytelling are vital for metabolizing moral injury and cumulative stress, as others who have faced similar experiences offer unique understanding.
The cycle of works relies on external validation and eventually leads to burnout, while the cycle of grace flows from knowing one is loved and accepted by God.
Jesus' ministry flowed from His identity as the beloved Son (Mark 1:9-11), not from striving for approval.

episodes.title: Dr. Jeff Perry on Hip Maladies
episodes.speaker: Jeff Perry
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers non-fracture, non-osteoarthritis hip maladies including osteitis pubis, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, avulsion fractures, stress fractures, adductor strains, and iliopsoas-related conditions. Dr. Perry emphasizes anatomy, clinical presentations, diagnostic maneuvers (e.g., resisted adduction, one-leg hop, flexion-external rotation), and imaging findings. Treatment focuses on relative rest, activity modification, NSAIDs, physical therapy, and referral for persistent or severe cases. The talk also includes a biblical reflection on Jacob's hip injury.
key_points: Osteitis pubis presents with progressive groin pain, pain with resisted adduction, and positive one-leg hop test; X-rays may show erosions or sclerosis late.
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease typically occurs in males aged 5–8 with insidious limp and loss of hip rotation; early MRI is more sensitive than X-ray.
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) is seen in obese adolescents with delayed puberty; X-ray shows the classic 'ice cream slipping off the cone' appearance.
Avulsion fractures of the hip result from forceful muscle contraction (e.g., blocked kick) and are managed with rest, ice, and progressive weight bearing.
Stress fractures of the femoral neck are associated with the female athlete triad (amenorrhea, overtraining, low bone density); bone scan is the earliest diagnostic test.
Hip adductor strains often occur from forced abduction (e.g., slipping on ice) and present with pain on resisted adduction.
Snapping hip syndrome and iliopsoas bursitis cause deep groin pain with snapping during flexion; tenderness may be found lateral to the femoral neurovascular bundle.
For most sports-related hip conditions, initial management includes relative rest, ice, NSAIDs, and physical therapy, with referral if no improvement after 6 weeks.
The 10% rule for increasing exercise volume (no more than 10% per week) is a key principle to prevent overuse injuries.
Referral to orthopedics is indicated for suspected LCP, SCFE, or when conservative measures fail for conditions like osteitis pubis or iliopsoas bursitis.
Psoas abscess can present with non-specific back pain, muscle spasms, and fever; consider CT/MRI for diagnosis.
Passive hip extension may reproduce pain in psoas irritation.

episodes.title: Dr. John Ashley on Vesiculobullous 11/20/25
episodes.speaker: John Ashley
episodes.abstract: Dr. John Ashley presents a fast-paced lecture on common vesiculobullous rashes, emphasizing clinical recognition and management. He covers poison ivy, herpes simplex, varicella, zoster, monkeypox, blistering dactylitis, bullous impetigo, scabies, dermatitis herpetiformis, and eczema herpeticum. Key themes include the importance of examining the whole patient, adjusting steroid doses based on patient factors, and using appropriate antiviral and topical therapies. The talk provides practical pearls on dosing, pitfalls, and red flags for primary care clinicians.
key_points: Poison ivy contact dermatitis typically lasts about a month without treatment; systemic or potent topical steroids can speed resolution.
Medrol dose packs are less preferred due to nighttime dosing; give prednisone once daily in the morning instead.
For severe poison ivy, start with 20 mg prednisone in the afternoon then 60 mg the next morning, adjusting for patient size and sensitivity.
Herpetic whitlow presents with grouped vesicles on a finger and is pathognomonic for herpes simplex.
Acyclovir for varicella is dosed five times daily, but four times daily is acceptable if compliance is an issue.
Suppressive valacyclovir 500 mg daily is appropriate for patients with more than 3–4 herpes outbreaks per year.
Eczema herpeticum should be suspected when an atopic patient develops widespread vesicles; treat with acyclovir and topical steroids.
Varicella is characterized by lesions in different stages (papules, vesicles, ulcers) in the same area.
Antivirals are renally excreted; ensure adequate hydration to prevent nephrotoxicity.
Early low-dose gabapentin in older adults with zoster may reduce postherpetic neuralgia.
Blistering dactylitis in a child with high fever and inability to move the finger warrants referral to a hand surgeon.
Bullous impetigo may initially present without honey-colored crust; recheck in a few days if uncertain.

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 12/4/25
episodes.speaker: Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert discusses the evaluation and management of adnexal masses, emphasizing the importance of classifying masses as neoplastic or nonneoplastic. Nonneoplastic masses include functional cysts (follicular and corpus luteum) and organic pathologies (endometrioma, tubo-ovarian abscess). He reviews bimanual examination technique, noting that uterine position affects palpation, and that the ovary is roughly the size of the distal thumb phalanx. Ultrasound findings of simple versus complex cysts guide management, with simple cysts having a 90% chance of benignity and often resolving spontaneously. Key clinical pearls include the need for endometrial monitoring in PCOS, observation of hemorrhagic cysts, and prompt antibiotic therapy for tubo-ovarian abscess.
key_points: Adnexal masses are divided into neoplastic (benign or malignant) and nonneoplastic; common nonneoplastic masses include follicular cysts, corpus luteum cysts, endometriomas, and tubo-ovarian abscesses.
Bimanual exam technique: place fingers in the posterior fornix and lift; if the uterus is retroverted, the fundus may not be felt because the cervix is pushed forward instead.
Ovary size equals the distal phalanx of the thumb; in obese women, ovaries are often not palpable, and in postmenopausal women they become even smaller.
On ultrasound, a simple cyst (anechoic, thin-walled) has a 90% chance of being benign; complex cysts (loculated or with solid excrescences) require further workup.

PCOS diagnosis requires irregular menses, hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovaries on ultrasound; management includes ensuring endometrial shedding at least once a year to prevent hyperplasia and screening for diabetes.
Functional cysts (follicular, corpus luteum) are common and often resolve spontaneously; simple cysts less than 10 cm can be followed with repeat ultrasound in 3 months.
Hemorrhagic ovarian cyst presents with acute pain near ovulation and shows internal echoes/clot on ultrasound; management is observation, not surgery.
Tubo-ovarian abscess from PID requires IV antibiotics; fertility prognosis is guarded due to tubal damage.
In postmenopausal women, any palpable ovary should be evaluated with ultrasound, as it may indicate malignancy.
Timing of pelvic pain in relation to menstrual cycle is critical: mid-cycle pain (Mittelschmerz) is benign and self-limited.

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Adnexal Masses 1/22/26
episodes.speaker: Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Jon Calvert covers the classification and evaluation of adnexal masses. It distinguishes between non-neoplastic (functional vs organic) and neoplastic (benign vs malignant) masses. Key ultrasound findings differentiate simple cysts (benign) from complex cysts (suspicious for malignancy). Specific conditions discussed include hemorrhagic cysts, endometriomas, hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, and fibroids. The importance of bimanual pelvic examination and appropriate referral is emphasized.
key_points: Adnexal masses are classified as non-neoplastic (functional vs organic) or neoplastic (benign vs malignant).
Simple cysts on ultrasound are anechoic, thin-walled, and benign; complex cysts have septations, solid components, or irregular walls and are suspicious for malignancy.
Normal ovaries measure approximately 3.5 x 2 x 1.5 cm and become non-palpable after menopause; inability to feel ovaries in a 65-year-old is normal.
Hemorrhagic cysts present with sudden severe pain often during activity, may have shifting pain due to fluid, and can be managed with repeat ultrasound in two weeks.
Endometriomas have a characteristic 'frosted glass' appearance on ultrasound.
Hydrosalpinx is a fluid-filled fallopian tube, usually an incidental finding, often from prior infection.
Tubo-ovarian abscess appears as a complex mass with mixed echogenicity ('garbage') and irregular margins.
Fibroids are classified by location: submucosal (menorrhagia), intramural (bleeding), subserosal (palpable masses).
Bimanual exam is essential for detecting adnexal masses; check uterine mobility in patients with history of STDs.
Patients with physiologic follicles on ultrasound should be reassured that these are normal and not cancer.

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Infections Genitalia
episodes.speaker: Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers common genital infections in both males and females, including bacterial vaginosis, herpes simplex virus, gonorrhea, chlamydia, trichomoniasis, and syphilis. The speaker emphasizes diagnostic criteria such as the Amsel criteria for bacterial vaginosis, the importance of distinguishing primary from recurrent HSV for treatment decisions, and the clinical presentation of gonorrhea/chlamydia with endocervical discharge. Key teaching points include the role of pH in vaginal infections, the necessity of physical exam for herpes lesions in pregnancy, and the high prevalence of syphilis in Oklahoma.
key_points: Bacterial vaginosis diagnosis requires three of four Amsel criteria: thin milky discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test, and clue cells on wet prep.
Normal vaginal pH is ≤4.5, maintained by lactobacillus; elevated pH from semen, menses, or trichomonas predisposes to bacterial vaginosis.
Primary HSV infection is treated more aggressively than recurrent episodes and can cause systemic symptoms requiring hospitalization.
In pregnancy with active herpetic lesions near delivery, cesarean section is indicated to prevent neonatal transmission.
Gonorrhea and chlamydia are intracellular organisms in columnar cells of the endocervix, producing purulent discharge from the cervical os.
When the specific organism is unknown, presumptive treatment for both gonorrhea and chlamydia is recommended.
Trichomoniasis presents with frothy yellow-green discharge, vaginal irritation, postcoital spotting, and strawberry cervix on exam.
Syphilis rash can be subtle, variable in appearance, and may be transient; testing is essential if syphilis is suspected.
Pearly penile papules and Fordyce spots are benign and distinguished from genital warts by their soft texture and lack of hardness.
Asymptomatic HSV transmission can occur when lesions are present but painless; daily suppressive therapy reduces recurrence and transmission risk.

episodes.title: Dr. Jon Calvert on Pelvic Pain Cases
episodes.speaker: Jon Calvert
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jon Calvert presents a framework for evaluating pelvic pain by asking about location, quality, frequency, duration, aggravating/relieving factors, radiation, and change over time. He then walks through seven cases to illustrate key diagnoses: endometriosis, adenomyosis, interstitial cystitis, abdominal wall hematoma, Bartholin gland cyst, mittelschmerz, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Emphasis is placed on distinguishing cyclic from random pain to narrow the differential, and on using history and physical exam findings—such as cervical displacement and uterine mobility—to guide management.
key_points: Cyclic pain is physiologic (e.g., dysmenorrhea, ovulation); random pain suggests pathology (e.g., scar tissue, infection).
Endometriosis presents with two phases: cyclic dysmenorrhea from endometrial implants and random pain from scar tissue formation.
Adenomyosis causes worsening dysmenorrhea and increased menstrual flow due to endometrial pockets within the myometrium.
Interstitial cystitis presents with chronic dysuria and suprapubic pain that worsens with bladder filling and improves with emptying; urine cultures are typically negative.
Bartholin gland cysts: initial management with Word catheter; recurrence requires marsupialization; consider malignancy in noninfectious cysts.
Mittelschmerz (ovulation pain) is cyclic, unilateral, and may alternate sides; treatment with combination oral contraceptives to suppress ovulation.
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) can involve any part of the upper genital tract (cervix, endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries); uterine tenderness is a key exam finding.
Cervical displacement on bimanual exam suggests either scar tissue pulling the uterus (ipsilateral) or a mass pushing it (contralateral).
Chronic pelvic pain is defined as pain lasting more than three months.
Combination oral contraceptives are preferred for endometriosis and mittelschmerz because they suppress ovulation and provide a steady hormonal state.
Chronic endometritis is an infection of the endometrium that can persist for months to years and should be considered in patients with pelvic pain after gynecologic procedures.
The classic presentation includes dysmenorrhea and heavy menstrual bleeding beginning immediately after the inciting event (e.g., laparoscopic surgery with uterine manipulation).

episodes.title: Dr. Jordan Dever on Pregnancy and Respiratory Diseases
episodes.speaker: Jordan Dever
episodes.abstract: Dr. Jordan Dever reviews normal physiological lung changes in pregnancy, asthma management during pregnancy, flash pulmonary edema, and pulmonary embolism. Key points include that asthma treatment should not be withheld in pregnancy, exacerbations peak between 24-36 weeks, and pulmonary edema management prioritizes diuresis over magnesium. The lecture emphasizes that pregnant patients often receive suboptimal acute care due to provider hesitation.
key_points: Pregnancy causes a compensated respiratory alkalosis with increased minute ventilation, decreased PaCO2, and decreased functional residual capacity.
FEV1 and FVC do not change significantly during pregnancy, making spirometry reliable for asthma diagnosis.
Uncontrolled asthma in pregnancy increases risks of preterm birth, low birth weight, congenital malformations, and NICU admission.
Asthma exacerbations in pregnancy are most common between 24 and 36 weeks gestation.
Acute asthma exacerbation treatment in pregnancy is identical to non-pregnant patients: oxygen, albuterol, ipratropium, systemic steroids, and magnesium if needed.
Pregnant women are less likely to receive appropriate corticosteroids for asthma exacerbations in the ED and on discharge.
Flash pulmonary edema in pregnancy can be caused by preeclampsia, fluid overload, peripartum cardiomyopathy, or sepsis.
In pulmonary edema with hypertension, furosemide is first-line; magnesium should be avoided initially due to fluid volume.
Labetalol is contraindicated if peripartum cardiomyopathy is suspected because it is a negative inotrope.
In septic shock with pulmonary edema, norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor; aggressive fluid boluses should be avoided.
Nitroglycerin infusion is a safe antihypertensive in pulmonary edema as it does not affect cardiac contractility.
VTE risk is 5-fold increased in pregnancy and 60-fold in the first 3 months postpartum.

episodes.title: Dr. Kaleigh Winters on PNG & Tuberculosis 2/29/26
episodes.speaker: Kaleigh Winters
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kaleigh Winters shares her experience as a Global Health fellow in Papua New Guinea, describing a typical post-call day marked by multiple deaths, births, and complex cases. She then presents a CDC-based tuberculosis review covering transmission, latent vs. active disease, risk factors (including diabetes and HIV), diagnostic tests (IGRA, TST, AFB smear, NAAT/GeneXpert, culture), and specimen collection. Key teaching points include the 10% lifetime risk of reactivation, the importance of clinical judgment over test results, and the limited utility of lung exam in pulmonary TB.
key_points: TB is transmitted via airborne droplet nuclei (1–5 microns) that reach alveoli and enter lymph/blood; immune response takes 2–8 weeks.
Latent TB has a 5% risk of reactivation in the first 2 years and another 5% over the rest of life (10% total); HIV increases risk to 7–10% per year.
Diabetes confers a 30% lifetime risk of reactivation, a frequently underappreciated association.
Extrapulmonary TB can occur in any organ and is more common in immunosuppressed patients; miliary TB is a life-threatening disseminated form.
Chest X-ray may show severe disease despite a normal lung exam; physical exam is not sensitive for pulmonary TB.
IGRA (QuantiFERON) is more sensitive and specific than TST (PPD) and is not affected by prior BCG vaccination.
NAAT (e.g., GeneXpert) provides rapid diagnosis and rifampin resistance testing in ~2 hours but requires sufficient bacterial load and may remain positive after treatment.
Culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis and drug susceptibility testing, but takes weeks; negative culture does not rule out disease.
Sputum cultures should be obtained monthly until two are negative to document treatment response and conversion to non-infectious status.
In resource-limited settings, clinical judgment often supersedes test results; cultures may be unavailable or unreliable.

Drug resistance definitions: mono (one drug), poly (≥2), multi-drug (isoniazid + rifampin), extensively drug-resistant (all classes). Penicillin-resistant TB can arise from person-to-person transmission or poor adherence.
Latent TB treatment in pregnancy can be delayed unless patient is HIV-positive; then treatment during pregnancy is recommended with isoniazid and vitamin B6.

episodes.title: Dr. Keller -GERD
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the spectrum of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), from physiologic to pathologic reflux, and emphasizes the importance of distinguishing typical symptoms like heartburn and regurgitation from alarm features such as dysphagia, weight loss, and iron deficiency anemia. The speaker reviews diagnostic classifications including erosive esophagitis (LA grades A-D), NERD, and functional heartburn, along with modalities like endoscopy, Bravo pH monitoring, and impedance testing. Practical management strategies include lifestyle modifications, proper PPI timing (30-60 minutes before first meal), and step-down therapy. The talk highlights that incomplete response to empiric PPI warrants endoscopic evaluation, and that refractory cases often involve improper dosing, functional heartburn, or visceral hypersensitivity.
key_points: GERD is defined as pathologic reflux causing troublesome symptoms or complications such as erosion, stricture, or Barrett's esophagus.
Typical GERD symptoms are heartburn (pyrosis) and acid regurgitation; dysphagia, especially solid food dysphagia, is an alarm symptom prompting urgent endoscopy.
Liquid dysphagia suggests esophageal dysmotility (achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm) rather than mechanical obstruction.
Pill dysphagia is common (up to 40% of patients) and, if not associated with solid food dysphagia, is less worrisome for stricture.
Extra-esophageal manifestations of GERD include chest pain, water brash, globus sensation, nausea, cough, and hoarseness.
Erosive esophagitis is graded LA A-D: A (<5 mm, not bridging), B (>5 mm, not bridging), C (bridging, <75% circumference), D (≥75% circumference).
NERD (nonerosive reflux disease) refers to reflux symptoms without endoscopic esophagitis; a subset has esophageal hypersensitivity or functional heartburn.
Empiric PPI trial: 2 months of single daily dose; if symptoms resolve, confirm GERD; if recurrent within 3 months, consider endoscopy.
PPI must be taken 30-60 minutes before the first meal of the day because proton pumps are activated by food and the drug needs to be in the bloodstream at that time.
Refractory GERD (incomplete response to BID PPI) warrants endoscopy; if negative, proceed to 24-hour impedance-pH probe to assess acid and nonacid reflux.

Alarm symptoms triggering urgent endoscopy: unexplained weight loss, dysphagia/odynophagia, iron deficiency anemia, persistent vomiting, GI cancer in first-degree relative, new onset dyspepsia in patients ≥60 years.
Long-term GERD management: use lowest effective PPI dose; step-down to H2 blocker after 2-3 months can be considered, but PPIs lack tachyphylaxis and H2 blockers do not.

episodes.title: Dr. Keller on GERD, Gastritis, and PUD
episodes.speaker: Keller
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers GERD, gastritis, and PUD for family-medicine residents. Dr. Keller emphasizes that GERD becomes disease only when symptoms are troublesome, highlights alarm signs for endoscopy referral, and details treatment options including lifestyle modifications, H2 blockers, and PPIs. Key teaching points include proper PPI timing, tachyphylaxis with H2 blockers, and long-term PPI risks such as hypomagnesemia and fractures. The talk also addresses complications like Barrett's esophagus and strategies for tapering PPIs.
key_points: GERD is defined by troublesome symptoms or mucosal damage; physiologic reflux is asymptomatic and universal.

Alarm signs requiring EGD include unintentional weight loss, progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, early satiety, unexplained vomiting, GI bleeding, and iron deficiency anemia in men or postmenopausal women.
NERD (nonerosive GERD) describes patients with reflux symptoms but no endoscopic findings.
Barrett's esophagus diagnosis requires intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells) on biopsy taken above the gastroesophageal junction; progression to adenocarcinoma is about 0.5% per year.
PPIs should be taken 30–60 minutes before breakfast for optimal efficacy; missing this timing reduces effectiveness by about 50%.
H2 blockers work faster than PPIs (within 1 hour) but develop tachyphylaxis after 3–4 weeks of twice-daily dosing, losing 50% of acid reduction.
Long-term PPI use increases risks of C. diff colitis, hypomagnesemia, fractures (especially in petite women), and possible chronic kidney disease.
Failed PPI trial is defined as daily standard-dose PPI for two months; consider impedance pH testing for nonacid or bile reflux if symptoms persist.
Patients who do not respond at all to PPIs are unlikely to benefit from surgical fundoplication.
Tapering PPIs requires managing rebound acid hypersecretion; one strategy is alternating H2 blockers with PPIs weekly.
Calcium citrate is preferred over calcium carbonate for patients on PPIs due to reduced absorption in higher gastric pH.
Patients with LA grade C or D esophagitis should have follow-up EGD at 8–12 weeks to rule out hidden Barrett's or cancer.

episodes.title: Dr. Keller on Infant Gastroesophageal 4/16/26
episodes.speaker: Keller
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers infant gastroesophageal reflux (GER) versus gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), emphasizing that most infants are 'happy spitters' whose symptoms peak at 3 months and resolve by 1 year. Dr. Keller reviews red flags requiring further evaluation (bilious vomiting, forceful vomiting, blood, poor weight gain, aspiration), conservative management (smaller frequent feedings, upright positioning, nipple flow adjustments, thickened feeds with oat cereal), and formula selection including hypoallergenic options for cow's milk protein allergy. The talk also addresses differential diagnoses such as pyloric stenosis, Sandifer syndrome, and mimics of blood in the diaper (urate crystals), as well as two related allergic conditions: IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy and non-IgE-mediated food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome.
key_points: About 80% of infants are 'happy spitters'; physiologic reflux peaks at 3 months and resolves by 1 year of age.
Bilious vomiting indicates small bowel obstruction until proven otherwise, requiring immediate evaluation.
Poor weight gain is the most common presentation of GERD in the clinic; feeding logs help assess caloric adequacy and food insecurity.
Thicken feeds with dry infant oat cereal (not rice cereal) at 1 tablespoon per ounce; do not use thickeners in breast milk because amylase digests them.
Positional therapy is limited: upright 20-30 minutes after feeds helps, but crib wedges and head propping are not recommended due to SIDS risk.
40% of infants with GERD have cow's milk protein allergy; trial of hypoallergenic formula (extensively hydrolyzed or amino acid-based) is indicated when reflux is excessive.
Watch for Sandifer syndrome: arching, neck extension, and chin lifting during or after feeds, signaling esophageal pain from reflux.
Urate crystals in the diaper (gritty, brick-red, not shiny) mimic blood in the first 1-3 days of life and are normal.
Bright red blood per rectum ± streaks in stool may indicate anal fissure, proctocolitis, or cow's milk protein allergy; perform a spread-sheet exam.
Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES) is non-IgE mediated, presents with vomiting and diarrhea hours after milk/soy/rice/oats, and is distinct from typical IgE-mediated allergy.
Most infants are 'happy spitters' who do not lose weight and require only parental reassurance.
Conservative measures (e.g., upright positioning, avoiding overfeeding) and a trial of hypoallergenic formula (or maternal dairy elimination if breastfeeding) should precede pharmacotherapy.

episodes.title: Dr. Kelly Dunn on IHI FM Board Review (9/11/25)
episodes.speaker: Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn reviews psychiatric board topics including bipolar disorder, PTSD nightmares, methadone complications, anorexia nervosa, speech delays, smoking cessation, and insomnia management. She emphasizes screening for mania before starting antidepressants and provides guidance on medication selection based on FDA indications and evidence-based algorithms. The talk also introduces the Spark hotline for provider-to-provider psychiatric consultation in Oklahoma. Key clinical pearls include the diagnostic criteria for bipolar I, contraindication of SSRI monotherapy in hypomanic patients, and first-line treatment for sleep-maintenance insomnia.
key_points: Bipolar I disorder requires only a single manic episode lasting ≥7 days or requiring hospitalization; depressive episodes are not necessary.
