SSRI or SNRI monotherapy is contraindicated in hypomanic or manic patients; stabilize mood before adding antidepressants.
Prazosin is effective for PTSD-related nightmares and mid-sleep awakening; doses may be titrated upward as tolerated.
Methadone requires baseline and monitoring EKG due to risk of QTc prolongation, especially with other QTc-prolonging drugs.
Family-based therapy is first-line for adolescents with anorexia nervosa, leading to higher remission rates than individual therapies.
Male sex is the strongest risk factor for speech and language delay; bilingual households do not increase risk.
Varenicline (Chantix) is the most effective pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation, especially when combined with nicotine replacement.
Doxepin (Silenor) has FDA indication for insomnia and is preferred over trazodone per American Academy of Sleep Medicine guidelines; benzodiazepines should be avoided for chronic insomnia.
Antipsychotics like quetiapine are not first-line for insomnia due to metabolic side effects without another indication.
The Spark hotline provides free peer-to-peer psychiatric consultation for Oklahoma healthcare providers.
Benzodiazepine overdose alone rarely causes respiratory depression; danger increases with polypharmacy.
SSRI is first-line treatment for panic disorder; benzodiazepines are not recommended as first-line due to risk of dependence and lack of acute efficacy.

episodes.title: Dr. Kelly Dunn on IHI FM Board Review 6/11/26
episodes.speaker: Kelly Dunn
key_points: Benzodiazepine deprescribing should be done slowly over months to a year; patients may experience temporary withdrawal and rebound anxiety but long-term benefits include reduced anxiety and improved family dynamics.
Serotonin syndrome is a life-threatening condition caused by overactivation of serotonin receptors, often from serotonergic drug combinations.
Clonus is a pathognomonic sign of serotonin syndrome, differentiating it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome which presents with rigidity.

Common serotonergic drugs include SSRIs, SNRIs, trazodone, mirtazapine, buspirone, ondansetron, opioids, buprenorphine, dextromethorphan, triptans, St. John's wort, and illicit drugs like MDMA, methamphetamine, and cocaine.
A single serotonergic agent can cause serotonin syndrome, though it is more common with polypharmacy.
Avoid prescribing two SSRIs or SNRIs simultaneously; this is a medicolegal risk.
Use promethazine instead of ondansetron when possible to reduce serotonergic load in patients on multiple serotonergic drugs.
Do not start multiple new medications in a single visit; layer them one at a time to monitor for adverse effects.
Informed consent and counseling about serotonin syndrome risk are important when prescribing serotonergic drugs.
For psychiatric conditions in adolescents, behavioral interventions should be attempted before medication.

episodes.title: Dr. Kelly Dunn on Sleep Disorders
episodes.speaker: Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Kelly Dunn covers the importance of sleep for physical, mental, and emotional health, the architecture of sleep (non-REM and REM), and the role of circadian rhythm. She discusses common sleep disorders such as insomnia, sleep apnea, narcolepsy, and restless leg syndrome, emphasizing a comprehensive evaluation using screening tools like the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, STOP-BANG, and insomnia severity index. The gold standard first-line treatment for insomnia is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT-I), which is more effective and safer than medications. Pharmacological options like doxepin and benzodiazepines are reserved for short-term use due to tolerance and dependence risks. The lecture also highlights how poor sleep can mimic attention problems and exacerbate psychiatric conditions like bipolar disorder.
key_points: Sleep is essential for cognitive function, immune health, memory consolidation, and physical restoration.
Non-REM sleep includes light (N1), deeper (N2) with memory consolidation, and deep (N3) for physical repair; REM sleep is critical for emotional processing and dreaming.
Circadian rhythm and homeostatic sleep drive regulate the sleep-wake cycle; disruptions can trigger mood episodes in bipolar disorder.
Comprehensive sleep evaluation includes sleep history, medical/psychiatric review, medication assessment, lifestyle factors, and screening tools.
Insomnia disorder requires difficulty initiating/maintaining sleep despite adequate opportunity, with daytime impairment, at least 3 nights/week for 3 months.
CBT-I is the first-line gold-standard treatment for insomnia, addressing thoughts, behaviors, and sleep anxiety.
Pharmacologic treatment (e.g., doxepin, benzodiazepines) should only be used short-term (4–5 weeks) due to tolerance, dependence, and cognitive side effects.
Choose benzodiazepines based on half-life: short-acting for trouble falling asleep, longer-acting for trouble staying asleep.
Sleep problems are a common cause of attention complaints; evaluate sleep before prescribing stimulants.
Social rhythm therapy, which stabilizes circadian rhythms, is an effective psychosocial treatment for bipolar disorder.
Screening for obstructive sleep apnea with the STOP-BANG questionnaire (snoring, tiredness, observed apneas, blood pressure, BMI, age, neck circumference, gender) is recommended.
Z-hypnotics (zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone) are benzodiazepine receptor agonists; zolpidem carries higher risk of sleepwalking and should be avoided.

episodes.title: Dr. Kim on Urban Missions
episodes.speaker: Kim
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kim shares the story of her Christian community health center in Staten Island, New York, highlighting its evolution from a warehouse to a federally qualified health center serving a diverse, underserved population. She describes the center's whole-person care model, including spiritual and behavioral health services, and details their recent work providing medical care to migrant families housed in local hotels. The talk emphasizes the importance of pausing to reflect on one's calling and the opportunities for cross-cultural service within the United States.
key_points: The health center in Staten Island serves 5,000-6,000 patients annually, with a mission to honor God by caring for physical, mental, and spiritual health.
Staten Island is known as the 'forgotten borough,' and the clinic serves the northwestern part, addressing a community that often feels neglected by city resources.
The clinic has expanded from primary care to include behavioral health, dental services, and psychiatric support, reflecting a whole-person approach.
The patient population is highly diverse, including Nigerian, Pakistani, Yemeni, Sri Lankan, and Liberian communities, with staff speaking eight languages.
The clinic intentionally serves people across the socioeconomic spectrum, from union workers and first responders to homeless individuals and migrants.
Since 2022, the clinic has provided care to migrants housed in two local hotels, seeing about 400 people in 80-90 rooms, mostly families from Venezuela and Colombia.
The migrant shelter work began with a request to triage sick children and evolved into a twice-weekly clinic using a massage table as an exam table.
The clinic respects the shelter's church-state boundaries but finds ways to build trust and provide compassionate care, often spending an hour per family.
Common health issues among migrants include respiratory infections, parasite concerns, blood pressure and sugar problems, and mental health issues.
The speaker encourages residents to consider their ten-year vision and highlights that cross-cultural mission opportunities exist within the US, such as in New York.
Shelter expiration dates of 30 days for singles and 60 days for families disrupt housing stability and continuity of care, especially for children in school.
Routine HIV screening in migrant populations can detect undiagnosed cases, including concurrent pregnancy, enabling early linkage to care.

episodes.title: Dr. Kirkpatrick on Bariatric Seminar Presentation 6/18/26
episodes.speaker: Kirkpatrick
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kirkpatrick, medical director of the bariatric program at St. John's, reviews surgical and endoscopic weight-loss options for primary care providers. He covers indications (BMI ≥35 with comorbidity or ≥40 alone, and BMI ≥30 with severe uncontrolled diabetes), compares the three main surgeries—vertical sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, and SADI (modified duodenal switch)—and highlights their hormonal effects, risks, and expected weight loss. He also introduces the newer endoscopic sleeve gastrectomy for lower-BMI patients and emphasizes key postoperative requirements such as smoking cessation, NSAID avoidance, and protein goals.
key_points: Bariatric surgery candidacy: BMI ≥35 with comorbidity, BMI ≥40 alone, or BMI ≥30 with severe uncontrolled diabetes.
Endoscopic sleeve gastrectomy is an incisionless option for BMI 30–40.
Vertical sleeve gastrectomy is restrictive and metabolic; it reduces ghrelin and has modest GLP-1 effect.
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass provides greater GLP-1 effect and better long-term weight loss and diabetes control than sleeve.
SADI (single anastomosis duodenal ileal bypass) combines sleeve restriction with greater malabsorption; reserved for BMI >50 with diabetes.
All surgeries are performed robotically with low complication rates (<2% for bleeding, infection, clots).
Smoking and NSAID use are contraindicated after gastric bypass due to ulcer risk at the anastomosis.
Postoperative protein goal is 70 g/day initially, increasing to 90 g/day for SADI patients.
Patients typically stay one night and return to work in two weeks.
Bariatric-specific multivitamins (or Centrum Silver) are required lifelong after bypass or SADI.
Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a safer, outpatient procedure for patients who cannot undergo surgery due to scar tissue or fear, but it lacks the incretin effect seen with surgical bypass.
Weight loss expectations: ESG 13-15%, sleeve gastrectomy ~20%, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass ~25-30% of total body weight.

episodes.title: Dr. Landreth on Bites and Stings in the Pediatric ER 11/20/25
episodes.speaker: Landreth
episodes.abstract: Dr. Landreth, a pediatric emergency medicine physician, presents a lecture on bites and stings in the pediatric ER, focusing on common and high-risk presentations in Oklahoma. She covers dog bites in detail, including wound management, antibiotic prophylaxis, tetanus and rabies considerations, and the importance of irrigation and primary closure for facial lacerations. The talk also addresses snake bites from local pit vipers (copperhead, rattlesnake, cottonmouth), emphasizing assessment of envenomation, serial monitoring of swelling, lab evaluation for coagulopathy, and indications for antivenom. Practical pearls include avoiding glue on dog bites, using LET for anesthesia, and calling poison control early for snake bites.
key_points: Dog bites in children most commonly involve the face/head; adults more often have extremity bites.
Irrigate dog bite wounds with at least 1000 mL saline; do not use glue for closure due to infection risk.
Facial dog bite lacerations should be repaired by primary closure; puncture wounds should not be repaired.
Antibiotic prophylaxis (amoxicillin-clavulanate for 3-5 days) is indicated for high-risk wounds: hands, puncture wounds, extensive wounds, immunocompromised patients.
Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis is not indicated for domestic dog bites if the dog can be monitored for 10 days; bat exposures and wild carnivore bites require prophylaxis.
Cat bites have a very high infection risk; treat with amoxicillin-clavulanate and ensure follow-up.
For snake bites, remove constricting items, do not use tourniquets or ice, and assess induration by palpating lateral borders of the extremity.
Mark the leading edge of swelling with a time-stamped line and recheck hourly to track progression.
Indications for pit viper antivenom include progressive local tissue injury, systemic toxicity, or significant coagulopathy.
Copperhead bites often cause less severe coagulopathy than rattlesnake or cottonmouth bites; minor envenomations may be observed without antivenom.
Brown recluse bites are most common in Oklahoma, peaking late spring to early fall, with highest risk of severe envenomation in children.
The classic brown recluse wound shows central pallor (ischemia) with surrounding erythema (red, white, and blue appearance) due to microvascular thrombosis.

episodes.title: Dr. Lawrence Lee on Morning Reports
episodes.speaker: Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: A 34-year-old woman with dermatomyositis and calcinosis cutis presents with purulent drainage from her thighs, initially diagnosed as cellulitis. Her white count is markedly elevated at 51.2, and she is tachycardic but not septic. The case sparks debate about whether to restart steroids after she was tapered off, balancing the risk of adrenal suppression against worsened immunosuppression during infection. Cultures eventually grow Staphylococcus aureus and Corynebacterium jeikeium, and rheumatology recommends restarting prednisone 10 mg.
key_points: Dermatomyositis is a rare autoimmune disease causing inflammation of skin and muscles, often associated with interstitial lung disease.
Calcinosis cutis involves calcium deposition in the skin; dystrophic calcinosis occurs with normal calcium and phosphate levels, often in autoimmune diseases like dermatomyositis.
Metastatic calcinosis is due to abnormal calcium or phosphate metabolism, typically from hyperparathyroidism or renal failure.
In patients chronically on steroids, adrenal suppression can persist up to a year after cessation, warranting stress-dose steroids during illness.
Immunosuppressed patients with cellulitis may require broader empiric antibiotics like vancomycin and Zosyn.
A normal white count and absence of fever in a patient with purulent drainage can be signs of adrenal insufficiency due to steroid withdrawal.
Pain management in complex patients may involve escalating from oral to IV opioids, but attention to pain-seeking behavior is important.
Cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus and Corynebacterium jeikeium, an unusual organism that may indicate polymicrobial infection or contamination.
Rheumatology consultation is crucial for managing dermatomyositis flares and deciding on immunosuppression during infections.
The case illustrates the tension between treating infection and managing underlying autoimmune disease with steroids.
When committing to a diagnosis and treatment plan, act with conviction rather than half-measures (e.g., treat a COPD exacerbation with both albuterol and steroids).
A patient who is eating, mobilizing, and functioning well despite reported severe pain may have pain that is not as severe as claimed.

episodes.title: Dr. Lawrence Lee on Morning Reports
episodes.speaker: Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: A 34-year-old female with dermatomyositis and calcinosis cutis presents with recurrent cellulitis and purulent drainage. The case highlights challenges in managing infections in immunosuppressed patients, including atypical presentation and antibiotic resistance. A debate on steroid use reveals the risk of adrenal suppression even after tapering. The teaching emphasizes the importance of recognizing calcinosis cutis types and considering endocrine complications of steroid therapy.
key_points: Dermatomyositis is a rare autoimmune disease causing proximal muscle weakness and a characteristic rash, including violaceous papules over joints.
Diagnosis is confirmed by muscle and skin biopsy, along with serology such as anti-synthetase antibodies and EMG.
Calcinosis cutis has distinct subtypes: dystrophic (normal calcium/phosphate) and metastatic (abnormal calcium/phosphate, often with hyperparathyroidism or renal disease).
In immunosuppressed patients, cellulitis and other infections may present without typical signs like fever or leukocytosis.
Steroid-induced adrenal suppression can persist for up to a year after discontinuation, necessitating stress-dose coverage during illness.
Prior antibiotic exposure increases the risk of resistant organisms; obtaining cultures before broad-spectrum antibiotics is critical.
Pain management in hospitalized patients requires strict adherence to medication orders: oral opioids before IV analgesics per protocol.
Multidisciplinary input from rheumatology and infectious disease is essential for managing complex autoimmune patients with superimposed infections.
First-line therapy for dermatomyositis includes corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents such as methotrexate or azathioprine.
Commit to a specific diagnosis and treatment plan; avoid half-measures like calling a COPD exacerbation but withholding steroids.
Functional status (eating, mobilizing) is a more reliable indicator than pain scores in patients with chronic pain.
A sudden change in pain pattern with new autonomic symptoms (headache, hypertension, bradycardia) should raise concern for aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, or spinal abscess.

episodes.title: Dr. Lawrence Lee on Morning Reports 2/9/26
episodes.speaker: Lawrence Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lawrence Lee presents a case of an 86-year-old nursing home resident with a right foot infection and known osteomyelitis, highlighting the importance of a thorough skin exam and the diagnostic gold standard of bone biopsy. The lecture reviews osteomyelitis classification (hematogenous vs. nonhematogenous), common pathogens, and empiric antibiotic choices, emphasizing the need to hold antibiotics before biopsy when possible. Key teaching points include the significance of ESR >100 in osteomyelitis, the role of sequestra and sinus tracts, and practical workflow tips for examining wounds in immobile patients.
key_points: Osteomyelitis is classified as hematogenous (blood-borne seeding) or nonhematogenous (direct inoculation from trauma, puncture, surgery, or diabetic ulcers).
The most common cause of nonhematogenous osteomyelitis is contiguous spread from a diabetic foot ulcer.
Bone biopsy is the definitive diagnostic test for osteomyelitis; MRI can infer but not confirm the diagnosis.
ESR >100 is highly suggestive of osteomyelitis or malignancy.
Empiric antibiotics for osteomyelitis should cover MRSA (vancomycin) and gram-negative rods (third-generation cephalosporin).
For MSSA, IV cefazolin is a highly effective and commonly stocked alternative to nafcillin.
Antibiotics should ideally be held until after bone biopsy to optimize culture yield; a 2-week antibiotic-free window is suggested by studies.
A sequestrum is a fragment of dead bone separated from healthy bone that cannot be penetrated by IV antibiotics.
A sinus tract is a soft tissue channel from infected bone to the skin surface, often draining pus.
Always examine every wound and under every dressing on admission; failure to do so can lead to missed tunneling, sepsis, and medicolegal liability.
When a nurse reports abnormal vital signs, first obtain a fresh set of vitals, a stat EKG, and assess the patient.
The differential diagnosis should guide clinical actions, not the other way around.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter describes a practical approach to tapering patients off benzodiazepines using the Ashton Manual. He emphasizes transitioning patients to diazepam due to its longer half-life and less potent dosing, which allows for smaller, more manageable cuts. The process involves gradual substitution of the original benzo with diazepam over weeks, followed by a slow taper of diazepam itself. Close monitoring via patient portal and individualized pace adjustments are critical, and the speaker notes that not all patients need to discontinue benzodiazepines if the benefits outweigh risks.
key_points: Transition patients to diazepam because it is less potent and allows smaller dose cuts.
Replace one dose of the original benzo at a time, typically starting with the evening dose.
Use the Ashton Manual conversion charts as guide rails, not rigid rules.
Monitor patients closely via portal for sedation or withdrawal symptoms and adjust doses accordingly.
Taper every 1–2 weeks, but extend to 4 weeks if the patient needs psychological preparation.
At lower total daily doses, the same milligram cut represents a larger percentage reduction.
Microtapering with compounded liquid benzos (e.g., 0.1 mg cuts daily) is an option for sensitive patients.
Assess each patient individually; some are physically dependent while others struggle psychologically.
If a patient refuses to taper, provide a one-month supply and clearly document that future refills will not be given.
Benzodiazepines have a legitimate place; not every patient needs to be tapered off.
Patients on benzodiazepines often lack concurrent antidepressant therapy and counseling.
Initiate an SSRI or SNRI as a controller medication to facilitate tapering.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: This case-based lecture reviews cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for evaluating patients with dyspnea, hypotension, and shock. Dr. Ledbetter uses interactive audience response to teach focused ultrasound views, including lung ultrasound, IVC assessment, and cardiac views for left ventricular function, right heart strain, and pericardial effusion. Key teaching points include using E-point septal separation to estimate ejection fraction, recognizing bilateral B-lines for pulmonary edema, and identifying the D-sign for acute right heart strain. The session emphasizes integrating ultrasound findings with clinical context to guide management decisions.
key_points: E-point septal separation >8 mm predicts LVEF ≤40%.
Bilateral B-lines in multiple zones are highly specific for pulmonary edema.
The short-axis view at the papillary muscle level is best for assessing LV contractility.
A dilated RV with septal flattening (D-sign) indicates acute right heart strain, as in PE.
A plethoric IVC (non-collapsing) suggests elevated right atrial pressure.
In DVT ultrasound, failure to compress the vein despite arterial compression indicates thrombus.
The subxiphoid view is essential for detecting pericardial effusion and tamponade.
Sepsis can cause myocardial dysfunction with LV dilation and poor contractility.
Hyperdynamic LV with small cavity suggests hypovolemia; fluids are preferred over pressors.
Lung ultrasound is more sensitive than chest X-ray for pleural effusion and pneumonia.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter teaches cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) focusing on the parasternal long-axis and short-axis views to estimate left ventricular ejection fraction. He emphasizes three bedside methods: E-point septal separation, wall thickening (≥50% increase in myocardial thickness), and LV cavity size reduction (≥30% decrease in chamber area). He notes that wall thickening and cavity reduction are more reliable than E-point septal separation. Practical tips include probe positioning toward the patient's right shoulder for long axis, rotating 90° clockwise for short axis, patient rotation to bring the heart closer, and hand stabilization techniques.
key_points: Parasternal long-axis view: probe marker toward patient's right shoulder, start at left sternal border, window shop with sliding, then rotate/fan/rock to center.
Parasternal short-axis view: from long axis, rotate probe 90° clockwise toward left shoulder; fan up to base (aortic valve) or down to papillary muscle level.
E-point septal separation: anterior mitral leaflet should come within 1 cm of the septum; if >1 cm, suggests reduced EF.
Wall thickening: myocardial thickness should increase by at least 50% (almost double) from diastole to systole.
LV cavity reduction: the left ventricular chamber should shrink by at least 30% in area during systole.
Wall thickening and cavity reduction are considered more accurate than E-point septal separation for estimating EF.
Patient positioning: rotate the patient's left shoulder outward to bring the heart closer to the chest wall.
Hand stabilization: anchor with knee or pinky on the patient's body to minimize probe movement.
Fanning the probe changes the level: up toward base, down toward apex to see papillary muscles.
Goal is qualitative assessment (normal, reduced, severely reduced), not a precise EF number.
In the parasternal long axis view, assess three features: myocardial thickening, change in LV area, and mitral valve E-point septal separation.
Normal LV area change between systole and diastole is at least 30%; less suggests reduced function.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Hypertension
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Ledbetter covers the fundamentals of musculoskeletal ultrasound of the knee, including tissue appearance (muscle, tendon, bone) and the critical concept of anisotropy. The speaker demonstrates a systematic scanning protocol starting suprapatellar to evaluate the quadriceps and patellar tendons, menisci, and collateral ligaments. Clinical applications focus on detecting knee effusions and performing ultrasound-guided joint injections, emphasizing that ultrasound improves accuracy and patient satisfaction compared to blind techniques.
key_points: Muscle appears feathery in long axis and starry in short axis; tendon shows parallel hyperechoic lines in long axis and dots in short axis.
Anisotropy means tissue brightness changes with probe angle; always keep the probe perpendicular to tendon and nerve to avoid false-positive tears.
Start knee ultrasound suprapatellar in long axis to identify quadriceps tendon, patella, fat pads, and femur; then rotate to transverse view.
Joint effusion is seen as an anechoic space above the suprapatellar fat pad; the space is nearly absent when no fluid is present.
Follow the patellar tendon from patella to tibia in long and short axis; avoid injecting through the tendon as it is painful.
The medial meniscus anterior horn appears as a triangle; ultrasound can rule in a tear but cannot rule one out.
The MCL is seen as hyperechoic parallel lines; dynamic varus/valgus stress can reveal gapping compared to the contralateral side.
Ultrasound is superior to physical exam for detecting knee effusion; a focused scan takes only seconds.
For ultrasound-guided knee injection, use a lateral suprapatellar approach; visualize the needle entering the joint space under the probe.
When anatomy is difficult to palpate, use ultrasound to mark an injection site off the patellar tendon medially or laterally.
Mark the injection site by crossing two lines drawn from the center of the ultrasound probe positions.
Use the opposite end of the Betadine stick to mark the skin to maintain sterility.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers diagnosis and treatment of pneumonia in adults and children, with emphasis on point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS). For adults, typical lobar pneumonia is treated with amoxicillin 1000 mg three times daily, atypical with azithromycin 1500 mg total, and outpatient duration is three to five days, no more than seven. For children, IDSA still recommends amoxicillin, typically five to ten days. The lecture details lung ultrasound technique including probe selection, patient positioning, scanning zones, and key findings: A-lines, lung sliding, thickened pleural line, B-lines, hepatization, air bronchograms, and dynamic air bronchogram as pathognomonic for pneumonia.
key_points: For pediatric pneumonia suspicion, age less than three months is high risk; three to six months requires strong clinical justification to avoid ER referral.
In adults, typical lobar pneumonia is treated with amoxicillin 1000 mg three times daily (two 500 mg capsules) for three to five days.
Atypical pneumonia in adults is treated with azithromycin 1500 mg total (e.g., 500 mg for three days or 500 mg day one then 250 mg days two to five).
Outpatient pneumonia duration should be three to five days, no more than seven days; shorter courses are appropriate if rapid improvement occurs.
Lung ultrasound is superior to chest X-ray for diagnosing pneumonia in both children and adults, even by novice operators.
Use the lung preset on Butterfly for upper lung zones; switch to abdominal preset for the bases to avoid artifact.
Always orient the probe marker to the patient's head during lung ultrasound to maintain standard landmarks.
Normal lung ultrasound shows a thin, crisp pleural line, A-lines, and lung sliding; absence of these suggests pathology.
Pneumonia findings on ultrasound include thickened or irregular pleural line, B-lines, hepatization (tissue-like consolidation), and air bronchograms; a dynamic air bronchogram is pathognomonic.
If no pneumonia is found in the anterior zones, scan the posterior zones (zones 5 and 6) to complete the evaluation.
B-lines are ring-down artifacts that originate at the pleural line and extend to the edge of the screen; depth must be set to 12–15 cm to distinguish them from normal Z-lines.

Three or more B-lines in a single zone is considered pathologic, but B-lines are not specific for pneumonia—they can be seen in pulmonary edema, interstitial lung disease, ARDS, atelectasis, infarction, contusion, or mass.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter discusses the use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for diagnosing and managing abscesses, emphasizing that ultrasound reduces the failure rate of incision from 17% (physical exam alone) to 3.7%. The lecture covers probe selection (linear probe for superficial abscesses), scanning technique (two planes, entire area), and key sonographic findings including cobblestoning (fluid in subcutaneous tissue, seen in both cellulitis and edema) and abscess characteristics (anechoic or heterogeneous, with possible septations). It also highlights the importance of Doppler to distinguish abscess from vessels or lymph nodes, and demonstrates utility for foreign body detection and marking.
key_points: Ultrasound plus physical exam reduces abscess incision failure rate from 17% to 3.7%.
Use a linear probe for superficial abscesses; scan the entire area of concern in two planes.
Cobblestoning indicates fluid in subcutaneous tissue but cannot differentiate cellulitis from edema without clinical context.
Abscesses may be anechoic, hypoechoic, or heterogeneous; septations suggest need for open drainage rather than needle aspiration.
Doppler is essential to confirm an abscess is not a blood vessel and to identify nearby vessels before incision.
Lymph nodes can mimic abscesses; look for a central hilum with Doppler flow to avoid cutting into them.
Ultrasound effectively detects foreign bodies (splinters, glass, metal) and can guide removal, especially with a water bath technique.
Measure abscess in three dimensions (depth, width, length) by rotating the probe 90 degrees.
Compressibility and movement of fluid ("hustle stalsis") help identify isoechoic abscesses.
Probe safety: keep water level below the gasket; confirm with attending before submerging.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - GI
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter introduces point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the knee, emphasizing the importance of anisotropy in musculoskeletal imaging and how to avoid it by keeping the probe perpendicular to tissues. He demonstrates key views: the suprapatellar recess for fluid detection and injection, the infrapatellar patellar tendon view for static guidance, and the menisci and collateral ligaments. The session includes hands-on scanning practice with guidance on needle placement for injections and arthrocentesis.
key_points: Anisotropy causes tendons and ligaments to appear hypoechoic when the ultrasound beam is not perpendicular; always fan through to avoid mistaking artifact for pathology.
The suprapatellar recess is the preferred site for knee joint injection or arthrocentesis; it lies between the quadriceps tendon, the prefemoral fat pad, and the suprapatellar fat pad.
In a dry knee (no effusion), the suprapatellar recess may not be visible; inject a small amount of fluid to separate the fat pads and confirm needle position.

For dynamic ultrasound-guided injection, start with a long-axis view of the quadriceps tendon, center the probe over the target, then rotate 90° to short axis for needle insertion from the lateral side.
The patellar tendon is a linear hyperechoic structure connecting the patella to the tibial tuberosity; losing the tendon on ultrasound marks a safe needle entry zone for anterior knee injection.

The medial meniscus appears as a triangular hypoechoic (or variable echogenicity) structure between the femur and tibia on the medial joint line; the lateral meniscus is seen similarly on the lateral side.
The MCL is visualized in the same view as the medial meniscus, attaching femur to tibia; the LCL requires a more lateral and inferior view, attaching femur to fibula.
Bone appears as a hyperechoic line with posterior acoustic shadowing; muscle is hypoechoic with striations; nerves have a honeycomb pattern in short axis.
Patient positioning is critical: have the patient sit with leg straight and knee slightly flexed on a pillow for comfort and optimal probe access.
Using ultrasound for knee injections improves patient satisfaction and procedural accuracy; static guidance (marking the skin) is an alternative to dynamic needle tracking.
Use the long-axis view of the patella and quadriceps tendon to establish depth, then apply that knowledge to the short-axis view.
Center the probe over the suprapatellar recess, about 2 cm above the patella, to target the injection site.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter's lecture covers point-of-care lung ultrasound for diagnosing pneumonia, emphasizing its superiority over chest X-ray in sensitivity and radiation avoidance. Key findings include dynamic air bronchograms, focal B-lines (≥3 per zone), lung consolidation (hepatization), shred sign, and pleural effusion with spine sign. The lecture also reviews probe selection (linear probe, lung or abdominal preset in lower zones), scanning zones (four anterior per side plus two posterior), and normal artifacts (lung sliding, A-lines, curtain sign). Clinical context is stressed for accurate diagnosis, including distinguishing multifocal pneumonia from pulmonary edema.
key_points: Use a linear probe with marker toward the head; on Butterfly, use lung preset; for zones 4 and 6, switch to abdominal preset for better image quality.
Four anterior zones per side are split by nipple line (horizontal) and anterior axillary line (vertical); posterior zones 5 and 6 are above/below scapular angle.
Normal lung ultrasound shows lung sliding, A-lines (repetitions of pleural line), and curtain sign at the diaphragm without spine sign above.
Dynamic air bronchograms (moving hyperechoic dots) are super highly specific for pneumonia.
Focal B-lines (≥3 in a single zone) are 96% specific for pneumonia.
Lung consolidation (hepatization) is abnormal tissue visualized; shred sign (irregular interface between consolidated and aerated lung) is highly specific.
Pleural effusion allows spine sign above diaphragm; jellyfish sign indicates consolidated lung floating in effusion.
Thickened pleural line suggests infection; thin, crisp pleural line favors pulmonary edema over pneumonia.
Ultrasound is more sensitive than X-ray for pneumonia and pleural effusion, avoiding radiation exposure.
Bilateral symmetric B-lines with thin pleural line suggest pulmonary edema; asymmetric focal B-lines with subpleural consolidations suggest pneumonia.

episodes.title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid
episodes.speaker: Ledbetter
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the thyroid, including normal anatomy, scanning technique in transverse and sagittal planes, and measurement of lobes and isthmus. It reviews the sonographic features of thyroid nodules—location, size, shape, margins, echogenicity, calcifications, and vascularity—and how to apply TIRADS scoring to determine biopsy versus follow-up. Benign findings such as simple cysts, colloid cysts, spongiform nodules, and halo signs are distinguished from malignant features like microcalcifications, interrupted eggshell calcification, internal vascularity, and infiltrative margins. The importance of consistent measurement for serial follow-up is emphasized.
key_points: Normal thyroid is homogeneous and hyperechoic relative to strap muscles; the isthmus should measure <0.5 cm in transverse plane.
Scan the thyroid first in transverse view (where it looks most like a thyroid) then in sagittal view; use probe marker toward the patient's head for orientation.
Thyroiditis appears heterogeneous with black-and-white specks due to lymphocytic infiltration.

Nodule evaluation includes location, size (three reproducible planes), shape (taller-than-wide is suspicious), margins (halo sign benign, infiltrative malignant), echogenicity, calcifications, and vascularity.
Microcalcifications (<1 mm) are associated with psammoma bodies and papillary carcinoma; interrupted eggshell calcification is more likely malignant.
Internal or central vascularity is more concerning than peripheral or absent flow.
Spongiform nodules (>50% cystic) and simple cysts are benign; colloid cysts with hyperechoic comet-tail artifact are usually benign.
TIRADS scoring combines sonographic features; for TIRADS 3, biopsy if >2.5 cm, follow if <1.5 cm; for moderately suspicious, biopsy if ≥1 cm; for highly suspicious, biopsy if ≥0.5 cm.
Consistent measurement technique (AP and perpendicular planes or greatest dimensions) is critical for reliable follow-up.
Nodules <1 cm without concerning features are typically followed rather than biopsied.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee on Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Lee
episodes.abstract: A 55-year-old woman presented with bilateral arm pain and was found to have severe thrombocytopenia (platelets of 5). The case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential when clinical findings are unexpected, systematically evaluating thrombocytopenia with targeted diagnostic tests, and ensuring that assessment and plan are logically connected. Key teaching points include reopening the differential when something seems 'fishy,' confirming abnormal labs before assuming error, and matching each diagnostic consideration with an appropriate workup.
key_points: Bilateral arm pain has a broad differential including musculoskeletal, vascular, neurological, and rheumatologic causes; always consider serious etiologies.
When a lab value is unexpectedly abnormal, confirm with repeat testing before assuming error.
When the clinical picture is 'fishy' or unexpected, explicitly reopen and verbalize your differential diagnosis.
For thrombocytopenia, systematically consider HIT, ITP, DIC, TTP, splenic sequestration, bone marrow infiltration, medication-induced, and viral causes.
Each differential diagnosis should have a matching diagnostic plan (e.g., peripheral smear for ITP, ADAMTS13 for TTP, ultrasound for splenic sequestration).
The assessment and plan in a note must logically match; avoid non sequiturs.
Always check outside records for medication history when considering drug-induced cytopenias.
Severe pain out of proportion to exam or causing functional limitation (e.g., unable to hold a cup) is a red flag.
Clinical notes should avoid non-sequitur reasoning; each problem should have a clear status and a plan for resolution.
Peripheral smear findings of macrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophils, and severe thrombocytopenia raise concern for malignancy.
Rising LDH indicates cell death or tissue damage, not necessarily hemolysis, especially when haptoglobin is normal and reticulocyte count is low.
Parsonage-Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy) presents with acute, severe neuropathic pain and weakness, often improving with benzodiazepines.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee on Morning Reports
episodes.speaker: Lee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lee presents a complex case of a 63-year-old male with alcohol misuse, thrombocytopenia, and multiple systemic symptoms. The session emphasizes the importance of a structured differential diagnosis for thrombocytopenia, distinguishing between thrombotic and bleeding disorders. A detailed acid-base analysis using Winter's formula reveals a mixed metabolic and respiratory acidosis, highlighting the need for careful interpretation. Imaging findings suggest diffuse lymphadenopathy and possible metastatic disease, pointing toward lymphoma as a key diagnostic consideration.
key_points: Thrombocytopenia requires a broad differential diagnosis including cirrhosis, medication-induced, ITP, DIC, HIT, TTP, malignancy, infection, and bone marrow failure.
Distinguishing thrombotic thrombocytopenias (e.g., HIT, TTP, APS) from bleeding disorders (e.g., ITP) is critical for management.
Winter's formula (expected pCO2 = 1.5 x [HCO3-] + 8 ± 2) is used to determine if respiratory compensation is appropriate in metabolic acidosis.
A normal pCO2 (35-45) can still represent respiratory acidosis if the expected pCO2 is lower, as in this case with a low bicarbonate.
Anion gap calculation (Na - Cl - HCO3-) and delta-delta analysis help characterize mixed acid-base disorders.
CT findings of diffuse lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and suspicious osseous lesions raise concern for lymphoma in this patient.
Chronic liver disease signs on CT include cirrhotic morphology, recanalized umbilical vein, and caput medusae.
The patient's history of alcohol misuse, recent binge drinking, and thrombocytopenia with ecchymoses suggests possible alcoholic hepatitis or cirrhosis-related coagulopathy.
Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow aspiration are key workup steps for suspected malignancy or myelofibrosis.
Infection can cause thrombocytopenia via bone marrow suppression, immune-mediated mechanisms, or HUS/TTP.
For lymphadenopathy, excisional biopsy is preferred over FNA, core needle, or incisional biopsy to obtain diagnostic tissue and avoid repeat procedures.
FNA is a 'misdemeanor' for lymphadenopathy and should not be performed.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee on Morning Reports
episodes.speaker: Lee
episodes.abstract: A 63-year-old male with alcohol misuse presents with thrombocytopenia, ecchymosis, confusion, and bleeding. The discussion emphasizes generating a broad differential for thrombocytopenia, including bone marrow failure, medication-induced, ITP, TTP, HIT, DIC, and others, and distinguishing thrombotic from bleeding disorders. Acid-base analysis using Winters formula reveals a respiratory acidosis superimposed on metabolic acidosis. Imaging shows diffuse lymphadenopathy and osseous lesions suspicious for lymphoma, along with signs of chronic liver disease.
key_points: When encountering thrombocytopenia, always generate a differential diagnosis.
Thrombotic thrombocytopenias include TTP, HIT, DIC (half), APS, and vasculitides.
Use Winters formula (expected pCO2 = 1.5 x [HCO3] + 8 ± 2) to assess respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis.
A normal pCO2 does not rule out respiratory acidosis; calculate expected pCO2.
Calculate anion gap (Na - Cl - HCO3) and delta gap to identify mixed acid-base disorders.
Imaging findings of diffuse lymphadenopathy and osseous lesions are highly suspicious for lymphoma.
Chronic liver disease on CT: recanalized umbilical vein and caput medusae.
Bone marrow suppression can be caused by sepsis, infection, MDS, aplastic anemia, B12/folate deficiency.
Medication-induced thrombocytopenia requires thorough medication review.
ITP workup includes CBC, peripheral smear, and possibly bone marrow biopsy.
For lymphadenopathy suspicious for lymphoma, excisional biopsy is preferred over FNA or core needle biopsy.
FNA is not recommended for lymphadenopathy; it is considered a 'misdemeanor' in this context.

episodes.title: Dr. Lee's Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: A 68-year-old woman presents with the worst headache of her life, a classic red flag for subarachnoid hemorrhage. Despite a negative CT head, the case highlights the need for a broad differential including cerebral venous sinus thrombosis and dissection. The admitting physician's plan is criticized for lacking a differential diagnosis and failing to pursue advanced imaging (MRI/CTA). The lecture reviews migraine pathophysiology, epidemiology, and the importance of a structured approach to headache evaluation.
key_points: Worst headache of life demands immediate CT head and LP for xanthochromia to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage.
A negative CT does not exclude all dangerous causes; consider MRI/CTA for CVST, dissection, or stroke mimics.
Always maintain a differential diagnosis when the etiology of a symptom is not definitive.
Migraine pathophysiology is neurogenic inflammation, not primarily vascular; triptans may still involve vasoconstriction.
Prodrome occurs in 77% of migraineurs (e.g., yawning, constipation), aura in 25% and can mimic stroke.
Solu-Medrol (steroids) for status migrainosus can worsen hyperglycemia, as seen in this case.
Observation status is appropriate for unstable headache patients; discharge requires clear resolution and workup.
Red flags in headache (SUEP criteria) include age >50, sudden onset, progressive, focal deficits, and systemic symptoms.
Patients with new or atypical migraine and risk factors for stroke should undergo MRI to exclude ischemia.
Lisinopril and Fioricet were considered for headache management, but the plan lacked a structured differential.
Migraine subtypes include migraine with brainstem aura, hemiplegic migraine, retinal migraine, vestibular migraine, and chronic migraine.
Abdominal migraine is a pediatric condition presenting with recurrent central abdominal pain, often a prodrome to migraine later in life.

episodes.title: Dr. Leo on Advance Care Planning
episodes.speaker: Leo
episodes.abstract: Dr. Leo's lecture clarifies common terminologies in advance care planning, including advanced directives, living wills, POLST, DNR, comfort measures only, and hospice. The talk emphasizes that advance care planning is an ongoing process, and that a living will does not automatically include DNR orders. It also highlights the differences between a power of attorney and a health care agent, and explains that POLST is a portable medical order for patients with life-altering diagnoses. Practical tips include consulting palliative care for complex cases and understanding that hospice does not require a prior DNR.
key_points: Advance care planning is an ongoing process, not a one-time event.
An advanced directive is a legal document for future care decisions but is not legally binding in emergencies.
A POLST is a physician order for life-sustaining treatment, portable and intended for patients with life-altering diagnoses.
A living will may not include resuscitation orders; always verify its contents.
Comfort measures only (CMO) orders automatically include DNR at St. John.
Hospice care requires a prognosis of six months or less.
Palliative care can be combined with curative treatment.
A durable power of attorney overrides the default health care agent (e.g., spouse).
When a patient lacks capacity, the health care agent follows a state-specific pecking order (spouse, children, parents, siblings).
Observing palliative care consultations can improve a clinician's communication skills.
Initiate advance care planning early; it is a process that can be revisited.
Document the health care proxy in the H&P note per Ascension policy.

episodes.title: Dr. Leo on Epidemiology
episodes.speaker: Leo
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews fundamental epidemiology concepts including relative risk, absolute risk, confidence intervals, p-values, and the clinical application of NNT, NNH, and NNS. It also covers sensitivity and specificity with the mnemonic SnNOut and SpPIn. The second part introduces the 'Choosing Wisely' campaign and presents evidence that administering oxygen in the absence of hypoxemia does not benefit patients with myocardial infarction or dyspnea and can cause harm in COPD.
key_points: Relative risk is a ratio comparing incidence in exposed vs. unexposed groups; a point estimate requires a confidence interval.
A 95% confidence interval means we are 95% confident the true value lies within that range.
P-value is the probability results occurred by chance; it is the inverse of the confidence interval and does not prove causation.
Absolute risk reduction (ARR) and NNT/NNH/NNS are more clinically useful than relative risk because they account for baseline risk.
NNT is the number of patients needed to treat to prevent one adverse outcome; NNH is the number needed to cause one harm.
Sensitivity detects disease; a highly sensitive test rules out disease (SnNOut).
Specificity detects absence of disease; a highly specific test rules in disease (SpPIn).
Oxygen therapy in the absence of hypoxemia does not improve mortality or dyspnea and can increase mortality in COPD patients.
In COPD, titrated oxygen to a target saturation is superior to fixed high-flow oxygen.
Expert opinion (e.g., UpToDate) is Level C evidence and should be interpreted cautiously.
In patients without hypoxemia, liberal O2 supplementation increases in-hospital mortality (RR 1.21) and 30-day mortality (RR 1.14).
Titrating O2 to a target saturation in confirmed COPD reduces mortality from 9% to 4.2% and decreases hypercapnia.

episodes.title: Dr. Liening on Pediatric GI 1/8/26
episodes.speaker: Liening
episodes.abstract: Dr. Liening delivers a high-yield pediatric GI lecture covering neonatal jaundice, infant reflux, pyloric stenosis, and food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES). She emphasizes the critical distinction between conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, the importance of a rising bilirubin rate >0.2 mg/dL/hr, and the necessity of ultrasound for any infant with elevated direct bilirubin. The talk also reviews red flags that distinguish pathologic reflux from pyloric stenosis and highlights the importance of not dismissing parental concerns about worsening vomiting. Finally, she discusses FPIES as a non-IgE-mediated reaction to cow milk or soy protein, presenting with rectal bleeding in infants under one year.
key_points: Conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia always indicates post-hepatic obstruction and requires urgent ultrasound evaluation.
Unconjugated jaundice in newborns is often physiologic due to immature liver enzymes, but a rate of rise >0.2 mg/dL/hr is dangerous and warrants close monitoring.
Peak risk time for pathologic jaundice and kernicterus is the first 24 hours of life; bilirubin >20 mg/dL is the threshold for kernicterus risk.
Simple infant reflux is normal in about 50% of 2-month-olds and typically resolves by 9-12 months; management focuses on feeding technique, positioning, and parental support.

Pyloric stenosis presents with progressive projectile non-bilious vomiting in infants 4-6 weeks old, with weight loss and eagerness to feed after vomiting; abdominal ultrasound is the diagnostic test.
FPIES is a non-IgE-mediated food protein reaction presenting with bloody, mucoid stools in infants <1 year; it is not an allergy and is most often triggered by cow milk or soy protein.
Do not prescribe reflux medications like ranitidine for simple infant reflux; they impair vitamin absorption and are not recommended unless the infant is ill.
Wedge pillows can be safely used under the sheet to elevate the head of the bed for reflux; they are effective and safe for sleep positioning.
Metabolic disorders should be considered in sick neonates with feeding issues; always check the newborn screen.
Parental concern about worsening vomiting should not be dismissed; a missed pyloric stenosis diagnosis can lead to significant morbidity.

episodes.title: Dr. Liening on Shoulder Exam 9/18/25
episodes.speaker: Liening
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews high-yield shoulder examination topics for board preparation, focusing on understanding anatomy and special test names. Through sample board questions, the speaker covers acute vs chronic rotator cuff tears, adhesive capsulitis, cervical radiculopathy, AC joint injury, and biceps tendinopathy. The session includes a video demonstration of efficient exam techniques, emphasizing proper positioning for the empty can test, external rotation test, and the importance of observing the shoulder from behind during range of motion.
key_points: Understanding shoulder anatomy and pathophysiology can answer 50-75% of test questions.
Knowing special test names improves documentation and test performance.
Acute rotator cuff tear in young active patients requires MRI; chronic tears in elderly are managed conservatively with physical therapy.
Adhesive capsulitis presents with global stiffness, no point tenderness, and severe external rotation limitation.
Spurling's test (extension, lateral flexion, rotation with axial compression) indicates cervical radiculopathy.
Cross-body adduction test reproduces AC joint pain.
Empty can test is most specific for supraspinatus pathology.
Speed's and Yergason's tests suggest biceps tendinopathy.
Efficient ROM exam: sequence of forward flexion, abduction, external rotation, internal rotation, cross-body adduction.
Observe shoulder from behind to detect compensatory elevation during ROM.

episodes.title: Dr. Lucashu on Coronary Artery Disease
episodes.speaker: Lucashu
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Lucashu covers the prevention, risk assessment, and initial evaluation of coronary artery disease through a case-based approach. It distinguishes primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention, emphasizing modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors. The use of the ASCVD risk calculator for statin initiation, the current recommendation against aspirin for primary prevention, and appropriate screening tests such as coronary calcium scoring are discussed. For chest pain evaluation, the lecture reviews key history and physical exam elements, the HEART score for risk stratification, and interpretation of nonspecific ST changes on EKG.
key_points: Primary prevention prevents disease onset; secondary prevention screens for early disease; tertiary prevention minimizes complications.
Modifiable risk factors include smoking, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and stress; nonmodifiable include age, sex, family history, and postmenopausal state.
Aspirin is no longer recommended for primary prevention of cardiovascular events.
The ASCVD risk calculator should be used to guide statin initiation; the newer PREVENT calculator is not yet as user-friendly.
Screening EKG and baseline EKG are not indicated for asymptomatic patients.
Coronary artery calcium score (cardiac CT) can be used for risk assessment in asymptomatic patients aged 40–70 with risk factors.
For chest pain, key history elements include quality, location, radiation, duration, provoking factors, relieving factors, associated symptoms, and prior episodes.
The HEART score (without troponin) can be used in the office to estimate risk; a score of 0–3 allows discharge home, while higher scores require further evaluation.
Life-threatening differentials for chest pain include ACS, aortic dissection, tamponade, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, and esophageal rupture.
Nonspecific ST changes on EKG (e.g., inverted T wave in lead III, biphasic T wave in V4, flattened T waves in V5/V6) may be subtle but warrant attention.

The HEART score is used for chest pain workup: 0-3 (low risk) may be managed outpatient, 4-6 (moderate risk) warrants admission and inpatient stress test, 7-10 (high risk) requires immediate cardiology consultation likely for catheterization.
A troponin of 0.06 (above the 0.02 cutoff) is considered mildly elevated and not immediately concerning, prompting further evaluation with stress testing before cardiology consultation.

episodes.title: Dr. Lucashu on Outpatient Management
episodes.speaker: Lucashu
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lucashu delivers a practical, non-comprehensive lecture on outpatient diabetes management, emphasizing actionable steps for new diagnoses. The talk covers initial workup, the 12-point management checklist, first-line metformin dosing, shame-free lifestyle counseling, and a framework for selecting second-line agents based on comorbidities. Key themes include maximizing metformin before escalation, using a diabetic report card for comorbidities, and tailoring therapy to patient-specific factors like cost and hypoglycemia risk.
key_points: For a new diabetes diagnosis, order hemoglobin A1c and lipid panel per USPSTF screening guidelines; baseline chem 7 and CBC are not required but commonly added.

Initial visit management includes 12 items: ACE inhibitor for hypertension, moderate-intensity statin, foot exam, eye exam, urine microalbumin, nutrition referral, lifestyle counseling, home blood pressure log, recheck elevated office BP, one-month follow-up, and providing a diabetic education folder.
Metformin is first-line for all patients; start at maximum tolerated dose (1000 mg PO BID or XR 2000 mg daily) unless prior intolerance, and document failure at max dose before adding second agents.
Metformin XR is better tolerated but may require prior authorization for Medicaid; regular metformin or SR are tier 1 options.
Lifestyle modification should use a shame-free approach; focus on eliminating sugary drinks and the 'five whites' (sugar, bread, rice, potatoes, pasta).
Aerobic exercise goal is 150 minutes per week in sessions of at least 10 minutes; patients should achieve a heart rate that prevents completing a full sentence.
Bariatric surgery referral is appropriate for BMI ≥35 with a comorbidity like diabetes; no specific glycemic control is required for referral, though the center will manage perioperative glucose.
Moderate-intensity statin is indicated for all patients with diabetes regardless of baseline LDL; upgrade to high-intensity based on ASCVD risk calculator after lipid panel results.
Home glucose monitoring is needed for A1c >9%; for lower A1c, a monitor may still be provided but with less frequent checking.
Weight loss goal is 0.5–1 pound per week; some diabetes medications promote weight loss while insulin works against it.
GLP-1 agonists (e.g., Ozempic, Wegovy) and SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., Farxiga, Jardiance) are preferred for patients with ASCVD, CHF, or CKD due to cardiorenal benefits.
Only certain GLP-1s (first three listed) have cardiovascular benefit; Byetta and Adlyxin do not.

episodes.title: Dr. Lucashu speaks on Thyroid disease
episodes.speaker: Lucashu speaks
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the diagnosis and management of hypothyroidism in a family medicine setting, using a case-based approach. It reviews common symptoms, physical exam findings, and appropriate lab testing, emphasizing the use of TSH for screening and monitoring. Treatment initiation, dose titration, and long-term follow-up are discussed, along with special considerations for pregnancy. The talk also highlights pitfalls such as overcorrection, medication interactions, and the importance of patient education.
key_points: Hypothyroidism presents with vague symptoms like fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and hair loss; increased menstrual flow is a distinguishing feature.
Physical exam may reveal bradycardia, delayed reflex relaxation, dry skin, thyroid enlargement, and myxedema, but is often normal.
Order a thyroid analyzer for screening; for known thyroid disease, order TSH, T3, and T4 separately to avoid missing abnormal T4 with normal TSH.
Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism; other causes include post-op, iodine deficiency, drugs (lithium, amiodarone), and pituitary disease.
Start levothyroxine at 25-50 mcg daily; repeat TSH in 4-6 weeks after each dose change.
Goal TSH is within the normal range; avoid overcorrection, especially in the elderly, to prevent angina, atrial fibrillation, and osteoporosis.
Levothyroxine should be taken consistently, preferably in the morning on an empty stomach; compliance is more important than perfect timing.
In pregnancy, increase levothyroxine dose by 30-50% immediately and check TSH monthly; treat subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy.
Do not use Cerner reference ranges for thyroid labs in pregnancy; use perinatology guidelines and manage based on TSH alone.
Refer to endocrinology if levothyroxine dose exceeds 200 mcg daily or if symptoms persist despite adequate dosing and compliance.
American Thyroid Association recommends TSH screening every 5 years starting at age 35; USPSTF finds insufficient evidence for screening in asymptomatic adults.
Subclinical hypothyroidism (TSH 5.9, normal T4) usually requires reassurance and monitoring unless exceptions apply (symptomatic, TSH >10, goiter, pregnancy, high risk).

episodes.title: Dr. Mark Crouch on Ingestions 6/11/26
episodes.speaker: Mark Crouch
episodes.abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch presents a case-based discussion on ingestions, emphasizing the importance of obtaining the bottle, calling poison control, and assessing timing and symptoms. He highlights global health challenges such as paraquat poisoning in Papua New Guinea and cyanide toxicity from improperly prepared cassava or fava beans. Key principles include early IV access, checking blood glucose, and using local resources like package inserts for unfamiliar medications.
key_points: Always obtain the bottle or container of the ingested substance; it often contains poison control numbers and ingredient information.
Timing of ingestion is critical to determine GI location, absorption, and intervention window (e.g., activated charcoal).
In asymptomatic patients, still monitor closely as some toxins can cause rapid deterioration.
Early IV access should be established before circulatory collapse, even if no fluids are given immediately.
Check blood glucose in any ingestion patient, as hypoglycemia may coexist from other causes.
For unfamiliar medications, especially overseas, open the package insert for dosing and toxicity information.
Paraquat (Gramoxone) is a highly toxic weed killer banned in many countries; >30 mL ingestion is universally fatal due to pulmonary damage.
Cyanide poisoning from improperly prepared cassava or fava beans presents with confusion, agitation, and can be treated with an antidote (e.g., Nithiodote).
Naloxone is now widely available without prescription for opioid overdose reversal, similar to community defibrillators.
In global health settings, ask local staff or community members about common toxidromes and local poisons.

episodes.title: Dr. Mark Crouch on PNG Missions Pt.1 8/28/25
episodes.speaker: Mark Crouch
episodes.abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch shares his family's 12-year experience serving as family medicine physicians in rural Papua New Guinea at Nazarene Hospital, a 150-bed referral facility in the Highlands. He describes the challenges of practicing medicine in a setting with limited diagnostic and therapeutic options, where animistic beliefs coexist with Christianity, and domestic violence affects 80-90% of women. The lecture emphasizes the importance of being a 'doorkeeper' for patients, providing physical care while discerning opportunities for spiritual support, and highlights teaching and training local residents as a key development focus.
key_points: Papua New Guinea is the most rural country globally, with 87% of 8-9 million people living in remote areas accessible only by air or boat.
There are approximately 600 distinct languages in PNG, not dialects, making it a linguistically diverse region.
Syncretism is common: many profess Christianity while maintaining animistic practices like appeasing spirits with rituals.
Domestic abuse affects 80-90% of women in PNG, with sexual abuse in 50-60%; this drives a large proportion of clinical work.
Nazarene Hospital performs more deliveries annually than the entire St. John system, with over 2,100 deliveries per year.
In resource-limited settings, physicians often have only 5-6 therapeutic options; when exhausted, they must acknowledge 'there is nothing more I can do' and shift to comfort care.
The hospital was strategically placed on a tribal boundary to discourage warfare, reducing conflict nearly to zero.
Teaching and training local residents has become a major focus, growing from a dream to a reality over the past decade.
An electronic medical record (EMR) replaced paper charts in January, causing significant adjustment challenges.
The speaker's master's in public health has informed a passion for maternal and child health, particularly safe deliveries.
Giant condyloma acuminata in pregnancy can obstruct labor and necessitate cesarean section.
Administer corticosteroids at 28 weeks gestation for fetal lung maturity when preterm labor occurs.

episodes.title: Dr. McIntosh on Peds Respiratory Care 3/26/26
episodes.speaker: McIntosh
episodes.abstract: Dr. McIntosh presents a practical overview of pediatric upper respiratory infection (URI) management, emphasizing clinical diagnosis over unnecessary testing. He covers supportive care, including nasal irrigation and honey for cough, red flags requiring urgent evaluation, and appropriate antibiotic use for bacterial infections like strep pharyngitis and sinusitis. Case discussions highlight croup, peritonsillar abscess, and foreign body aspiration.
key_points: Clinical diagnostic acumen should guide URI evaluation; testing for flu, RSV, and strep is reserved for specific scenarios.
Supportive care (hydration, rest, saline irrigation) is the mainstay for viral URIs; honey is effective for cough in children over 1 year.
Avoid OTC cough and cold medications (dextromethorphan, phenylephrine) in children under 4 years due to overdose risk.
Antibiotics are rarely needed; prescribe for bacterial sinusitis only if symptoms persist >10 days or worsen after 5-7 days.
First-line treatment for strep pharyngitis is high-dose amoxicillin; amoxicillin-clavulanate is an alternative.
Red flags include tripoding, stridor at rest, refusal to swallow, fever >5 days, symptoms >14 days, and unilateral findings.
Croup presents with barking cough and inspiratory stridor; treat with dexamethasone.
Peritonsillar abscess presents with unilateral sore throat, drooling, and fever; requires imaging and drainage.
Persistent unilateral foul-smelling rhinorrhea suggests a foreign body in the nose.
Hand hygiene and avoidance of secondhand smoke are key prevention strategies.
Most URIs are viral; supportive care (saline, humidification, honey) is first-line.

For classic pertussis (paroxysmal cough with whoop/vomiting in unvaccinated child), treat empirically with a macrolide (azithromycin) and provide post-exposure prophylaxis for unvaccinated household contacts.

episodes.title: Dr. Megaly on Intro to Peripheral Arterial & Venous Disease
episodes.speaker: Megaly
episodes.abstract: Dr. Megaly discusses peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and venous disease, emphasizing that PAD is a marker of cardiovascular mortality and often asymptomatic. He advocates for screening with pulse exam rather than routine ABI, and highlights the importance of medical therapy (aspirin, statin, smoking cessation) to save lives. For DVT, he focuses on preventing post-thrombotic syndrome by treating iliac and femoral DVTs with catheter-directed thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy, and notes May-Thurner syndrome as a treatable cause of left DVT.
key_points: PAD is a marker of systemic atherosclerosis and carries high cardiovascular mortality; survival is nearly halved at 5 years for symptomatic patients.
Asymptomatic PAD occurs in 20–50% of patients; atypical leg pain is a common presentation.
Claudication location correlates with arterial segment: buttocks/hips for aortoiliac, thigh/knee for SFA (most commonly occluded), foot for tibial disease.
Screening with pulse exam is practical: if pedal pulses are normal (2+), no further testing is needed; if weak or absent, proceed to imaging.
ABI interpretation: normal >1.0; 0.91–0.99 is abnormal; >1.4 indicates noncompressible vessels (use toe-brachial index).
Duplex ultrasound waveforms: triphasic = normal, biphasic = mild disease, monophasic = severe stenosis.
Medical therapy (aspirin, statin, smoking cessation) is critical to reduce mortality in PAD patients.
For DVT, treat iliac and femoral DVTs to prevent post-thrombotic syndrome; below-knee DVTs are not treated.
May-Thurner syndrome (left iliac vein compression by right iliac artery) should be considered in acute left DVT and is treatable with stenting.
Post-thrombotic syndrome is staged with CEAP classification; treatment includes compression and possibly iliac vein stenting for proximal lesions.
Symptomatic DVT above the inguinal ligament (iliofemoral) indicates treatment, while below-inguinal DVT is treated only if symptomatic and involves deep veins.
The TRACK trial showed mechanical thrombectomy reduces moderate-to-severe post-thrombotic syndrome (18% vs 24%) and halves the rate of ulceration (8.7% reduction).

episodes.title: Dr. Miller on Pediatric Urology
episodes.speaker: Miller
episodes.abstract: Dr. Miller introduces pediatric urology as a reconstructive specialty focused on congenital anomalies and urinary tract infections. He emphasizes that there are only two true emergencies in pediatric urology: testicular torsion and posterior urethral valves, both occurring exclusively in boys. The talk highlights the critical role of antenatal imaging (hydronephrosis) and pressure dynamics in urologic disease, noting that men are at greater risk for renal injury from high pressure since they do not leak urine like women. Practical guidance is given on evaluating undescended testicles, with a low threshold for referral to a pediatric urologist.
key_points: Pediatric urology deals primarily with congenital issues and reconstruction, while adult urology is often deconstructive.
There are only two true pediatric urologic emergencies: testicular torsion and posterior urethral valves.
Testicular torsion is diagnosed by Doppler ultrasound—obtain imaging rather than relying on physical exam alone.
Posterior urethral valves occur only in boys and cause bilateral hydronephrosis from high bladder pressure; children may still pee normally.
Urine stream does not reliably indicate obstruction; pressure, not flow, damages kidneys.
Antenatal hydronephrosis is the most common clue for posterior urethral valves; involve a pediatric urologist early.
Undescended testicles are present in 3% of full-term boys and rarely descend after 1 year of age.
Surgery for undescended testicles before age 1 may improve fertility outcomes, though data are still evolving.
Retractile testicles can be observed, but any uncertainty warrants referral to a pediatric urologist.
Women leak urine under high pressure (relieving renal stress); men do not, placing them at risk for kidney damage.
Testicular torsion: always image with ultrasound—never regret getting an ultrasound.
Posterior urethral valves: place a catheter to reduce pressure; definitive treatment is endoscopic valve incision.

episodes.title: Dr. Morgan on Covid Pediatric Vaccines
episodes.speaker: Morgan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Morgan reviews the epidemiology, safety, and efficacy of COVID-19 vaccines for children aged 6 months to 5 years. Children in this age group have the highest hospitalization, ICU admission, and death rates among all pediatric age groups, with 46–68% of hospitalized children having underlying health conditions. The vaccine studies were small but well-designed, showing no myocarditis and rare febrile seizures, with local reactions worsening after the second dose. Efficacy ranged from 31–46% for Moderna and similar for Pfizer, and the vaccine is safer than COVID-19 infection in this population.
key_points: Children 6 months to 4 years have the highest hospitalization and death rates among pediatric age groups.
46–68% of hospitalized children in this age group had underlying health conditions.
COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths in this age group were as high or higher than for other vaccine-preventable diseases at the time their vaccines were developed.
The vaccine studies were observer-blind, placebo-controlled, and randomized, but small in sample size.
No cases of myocarditis were observed in the pediatric vaccine trials.
Local reactions (pain, redness, swelling) are common and may worsen with the second dose; Moderna reactions are generally worse than Pfizer.
Febrile seizures are a rare side effect (one case in the studies) but also occur with COVID infection.
Vaccine efficacy: Moderna 46% for ages 2–5 years and 31% for ages 6–23 months; Pfizer has similar percentages.
Pediatric COVID-19 vaccine (Pfizer) for ages 6 months–5 years was studied under EUA with 2-month seropositivity and 7-month safety follow-up.
Vaccine efficacy is about 80% in preventing infection, but data are limited to a few months.
Antibody duration in children is inferred from adult data (about 3 months).
The highest risk of hospitalization is in the youngest age group (6 months–5 years).

episodes.title: Dr. Morgan on Failure to Thrive
episodes.speaker: Morgan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Morgan's lecture on failure to thrive (FTT) emphasizes that most cases are straightforward if diagnosed early and managed with close follow-up. The two most critical skills are mastering growth curve interpretation and confidently applying the definition of FTT as a change of two standard deviations below the patient's norm. Organic (genetic/GI/feeding) and nonorganic (environmental/social) causes are distinguished, and symmetric vs. asymmetric growth patterns help identify underlying etiology. Dr. Morgan urges residents to overcome fear of labeling FTT, as early intervention prevents missed opportunities and serious outcomes.
key_points: Failure to thrive is defined as a change of two standard deviations below the patient's norm, usually based on birth percentile.
Weight loss occurs first, then length, then head circumference; symmetric decline in all parameters suggests a genetic or endocrine cause like growth hormone deficiency.
A baby born small for gestational age (SGA) is not automatically FTT; FTT requires a decline from a prior thriving trajectory.
Use CDC WHO growth curves for ages 0–24 months and CDC curves for >24 months; always verify measurements and remeasure if inconsistent.
Nonorganic FTT (environmental, social, feeding issues) is most common and modifiable with education and close monitoring.
Organic FTT includes genetic, GI, feeding, or absorption problems; asymmetric growth patterns often point to multifactorial causes.
Early diagnosis and intervention prevent progression; even severe cases with head circumference decline can improve with timely referrals.
Residents should not fear diagnosing FTT; most cases resolve with simple interventions like addressing feeding practices or social situations.
Symmetric growth failure (all parameters declining at same rate) is a red flag for endocrine or genetic disorders requiring specialist referral.
Documenting FTT in the chart is safe and necessary; it can be removed once resolved, but missing the diagnosis leads to lost intervention windows.
Use WHO growth charts for children 0–2 years and CDC charts for 2+ years; for preterm infants, use Fenton curves until they catch up.
Most failure to thrive is nonorganic (environmental/social), often due to feeding difficulties, maternal depression, or resource limitations.

episodes.title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne
episodes.speaker: Nakashima
episodes.abstract: Dr. Nakashima's lecture provides a family-medicine approach to classifying and treating acne and eczema. For acne, she distinguishes inflammatory and non-inflammatory types, grades severity by lesion count, and outlines a stepwise treatment algorithm starting with benzoyl peroxide and cleanser, then adding tretinoin or adapalene, topical clindamycin, and oral options (doxycycline, spironolactone, birth control) before referral for isotretinoin. The eczema portion emphasizes the atopic triad and risk factors such as low microbial exposure and high-sugar diets. The talk includes practical tips on medication dosing, patient counseling, and common pitfalls in primary care.
key_points: Acne is classified as inflammatory (papules, pustules, nodules, cysts) and noninflammatory (open and closed comedones) and occurs in sebaceous areas.
Severity grading: mild <30 lesions, moderate 30–125, severe >125; use clinical gestalt rather than exact counting.
First-line treatment for mild acne: gentle cleanser (Cetaphil/CeraVe), moisturizer, and benzoyl peroxide 5% applied for 1–2 minutes then rinsed.
If first-line fails after 6 weeks, add topical tretinoin (starting at 0.025% every other night) or adapalene gel; mix with moisturizer to improve tolerance.

For moderate acne, add topical clindamycin 1% lotion (max 4 months) and consider oral therapy: doxycycline 100 mg daily (max 4 months), spironolactone (for females, especially with PCOS), or combined oral contraceptives.
Severe or scarring acne warrants early dermatology referral for isotretinoin or scar management (laser, dermaplaning, silicone sheets).
DermNet NZ is a free, reliable resource for patient education images and handouts in multiple languages.
Eczema is strongly associated with atopic triad (asthma, allergies); family history present in ~70% of cases.
Risk factors for eczema include low microbial exposure in childhood, high-sugar diet, and high unsaturated fatty acid intake.
Clinical assessment for acne includes distinguishing papules from molluscum contagiosum (no central dimple) and sebaceous hyperplasia (yellow, translucent appearance).
Eczema triggers include dry/humid climate, pollen, stress, and irritants; risk factors are separate and not required for diagnosis.
First-line treatment is topical emollients; creams are preferred over lotions because they lack preservatives.

episodes.title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25
episodes.speaker: Nakashima
episodes.abstract: Dr. Nakashima presents updates from the AAFP Family Centered Pregnancy Conference, emphasizing care equity, family-centered continuity, and new screening guidelines. She highlights the decline of family physicians practicing obstetrics, the impact of obstetric deserts and racism on maternal mortality, and the unique value of continuity care. The lecture covers substance use disorder screening tools (NIDA-4 and 5 Ps), refugee prenatal care considerations, and management of fetal growth restriction including the Hadlock formula and umbilical artery Doppler monitoring.
key_points: Only 7% of family physicians now practice obstetrics, down from 45% thirty years ago, contributing to obstetric deserts.
Black women are 2-3 times more likely to die from pregnancy and have the highest cesarean delivery rates, driven by racism and social determinants of health.
