Continuity of care from preconception through the fourth trimester reduces mortality, hospitalization, and costs; 81% of studies show mortality reduction with continuity physicians.
Universal urine drug screening (UDS) is not recommended as a primary screening tool; validated questionnaires like NIDA-4 and the 5 Ps should be used first.
NIDA-4 asks about tobacco/vaping, heavy alcohol use (>4 drinks/day or >10/week), prescription misuse, and illicit drugs including marijuana.
The 5 Ps screening tool (Parents, Partner, Past, Prescriptions, Personal) uses indirect questioning to assess substance use risk.
For refugee prenatal care, educate patients on the rationale for frequent labs and monitoring, and consider PTSD as a risk factor for postpartum depression.
Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is defined as estimated fetal weight <10th percentile; the Hadlock formula is superior to NICHD and WHO for detection.
Umbilical artery Doppler monitoring in FGR can decrease stillbirth rate by 9%; perform weekly for first 2 weeks, then every 2-4 weeks if normal.
Aspirin is recommended for prevention of FGR in high-risk patients, similar to preeclampsia prophylaxis.
Universal TSH screening in pregnancy is not advised by guidelines, but is commonly performed in practice.
Lab values for TSH and free T4 differ by trimester; electronic health records may not adjust for pregnancy.

episodes.title: Dr. Newborn on OMT
episodes.speaker: Newborn
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Newborn covers osteopathic manipulative treatment (OMT) techniques including soft tissue, counterstrain, and myofascial release. It discusses appropriate referrals for OMT, emphasizing that somatic dysfunction in acute musculoskeletal issues is highly treatable, whereas chronic conditions require setting patient expectations and often multiple sessions. Practical demonstrations show how to apply soft tissue techniques to the thoracic, lumbar, and cervical spine, with attention to anatomical risks such as the vertebral artery. Key teaching points include the importance of targeting muscle (not skin), holding tension for 30–90 seconds, and using the Spurling's test before cervical work.
key_points: Soft tissue technique involves kneading muscles perpendicular to the spine or along the origin‑insertion plane until relaxation occurs.

Counterstrain is an indirect technique: identify the point of maximal tenderness, shorten the muscle, and hold for up to 90 seconds, then return to neutral without having the patient activate the muscle.
Appropriate OMT referrals are for musculoskeletal conditions with identifiable somatic dysfunction—acute problems are more responsive than chronic ones.
TART (tissue texture change, asymmetry, restriction of motion, tenderness) helps distinguish acute (boggy) from chronic (ropey/fibrotic) dysfunction.
OMT can effectively treat tension headaches, overuse injuries, and some acute rib or sciatic complaints, but not non‑musculoskeletal conditions or mechanical problems like herniated discs.
Chronic pain often requires home exercises and stretches; patient expectations should be set that improvement may take multiple visits.
Cervical soft tissue work requires awareness of the vertebral artery and nerve roots; a negative Spurling's test is recommended before treatment.
Soft tissue is very low‑risk; avoid rubbing the skin by engaging the muscle layer with thenar eminences or thumbs.
Stress‑related tension in the neck and shoulders is a common contributor to chronic myofascial pain that OMT can address.
The same soft tissue principles apply to cervical spine, but with gentler technique and attention to the vertebral artery course through the transverse foramina.
The suboccipital release targets the nuchal line, where the rectus capitis and obliquus capitis muscles attach.
The greater and lesser occipital nerves exit the skull at the nuchal line; tension here can cause nerve impingement and headache.

episodes.title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain
episodes.speaker: Newborn
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers pain in pregnancy, beginning with a biblical perspective and the concept of pain as a gift. It reviews types of pain across trimesters, warning signs for non-obstetric causes, and appropriate imaging (ultrasound, MRI, CT) with radiation safety. Specific conditions like appendicitis, kidney stones, placental abruption, round ligament pain, and lightning crotch are discussed. The talk concludes with labor pain management, emphasizing ACOG recommendations for neuraxial anesthesia at any stage and debunking myths about early epidurals.
key_points: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy affects 80% of women in the first trimester; persistence after 16–20 weeks with abdominal pain is abnormal.
Warning signs for non-obstetric abdominal pain include localized/abrupt onset, constant/severe pain, and association with nausea/vomiting, fever, or vaginal bleeding.
A single CT abdomen/pelvis delivers about 10 rads, well below the 50-rad threshold for fetal harm; it should not be withheld if clinically indicated.
Appendicitis is the most common acute surgical abdomen in pregnancy (1 in 1500); ultrasound is the best initial test, followed by MRI or CT if needed.
Placental abruption is the most dangerous cause of third-trimester pain, typically intense and unrelenting, with or without vaginal bleeding.
ACOG recommends offering neuraxial anesthesia at any stage of labor; early epidural prolongs labor by only about 7 minutes.
Round ligament pain occurs at the end of the second trimester/beginning of the third; lightning crotch is a distinct nerve pain in the groin/inner thigh.
For kidney stones, hydronephrosis, clinical picture, and hematuria often suffice for diagnosis without CT.
CT scan in pregnancy should only be obtained after obstetrical consultation.
The most common concerning causes of early pregnancy pain are ectopic pregnancy and spontaneous abortion.

episodes.title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)
episodes.speaker: Nichols
episodes.abstract: Dr. Nichols presents an outpatient-focused approach to acute kidney injury (AKI) using a case of a 66-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes, and medications including lisinopril and omeprazole who is found to have elevated creatinine and BUN. The lecture covers differential diagnosis, classification into prerenal, intrinsic, and postrenal AKI using BUN-to-creatinine ratio and other tests, and emphasizes the importance of recognizing false positives from medications like Bactrim. Key management steps include holding nephrotoxic drugs, assessing severity with RIFLE criteria (assuming baseline GFR of 75 if unknown), and bringing the patient back to clinic rather than managing by phone. Specific UA findings and clinical clues for intrinsic causes such as AIN (rash, eosinophils) and ATN are discussed.
key_points: AKI is classified as prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal; the BUN-to-creatinine ratio helps differentiate (prerenal >20:1, intrinsic 10-20:1).
Prerenal AKI is the most common type; when in doubt, assume prerenal.
False elevations of creatinine can be caused by Bactrim, protein supplements, ketoacidosis, and lab error; false BUN elevations can be caused by upper GI bleed, steroids, and high protein intake.
Risk factors for AKI include elderly age, female sex, Black race, diabetes, hypertension, ACEi/ARBs, NSAIDs, PPIs, hypovolemia, sepsis, and obstruction.
If baseline creatinine is unknown, assume a GFR of 75 to apply RIFLE criteria for severity assessment.
Intrinsic AKI includes ATN (prolonged prerenal, nephrotoxins), AIN (drugs, infections, with fever/rash/arthralgias), and glomerulonephritis.
Postrenal AKI causes include prostatic hypertrophy, stones, neurogenic bladder, and severe constipation.
Diagnostic workup includes CBC, electrolytes, urine studies (osmolality, sodium, UA for casts/crystals/hemoglobin), and renal ultrasound (normal in prerenal, shows chronic changes or obstruction).
Specific UA findings: muddy brown casts in ATN, white cell casts in AIN, eosinophils in AIN, hemoglobin without RBCs in rhabdo, macroscopic hematuria in vascular causes.
Management: hold nephrotoxic medications, address underlying cause, rehydrate if prerenal, avoid contrast, and monitor urine output and creatinine.
Use RIFLE criteria to determine admission: failure class or below requires admission; injury class can be managed with close outpatient follow-up.
For prerenal AKI, trial holding nephrotoxic medications and encourage oral rehydration if no obstruction is present.

episodes.title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25
episodes.speaker: Nicole Tipton
episodes.abstract: This emergency-medicine lecture covers cold-related environmental exposures, focusing on hypothermia and frostbite. The speaker reviews staging of hypothermia (mild, moderate, severe, cardiac arrest), ECG findings such as Osborn waves, and systematic rewarming strategies from passive external methods to invasive techniques like ECMO. For frostbite, the lecture parallels burn classification (first through fourth degree), discusses blister management controversies, and uses a clinical case to illustrate management decisions. At-risk populations (elderly, young, trauma patients, military, homeless) and practical tips for undressing and preserving patient belongings are also emphasized.
key_points: At-risk populations for cold injury include elderly, very young, trauma patients after undressing, military personnel, homeless individuals, and those with Raynaud's phenomenon.
Hypothermia staging: Stage I (32–35°C, shivering, tachycardia), Stage II (28–32°C, bradycardia, confusion), Stage III (24–28°C, no shivering, cyanosis, unconscious), Stage IV (<24°C, cardiac arrest).
The Osborn wave (J wave) on ECG is characteristic of hypothermia; its height correlates with the degree of hypothermia and can also be seen in myxedema coma.

First-degree frostbite (frostnip) involves partial skin freezing with redness, numbness, and burning pain; second-degree presents with clear blisters; third-degree shows hemorrhagic or necrotic blisters with subdermal plexus involvement; fourth-degree extends to tendons, bone, and muscle with tissue necrosis.
Blister management in frostbite is controversial; the speaker's general rule is not to open blisters unless infection is present.
Initial management of hypothermia: remove all wet clothing (patient safety justifies rapid undressing; consider offering replacement clothes, especially for homeless patients).

Passive external rewarming (bear hugger, warm blankets) is appropriate for mild hypothermia; active rewarming (warmed IV fluids, gastric lavage, bladder irrigation) is needed for moderate to severe cases.
For patients in hypothermic cardiac arrest, 'you must be warm and dead' — aggressive rewarming (e.g., ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass) is essential before declaring death; call ECMO early.
In trauma patients, after undressing and procedures, covering the patient back up is often forgotten, leading to iatrogenic hypothermia and coagulopathy.
Hypothermia-induced bradycardia is common in stages II–III; warmed IV fluids raise core temperature by approximately 0.5°C per hour.
Timing of environmental exposure within a year can affect clinical significance.
A January exposure may have different health impacts than an exposure in another month.

episodes.title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist
episodes.speaker: Okeefe
episodes.abstract: Dr. Okeefe provides a practical approach to coma and disordered consciousness for non-neurologists, emphasizing the importance of accurate terminology and recognizing the spectrum from confusion to coma. He explains the Monro-Kellie doctrine and a simplified model of consciousness requiring intact cortices, thalami, and reticular activating system. The lecture covers common causes of cortical dysfunction (metabolic, toxic, seizures, hypoperfusion) and stresses the role of delirium in hospitalized patients, particularly those with preexisting brain vulnerabilities. Key pearls include differentiating coma from sleep, identifying dangerous transitions between consciousness states, and advocating for environmental interventions to reduce hospital-acquired delirium.
key_points: Use precise terminology (awake, confused, lethargic, stuporous, obtunded, comatose) to communicate patient status accurately.
The transition from lethargic to stuporous is dangerous because protective reflexes and ability to follow commands diminish.
Coma differs from sleep in that a comatose patient cannot be aroused by external stimuli, whereas a sleeping patient can.
Preexisting structural brain issues (cortical atrophy, stroke history, TBI, dementia, Parkinson's) increase susceptibility to delirium.
The Monro-Kellie doctrine describes a fixed intracranial volume; cellular damage begets more damage via edema, hypoperfusion, and secondary infarction.
Consciousness requires three intact components: bilateral cortices (bulb), thalami (switch), and reticular activating system (cord).
Cortical dysfunction is often non-anatomical: metabolic derangements, intoxication, seizures, global hypoperfusion, or toxic-metabolic syndromes.
Bilateral thalamic injury can occur from carbon monoxide poisoning or artery of Percheron stroke (a rare variant).
Delirium in hospitalized elderly is multifactorial: sleep disruption, sensory deprivation, immobility, and underlying medical illness.
Correcting the underlying disturbance does not immediately reverse delirium; consistent daily interventions (mobility, lights on, glasses/hearing aids) are needed.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage and diffuse processes like encephalitis often cause coma due to global cerebral involvement.
The medial thalami are critical for consciousness; bilateral infarction from a single arterial variant can cause prolonged coma despite tiny strokes.

episodes.title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions
episodes.speaker: Papp speaks
episodes.abstract: Dr. Esther Papp, a family medicine graduate, shares her experience working in Togo, West Africa with Samaritan's Purse. She presents multiple cases highlighting common tropical pathologies: cerebral malaria, typhoid fever, severe acute malnutrition, and neonatal sepsis. She emphasizes the need for rapid intervention, such as physically carrying a seizing child to the ER, and provides specific treatment protocols for seizures, malaria, typhoid, and refeeding. She also discusses the emotional challenges and the role of faith in her practice.
key_points: In resource-limited settings, standard of care may require physically carrying a critically ill child to the ER to avoid delays.
Cerebral malaria presents with seizures and severe anemia; treat empirically with IV artesunate before lab results return.
Seizure management protocol: start with phenobarb 20 mg/kg, then escalate through levetiracetam and phenytoin, waiting 5–10 minutes between doses.
Typhoid fever is the top differential for fever and abdominal pain in Togo; treat with IV ceftriaxone inpatient or ciprofloxacin/azithromycin outpatient.
Severe acute malnutrition requires careful refeeding with electrolyte monitoring, prophylactic antibiotics, and vitamin supplementation.
Neonatal feeding depends on gestational age: NG tube for <32 weeks, trial of PO for >34 weeks, with careful monitoring for aspiration.
Conjunctival pallor can guide transfusion decisions in anemic children with malaria.
Serial abdominal exams are critical for typhoid patients to detect perforation early.
Avoid saying a patient 'needs to go to the ER' as it causes delays; physically escort the patient instead.
Faith and prayer can play a role in clinical decision-making and coping with traumatic cases.
In resource-limited settings, ultrasound is a versatile diagnostic tool that can guide management and treatment decisions.
For acute stroke, always check a blood sugar first to rule out hypoglycemia causing stroke-like symptoms.

episodes.title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals
episodes.speaker: Patrick
episodes.abstract: Dr. Patrick contrasts mid-20th-century medicine with today's complex, lifestyle-driven practice, emphasizing how ethical foundations and patient trust have eroded. He highlights the Hippocratic Oath's original role in establishing trust, and stresses the importance of questioning patients sensitively rather than imposing politically correct agendas. The lecture connects biblical literacy, cultural change, and moral relativism to modern clinical challenges, urging physicians to deepen their relational and ethical skills.
key_points: Medicine has shifted from acute infectious disease to chronic lifestyle-related conditions, with most patients now partly responsible for their illness.
The Hippocratic Oath was originally taken at the start of training to establish ethical commitments, not at graduation.
Before 1860, seeing a doctor for a serious illness actually increased short-term mortality; patient trust was the foundation of medical practice.
Paternalistic mentoring in the past included honest career guidance and personal engagement, which built strong doctor-patient and doctor-doctor relationships.
Listening to the abdomen with a stethoscope can detect a liver rub caused by cancer breaching the capsule — a late-stage sign in hepatoma.
Patients often thank physicians for giving them a clear diagnosis and prognosis, because it allows them to plan reconciliation and closure.
Young physicians face high rates of anxiety and suicide; the profession needs to address this openly rather than with denial.
Learning to ask sophisticated, sensitive, and kind questions is more important than making statements, especially when discussing death and serious illness.
Biblical literacy is declining, weakening cultural and metaphysical foundations that underpin Western medicine and its ethical framework.
Moral relativism is pervasive; reading authors like Peter Kreeft can help physicians navigate these ethical challenges.
Cultural narratives of meaning enrich lives and enable ethical action more effectively than abstract ethics lectures.
Rising anxiety rates correlate with smartphone use; Jonathan Haidt's 'The Anxious Generation' is referenced.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
episodes.speaker: Place
episodes.abstract: This lecture on benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) defines the condition as a true hyperplasia causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). The speaker emphasizes using validated instruments like the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) to quantify symptoms and distinguish between obstructive and irritative complaints. A case of a 65-year-old male with nocturia, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, and post-void dribbling illustrates typical presentation. The talk also reviews prevalence (50% by age 50, 80% by age 80) and the importance of correct terminology.
key_points: BPH is a true hyperplasia (increase in cell number), not hypertrophy (increase in cell size).
Prevalence follows the '50 by fifty and eighty by 80' rule: 50% of men in their 50s and 80% in their 80s have symptoms.
Use the term 'lower urinary tract symptoms' (LUTS) instead of 'BPH symptoms' to avoid diagnostic anchoring.
The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) is a validated instrument to quantify and characterize LUTS.
Key symptoms include sensation of incomplete emptying, frequency (≤2 hours), intermittency, urgency, weak stream, straining, and nocturia.
Nocturia is the most common reason patients seek care for LUTS.
Straining to urinate involves a Valsalva maneuver to assist the detrusor muscle in emptying the bladder.
Obstructive symptoms (hesitancy, weak stream, straining, incomplete emptying) and irritative symptoms (frequency, urgency, nocturia) help categorize LUTS.
The case of TW highlights typical BPH presentation: nocturia 3×/night, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, and post-void dribbling.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
episodes.speaker: Place
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews the basics of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), a common age-related condition causing lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). The speaker emphasizes that BPH is a symptom-based diagnosis supported by history, digital rectal exam, and selective laboratory tests. Management includes lifestyle modifications, alpha blockers, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, and surgical options like TURP. The lecture distinguishes between obstructive and irritative symptoms and highlights the utility of the IPSS score for quantification.
key_points: BPH is benign hyperplasia (increased cell number, not cell size) causing lower urinary tract symptoms; prevalence is 50% at age 50 and 80% at age 80.
Diagnosis requires symptoms; it is not a radiologic or physical exam diagnosis alone.
Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) are classified as obstructive (weak stream, hesitancy, straining, incomplete emptying, post-void dribbling) or irritative (frequency, urgency, nocturia, dysuria).
The IPSS (International Prostate Symptom Score) is a validated tool to quantify symptoms and should be used, especially when objective measurement is needed.
Digital rectal exam is mandatory in symptomatic patients to assess prostate size (big vs. not big) and to check for nodules.
Urinalysis should be performed to rule out hematuria, infection, or other pathology.
PSA can be supportive but is not diagnostic for BPH; a very low PSA (<0.1) may indicate hypogonadism warranting testosterone evaluation.
Percent-free PSA can help in gray zones: low percent-free suggests higher malignancy risk, high percent-free is more associated with BPH.
First-line management includes lifestyle changes: avoid fluids after 6 PM, limit caffeine, alcohol, and carbonated drinks; double voiding before bed.
Medical therapy includes alpha-blockers (relax prostate/bladder neck) and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (reduce prostate volume); TURP remains the standard surgical option.
Lifestyle interventions include double voiding, urethral milking, sitting to urinate, and treating constipation to reduce pelvic pressure on the prostate.
Alpha-1 antagonists are first-line for BPH; they relax the prostatic urethra and bladder neck smooth muscle by blocking alpha-1 receptors.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension
episodes.speaker: Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place argues that hypertension management is one of the most important clinical interventions in all of medicine, second only to smoking cessation. He reviews the pathophysiology of hypertension, emphasizing the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system as the central mechanism. The lecture covers proper blood pressure measurement technique, evidence-based targets, and the importance of accurate home monitoring. Dr. Place aims to inspire residents to become passionate about controlling blood pressure to reduce cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease.
key_points: Hypertension is the number one risk factor for ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease, killing more people than all top cancers combined.
The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is the dominant pathophysiologic mechanism in over 90% of hypertension cases.
Proper blood pressure measurement requires the patient to be seated with feet flat, back supported, arm at heart level, no caffeine or exercise within 30 minutes, and the cuff on bare skin.
At the first visit, check both arms and use the higher reading for diagnosis and management.
Home blood pressure monitors should be validated (e.g., Omron brand) and patients should record readings; many devices can average three readings taken five minutes apart.
Normal blood pressure is <120/80 mm Hg; elevated is 120-129/<80; stage 1 hypertension is 130-139/80-89; stage 2 is ≥140/90.
Clinic blood pressures are often unreliable due to patient rushing, caffeine, or improper technique; home monitoring provides more accurate data.
The endothelium is a dynamic organ, not a passive lining; it can be damaged by smoking and alcohol, contributing to hypertension.
Angiotensin II is the key molecule in hypertension management, causing vasoconstriction, increased sympathetic activity, sodium retention, and aldosterone release.
Cardiovascular disease kills about 18 million people annually; controlling blood pressure and smoking cessation are the two most impactful interventions in family medicine.
Clinic blood pressure readings are unreliable; base management on home or ambulatory monitoring.
Target BP is <130/80 for most patients, but communicate it as 'the 120s over 70s' to avoid false reassurance.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26
episodes.speaker: Place
episodes.abstract: This lecture emphasizes hypertension as the most important clinical intervention in family medicine, given its role as the leading risk factor for cardiovascular disease and death worldwide. The speaker reviews seven pathophysiologic mechanisms, focusing on the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and angiotensin II as the central molecule. Proper blood pressure measurement technique is demonstrated, highlighting common errors in clinic settings. The goal is to inspire residents to become passionate about blood pressure management as a high-impact, evidence-based practice.
key_points: Hypertension is the number one modifiable risk factor for ischemic heart disease and cerebrovascular disease, the leading causes of death globally.
Controlling blood pressure and smoking cessation are the two most impactful interventions in family medicine.

The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is central to hypertension pathophysiology; angiotensin II is the master molecule driving vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and aldosterone/ADH secretion.
Seven pathophysiologic mechanisms include vascular remodeling, sympathetic activation, neurogenic factors, endothelial dysfunction, RAAS, renal mechanisms, and oxidative stress.

Proper blood pressure measurement requires: patient seated >5 minutes, feet flat, back supported, arm at heart level, bare arm, correct cuff size (80-100% arm circumference), no talking, no caffeine/exercise/smoking within 30 minutes.
Using a cuff that is too small falsely elevates blood pressure readings.
Patients cannot reliably sense their blood pressure; symptoms only occur at very high levels (e.g., >180/110).
Second blood pressure readings in clinic are important for accuracy and are audited for quality metrics.
Most hypertension is essential (primary); rare secondary causes like pheochromocytoma (0.6/100,000 patient-years) should not be over-searched.
Endothelial dysfunction is a dynamic process involving inflammation and damage from pressure, smoking, and toxins.
Use a validated home blood pressure monitor with an arm cuff; wrist cuffs are inaccurate and should only be used if the arm is too large for an arm cuff.
Normal blood pressure is <120/80; elevated is 120–129/<80; stage 1 is 130–139/80–89; stage 2 is ≥140/90.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25
episodes.speaker: Place
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Place covers the diagnosis and management of male hypogonadism, emphasizing the importance of accurate symptom assessment and laboratory testing. The most common symptom is reduced libido, not erectile dysfunction, which is often vascular in origin. The talk distinguishes primary, secondary, and functional hypogonadism, with functional hypogonadism due to obesity and diabetes being the most prevalent. Practical guidance is given on ordering the correct lab tests, including the use of LCMS total testosterone and the need for fasting morning draws, as well as the role of SHBG and free testosterone in borderline cases.
key_points: Reduced libido is the most important symptom of male hypogonadism; ask about sex drive compared to a few years ago, not to age 20.
Erectile dysfunction is mostly vascular and often does not improve with testosterone therapy; avoid creating false expectations.
Functional hypogonadism (due to obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism) is the most common cause and represents a secondary type with low-normal FSH/LH.
Primary hypogonadism involves a sick testis (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, trauma, mumps orchitis); secondary hypogonadism involves pituitary/hypothalamus lesions (e.g., prolactinoma).
Total testosterone should be drawn fasting between 7-10 AM; non-fasting can lower levels by 30-50 points.
Use LCMS total testosterone (gold standard) rather than the older total testosterone assay, which is inaccurate at low levels.
If initial total T is low or borderline, repeat in 2-3 weeks with SHBG, free T, FSH, and LH to confirm and classify.
SHBG is downregulated in obesity/diabetes (low total T, free may be normal) and upregulated with aging/liver disease (low free T).
For patients with BMI >35, prediabetes, or sedentary lifestyle, order the full panel upfront due to high likelihood of functional hypogonadism.
Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) is missed in about 50% of cases; consider karyotype in primary hypogonadism.
Interpret FSH and LH to differentiate primary (high FSH/LH) from secondary (low/inappropriately normal FSH/LH) hypogonadism.
In primary hypogonadism, the testis is failing; the pituitary tries to compensate by raising FSH and LH.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Obesity
episodes.speaker: Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place discusses the critical importance of obesity in clinical practice, emphasizing its high prevalence (estimated 50% post-COVID) and profound impact on metabolic and cardiovascular disease. He presents three patient stories illustrating the spectrum of outcomes—from successful weight loss to persistent complications. The talk covers obesity definitions (class 1-3), limitations of BMI, phenotypic presentations (e.g., obese clueless, metabolic obese), and a basic management framework. He stresses avoiding stigmatizing language like 'morbid obesity' and addressing obesity as a primary driver of disease.
key_points: Obesity prevalence is about 50% post-COVID, with class 3 (BMI >40) now 10%.
Do not use the term 'morbid obesity'; use class 3 instead.
BMI has limitations: inaccurate in Asians, athletes, very short/tall individuals, and ethnic differences exist.
Obesity is a genetic propensity toward adiposity accelerated by environment and lifestyle.
Adipose tissue is hormonally active and causes chronic inflammation, contributing to cytokine storm in COVID-19.
Obesity is associated with a 7x risk of diabetes in men and 12x risk in women; check A1C in obese patients.
ASCVD (heart attack/stroke) kills 20 million per year globally; all cancers combined kill 10 million.
Identify phenotypes: obese clueless (unaware, unmotivated), metabolic obese (motivated, diabetes spectrum), and others.
Some medications like mirtazapine cause significant weight gain; consider stopping them.
Weight circumference has better outcome data than BMI but is rarely measured in clinic.
Bariatric surgery can have complications such as phrenic nerve injury causing chronic hiccups.
Obesity rates in disabled populations (e.g., Down syndrome, cerebral palsy) are ~80%.

episodes.title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment
episodes.speaker: Place
episodes.abstract: Dr. Place emphasizes that preoperative assessment is a valuable opportunity to reduce surgical risk and improve patient outcomes. He distinguishes surgical risk factors (e.g., procedure type, duration, urgency) from patient-specific factors, highlighting the need for a comprehensive evaluation that includes spiritual, mental health, nutritional, medical, and social support domains. He introduces the NSQIP risk calculator as the gold-standard tool for estimating personalized risks and generating a detailed report for the surgeon. The lecture stresses the importance of a face-to-face visit, not just chart review, and encourages documenting findings in a formal report to enhance care and strengthen surgeon relationships.
key_points: Surgical risk is defined by procedure type (local, neuraxial, general anesthesia), duration (less than or greater than one hour), and urgency (elective, urgent/emergent).
Patient risk factors span head-to-toe: spiritual beliefs, mental health, cardiac/pulmonary status, nutrition, medical comorbidities, and social support.
The NSQIP (National Surgical Quality Improvement Program) online calculator is the gold standard for estimating individualized surgical risk and should be used during preoperative evaluation.
Preoperative visits should be scheduled in person, not conducted via chart review or email, to allow comprehensive assessment and shared decision-making.
A formal written report (including NSQIP results) should be sent to the surgeon, not just a signed clearance form, to demonstrate thoroughness and improve communication.
About 30% of patients develop clinical major depressive disorder within one year after CABG, supporting preoperative consideration of SSRI/SNRI therapy.
Many patients enter elective surgery with suboptimal nutritional status, which delays recovery; addressing nutritional deficits preoperatively is important.
Social support (family, caregivers, socioeconomic status) significantly impacts postoperative outcomes and must be assessed.
The NSQIP tool provides predicted risks for serious complications, pneumonia, cardiac events, surgical site infection, UTI, venous thromboembolism, and discharge to a nursing facility.
Even low-risk patients have non-zero risks; discussing individualized risk estimates with patients aids informed consent and shared decision-making.
Use the ACS NSQIP risk calculator to estimate serious complication risk and guide conversations about postponing surgery when risk exceeds 10%.
Screen functional capacity with the ability to climb two flights of stairs (4 METs); inability indicates need for further cardiac evaluation.

episodes.title: Dr. Place Outpatient Lecture
episodes.speaker: Unknown
key_points: Hepatitis C is often asymptomatic or presents with mild, self-limited symptoms such as low-grade jaundice and transaminitis.
Diagnosis requires HCV RNA to confirm active replication; antibody positivity alone is insufficient.
Genotype 1 is the most common genotype in the United States; genotype 3 is associated with resistance and requires caution.
Fibrosis assessment is the key fork in management: use FIB-4, APRI, Fibrospect, and ultrasound; biopsy is rarely needed.
Over 90% of otherwise healthy patients with HCV antibody have no fibrosis on workup.
Simplified treatment is for chronic HCV, any genotype, without cirrhosis and without prior treatment.
First-line regimens: Mavyret (glecaprevir/pibrentasvir) 3 tablets daily for 8 weeks or Epclusa (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir) 1 tablet daily for 12 weeks.
No routine lab monitoring is required during treatment; check drug interactions using the University of Liverpool checker.
Post-treatment HCV RNA at 12 weeks confirms sustained virologic response (cure).
Non-cirrhotic patients who achieve SVR need no further liver-related follow-up.
Refer complicated cases (prior treatment failure, cirrhosis, HBV coinfection, pregnancy, HCC, transplant) to a hepatologist or ID specialist.
Check HCV viral load at 12 weeks after treatment to document sustained virologic response.

episodes.title: Dr. Price on Pelvic Floor Dysfunction
episodes.speaker: Price
episodes.abstract: Pelvic floor disorders affect 1 in 3 women and include bladder control problems, pelvic organ prolapse, and bowel control problems. Risk factors include modifiable lifestyle factors such as smoking, obesity, extreme sports, constipation, and uncontrolled diabetes. Diagnosis relies on recognizing symptoms like pressure, bulge, urinary leakage, and incomplete emptying. Treatment starts with conservative measures including pelvic floor exercises, dietary changes (avoiding the four C's), and weight loss, with surgical options reserved for refractory cases.
key_points: One in three women will experience a pelvic floor disorder in their lifetime.
Pelvic floor disorders include urinary incontinence (16% of women), pelvic organ prolapse (3%), and accidental bowel leakage (9%).
Modifiable risk factors include smoking, obesity, extreme sports (e.g., CrossFit), constipation, and uncontrolled diabetes.
Losing 10% of BMI improves urinary symptoms by 50%.
Patients often wait years to seek help; 26% wait over five years.
Educate patients that the urethra, vagina, and rectum are three separate openings.
Urinary incontinence types: stress (leakage with activity), urge (overactive bladder), mixed (30% of women), and continuous.
Avoid the four C's: carbonated drinks, citrus, caffeine, and chocolate to reduce bladder irritation.
Kegel exercises: squeeze for 10 seconds, do sets of 10, twice daily.
Surgical options for stress incontinence (e.g., bladder sling) are 85-95% effective but carry a 1-5% risk of mesh exposure.
Bladder training gradually increases voiding intervals to restore normal bladder capacity.
Anticholinergic medications for OAB cause dry mouth in 80% of patients; oxybutynin has the worst tolerability.

episodes.title: Dr. Price on Vector Transmitted Disease 6/18/26
episodes.speaker: Price
episodes.abstract: Dr. Price discusses vector-borne diseases increasingly seen in Houston, including typhus (murine, epidemic, scrub), Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, STARI syndrome, tick paralysis, and mosquito-borne viruses. He emphasizes that murine typhus is now encountered two to three times weekly, often in non-travelers, and that doxycycline is the treatment of choice for most rickettsial diseases. He highlights diagnostic challenges, such as the unreliability of Lyme serology in non-endemic areas and the importance of recognizing STARI syndrome in the southern US. Key clinical pearls include the petechial rash of Rocky Mountain spotted fever starting at the ankles, the need to treat empirically with doxycycline when suspicion is high, and the management of tick paralysis by simply removing the tick.
key_points: Murine typhus (Rickettsia typhi) is transmitted by fleas and presents with fever, headache, thrombocytopenia, and elevated LFTs; it is now seen 2-3 times weekly in Houston.
Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) causes a petechial rash that typically begins on the ankles and can spread centrally; doxycycline is the only effective treatment and must be started empirically.
Lyme disease is rare in Texas; a rash in a non-endemic area is more likely STARI syndrome (southern tick-associated rash illness), which is treated similarly with doxycycline.
STARI syndrome is transmitted by the Lone Star tick, presents with erythema migrans-like rash, but rarely causes cardiac or neurologic complications.
Tick paralysis presents as ascending flaccid paralysis in children; removal of the tick leads to recovery within 24-48 hours.
Doxycycline is safe for children under 8 and pregnant women for short courses when treating rickettsial diseases; older tetracyclines had more risk of tooth staining.
Empiric doxycycline should be started when RMSF or typhus is suspected, even before confirmatory testing, because delays increase mortality.
Lyme serology (ELISA followed by Western blot) is only reliable in endemic areas; a positive IgG can persist for years after treated infection, making it useless for diagnosing recurrence.
Mosquito-borne diseases like West Nile and Zika are present in the US; most West Nile infections are asymptomatic or mild.
Poor sanitation and open defecation contribute to 10% of global disease burden, especially in children under 5.
Soil-transmitted helminthiases cause fatigue and poor school performance, perpetuating poverty.
Pit latrines propagate disease; compost toilets are a sustainable, low-tech alternative.

episodes.title: Dr. Purser on Allergic Rhinitis 4/16/26
episodes.speaker: Purser
episodes.abstract: Dr. Purser emphasizes that nasal congestion is the primary symptom driving patients to seek care for allergic rhinitis, not sneezing or itching. He stresses the importance of using visual aids to educate patients about nasal anatomy, particularly the turbinates and their functions. He differentiates allergic from nonallergic rhinitis, noting that antihistamines are not anti-inflammatory and that avoidance is the first step in management. He also discusses the value of early skin prick testing in infants and the clinical consequences of mouth breathing in children, including sleep disturbances and dental caries.
key_points: Nasal congestion is the most common symptom that brings patients to the clinic for allergic rhinitis.
Antihistamines (e.g., Zyrtec, Claritin, Allegra) are not anti-inflammatory and do not treat congestion directly.
Nonallergic rhinitis (vasomotor) is common, often triggered by cold, perfumes, or eating, and does not respond to antihistamines.
Family history and the presence of itching or sneezing help differentiate allergic from nonallergic rhinitis.
Skin prick testing can be performed as early as 2–6 months of age, especially for indoor allergens or food allergies.
Avoidance of identified allergens is the first-line intervention for allergic rhinitis.
Mouth breathing in children can lead to attention deficit, poor sleep, and increased risk of dental cavities.
Turbinates function to warm, filter, and humidify inspired air; excessive surgical removal can impair these functions.
Using pictures to explain nasal anatomy (e.g., turbinates, septum, nasolacrimal duct) improves patient understanding and compliance.
Pollen counts from local monitoring stations can guide patients on when to avoid outdoor exposure.
Start topical nasal steroid 4 weeks before the expected allergy season for seasonal allergic rhinitis.
Fluticasone propionate (Flonase) is cheap but has a higher risk of epistaxis due to alcohol; fluticasone furoate and mometasone have lower systemic absorption.

episodes.title: Dr. Purser on Anaphylaxis 2/26/26
episodes.speaker: Purser
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Purser focuses on differentiating acute from chronic urticaria, emphasizing the importance of blanching versus non-blanching lesions and the 6-week cutoff. Histaminergic hives are itchy, transient, and blanch, while vasculitic hives are painful and non-blanching. Chronic spontaneous urticaria is often autoimmune, triggered by viral infections (especially Epstein-Barr virus) or lymphoma, and requires workup with ESR, CRP, and TSH. Management includes antihistamines, longer prednisone tapers for flares, and biologics for refractory cases, with attention to physical urticarias such as cold and cholinergic.
key_points: Differentiate acute (<6 weeks) from chronic (≥6 weeks) urticaria using the 6-week cutoff.
Blanching hives are histaminergic; non-blanching suggests vasculitis.
Histaminergic hives itch, blanch, resolve within 24 hours, and respond to antihistamines.
Angioedema often accompanies hives, lasts 1–2 days, and may require steroids.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria is often autoimmune, triggered by viral infections (especially EBV) or lymphoma.
Workup for chronic urticaria includes ESR, CRP, TSH, and thyroid antibodies.
First-line treatment is non-sedating antihistamines; for severe flares, use a longer prednisone taper (e.g., 2 weeks) rather than a short Medrol dose pack.
Physical urticarias (inducible) include cholinergic, cold, pressure, solar, and dermatographism.
Biologics (e.g., omalizumab) are available for refractory chronic urticaria.
Patient education should reassure that hives are not dangerous but monitor for anaphylaxis.
Chronic urticaria often requires up to four times the standard dose of second-generation antihistamines.
Tryptase is a serum test; avoid ordering trypsin by mistake.

episodes.title: Dr. Richard on Outpatient Peds - Common Respiratory Disorders 3/19/26
episodes.speaker: Richard
episodes.abstract: Dr. Richard discusses common outpatient pediatric respiratory disorders, emphasizing clinical decision-making for conditions like strep pharyngitis, RSV, influenza, COVID-19, and croup. He reviews the Centor criteria for strep testing, RSV prevention strategies including maternal vaccination and monoclonal antibodies, and appropriate use of antipyretics. The lecture also covers judicious antibiotic use, indications for antivirals and steroids, and recognition of serious post-COVID complications like MIS-C and Kawasaki disease.
key_points: Centor criteria should guide strep testing in children; avoid indiscriminate swabbing due to high colonization rates in young children.
Maternal RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) given at 32-36 weeks protects infants for about 6 months; infants born <14 days after maternal vaccination still need RSV prophylaxis.
High-risk infants may qualify for monoclonal antibody RSV prophylaxis in their second RSV season.
Nasal suctioning with saline before feeds and sleep is the mainstay of supportive care for viral upper respiratory infections in infants.
Max dose of acetaminophen is 15 mg/kg; max dose of ibuprofen is 10 mg/kg; use weight-based calculations rather than age-based estimates.
Steroids are not routinely indicated for RSV or influenza unless comorbid asthma or croup is present.
Antibiotics should be prescribed cautiously in children due to risks of gut dysbiosis, neurodevelopmental delays, allergies, and obesity.
Tamiflu reduces influenza duration by less than one day; Xofluza is an alternative with single-dose convenience and no renal adjustment needed.
Paxlovid for pediatric COVID-19 requires age ≥12 years, weight ≥40 kg, symptoms ≤5 days, and comorbidities or immunocompromise.
MIS-C should be considered in children presenting 2-3 weeks after COVID-19 with unexplained systemic illness; IVIG and steroids are mainstays of treatment.
Croup severity is assessed by stridor at rest and retractions; dexamethasone is first-line but takes time to act; avoid examining the throat in suspected croup.
More than 200 viruses cause the common cold; supportive care is the main treatment.

episodes.title: Dr. Richard on UTIs 10/2/25
episodes.speaker: Richard
episodes.abstract: Dr. Richard reviews uncomplicated urinary tract infections (UTIs) in women, emphasizing the importance of distinguishing lower from upper tract disease through history and exam. He covers best practices for urine sample collection (midstream clean-catch), interpretation of dipstick nitrites, and common pitfalls including false-negative nitrite results. The lecture also addresses when virtual visits are appropriate, management of recurrent UTIs, and the 2022 IDSA guidelines allowing watchful waiting in low-risk young women. Throughout, he stresses antibiotic stewardship and awareness of multidrug-resistant organisms.
key_points: Uncomplicated UTI is limited to the lower urinary tract (bladder/urethra) in non-pregnant women without systemic signs or comorbidities.
The ideal urine specimen for culture is a midstream clean-catch sample processed within 1–2 hours to avoid false growth from E. coli proliferation.

Nitrite-negative dipstick can still occur in true UTI due to organisms that do not reduce nitrate (Enterococcus, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Group B Strep), short bladder incubation time, acidic urine (cranberry), or frequent voiding.
Hematuria combined with positive nitrite is the symptom pairing with highest predictive value for UTI.
Sterile pyuria should prompt consideration of partially treated infection, STIs, or urologic conditions such as interstitial cystitis.
Self-diagnosis of UTI by women is a strong predictor; virtual visits can be acceptable for uncomplicated presentations, but recurrent UTIs (≥3 per year) require in-person evaluation and culture.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria generally does not require treatment except in pregnancy or prior to urologic procedures.
For E. coli and Staphylococcus saprophyticus, a colony count of ≥10³ CFU/mL can be diagnostic in symptomatic patients, not the traditional ≥10⁵ threshold.
In healthy young women with mild symptoms and no risk factors, watchful waiting with hydration is an option to reduce antibiotic resistance.
Clinicians should consider geographic/local antibiogram data when selecting empiric therapy due to rising multidrug resistance.
Differential for dysuria includes STI, atrophic vaginitis, interstitial cystitis, and pyelonephritis.
Burning at the end of urination (post-void burning) suggests vaginal irritation or atrophy rather than typical cystitis.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Acute and Chronic Low Back Pain
episodes.speaker: Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander teaches how to distinguish disc, facet joint, and spinal stenosis causes of low back pain using history and physical exam, emphasizing that disc pain is acute with paraspinal spasms, facet pain is chronic and lateralized with extension worsening, and spinal stenosis presents with neurogenic claudication relieved by bending forward. He contrasts neurogenic claudication with vascular claudication, noting that vascular pain is more distal, asymmetric, and slowly resolves with rest. Radicular pain from nerve compression is typically unilateral and follows a specific nerve root distribution. The speaker cautions against prolonged bed rest, recommending activity modification and conservative therapy before imaging.
key_points: Disc pain presents as acute onset with bending/lifting, localized back pain, paraspinal spasms, and no radicular symptoms unless extrusion occurs.
Facet joint pain is more chronic, lateralized, worsened by extension, and better when lying down, without true radicular leg pain.
Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication: bilateral, upper-leg pain on walking, relieved immediately by bending forward or sitting.
Vascular claudication differs by being more distal, asymmetric, slowly progressive, and resolves over minutes of rest, not immediately with bending.
Foraminal stenosis narrows the nerve root exit due to disc herniation anteriorly or facet hypertrophy posteriorly, causing unilateral radicular pain.
MRI is used to confirm a clinical diagnosis after X-ray and failed conservative therapy, not as a first-line test.
Prolonged bed rest is discouraged; advise activity modification and gradual return to activity to avoid complications like DVT.
Radicular pain is mechanical; movements that narrow the foramen (e.g., extension) typically worsen pain regardless of the exact motion.
Most patients have mixed pathology, but identifying the predominant pattern guides treatment—e.g., nerve pain is treated differently than disc degeneration.
Avoid bed rest for acute low back pain; encourage staying upright and walking.
For back pain, use cyclic heat/ice therapy (ice 10 min, heat 10 min, repeat) 2-3 times daily, starting with ice and ending with heat.
Acetaminophen is effective for pain control; limit to 3,000-3,500 mg/day due to risk of hepatic toxicity.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Chronic Abdominal Pain
episodes.speaker: Rylander
key_points: Normalize bowel function first with soluble fiber, probiotics, Miralax, and loperamide to achieve 1-2 bowel movements per day.
Use the gastrocolic reflex after meals to encourage bowel movements.
Gradual stepwise dietary approach: FODMAP diet, then gluten-free diet, then IgG elimination diet for refractory cases.
Dietary changes require 10-12 weeks to see effect due to antibody and inflammation resolution time.
IgG testing interpretation: class 2 or higher is clinically significant; start with highest class foods.
Customize diet based on patient preferences to improve compliance.
Long-term maintenance is needed; stopping interventions leads to relapse.
Peppermint oil may have anti-inflammatory and antispasmodic effects in the GI tract.
Use IgG testing as a surrogate marker when other diets fail, and interpret with caution.
Do not change dietary interventions more frequently than every 10 weeks.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on COPD and Asthma
episodes.speaker: Rylander
key_points: Renal indices (BUN/creatinine) are unreliable for prerenal assessment if the patient has received IV fluids or diuretics within 48 hours.
Patients with heart failure exacerbation have increased intravascular volume, not dehydration; do not give IV fluids for presumed prerenal azotemia in this setting.
In septic patients with heart failure, give fluids and inotropes early; use point-of-care ultrasound to assess cardiac function.
Surviving Sepsis guidelines now recommend early vasopressors to avoid fluid overload and cardiac mortality.
Distinguish COPD exacerbation from heart failure by history: gradual worsening over days suggests COPD; abrupt onset after a large meal or alcohol suggests aspiration, MI, or atrial fibrillation.
For COPD or asthma exacerbation, use muscarinics and steroids first; reserve beta-agonists for second-line due to cardiac arrhythmia risk.
IV magnesium reduces hospitalization time and repeat admissions in COPD and asthma exacerbations.
Steroids take 24-48 hours to work; do not judge their efficacy within a few hours.
High-dose vasopressors that rely on vasoconstriction decrease cardiac output and worsen outcomes; norepinephrine at high doses is associated with increased mortality.
Aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical reaction that does not require antibiotics initially; steroids are the mainstay.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Dementia
episodes.speaker: Rylander
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the four main types of dementia: Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, and vascular dementia. The speaker explains the role of tau protein in neurodegenerative diseases, distinguishing between tauopathies and vascular dementia. Key clinical skills include using the FAST scale to grade dementia severity and differentiating delirium from dementia. Vascular dementia is highlighted as the only treatable form, managed with lifestyle changes, high-dose statins, and antiplatelet therapy.
key_points: Tau protein governs microtubules in axons; its dysfunction underlies most neurodegenerative diseases.
Alzheimer's disease involves tau aggregation outside cells forming amyloid plaques; frontotemporal dementia involves tau tangles inside cells.
Lewy body dementia features alpha-synuclein deposits and has a faster progression (about 7 years) than Alzheimer's (14 years).
Vascular dementia is caused by small infarctions leading to stepwise decline and is the only treatable dementia.
Treat vascular dementia with lifestyle changes (no smoking), high-dose statins (e.g., Crestor 40 mg), and antiplatelets (e.g., Plavix).
The MIND diet combines Mediterranean and DASH diets with limited wine; alcohol in excess worsens dementia.
Differentiate delirium from dementia by assessing baseline function; delirium involves disorganized thought and inattention.
Use the FAST scale to grade dementia severity and detect acute mental status changes.
Alzheimer's hallmark is short-term memory loss with preserved long-term memory; patients may wander and repeat questions.
Vascular dementia has a stepwise decline tied to infarctions, unlike the predictable temporal decline of Alzheimer's.
Alzheimer's disease follows a predictable progressive course on the FAST scale, while other dementias progress in a haphazard fashion through the same steps.
Visual hallucinations are a hallmark of Lewy body dementia; any dementia patient with visual hallucinations should be assumed to have Lewy body until proven otherwise.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Gout: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 12/18/25
episodes.speaker: Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander emphasizes that gout is primarily a disorder of uric acid underexcretion rather than overproduction, making clearance the key defect. The lecture covers correct dietary counseling (beer, other alcohols, and high-fructose corn syrup are the top three offenders, ahead of high-purine animal foods), the treatment goal of serum uric acid below 6 mg/dL, and the importance of titrating allopurinol to achieve that goal. Acute management options include colchicine, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids, with choice guided by comorbidities. The talk also reviews diagnostic methods including joint aspiration, point-of-care ultrasound, and dual-energy CT, and notes the need to check for HLA-B*5801 in Southeast Asian patients before starting allopurinol.
key_points: The primary defect in gout is underexcretion of uric acid, not overproduction; 90% of cases are due to impaired renal clearance.
The three most important dietary interventions for gout are avoiding beer, other alcohols, and high-fructose corn syrup; high-purine animal foods are fourth.
Serum uric acid treatment goal is <6 mg/dL for most patients; <5 mg/dL for those with tophaceous gout.
Allopurinol should be started at 100 mg daily and titrated upward (typically to 200-300 mg) until the goal is reached; most patients require >100 mg.
Before starting allopurinol in patients of Southeast Asian descent, screen for HLA-B*5801 to prevent severe hypersensitivity.
Acute gout management options include colchicine, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids; choice depends on comorbidities (e.g., CKD, diabetes, heart failure).
Colchicine should be given as low-dose therapy (not high-dose) and is most effective within 24 hours of flare onset; hold statins during colchicine use.
Do not stop maintenance urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare, as rapid changes in uric acid level can precipitate or worsen flares.
Febuxostat is an alternative for patients who fail to reach goal on allopurinol 300 mg; the FAST trial showed no excess cardiovascular risk compared to allopurinol.
Dual-energy CT can reveal the total body burden of urate crystal deposition, which is often more extensive than clinically appreciated.
Treat gout to a target serum urate below 6 mg/dL; do not simply start allopurinol and treat flares as they occur.
If a patient continues to flare after achieving urate goal, reconsider pseudogout or other crystal arthropathies.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Gout - Diagnostic and Therapeutic Principles 1/15/26
episodes.speaker: Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander's lecture on gout emphasizes that the primary defect is underexcretion of uric acid, not overproduction, and that dietary triggers such as beer, other alcohols, and high fructose corn syrup are more important than purine-rich foods. The treatment goal is a serum uric acid level below 6 mg/dL, as this dissolves crystals and prevents flares. Acute management should begin within 24 hours using colchicine, NSAIDs, or corticosteroids based on comorbidities, and chronic management involves titrating allopurinol from 100 mg to 300 mg, with febuxostat as a second-line option. Key pitfalls include failing to follow up to goal and not screening Southeast Asian patients for HLA-B*5801 before starting allopurinol.
key_points: Dietary triggers in order of importance: beer, other alcohols, high fructose corn syrup, then animal purines; plant purines are not a concern.
Gout is primarily due to underexcretion of uric acid (90% of cases), not overproduction.
Treatment goal is serum uric acid <6 mg/dL; for tophaceous gout, target <5 mg/dL.
Most common chart review error is focusing on dietary advice without following up to ensure the goal is met.
Acute gout management: start within 24 hours; choose colchicine, NSAIDs, or corticosteroids based on comorbidities (avoid NSAIDs in CKD, avoid steroids in diabetes).
Colchicine: use low-dose therapy, hold statins during flare, monitor renal function.
Allopurinol: start at 100 mg daily, titrate up to 300 mg, checking labs every 1-2 months until goal is reached.
Screen Southeast Asian patients for HLA-B*5801 before starting allopurinol.
If allopurinol fails to achieve goal at 300 mg, switch to febuxostat.
Do not stop maintenance urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare, as rapid changes in uric acid can worsen flares.
Gout is a crystal deposition disease driven by chronic hyperuricemia.
Definitive diagnosis requires joint aspiration with crystal analysis; ultrasound can detect crystal disease but cannot distinguish gout from pseudogout.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Knee Pain and Problems
episodes.speaker: Rylander
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the evaluation and management of common knee injuries, emphasizing the importance of distinguishing surgical emergencies from minor sprains. Key points include taking a detailed history of the mechanism of injury, differentiating hemarthrosis from effusion, and performing specific physical exam tests such as the Thessalie test for meniscal tears and the Lachman test for ACL injuries. Management focuses on topical therapies like CBD and Voltaren to avoid systemic NSAID risks, and specific reduction techniques for patellar dislocation.
key_points: The mechanism of injury (twisting, direct blow, fall, deceleration) is critical for diagnosing knee injuries.
Hemarthrosis (blood in the joint) causes rapid swelling within hours, while effusion (delayed swelling) occurs >12 hours and suggests meniscal injury.
The Thessalie test (weight-bearing rotation on a bent knee) is more sensitive than McMurray for meniscal tears.
Lachman test (anterior drawer at 30° flexion) is the primary test for ACL injury; a hard stop at <1 cm is normal, soft or absent stop indicates tear.
Posterior drawer test and sag sign are used for PCL injury, often from a blow to the tibia or deceleration.
MCL/LCL injuries are graded by laxity compared to the unaffected side; always compare both knees.
Topical CBD (without THC) and Voltaren gel are effective first-line treatments, avoiding systemic NSAID risks (ulcers, kidney injury, stroke).
Patellar dislocation reduction requires hyperextending the knee to create a window, then gentle medial pressure; avoid forcing it back in flexion.
Ottawa knee rules guide imaging; MRI is gold standard but usually requires prior X-ray per insurance.
Always document functional impact (what the injury prevents the patient from doing).
Patellar dislocation is far more common than true knee dislocation; most patients who think they dislocated their knee actually had patellar dislocation.
Patellar dislocation typically occurs laterally; medial or superior displacement is rare and requires urgent orthopedic evaluation.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on Nerve Blocks
episodes.speaker: Rylander
episodes.abstract: Dr. Rylander's lecture covers the technique for performing common nerve blocks in a family medicine clinic, including occipital, dorsal scapular, suprascapular, and cluneal blocks. He details the preparation of a standard injectate solution (2% lidocaine and 80 mg Kenalog), the use of a 27-gauge needle, and landmark-based approaches to ensure accurate placement. Emphasis is placed on safety measures such as aspiration to avoid intravascular or pleural injection, and the importance of selecting the appropriate CPT code for billing. The lecture also reviews clinical indications for each block, primarily neuropathic pain in the corresponding nerve distribution.
key_points: Use a 27-gauge, 1.5-inch needle for all nerve blocks and joint injections.
Standard solution: 2 mL of 40 mg/mL Kenalog plus 2 mL of 1-2% lidocaine, yielding 80 mg Kenalog in 4 mL total.
For occipital nerve block, landmarks are one-third and two-thirds of the distance from the occipital midline to the mastoid process; inject at the hairline with the patient sitting forward.
Always aspirate before injecting; if blood returns, do not inject; if air returns, suspect pneumothorax and obtain a post-procedure chest X-ray.

Dorsal scapular block uses three injection points: superior (just above the scapular spine at the medial border), medial (midpoint of the scapular body), and inferior (midpoint of the scapula, inferior angle).
Suprascapular block is performed at the midpoint of the scapular spine, with the needle angled 45 degrees upward and medially to reach the suprascapular notch.
Cluneal block involves dividing the upper gluteal region into thirds: medial and superior injections at one-third of the way from the midline, and lateral injection at two-thirds of the way.
Each nerve block has a specific CPT code; occipital block (64405) is 0.9 RVU, lesser occipital and other peripheral nerve blocks (64400) are 0.75 RVU.
Blocks are indicated for neuropathic pain (electric, tingling, or shocking) in the nerve distribution, and can be used for occipital headache, scapular pain, or hip pain.
Ultrasound is not required for these blocks but can be used for confirmation; the landmark-based technique is safe and effective.

episodes.title: Dr. Rylander on PVD/PAD 5/28/26
episodes.speaker: Rylander
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Rylander covers peripheral vascular disease (PVD) and peripheral arterial disease (PAD), emphasizing that arterial and venous disease often coexist and must be assessed as a spectrum rather than mutually exclusive conditions. Key concepts include the importance of distinguishing proximal macrovascular blockages from distal microvascular disease, as well as recognizing that arterial disease in the limb signals high systemic cardiovascular risk. Practical skills reviewed include bedside vascular exams, ankle-brachial and toe-brachial indices, ulcer identification, appropriate use of imaging (duplex, CTA, MRA), and referral thresholds for vascular surgery.
key_points: Arterial and venous disease are not mutually exclusive; always quantify how much of each is present.
Compression therapy for venous disease can worsen arterial disease if applied above arterial perfusion pressure, risking critical limb ischemia.
Microvascular circulation problems are often more important than proximal blockages in determining outcomes.
Toe-brachial index is sometimes more useful than ankle-brachial index when calcified vessels prevent compression.
Arterial ulcers have sharp, punched-out borders with clean pink skin and minimal hemosiderin deposits.
Peripheral arterial disease is a marker for systemic cardiovascular risk (CAD, stroke, carotid disease) requiring aggressive risk reduction.
Exercise therapy for claudication stimulates neovascularization and should be prescribed as walking to near-maximal pain, then rest, repeating cycles.
Patient education must include foot inspection, recognition of worsening ischemia, and urgency to seek care for new wounds.
Referral to vascular surgery is appropriate for active critical limb ischemia (urgent) or for patients who remain symptomatic after risk reduction and exercise.
Avoid referring patients who are not surgical candidates (e.g., active smoking, uncontrolled diabetes) to prevent overwhelming vascular services.
Differentiate arterial claudication from neurogenic claudication using the shopping cart test: bending forward relieves neurogenic but not arterial claudication.
For critical limb ischemia, initiate early vascular consultation and start anticoagulation (e.g., low-molecular-weight heparin) while awaiting evaluation.

episodes.title: Dr. Sakirgil on Abdominal Pain
episodes.speaker: Sakirgil
key_points: Renal colic presents with acute, severe, dull, achy flank pain radiating to the abdomen or groin with vomiting; fever is unusual.
For suspected renal stones without obstruction or toxicity, obtain an urgent CT, start Flomax, and if stone is <5 mm it is likely to pass spontaneously.
Diverticulitis typically presents with left lower quadrant pain; peritoneal signs suggest abscess or perforation requiring ER referral.
Uncomplicated diverticulitis can be treated outpatient with a liquid diet for 2 days and antibiotics (e.g., ciprofloxacin 500 mg TID plus metronidazole 500 mg TID for 10 days).
Testicular torsion must be diagnosed emergently; salvage rate is 80-100% if repaired within 6 hours.
For dyspepsia, a 4-week PPI trial is reasonable; if symptoms persist, test for H. pylori (stool antigen is easier than breath test as it does not require stopping PPIs).
Alarm features for peptic ulcer disease requiring GI referral include age >45, weight loss, anemia, and persistent anorexia ("I eat, and I'm not hungry anymore").
Pancreatitis is diagnosed with lipase >2 times normal and managed with IV fluids; early refeeding as tolerated is now preferred over prolonged NPO.
Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising) are late signs of hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
AAA should be suspected in older patients with sudden-onset abdominal or back pain, syncope, or hypotension; a tender, enlarged aorta on palpation is a key finding.

episodes.title: Dr. Santillano on Breast Feeding
episodes.speaker: Santillano
episodes.abstract: Dr. Santillano's lecture covers breastfeeding fundamentals, including colostrum composition, milk adaptation to the baby's needs, and the importance of proper latch to prevent nipple trauma. She discusses strategies for managing engorgement, waking sleepy babies, and maintaining milk supply through hydration and calorie intake. The lactational amenorrhea method criteria and the role of hand expression and nipple shields are also addressed. Practical pearls include using ibuprofen for engorgement, hand-expressing colostrum into a spoon for supplementation, and recognizing when a baby is in deep sleep by testing arm tone.
key_points: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first 6 months, then continued with complementary foods.
Breast milk supply stabilizes at 24–32 ounces per day after the first month, about 1–1.25 ounces per hour.
Colostrum is thick, cathartic, and rich in antibodies; it helps clear meconium and is harder to express than mature milk.
Milk composition adjusts to the baby’s needs – maternal breast tissue can produce antibodies in response to pathogens from the baby’s saliva.
Engorgement involves both milk and inflammation; ibuprofen is recommended postpartum to reduce inflammation and pain.
Painful latch indicates poor positioning; the nipple should point toward the soft palate, and asymmetric latch with more breast below the nipple is correct.
Sleepy newborns can be stimulated to feed with breast compression, unwrapping, or checking arm tone for deep sleep before attempting to put them down.
Hydration and caloric intake are critical for milk production; electrolyte solutions like Gatorade help maintain supply.

Lactational amenorrhea method for contraception requires exclusive breastfeeding every 4 hours during the day and every 6 hours at night, no supplementation, and is effective only for the first 6 months.
Hand expression of colostrum can begin at 36 weeks, particularly for mothers at risk of needing supplementation (e.g., diabetics).
Milk supply is demand-driven, so supplementation reduces supply by the amount supplemented.
Power pumping can help increase supply: 20 min pump, 10 min rest, 10 min pump, 10 min rest, 10 min pump.

episodes.title: Dr. Santillano on Decreased Fetal Movement
episodes.speaker: Santillano
episodes.abstract: Decreased fetal movement (DFM) is a marker for increased risk of fetal death, though the absolute risk remains low. Maternal perception of DFM can be influenced by factors such as placental location, parity, and maternal activity level. Evaluation includes history, fundal height measurement, nonstress test (NST), and amniotic fluid index (AFI). A reactive NST requires two accelerations in 20 minutes with moderate variability and no decelerations; nonreactive NST or abnormal AFI warrants referral for a full biophysical profile (BPP).
key_points: Quickening is the onset of fetal movement perception; multiparous women feel it earlier than primiparous, and anterior placenta can delay perception.
Fetal sleep cycles last 20–40 minutes; if no movement is felt after one hour of lying down, the patient should seek evaluation.
Kick counts: use the 'two hours, two hands, ten fingers, ten movements' rule; once 10 movements are felt, counting can stop.
DFM evaluation should include history (duration, intensity vs. number of movements), risk factors (IUGR, preeclampsia, diabetes, smoking, prior DFM), and fundal height.
Initial assessment in the office includes auscultation of fetal heart tones; if not quickly obtained, proceed to ultrasound.
A reactive NST requires two accelerations in 20 minutes, moderate variability (5–25 bpm), and no decelerations.
If NST is nonreactive after 20–30 minutes or if AFI is abnormal, refer for full BPP.
Cord entanglement (nuchal cord, true knot) can cause DFM even with a normal BPP the day before; clinical suspicion should remain high.
Uteroplacental insufficiency (from preeclampsia, IUGR, abruption, smoking) is a key risk factor for adverse outcomes with DFM.
Early labor can cause DFM due to uterine contractions squeezing the baby; this does not rule out the need for monitoring.
Decreased fetal movement at 39 weeks or greater warrants delivery regardless of testing results.
Between 37 weeks 0 days and 38 weeks 6 days, persistent decreased movement should lead to delivery; resolved cases may be managed with reassuring testing and discharge with precautions.

episodes.title: Dr. Santillano on OTC tips
episodes.speaker: Santillano
episodes.abstract: Dr. Santillano provides practical tips on over-the-counter medications, emphasizing the importance of educating patients about active ingredients to avoid accidental overdose, especially with NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and cold medicines. She highlights specific recommendations for choosing the correct formulations (e.g., Unisom doxylamine, infant ibuprofen concentration), safe use during pregnancy, and appropriate dosing of vitamins and supplements. Additionally, she covers allergy treatments, nasal spray technique, and OTC options for back pain and UTIs, stressing that OTC does not mean risk-free.
key_points: Educate patients on specific NSAID names to prevent accidental double-dosing.
Choose Unisom sleep tabs (doxylamine) over sleep gels (diphenhydramine) for better efficacy and dose splitting.
Cold medicines often contain acetaminophen; warn patients about overdose risk when combining with Tylenol.
In pregnancy, avoid decongestants (phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine) and medications with '-D' suffix.
Infant and children's ibuprofen have different concentrations; always specify concentration when prescribing weight-based doses.
Limit vitamin D to 2000 IU daily unless deficiency; high doses (10,000 IU) should be taken weekly.
Supplements are not FDA-regulated; consider NSF-certified brands for quality assurance.
For allergic rhinitis, Flonase Sensimist may be better tolerated due to smaller droplets.
Nasal saline rinses require sterile or distilled water to prevent Naegleria fowleri infection.
OTC lidocaine patches (Salonpas 4%) can be used as an alternative to prescription 5% patches.
Resistant lice may require prescription treatments like permethrin or ivermectin; OTC options may fail.
Clotrimazole OTC is effective for fungal infections and works faster than nystatin for hyperdermatitis.

episodes.title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25
episodes.speaker: Satterlee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Satterlee uses a Chinese finger trap metaphor to illustrate the paradox of anxiety: telling someone to relax often worsens it. The lecture then systematically reviews key differential diagnoses for anxiety in primary care, including GAD, panic disorder, social anxiety, adjustment disorder, and ADHD. Emphasis is placed on using ICD-10 codes carefully (e.g., F41.9 for unspecified anxiety vs. F41.1 for GAD) and on practical clinical distinctions such as the role of compulsions in OCD and the importance of ruling out medical causes and safety concerns first.
key_points: Anxiety is a normal adaptive state; the problem is when it becomes the default or is difficult to shift out of.
The Chinese finger trap demonstrates that direct resistance (e.g., 'just relax') worsens anxiety; a paradoxical approach (easing into it) is more effective.
GAD (F41.1) requires six months or more of pervasive, global anxiety; unspecified anxiety (F41.9) is a safer code when the diagnosis is uncertain.
Panic attacks are discrete episodes; panic disorder involves a preoccupation with future attacks leading to behavioral changes.
Adjustment disorder with anxiety is triggered by a specific stressor and is a better initial diagnosis than GAD when the history is unclear.
Differentiating anxiety from ADHD is clinically challenging; consider a trial of ADHD medication (works in 30 minutes) vs. an SSRI (takes 5-6 weeks) as a diagnostic clue.
OCD is distinguished from anxiety by the presence of compulsions and significant time lost to rituals (e.g., hours to leave the house).
In the first encounter for anxiety, essential steps are to assess safety (suicidality, environmental threats) and rule out medical causes (e.g., cardiac, thyroid).
Acute stress disorder (up to 1 month) and PTSD are triggered by life-threatening events, with different diagnostic gate criteria for adults vs. children.
Mixed anxiety and depressive disorder (F41.2) is a useful ICD code when both mood and anxiety symptoms are present but not fully differentiated.
For panic, true panic attacks last minutes, not hours; prolonged symptoms suggest elevated anxiety rather than panic.
First appointment must assess safety, rule out medical causes, and characterize duration, onset, frequency, intensity, and substance use.

episodes.title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain
episodes.speaker: Satterlee
episodes.abstract: This lecture focuses on establishing a framework for managing chronic pain in primary care, emphasizing expectation setting, understanding the patient's experience, and differentiating between addiction and pseudoaddiction. The discussion covers the impact of psychosocial factors such as depression, stress, and caregiver burden on pain perception. Practical strategies include using the VA Whole Health model, recognizing markers of pseudoaddiction, and considering alternative diagnoses like spinal stenosis and post-traumatic arachnoiditis. The importance of maintaining a collaborative, non-judgmental stance is highlighted.
key_points: Set realistic expectations with patients about functional goals rather than complete pain relief.
Use the VA Whole Health infographics to address multiple life domains affecting pain.
Depression and stress significantly distort perception of pain, distance, weight, and time.
Pseudoaddiction (inadequate pain relief leading to medication-seeking) can be distinguished from true addiction by patient's self-modulation of dose and lack of insight in addiction.
Caregiver burden and mental health issues are common comorbidities in chronic pain patients.
Spinal stenosis presents as neurogenic claudication (radiculopathy worse with exertion).
Post-traumatic arachnoiditis is a possible cause after spinal trauma.
Self-harm alternatives like snapping a hair tie can provide sensory feedback without damage.
Assume patients are doing their best; maintain a collaborative, non-judgmental approach.
Use patient's history of dose adjustment (e.g., reducing from 4 to 3 times/day) as a marker against addiction.
Conduct your own history and workup for chronic pain patients instead of relying on prior evaluations.
Flexion-extension X-rays are needed alongside MRI to assess spinal instability in post-traumatic stenosis.

episodes.title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder
episodes.speaker: Satterlee
episodes.abstract: Dr. Satterlee discusses conversion disorder (now called functional neurological symptom disorder) within the context of somatic symptom and related disorders. She emphasizes the need for thorough medical evaluation before making the diagnosis, using the example of a teenage girl initially diagnosed with conversion disorder who later was found to have perilymph fistula—a treatable inner ear condition.
