The lecture covers key distinctions among somatic symptom disorder, illness anxiety disorder, functional neurological symptom disorder, and factitious disorder, focusing on diagnostic criteria and clinical pearls for distinguishing them. She cautions against premature labeling and highlights the importance of thoughtful application of these diagnoses.
key_points: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) requires evidence that symptoms are incompatible with recognized neurological or medical conditions, not merely that no cause is found.
Perilymph fistula is a subtle inner ear condition that can mimic conversion disorder; symptoms may include hearing internal body sounds and coordination difficulties.
Somatic symptom disorder involves distressing somatic symptoms with disproportionate thoughts, feelings, or behaviors related to them.
Illness anxiety disorder centers on preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness, often with minimal or no somatic symptoms.
Factitious disorder involves deliberate deception or self-harm in the absence of obvious external incentives.
These disorders rarely occur in isolation; comorbidity with depression, anxiety, or trauma history is common.
A history of extensive diagnostic testing across multiple healthcare systems should raise suspicion for a somatic symptom disorder.
The diagnosis of functional neurological symptom disorder should be used thoughtfully, as mislabeling can lead to missed treatable conditions and stigma.
The DSM-5-TR groups these conditions under somatic symptom and related disorders, replacing older terms like somatization disorder and hypochondriasis.
Patients with neurodivergent traits may present with either hyperawareness or hypoawareness of bodily sensations, complicating diagnosis.
Illness anxiety disorder is characterized by fear of having or developing a serious illness, not by distress from existing symptoms.
Maladaptive avoidance in illness anxiety can manifest as either care-seeking or care-avoiding behavior.

episodes.title: Dr. Sean Doyle on Common Urologic Problems
episodes.speaker: Sean Doyle
episodes.abstract: Dr. Doyle covers common urologic issues encountered in primary care: hematuria, BPH, UTIs in women, and prostate cancer screening. He emphasizes that hematuria must be confirmed by microscopy, not dipstick alone, and that gross hematuria or persistent microscopic hematuria requires urology referral. He discusses risk stratification for microscopic hematuria workup, noting that renal ultrasound is replacing CT urography for intermediate-risk patients. He highlights that recurrent UTIs may mask bladder cancer, and that vaginal atrophy is a frequent cause of urinary symptoms in older women.
key_points: Hematuria must be confirmed by microscopic urinalysis (>3 RBC/hpf on one specimen); dipstick alone is insufficient.
Anticoagulant use does not exclude the need to work up hematuria.
Gross hematuria is the highest-risk finding and mandates urology referral.
Persistent microscopic hematuria after UTI treatment should prompt further evaluation, as bladder cancer can present as recurrent UTIs.
Low-risk hematuria (women <60, men <40, <10 pack-years, no other risk factors) may be followed with repeat urinalysis in 6 months.
Intermediate-risk hematuria workup includes renal ultrasound and cystoscopy; CT urography is reserved for high-risk patients.
Recurrent UTIs in older women are often due to vaginal atrophy, which alters vaginal flora and predisposes to true infection.
Irritative voiding symptoms, prior pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide, Lynch syndrome, and chronic indwelling catheters are risk factors for bladder cancer.
BPH symptoms in men under 30 or with alarming features should prompt urology referral.
Patients with chronic indwelling catheters need urology surveillance every 1-2 years for squamous cell carcinoma.
Not all patients with BPH need medication; if symptoms don't bother the patient, treatment may be deferred.
Once a man reports urinary symptoms, digital rectal exam (DRE) and PSA are diagnostic, not screening tests.

episodes.title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Ectopic Pregnancy 2/9/26
episodes.speaker: Seeley-Hacker
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the clinical presentation, risk factors, diagnosis, and management of ectopic pregnancy for family medicine residents. The speaker emphasizes keeping ectopic pregnancy high on the differential for reproductive-age women with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, even without classic risk factors. Key topics include the pathophysiology of tubal implantation, the importance of transvaginal ultrasound as the gold standard for diagnosis, and the role of serum hCG and other labs in evaluation. The talk also addresses the moral considerations of treating ectopic pregnancy within Catholic hospital systems.
key_points: Ectopic pregnancy occurs in 1-2% of all pregnancies and accounts for 2.7% of pregnancy-related deaths.
95% of ectopic pregnancies implant in the fallopian tube, most commonly in the ampulla.
Interstitial (cornual) ectopic pregnancies are more likely to rupture due to limited space.
50% of patients with ectopic pregnancy have no identifiable risk factors.
Prior ectopic pregnancy confers a 10% recurrence risk after one episode and >25% after two or more.
Chlamydia trachomatis is a major cause of PID-related ectopic pregnancy due to scarring and interleukin-1 secretion.
If pregnancy occurs with an IUD in place, 50% are ectopic.
Transvaginal ultrasound is the gold standard for diagnosis; MRI may be used for stable patients with suspected extratubal implantation.
A closed cervical os on exam helps differentiate ectopic from threatened or incomplete miscarriage.
Rh typing is essential because ectopic pregnancy can cause alloimmunization in Rh-negative patients.
Pregnancy of unknown location is the term when no intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy is seen despite rising hCG.
Heterotopic pregnancy (simultaneous intrauterine and ectopic) is rare naturally but more common with ART.

episodes.title: Dr. Seeley-Hacker on Pre-Labor Rupture of Membranes (PROM)
episodes.speaker: Seeley-Hacker
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers prelabor rupture of membranes (PROM) and preterm prelabor rupture of membranes (PPROM). Diagnosis relies on speculum examination with pooling, ferning (if microscope available), and nitrazine test for pH change; AmniSure is a second-line test with high sensitivity but low specificity (17-30% false positive). Management is gestational age-dependent, with a goal of prolonging pregnancy to 34 weeks when possible. Indications for delivery include infection (maternal fever, fetal tachycardia), spontaneous labor, and fetal intolerance (abruption, cord compression). Interventions include steroids for lung maturity, magnesium for neuroprotection, and tocolytics for short-term labor suppression, while antibiotics are used as indicated.
key_points: PROM is defined as rupture of membranes before labor onset; PPROM is preterm (<37 weeks) PROM.
Diagnostic triad: pooling of fluid on speculum exam, ferning pattern on microscopy, and nitrazine turning blue (pH shift from acidic to basic).
Avoid digital cervical exam in PPROM due to infection risk; use speculum exam only.
AmniSure test is highly sensitive (>95%) for ruling out rupture but has high false positive rate (17-30%), so it should be used as second-line after clinical exam.
Goal gestational age for management is 34 weeks; beyond that, risks of infection outweigh benefits of prolonging.
40-50% of PPROM patients deliver within 1 week; 70-80% within 2-5 weeks.
Indications for delivery: chorioamnionitis (maternal fever + fetal tachycardia), spontaneous labor, fetal intolerance (abruption or cord compression due to oligohydramnios).
Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone) given to enhance fetal lung maturity in PPROM between 24-34 weeks.
Magnesium sulfate given for neuroprotection to reduce cerebral palsy risk in preterm deliveries before 32 weeks.
Tocolytics should only be used for short-term (48 hours) to allow steroid benefit, not to prolong pregnancy long-term.
Patients with PPROM before 23-24 weeks can be managed outpatient with strict return precautions after counseling about risks.
For PROM <20 weeks, no interventions are indicated; monitor expectantly.

episodes.title: Dr. Shah on Diabetes 12/4/25
episodes.speaker: Shah
episodes.abstract: Dr. Shah's lecture on diabetes emphasizes the critical distinction between insulin deficiency (type 1) and insulin resistance (type 2) for proper diagnosis and management. He reviews pancreatic physiology, the role of C-peptide as a surrogate marker for insulin secretion, and the importance of interpreting C-peptide alongside a simultaneous glucose level. The lecture covers type 1 diabetes autoantibodies, the pitfalls of antibody testing in insulin-treated patients, and the necessity of never withholding basal insulin in insulin-deficient patients to prevent DKA. Finally, Dr. Shah introduces teplizumab, a monoclonal antibody that can delay the onset of type 1 diabetes in presymptomatic individuals with two or more autoantibodies.
key_points: Classify diabetes by pathophysiology: insulin deficiency (type 1) vs. insulin resistance (type 2).
C-peptide is a surrogate for insulin secretion; always interpret with a concurrent glucose level.
In hyperglycemic states (e.g., DKA), C-peptide can be artificially low due to glucotoxicity; do not use it for diabetes typing in uncontrolled settings.
Type 1 diabetes can present in adults, often with a slower, smoldering onset; obtain all four autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2, ICA, ZnT8) when suspecting type 1.
Insulin autoantibodies are not reliable after exogenous insulin exposure; test early if needed.
Treat type 1 diabetes with insulin – basal insulin is essential to prevent DKA; never withhold long-acting insulin in admitted patients.
Teplizumab (Tzield) can delay type 1 diabetes onset by 2–3 years in presymptomatic individuals (stage 2: two or more antibodies with dysglycemia).
Screen for type 1 diabetes in patients with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., hypothyroidism, celiac) using antibody testing.
In the hospital, start insulin drip for DKA, transition to subcutaneous insulin, and determine diabetes type after metabolic control is achieved.
When in doubt, start basal insulin first; you will not be faulted for controlling glucose with insulin.
Screen for presymptomatic type 1 diabetes in patients with a family history of type 1 diabetes, thyroid disorders, or celiac disease by checking islet autoantibodies.
Teplizumab (TZield) is approved for stage 2 type 1 diabetes; candidates must have at least two positive autoantibodies, and the infusion is given over 14 days (30 minutes each).

episodes.title: Dr. Shields on Shortness of Breath in Tuberculosis Endemic Nepal
episodes.speaker: Shields
episodes.abstract: Dr. Shields presents a case of a 7-year-old female from India with shortness of breath, facial swelling, and crepitus in the neck and chest wall. She had a history of incomplete TB treatment. The case illustrates pneumomediastinum with subcutaneous emphysema, likely due to tuberculosis. Key teaching includes manually verifying abnormal vital signs, recognizing crepitus as a sign of pneumomediastinum, using butterfly ultrasound to assess for pneumothorax or cardiac tamponade, and treating with high-concentration oxygen and anti-TB therapy when indicated.
key_points: Always verify abnormal vital signs by checking them manually; pulse oximetry and heart rate readings can be inaccurate.
Crepitus in the neck and chest wall suggests pneumomediastinum or subcutaneous emphysema.
Pneumomediastinum often results from alveolar rupture with air tracking along bronchial sheaths into the mediastinum.
Subcutaneous emphysema feels like bubble wrap and may cause pain with stethoscope pressure.
Butterfly ultrasound can help detect pneumothorax or cardiac tamponade by displacing subcutaneous air.
Pneumomediastinum usually self-resolves; give high-concentration oxygen to accelerate air resorption.
In TB-endemic areas, consider tuberculosis as the underlying cause even if sputum is negative; GeneXpert tests for rifampin resistance.
Obtaining sputum for acid-fast bacilli in children is difficult; clinical diagnosis may be necessary.
Fluid resuscitation with 20 mL/kg of normal saline is appropriate for dehydration or shock.
When confirmatory testing is unavailable and clinical suspicion for TB is high, empiric treatment may be justified but should be weighed against risks.

In resource-limited settings, a patient with TB risk factors presenting with hypotension, tachycardia, distant heart sounds, and crackles should raise immediate suspicion for cardiac tamponade from tuberculous pericardial effusion.
Pericardial effusion does not equal tamponade; tamponade is diagnosed when right atrial or right ventricular diastolic collapse is seen on ultrasound, indicating impaired cardiac filling.

episodes.title: Dr. Simpson on Connections
episodes.speaker: Simpson
episodes.abstract: Dr. Simpson presents on the critical role of compassion in medicine, drawing on research showing that patients remember a lack of compassion years after a traumatic event. He reviews systematic evidence that physician compassion improves clinical outcomes—including better glycemic control, enhanced immune response, and higher medication adherence—while also reducing costly tests and referrals. A randomized trial found that just 40 seconds of a compassionate statement meaningfully reduced patient anxiety. Dr. Simpson argues that compassion is not only therapeutic for patients but can also counteract burnout in clinicians, and he shares a personal n-of-1 experiment in which leaning into connection lifted his own burnout.
key_points: A compassion crisis exists in healthcare: nearly 50% of Americans perceive the system as uncompassionate, and 70% of opportunities for compassion are missed by physicians.
Compassion is defined as an emotional response to another’s pain involving an authentic desire to help, distinct from sympathy or empathy by including action.
A systematic review identified over 20 mechanisms by which compassion benefits patients: buffering stress, modulating pain, and enhancing immune and neuroendocrine function.
High physician compassion is associated with an 80% higher odds of optimal blood sugar control in diabetes and 40% lower odds of acute metabolic complications.
In a University of Wisconsin study, high clinician compassion correlated with shorter duration and lower severity of common cold symptoms.
A Johns Hopkins HIV study found that patients who felt their physician knew them as a person had 33% higher odds of medication adherence and 20% higher odds of undetectable viral load.
Compassionate, patient-centered care in primary care is linked to fewer diagnostic tests, fewer specialist referrals, fewer unnecessary hospitalizations, and lower total charges.
A randomized controlled trial showed that a 40-second compassionate statement from an oncologist significantly reduced patient anxiety compared to usual care.
Compassion activates reward pathways in the brain of the giver, buffering stress and offering a potential antidote to burnout.
Compassionate behaviors can be learned; they are not a fixed trait.
Dr. Simpson’s personal n-of-1 experiment: leaning into connection rather than detaching lifted the fog of burnout.
The compassion hypothesis posits that giving compassion can reenergize providers, not just drain them.

episodes.title: Dr. Simpson on Exploring Clinical Cases Using the DSM-5 11/13/25
episodes.speaker: Simpson
episodes.abstract: Dr. Simpson leads a family medicine residency lecture using a case-based small group format to practice DSM-5 differential diagnosis. Residents work in groups to formulate diagnoses and treatment plans, then reconvene to discuss their reasoning. The session emphasizes that traumatic exposure via media does not meet DSM-5 criteria for PTSD, shifting the diagnosis instead to adjustment disorder or acute stress disorder. The discussion also highlights the importance of psychosocial, spiritual, and cultural factors—including race, trust in institutions, and patient self-perception—in formulating a comprehensive case conceptualization.
key_points: Traumatic exposure via media or video does not satisfy DSM-5 Criterion A for PTSD unless it is occupational (e.g., first responders repeatedly exposed to details of traumatic events).
In the absence of direct or occupational exposure to a traumatic event, the differential should shift toward adjustment disorder or acute stress disorder.
Increases in substance use (alcohol, cannabis) to manage nightmares and sleep disturbance should be assessed as part of the clinical picture and may meet criteria for a substance use disorder.
Avoidance behaviors (stopping jogging, avoiding social media) and hypervigilance (concern for personal and family safety) are core symptoms that must be mapped to specific DSM-5 criteria.
Nightmares, sleep disturbance, and increased alcohol/marijuana use are clinically important flags that warrant further exploration and did not necessarily predate the current stressors.

Psychosocial and cultural factors—including historical marginalization, trust in law enforcement and medical institutions, and desire to be perceived as 'normal'—significantly influence the presentation and rapport.
When interviewing patients from a different background, clinicians must navigate unspoken dynamics related to race, trust, and cultural context even when the same language is spoken.

A thorough differential for a patient with anxiety and avoidance after a stressful event includes acute stress disorder, adjustment disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, depression, OCD, substance use disorder, and medical causes such as hyperthyroidism.

A 32-year-old male with new-onset anxiety after viewing racially charged violence, who denies paranoia and explicitly states he is 'not overtly sensitive about racism,' suggests insight and distress that should be validated.
Residents should use DSM-5 directly during group discussions to ensure diagnostic criteria are accurately applied, as 'it feels like that when you read the back' of the manual.
PTSD requires direct exposure, witnessing, or learning of trauma to a close person; media exposure does not count unless work-related.
Adjustment disorder is diagnosed when distress and impairment are out of proportion to a stressor but do not meet full criteria for another disorder.

episodes.title: Dr. Simpson on Foundational Skills for Physician Counseling
episodes.speaker: Simpson
episodes.abstract: Dr. Simpson opens with a prayer and discussion of the fruit of the spirit and the love chapter to ground counseling in Christian faith. He emphasizes that continuity of care distinguishes family medicine and makes relationship-building essential. He presents research on therapeutic factors showing that extra-therapeutic factors (40%), relationship (30%), and expectancy/hope (15%) outweigh specific technique (15%). He stresses that belief in the technique is key and that social context must be considered. He introduces the BATHE technique as a structured approach to foster emotional connection.
key_points: The fruit of the spirit are relationally oriented and foundational for patient interactions.
Continuity of care is the cornerstone of family medicine and allows deeper relationships.
Research shows extra-therapeutic factors account for 40% of change, relationship factors 30%, expectancy/hope 15%, and specific technique only 15%.
The therapeutic relationship is crucial; if patients leave without hope and expectation, they won't return.
A physician's belief in the treatment technique is more impactful than the technique itself.
Social determinants (e.g., neighborhood safety, food deserts) must be considered when giving advice.
The ACGME requires training in relationship skills because of their proven impact on outcomes.
The BATHE technique is an evidence-based intervention for fostering emotional connection.
Agenda setting is critical: ask for the patient's complete list of concerns using 'Is there something else?' until they say no, and avoid diving in until the list is complete.
Prioritize the patient's agenda and seek confirmation on what can be addressed today; schedule follow-up for remaining issues.
Use the three Es (Excuse, Empathize, Explain) to politely interrupt patients when they go off-task, ensuring the encounter stays on track.
Basic listening skills include attending (being present, eye contact, leaning in), open-ended questions, and reflection of meaning to deepen understanding.

episodes.title: Dr. Simpson on The Caregiver Role in Neurocognitive Disorders
episodes.speaker: Simpson
episodes.abstract: The lecture uses a case of a 76-year-old divorced woman caring for her ex-husband with dementia to explore the caregiver's experience. It stresses the importance of focusing on the caregiver as the patient, not just the dementia details. Practical strategies are offered for assessing caregiver stress, safety risks, and support needs, including medication simplification, respite, and community resources.
key_points: Caregivers are often unpaid, older, female, and may have their own health issues while providing 40+ hours of care weekly.
When a caregiver presents, resist the temptation to focus on the dementia patient's details; instead, center the caregiver's own emotional and physical status.
Assess for elder abuse risk by explicitly asking about caregiver frustration and potential violence.
Evaluate the need for alone time and respite care; 24/7 care without breaks is unsustainable.
Simplify medication regimens for caregivers who manage both their own and the patient's medications, using once-daily dosing when possible.
Encourage caregivers to build community support (e.g., church, support groups) early, as it provides long-term practical and emotional help.
Consider legal and financial planning, such as consultation with an elder law attorney, especially when long-term care eligibility is a concern.
Ask about the caregiver's emotional state, including guilt, anger, sadness, and any irrational but real feelings they may be experiencing.
Recognize the myriad tasks caregivers handle: ADLs, medication tracking, transportation, appointment scheduling, shopping, cooking, cleaning, and managing incontinence.
Caregivers often manage multiple tasks including toileting, feeding, bill paying, and legal decisions, which can be overwhelming.
The caregiver's own health suffers: they are three times more likely to feel extreme stress and 15% are hospitalized since becoming a caregiver.
Personality and baseline coping style influence how a caregiver handles the role, but even resilient individuals eventually exhaust their resources.

episodes.title: Dr. Slaughter, DO on Extrahepatic Cholestasis
episodes.speaker: Slaughter
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Slaughter covers the basics of hyperbilirubinemia, distinguishing between direct (conjugated) and indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin, and their clinical significance. It focuses on extrahepatic cholestasis, with choledocholithiasis as the most common cause, and outlines the imaging and procedural workup including ultrasound, MRCP, ERCP, and CT. The talk also addresses malignant causes such as pancreatic cancer, the role of CA 19-9 in monitoring rather than diagnosis, and common pitfalls like persistent bilirubin elevation due to albumin binding and mixed hyperbilirubinemia after surgery.
key_points: Direct (conjugated) bilirubin is water-soluble and excretable; indirect (unconjugated) is not and requires hepatic conjugation.
Chronic hyperbilirubinemia can cause bilirubin to bind to albumin, leading to a persistently elevated bilirubin even after the underlying cause is resolved.
Alkaline phosphatase elevation does not distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic cholestasis; GGT or 5'-nucleotidase helps when the source is unclear.
High-risk criteria for choledocholithiasis (stone on imaging, acute cholangitis, bilirubin >4 with dilated CBD) allow direct ERCP without MRCP.
Intermediate-risk patients (abnormal LFTs, dilated CBD but not markedly elevated bilirubin) should undergo MRCP before ERCP.
When ERCP fails, alternatives include endoscopic ultrasound with guidewire placement, external biliary drain, or intraoperative cholangiography.
CA 19-9 is not diagnostic for pancreatic cancer but is useful for monitoring treatment response after a baseline level is established.
Pancreatic head cancer typically presents with painless jaundice, weight loss, and abdominal pain; CT with contrast is the preferred imaging modality.
Post-surgical hyperbilirubinemia can be mixed due to hematoma breakdown (unconjugated) and impaired hepatic excretion (conjugated), especially in patients with underlying liver disease.
Isolated alkaline phosphatase elevation should prompt measurement of GGT or 5'-nucleotidase to confirm hepatic origin.
Pancreatic head tumors cause jaundice due to proximity to the common bile duct and are managed with pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple).
The Whipple procedure is a long, high-morbidity surgery (about 8 hours, 40% morbidity) with a mortality rate of about 0.4% recent.

episodes.title: Dr. Slaughter on Acute Diarreal Illness 1/8/26
episodes.speaker: Slaughter

episodes.title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #1: Going Deeper in Trust 1/16/26
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Sutton shares a story from his missionary work in Chad about a patient with a severe donkey bite that became gangrenous due to traditional treatment with donkey dung. Despite IV antibiotics and debridement, the gangrene progressed, requiring amputation to save her life. The case illustrates the importance of trust in the patient-physician relationship, especially when asking patients to accept difficult treatments. It also highlights challenges of practicing medicine in resource-limited settings.
key_points: Trust is essential for patients to accept life-saving but difficult interventions.
Donkey bites can cause severe tissue damage and high infection risk.
Traditional remedies like applying dung introduce pathogens and worsen infection.
Gangrene requires aggressive treatment with IV antibiotics and debridement.
Progressive gangrene despite medical management may necessitate amputation to prevent systemic sepsis.
In resource-limited settings, family physicians may need to perform procedures outside typical scope.
Building trust through demonstrated care and competence enables shared decision-making.
Delayed presentation due to distance or traditional remedies leads to advanced disease.
Close monitoring for ascending infection is critical in gangrene management.
Trust is a key component of the healing relationship, especially in cross-cultural contexts.
Trust is defined as 'really, really believe'—not just intellectual assent but deep, action-guiding conviction.
Trust in God is good for us, bringing peace and joy as seen in Scripture (Isaiah 26:3, Romans 15:13).

episodes.title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #2: Biblical Types of Trust 1/17/26
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Sutton discusses biblical expressions of trust, emphasizing that trust is not a single emotion but can manifest in different forms. He contrasts the peaceful, joyful trust of a child resting in a grandfather's lap with the agonizing trust of Jesus in Gethsemane. Using personal stories from his medical work in Chad, he illustrates how trust can be expressed even in crisis and uncertainty, and he encourages believers to recognize authentic trust even when it does not feel serene.
key_points: Trust is not merely intellectual agreement but deep, action-impacting belief in God's goodness and ability.
Jesus calls believers to trust in God and in Himself, especially when hearts are troubled.
Trust honors God and brings peace to the mind and heart, as described in Isaiah 26:3.
There are different biblical expressions of trust, including peaceful trust and trust in crisis.
The story of the sultan's grandson illustrates joyful, unrestrained trust in a powerful authority.
Jesus in Gethsemane demonstrates trust that coexists with deep sorrow and anguish.
God can supernaturally enable trust in moments of crisis, as seen in Psalm 22 and personal testimony.
Trust does not always look like serenity; it can be expressed through dependence and action in dire circumstances.
The worthiness of the object of trust (God) is more important than the intensity of the believer's feeling.
Recognizing different expressions of trust can prevent false guilt when one's experience does not match a stereotype.
Trust is not the absence of fear; it can be a response to fear, as seen in Psalm 56: 'When I am afraid, I will trust in you.'
Peaceful trust is a supernatural gift from God, often experienced when many are praying, providing calm without knowing the outcome.

episodes.title: Dr. Sutton Lecture #3: Trust and Uncertainty 1/17/26
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Sutton's final lecture in the trust series addresses the relationship between trust and uncertainty, arguing that real faith and good medicine can coexist with unanswered questions. Using the story of Jonathan and his armor-bearer, he shows that biblical risk is obedience in uncertainty. He applies this to clinical practice by warning against formulaic decisions and false certainty in patient outcomes, and encourages residents to hold sound principles while remaining open to Spirit-led, case-by-case discernment.
key_points: Trust does not mean the absence of uncertainty; the myth that it does undermines genuine faith.
Biblical risk is obedience in uncertainty, demonstrated by Abraham leaving without knowing the destination and Esther approaching the king without knowing the outcome.
Cultural background affects how much uncertainty people can tolerate, as illustrated by Hofstede's uncertainty-avoidance dimension.
Evidence-based medicine provides powerful data, but there is never a 100% guarantee that a specific treatment will work for the patient in front of you.

A rigid one-size-fits-all decision rule (always say yes, or always say no) is not the best approach in clinical or ethical dilemmas; maintain principles while using Spirit-led judgment for each patient.
Doctors and leaders feel pressure to appear confident and certain, but acknowledging uncertainty is compatible with competence.
Retrospective storytelling can give the false impression that faithful decisions were made with complete certainty at the time.
When caring for communities, public health considerations and long-term trust may require redirecting patients to appropriate health systems rather than providing ad hoc care.
No formula can put a doctor in complete control; comfort with uncertainty is essential in medicine and in faith.
Trust does not mean the absence of uncertainty; it means confidence in someone's character despite unknown outcomes.
Jonathan expressed uncertainty with 'perhaps the Lord will act,' yet his certainty in God's power enabled him to act boldly.
Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving, whether by many or by few—this certainty undergirds action amid uncertainty.

episodes.title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Disease 12/18/25
episodes.speaker: Swan
episodes.abstract: Dr. Swan discusses common pediatric eye conditions encountered in primary care, including dacryostenosis, retinoblastoma, congenital glaucoma, strabismus, amblyopia, preseptal/orbital cellulitis, conjunctivitis, and hordeolum/chalazion. She emphasizes key diagnostic maneuvers such as red reflex and corneal light reflex testing, and provides management guidelines including lacrimal massage for blocked tear ducts, urgent referral for leukocoria or dacrocystocele, and differentiation between preseptal and orbital cellulitis. Practical pearls include antibiotic choices, referral timing, and recognizing red flags. The lecture also incorporates shared clinical experience and community resources.
key_points: Dacryostenosis (blocked tear duct) is common; manage with lacrimal massage (light downward pressure 3-5 times, three times daily) and refer by one year (or six months per some specialists) if unresolved.
Leukocoria on red reflex exam is a red flag for retinoblastoma; requires urgent ophthalmology referral and brain imaging.
Strabismus is diagnosed by corneal light reflex asymmetry; refer constant strabismus at any age or intermittent after four to six months.
Pseudostrabismus due to epicanthal folds is a normal variant and does not require referral.

Differentiate preseptal cellulitis (anterior eyelid infection) from orbital cellulitis (pain with eye movement, ptosis, vision changes, fever). Preseptal: oral antibiotics with follow-up in 24-48 hours; orbital: emergency department.
For conjunctivitis in contact lens users, antibiotic drops must cover Pseudomonas.
Hordeolum (stye) is painful; chalazion is painless. Stye: warm compresses; refer if >2 weeks. Chalazion: refer if >1-2 months.
Doxycycline is preferred for adult chalazion due to lipophilic penetration; avoid in children <8 years. In children, use Augmentin or cephalexin.
Congenital glaucoma presents with tearing, photophobia, eye rubbing, and cloudy cornea; requires urgent ophthalmology referral.
Amblyopia from untreated strabismus, anisometropia, or deprivation (e.g., cataracts) can cause permanent vision loss; early vision screening is critical.
Topical antibiotics are essential for all corneal abrasions, with choice influenced by contact lens use.
Avoid topical anesthetics and NSAIDs for pain control; use oral ibuprofen or opiates for severe pain.

episodes.title: Dr. Swan on Pediatric Eye Diseases 1/15/26
episodes.speaker: Swan
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers common pediatric eye conditions encountered in primary care, including dacryostenosis, retinoblastoma, congenital glaucoma, strabismus, amblyopia, preseptal and orbital cellulitis, conjunctivitis, and hordeolum/chalazion. Key diagnostic techniques such as red reflex testing and the corneal light reflex are emphasized, along with management strategies including pressure massage for blocked tear ducts, urgent ophthalmology referral for leukocoria or orbital cellulitis, and appropriate antibiotic selection. The talk also highlights important red flags and referral timing to prevent vision loss or serious complications.
key_points: Dacryostenosis (blocked nasolacrimal duct) is common in infants; manage with digital pressure massage 3-5 times daily and refer if not resolved by 6-12 months.
Leukocoria (absent red reflex) is a red flag for retinoblastoma; requires immediate ophthalmology referral and brain imaging.
Congenital glaucoma presents with tearing, photophobia, and cloudy cornea; needs urgent ophthalmology referral.
Strabismus is diagnosed by asymmetric corneal light reflex; refer constant strabismus at any age or intermittent strabismus after 4-6 months.
Amblyopia results from abnormal visual development; screen by asking parents about vision concerns at every well-child visit.
Preseptal cellulitis is managed with oral antibiotics and close follow-up in 24-48 hours; orbital cellulitis requires emergency department referral.
For preseptal cellulitis in children under 8 years, cephalexin is preferred; older children may receive doxycycline or Augmentin.
Bacterial conjunctivitis in contact lens users requires pseudomonas coverage; otherwise, supportive care is often sufficient.
Topical steroids and NSAIDs should be avoided in conjunctivitis due to risk of corneal melting.
Hordeolum (stye) is painful and acute; chalazion is painless and chronic. Refer if not resolved in 2 weeks (stye) or 1-2 months (chalazion).
Corneal abrasions require fluorescein staining and ruling out globe rupture before management.
Topical antibiotics are indicated for all corneal abrasions, regardless of contact lens use.

episodes.title: Dr. Tischler on Abiding in Christ
episodes.speaker: Tischler
episodes.abstract: Dr. Tischler shares his personal testimony of faith, struggles with anger and perfectionism, and how God worked through hardships including a friend's suicide, miscarriage, and the pressures of residency. He emphasizes that true rest comes from coming to Jesus with our burdens, not from performance or perfection. The talk encourages honesty and vulnerability in community, and highlights that our value is found in Christ, not in our achievements or others' opinions.
key_points: Personal testimony illustrates how God transforms character flaws like anger and perfectionism over time.
Residency and medicine create a performative culture that can wrongly tie self-worth to outcomes and approval.
The Greek word 'herkypto' (to thoroughly examine) illustrates the depth of examining the reality of Christ's resurrection.
Hardships such as loss, miscarriage, and marital struggles can deepen one's relationship with God when faced honestly.
Jesus describes Himself as 'gentle and humble in heart,' inviting the weary and burdened to find rest in Him.
Coming to God with our weaknesses and sins glorifies Him because it acknowledges Him as the provider of mercy and grace.
The burden of trying to be the best doctor, spouse, and parent is heavy; Jesus offers a yoke that is easy and a burden that is light.
Vulnerability and honesty in community are essential for spiritual growth and mutual encouragement.
God's faithfulness is evident even in the midst of suffering and failure; He does not tire of us coming to Him.
Our identity and value are rooted in Christ, not in performance, scores, or patient outcomes.
Christ never tires of His people coming to Him, regardless of how many times they fail; each approach honors Him.
Our sins and weaknesses are not reasons for Christ to close His heart; no such reason exists.

episodes.title: Dr. Tischler on COPD
episodes.speaker: Tischler
episodes.abstract: Dr. Tischler presents a comprehensive lecture on COPD diagnosis and management based on the 2023 GOLD guidelines. He emphasizes that COPD must be confirmed by spirometry showing a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio less than 0.7, and that severity is now classified by symptoms and exacerbation history rather than spirometry alone. The lecture introduces the new GOLD groups A, B, and E, which guide initial pharmacotherapy, with long-acting muscarinic antagonists (LAMA) and long-acting beta-agonists (LABA) as the mainstay of treatment, moving away from inhaled corticosteroids. Key clinical tools include the modified MRC dyspnea scale and the COPD Assessment Test (CAT) for symptom assessment, both available on MDCalc.
key_points: COPD is characterized by chronic respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, cough, sputum) due to airway/alveolar abnormalities causing persistent airflow obstruction.
Spirometry is required for diagnosis: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.7 confirms COPD; clinical suspicion alone is insufficient.
Chest X-ray is not required by GOLD but is recommended by UpToDate to evaluate differential diagnoses (e.g., CHF, bronchiectasis, interstitial lung disease).
Severity classification in 2023 GOLD is based on symptoms (using mMRC or CAT) and exacerbation history, not FEV1 alone.
GOLD groups: A (low symptoms, 0-1 moderate exacerbations), B (high symptoms, 0-1 moderate exacerbations), E (≥2 moderate exacerbations or ≥1 hospitalization).
A moderate exacerbation is defined as one requiring treatment with steroids or antibiotics, not necessarily hospitalization.
Initial pharmacotherapy: Group A – bronchodilator (SABA or SAMA); Group B – LAMA + LABA; Group E – LAMA + LABA, with ICS added only for specific indications (e.g., eosinophilia).
Inhaled corticosteroids are no longer first-line; LAMA and LABA combinations are the mainstay.

Common inhalers: SABA (albuterol), SAMA (ipratropium), LABA (salmeterol, formoterol), LAMA (tiotropium, umeclidinium), LAMA/LABA (umeclidinium/vilanterol), triple therapy (fluticasone/umeclidinium/vilanterol).
Pre-COPD (preserved ratio impaired spirometry) is a new concept for symptomatic patients with normal spirometry who are at risk for progression.
COPD is diagnosed by spirometry with a post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio < 0.70.
Severity is now classified using the ABE system, which combines symptom burden and exacerbation history, not spirometry grades.

episodes.title: Dr. Tischler on Counterstrain
episodes.speaker: Tischler
episodes.abstract: Counterstrain is a low-risk osteopathic manipulative technique developed accidentally by Dr. Jones in the 1950s. It is based on the theory that many musculoskeletal pains arise from a dysfunctional nerve-muscle signaling cycle rather than actual tissue damage. The treatment involves finding a tender point, positioning the patient to relax the involved muscle, and holding that position for 90 seconds to reset the signaling. Common applications include anterior and posterior cervical regions and the upper back, with specific positioning rules (flexion/sidebend/rotate away for anterior points, extension for posterior points).
key_points: Counterstrain was discovered by Dr. Jones when a patient's back pain resolved after being left in a comfortable position.
The proposed mechanism is resetting aberrant nerve-muscle signaling that maintains muscle tightness after minor strain.
Treatment requires finding the most tender point using finger pad or thumb pad, not jabbing.
Position the patient to passively relax the involved muscle (shorten it) based on muscle action.
Hold the position for 90 seconds while monitoring tenderness; aim for two-thirds reduction in pain.
Return to neutral very slowly, especially the first 15 degrees, to avoid re-triggering the protective reflex.
For anterior cervical tender points: flex, sidebend away, and rotate away from the tender point.
For posterior cervical tender points: extend the neck (opposite of anterior).
Upper back T1-T3 tender points: patient hugs the table (arms crossed) with neck extended.
Upper back T4-T6 tender points: patient positions arms like sticks (or Superman) with neck extended.
Counterstrain is low risk and can be taught to patients for self-treatment at home.
Verbal consent and communication throughout treatment are essential.

episodes.title: Dr. Tischler on Gout
episodes.speaker: Tischler
episodes.abstract: Dr. Tischler reviews the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and management of gout and pseudogout. Gout requires elevated uric acid, which forms crystals in cooler peripheral joints, triggering acute inflammation. Key diagnostic pearls include rapid onset within 12–24 hours, classic first metatarsophalangeal joint involvement, and the fact that serum urate can be normal during a flare. Septic arthritis must be ruled out, ideally by arthrocentesis, before assuming gout.
key_points: Gout requires hyperuricemia at some point, but not all hyperuricemic patients develop gout.
Uric acid crystals form when serum concentration exceeds solubility (~6.8 mg/dL), especially in cooler peripheral joints.
Acute gout flares peak within 12–24 hours, often at night or early morning.
The first metatarsophalangeal joint is the most common site; erythema is typically confined to the joint, unlike cellulitis.
Up to 40% of gout flares have normal serum urate levels due to acute-phase shifts.
Septic arthritis must be excluded; arthrocentesis is the gold standard when suspicion is high.
Risk factors for hyperuricemia include male sex, obesity, hypertension, CKD, diuretics, and alcohol.
Common triggers for flares include trauma, surgery, dehydration, starvation, fatty meals, and thiazide or loop diuretics.
Tophi represent chronic granulomatous reactions to urate crystals and indicate long-standing disease.
Pseudogout (CPPD) affects 4–7% of adults and is underdiagnosed, especially in the elderly.
Arthrocentesis with crystal analysis is the gold standard for diagnosing gout; crystals are negatively birefringent and yellow.
Gout and septic arthritis can coexist; always wait for Gram stain and culture before ruling out infection.

episodes.title: Dr. Tischler on Syncope
episodes.speaker: Tischler
episodes.abstract: This lecture on syncope defines it as a transient loss of consciousness due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, leading to loss of postural tone, brief duration, and spontaneous recovery. The three main categories are reflex (e.g., vasovagal, carotid sinus sensitivity), cardiac (arrhythmias, structural disease, pulmonary embolism), and orthostatic hypotension. Workup emphasizes a thorough history and physical, orthostatic vital signs, and universal EKG, while head imaging is reserved for patients with neurologic deficits or head trauma. Key pitfalls include the importance of distinguishing exertional syncope (cardiac until proven otherwise) and the fact that a negative orthostatic workup does not rule out the condition, especially in the elderly.
key_points: Syncope is defined as transient loss of consciousness due to global cerebral hypoperfusion, with loss of postural tone, brief duration (5–10 seconds), and spontaneous complete recovery.
The three main categories of syncope are reflex (neurally mediated), cardiac (arrhythmic or structural), and orthostatic hypotension.
Vasovagal syncope is the most common cause, often triggered by stress, pain, prolonged standing, or sight/sound/smell.
Exertional syncope during exercise is a red flag for cardiac causes; syncope after exertion is more likely reflex or orthostatic.
Pulmonary embolism can present as syncope and may be missed; suspect when syncope is unexplained and not associated with spontaneous recovery.

Orthostatic vital signs should be checked in all patients, but a negative result does not rule out orthostatic hypotension, especially if history is suggestive or in elderly patients with delayed orthostatic hypotension.
Universal workup includes EKG; head imaging is indicated only when there are neurologic deficits or head trauma.
Sudden onset palpitations followed by syncope strongly suggests cardiac arrhythmia.
Carotid sinus sensitivity (e.g., from tight collars) can cause reflex syncope; carotid massage should be avoided in the emergency setting.
A long history of recurrent syncope over years points toward vasovagal syncope rather than a cardiac cause.
Syncope definition: transient loss of consciousness from cerebral hypoperfusion, loss of postural tone, spontaneous recovery.
Causes: reflex (vasovagal), orthostatic hypotension, cardiogenic (arrhythmia, structural heart disease).

episodes.title: Dr. Travis Eden on Nutrition and Lifestyle for Obesity Treatments
episodes.speaker: Travis Eden
episodes.abstract: Dr. Travis Eden discusses nutrition and lifestyle interventions for obesity, emphasizing the importance of preserving lean body mass during weight loss, especially with GLP-1/GIP agonist medications. He highlights risks of muscle wasting and sarcopenic obesity from rapid weight loss and weight cycling, and provides practical guidance on optimizing protein intake (1.2-2 g/kg ideal body weight), spacing protein throughout the day, and incorporating strength training. The talk also covers the plate method for meal planning, selecting high-quality protein sources, and behavioral strategies like food tracking to support consistency.
key_points: GLP-1/GIP agonist medications can lead to 20-25% loss of skeletal muscle, similar to weight loss without medications, but risk increases with more potent agents and very low-calorie diets.
Weight cycling (losing and regaining weight) preferentially depletes lean body mass over time, as regained weight is predominantly fat, lowering metabolism and making future weight loss harder.
Sarcopenic obesity is increasingly seen in younger populations, defined by loss of lean body mass and muscle function, not just in the elderly.
Protein intake should be 1.2-1.6 g/kg ideal body weight (up to 2 g/kg), dosed to feed lean mass, not actual body weight, to avoid excessive protein in patients with high BMI.
Spacing protein throughout the day (25-45 g per meal) optimizes muscle protein synthesis; single large doses above 45 g are likely overkill.
Leucine is a key amino acid for stimulating muscle protein synthesis; collagen protein is low in leucine and not optimal as a primary protein source.
Strength training is the most potent stimulus for muscle protein synthesis and can mitigate but not fully prevent lean mass loss during caloric restriction.
The plate method prioritizes lean protein (20-30 g per meal), low-carb vegetables for fiber, and optional healthy fats, focusing on satiety and reducing hyperpalatable foods.
Food tracking (via app or pen/paper) improves accountability and awareness of calorie content, helping patients modify decisions.
Bariatric surgery (sleeve gastrectomy, Roux-en-Y, SADI-S) achieves weight loss comparable to or greater than pharmacotherapy, but body composition preservation remains critical.
Very low-calorie diets (800-1,200 kcal/day) are manageable on GLP-1s but should not be prolonged; patients with lower BMI have less fat tissue and are more prone to lean mass loss.
Hydration and fiber intake are important for patients on GLP-1s to manage gastrointestinal side effects and satiety.

episodes.title: Dr. Warman on Medicare Wellness Visits
episodes.speaker: Warman
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Warman covers Medicare Wellness Visits, focusing on the Initial Annual Wellness Visit (G0438), Subsequent Annual Wellness Visit (G0439), and Welcome to Medicare Visit (G0402). It details the required components of each visit, including the health risk assessment, list of providers, history updates, vitals, cognitive screening, written screening schedule, and health advice. The talk emphasizes common billing pitfalls, such as the all-or-nothing rule for wellness visits, the importance of accurately documenting family history, and the correct use of modifier 25 when billing an E&M service concurrently. Residents are encouraged to leverage MA support, use the ad hoc form for compliance, and perform all elements routinely to avoid unbillable visits.
key_points: Welcome to Medicare (G0402) requires a visual acuity screening, which is often missed; the other annual wellness visits (G0438, G0439) do not.
Annual wellness visits are all-or-nothing billing: missing one required element makes the entire visit unbillable.
Family history cannot be left blank; at minimum document parents' status, and do not use 'noncontributory' – it does not qualify.
The written screening schedule (for next 5 years) must be generated in patient instructions; it is the provider's responsibility.
When billing an E&M with a wellness visit, append modifier 25 to the E&M code; the Medicare code takes precedence in visit hierarchy.
Advanced care planning (ACP) is separately billable only if the teaching physician documents >15 minutes; modifier 33 can waive patient cost-sharing.
Depression screening (PHQ-2/9) is bundled with initial AWV (G0438) but can be billed separately with subsequent AWV (G0439).
Social determinants of health (SDOH) risk assessment is a new separate billable code; only teaching physician time counts for time-based codes.
Use the national ad hoc form at every visit; performing all elements routinely avoids confusion over which wellness code to apply.
If patients also need chronic disease management, document separate chief complaint and plan to justify the E&M service.
The 4Ms (Mobility, Medications, Mind, and what Matters) must be documented in the HPI section, including the patient self-assessment of health (excellent, fair, poor, good).
Mark histories as reviewed in the EMR to ensure bulletproof documentation for audits.

episodes.title: Dr. Whitaker on CVA Management
episodes.speaker: Whitaker
key_points: Use isotonic saline (normal saline or LR); avoid half-normal saline and glucose-containing fluids.
Maintain blood glucose between 40–180 mg/dL; correct both hypo- and hyperglycemia.
Order head-of-bed elevation at 30 degrees with fall and aspiration precautions on admission.
Treat fever and rule out infection; do not give antipyretics prophylactically.
Start DVT prophylaxis (enoxaparin/heparin or SCDs) within 48 hours unless contraindicated; wait 24 hours after tPA.
Prescribe high-intensity statin therapy before discharge.
For patients with high-risk TIA or mild-to-moderate ischemic stroke, start dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 21–30 days after a noncontrast CT rules out hemorrhage.
In the first 24 hours without tPA, allow permissive hypertension (do not treat unless >220/120); if treating, aim for a 15% reduction.
After 24 hours, target BP gradually to 130–145 mmHg using IV labetalol or nicardipine; avoid hydralazine due to unpredictable drops.
Consider a 30-day event monitor (MCOT) for cryptogenic stroke to detect occult atrial fibrillation.

episodes.title: Dr. Williams on Skin Cancer Basics 9/3/26
episodes.speaker: Williams
episodes.abstract: Dr. Williams provides a practical overview of skin cancer basics for family medicine residents, emphasizing their role as first contact for patients unaware of skin cancer. He covers nonmelanoma skin cancers (basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), risk factors including ultraviolet radiation and immunosuppression, and the distinction between precancerous actinic keratosis and invasive cancers. Clinical features, diagnostic biopsy techniques, and treatment options such as cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy, and topical chemotherapy are discussed. Key pearls include recognizing persistent non-healing lesions as potential skin cancers, understanding the high morbidity of squamous cell carcinoma, and the importance of skin checks in high-risk populations.
key_points: Nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) comprises basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC); melanoma is the third major type.
Major risk factors: ultraviolet radiation (sun exposure, tanning beds), immunosuppression (transplant, HIV, certain medications), chemical exposures, and ionizing radiation.
Actinic keratosis (AK) is a precancerous lesion; treatment includes cryotherapy, photodynamic therapy (PDT), and topical fluorouracil.
BCC is slow-growing, often a pink pearly papule with telangiectasias, and rarely metastasizes; SCC grows quickly, is painful, and can metastasize with morbidity similar to melanoma.
Immunosuppressed patients (e.g., on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, azathioprine) have greatly increased SCC risk; transplant patients should see a dermatologist every 6–12 months.
Biopsy (typically shave biopsy) is necessary for diagnosis; do not rely on biopsy margin reports as evidence of complete removal.
High-risk areas for SCC include genitalia, hands/feet, and head/neck; untreated condyloma can transform to SCC.
Persistent non-healing lesions, especially those described as 'spider bites' or 'wasps stings,' should be evaluated for skin cancer.
BRCA1/2 mutation carriers have increased melanoma risk and should have annual skin checks.
Sun protection starting in childhood (sunscreen after 6 months, rash guards, hats) is more effective than starting later; best time to start is now.
Broad shave biopsies are preferred for melanoma to avoid false diagnosis from punch biopsies that may miss invasive components.
Breslow depth is the most important prognostic factor for melanoma, determining treatment and staging.

episodes.title: Dr. Williston on Sleep Disorders
episodes.speaker: Williston
episodes.abstract: Dr. Williston provides a practical overview of sleep disorders for family medicine, separating them into dyssomnias (insomnia, sleep apnea, narcolepsy) and parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors, REM behavior disorder). Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is emphasized as the first-line gold standard for chronic insomnia, though access remains a major barrier. Pharmacologic options, including Z-drugs, trazodone, and low-dose mirtazapine, are discussed with caveats about their risks and limitations. Sleep apnea diagnosis, CPAP therapy, and surgical alternatives like the Inspire device are reviewed, along with practical sleep hygiene recommendations.
key_points: Distinguish acute insomnia (<1 month, often stressor-related) from chronic insomnia (≥1 month) to guide treatment.
CBT-I is first-line gold standard for chronic insomnia (A evidence) but difficult to access; primary care delivery is possible (B evidence).
Sedatives (benzodiazepines and Z-drugs) induce unconsciousness, not restorative sleep; avoid as primary therapy for chronic insomnia.
Z-drugs like zolpidem can cause complex sleep-related behaviors (e.g., eating, driving, burns) and long-term memory loss.
Low-dose mirtazapine (≤7.5-15 mg) improves sleep; higher doses lose hypnotic effect but retain appetite stimulation.
Trazodone use for insomnia requires warning male patients about priapism.
Obstructive sleep apnea leads to hypertension, atrial fibrillation, morning headaches, and decreased libido; treatment includes CPAP, weight loss, alcohol avoidance, and ENT referral.
Home sleep studies are an option; if patients struggle to sleep, Ambien may be prescribed to facilitate the study.
The Inspire device (hypoglossal nerve stimulator) is an effective alternative for patients who cannot tolerate CPAP.
Restless leg syndrome: nonpharmacologic interventions first line, then alpha-2-delta ligands, then dopaminergic agents.
Nightmare disorder (REM) responds to imagery rehearsal therapy; non-REM parasomnias (sleepwalking, night terrors) require a safe environment and parental reassurance.
Avoid sleep studies for chronic insomnia unless other sleep disorder symptoms are present (Choosing Wisely).

episodes.title: Dr. Winters on Malawi & Parasites 5/14/26
episodes.speaker: Winters
episodes.abstract: Dr. Winters presents a structured approach to classifying parasitic infections, dividing them into ectoparasites and endoparasites (protozoa and helminths). He emphasizes that endoparasites like helminths cause eosinophilia due to tissue migration, while protozoa generally do not. The talk focuses on schistosomiasis in Malawi, detailing its life cycle, acute and chronic pathology, and treatment with praziquantel. Key clinical takeaways include the four-to-six-week delay before treatment is effective, the association of Schistosoma haematobium with bladder carcinoma, and the importance of eosinophilia as a diagnostic clue for helminth infections.
key_points: Parasites are broadly classified as endoparasites (helminths and protozoa) and ectoparasites; ectoparasites cause localized infestations without eosinophilia.
Protozoa (e.g., amoebas, Giardia, malaria) are unicellular, lack a tissue migratory phase, and do not typically cause eosinophilia.
Helminths (flatworms and roundworms) are multicellular, have tissue migration, and routinely cause eosinophilia.
Schistosomiasis is a platyhelminth (flatworm) that enters through intact skin in freshwater; the cercariae penetrate painlessly within minutes.
Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) occurs 4–6 weeks post-exposure as eggs are first laid, presenting with fever, urticaria, and eosinophilia; treatment is supportive plus steroids if severe.
Chronic schistosomiasis pathology is granulomatous and fibrotic due to host reaction to eggs; Schistosoma haematobium causes hematuria and is linked to bladder carcinoma.
Praziquantel is the treatment for schistosomiasis but is only active against adult worms, so it must be given at least 4–6 weeks after exposure to be effective.
Diagnosis is by finding eggs in stool or urine (depending on species), or via antibody/antigen detection, ultrasound, endoscopy, or biopsy.
Praziquantel costs $10–20 in Malawi versus approximately $300 in the United States.
For all parasites, a useful clinical framework is to ask: what is the disease, organism, geographic distribution, vector, and treatment of choice.
Schistosomiasis diagnosis standards vary by setting; in Malawi, freshwater exposure and snail vectors are key.
Praziquantel for schistosomiasis is a single-day dose; larger patients may split the dose morning and night for tolerability.

episodes.title: Dr. Yasmin Keefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist
episodes.speaker: Yasmin Keefe
episodes.abstract: Dr. Yasmin Keefe presents a practical approach to coma and disorders of consciousness for non-neurologists. She emphasizes the importance of using precise terminology to describe a patient's level of consciousness, as this directly guides the urgency of response. The lecture breaks down consciousness into three essential components—cortex, thalami, and reticular activating system—using a lamp analogy to simplify the concept. Dr. Keefe also highlights the critical role of delirium prevention and management, especially in patients with preexisting brain vulnerabilities, and provides actionable environmental strategies for the hospital setting.
key_points: Use precise terminology (awake, confused, lethargic, stuporous, obtunded, comatose) to describe consciousness; 'unresponsive' is too vague.
The transition from lethargic to stuporous is a dangerous inflection point because protective reflexes and communication are lost.
A comatose patient differs from a sleeping patient in that they cannot be aroused to wakefulness.
Patients with preexisting structural brain issues (dementia, stroke, TBI, Parkinson's) are more susceptible to delirium.
The Monro-Kellie doctrine explains that any cellular damage can lead to a cascade of edema, herniation, and secondary infarction.
Consciousness requires three intact components: bilateral cortices, thalami, and the reticular activating system (RAS).
Most causes of coma are non-anatomical: metabolic disturbances, intoxications, seizures, and global hypoperfusion.
Delirium in the hospital is driven by environmental factors (dark rooms, sleep disruption, sensory deprivation) and underlying medical illness.
Correcting the underlying disturbance does not immediately reverse delirium; consistent daily management is required.
Specific anatomical causes of coma include large strokes, subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, and anoxic injury.
The reticular activating system (midbrain, pons, medulla) and medial thalami are critical for consciousness; focal injuries like artery of Percheron stroke cause profound coma despite tiny lesions.
Blown pupil in comatose patient suggests uncal herniation; in awake patient, consider ipratropium, scopolamine patches, or trauma.

episodes.title: Dr. Youmans on Preemies in Primary Care
episodes.speaker: Youmans
key_points: Corrected age (gestational age at birth plus weeks since birth) should be used to evaluate growth and developmental milestones for preterm infants.
Late preterm infants (born within 5 weeks of due date) typically catch up by 24 months; extremely preterm infants may not fully catch up by that age.
The CDC milestone tracker app adjusts milestone expectations based on gestational age at birth, helping parents set realistic goals.
Preterm infants are at higher risk for feeding problems due to difficulty waking to feed and tiring easily; using a slow-flow nipple can reduce energy expenditure.
Reflux is common in preemies because of poorly developed lower esophageal sphincter and gut peristalsis; spitting up is expected.
Vaccinations should follow the standard CDC schedule based on chronological age (not corrected age), even for preterm infants.
The new RSV biologic (nirsevimab) is recommended for preterm infants to protect against RSV for the first 6 months of life.

Breastfeeding is particularly beneficial for preemies due to transfer of immune cells and antibodies; mothers should wash pump parts thoroughly after each use and avoid the 'fridge hack' to reduce infection risk.

Preterm infants may require referrals to specialists: dietitians for poor weight gain, lactation consultants for breastfeeding challenges, and physical/occupational/speech therapists for developmental delays.
Parental mental health is critical; rates of postpartum depression are significantly higher in parents of preemies, so clinicians should ask about emotional, relational, and financial stressors.

episodes.title: Dr. Zachary Youmans on Common Orthopedic Injuries for Elbow & Wrist 10/23/25
episodes.speaker: Zachary Youmans
episodes.abstract: This lecture provides a family medicine-focused overview of common elbow and wrist orthopedic injuries, integrating board review questions. Key conditions covered include lateral and medial epicondylitis (tennis and golfer's elbow), olecranon bursitis, cubital tunnel syndrome, and De Quervain's tenosynovitis. The speaker emphasizes conservative management, clinical diagnosis, and appropriate indications for orthopedic referral.
key_points: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) presents with lateral elbow pain and is reproduced on resisted wrist extension; the Cozen test is a specific diagnostic maneuver.
Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) presents with medial elbow pain and pain with resisted wrist flexion.
Both epicondylopathies are overuse syndromes with microtrauma and disordered tendon healing; initial management is conservative with rest, ice, and NSAIDs, typically resolving in 6-12 weeks.
Olecranon bursitis presents with posterior elbow swelling and must be differentiated from septic bursitis; aspiration is indicated if infection or crystalline arthropathy is suspected.
Septic bursitis is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and requires prompt diagnosis with Gram stain, culture, and cell count.
Cubital tunnel syndrome involves ulnar nerve compression at the elbow; Tinel sign at the elbow and elbow flexion test reproduce paresthesias in the ulnar distribution.
EMG/nerve conduction studies are standard for confirming cubital tunnel syndrome, even in straightforward cases.
De Quervain's tenosynovitis causes pain at the dorsal radial wrist and base of the thumb; histopathology shows disorganized collagen rather than inflammation.
Conservative treatment is first-line for all discussed conditions; intra-articular steroid injections for superficial bursae are generally avoided.
Indications for orthopedic referral include failed conservative therapy, significant neuropathy, or evidence of structural pathology like mass effect or fracture.
De Quervain's tenosynovitis is diagnosed clinically with a highly specific Finkelstein test; treatment includes splinting, topical/oral analgesics, and steroid injection.
Carpal tunnel syndrome results from median nerve compression at the wrist; the flick sign (shaking hand to relieve symptoms) is 93% sensitive and 96% specific.

episodes.title: Dr. Zachary Youmans on Lipids in Primary Care
episodes.speaker: Zachary Youmans
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews lipid management in primary care, emphasizing the pathophysiology of atherosclerosis and the roles of LDL and HDL. It covers risk stratification using the Pooled Cohort Equations and the newer PREVENT calculator, highlighting differences in screening recommendations between USPSTF and AHA/ACC. The speaker discusses secondary causes of dyslipidemia, indications for advanced lipid testing (ApoB and Lp(a)), and practical tips for fasting lipid panels. Key takeaways include starting screening at age 20 per AHA/ACC, using risk-enhancing factors, and understanding limitations of risk calculators.
key_points: ASCVD is the leading cause of death; lipid management is crucial.
Atherosclerosis begins with endothelial dysfunction from hypertension, leading to LDL oxidation and foam cell formation.
HDL is protective via reverse cholesterol transport; LDL is atherogenic.
Secondary dyslipidemia (diabetes, hypothyroidism, CKD) is more common than primary genetic forms.
The Pooled Cohort Equations underestimate risk in chronic inflammation and socioeconomic disadvantage; PREVENT includes renal function and A1C but cannot calculate for BMI >40.
USPSTF recommends screening starting at age 40; AHA/ACC recommends starting at age 20 with reassessment every 4-6 years.
Fasting for lipids is recommended for accurate triglycerides, especially if borderline.
ApoB testing can help when triglycerides are high and confound LDL calculation.
Lp(a) testing is indicated for unexplained premature ASCVD or strong family history.
Statin initiation threshold: USPSTF at 10% 10-year risk; AHA/ACC at 7.5%.
CAC score (low-dose cardiac CT) can help stratify intermediate-risk patients who are uncertain about starting a statin.
High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) lower LDL by at least 50% and are preferred in diabetics with additional risk factors.

episodes.title: Drs. Greuel and White on Business of Medicine
episodes.speaker: s. Greuel and White
episodes.abstract: Two family physicians, Dr. Greuel and Dr. White, share their career paths including private practice, OB fellowship, health system employment, telemedicine, and direct primary care (DPC). They discuss financial strategies after residency: renting before buying a house, refinancing student loans, and avoiding lifestyle inflation. They emphasize finding therapeutic outlets outside medicine and considering whole-person care. The speakers encourage residents to seek God's leading in their career decisions.
key_points: Consider various practice models: private practice, health system employment, DPC, telemedicine.
DPC involves no insurance and a monthly membership fee, allowing more time with patients.
After residency, rent before buying a house to understand your true income and avoid overextending.
Be cautious of financial advisors and lenders who target doctors with expensive products.
Evaluate student loan strategy: low fixed interest rates may favor investing over rapid repayment.
Refinance student loans with a fixed term if beneficial for monthly cash flow.
Find therapeutic side projects (e.g., writing) to prevent burnout.
Transitioning to a new clinical area (e.g., OB fellowship) is humbling and requires a learning curve.
Whole-person care takes extra time; consider DPC if traditional settings lead to burnout.
Keep living on a residency budget to pay off loans faster.
DPC uses a monthly membership model, not fee-for-service, providing predictable revenue independent of patient visit volume.
DPC allows for smaller patient panels (500–600 vs. 2,000–3,000 in corporate medicine), enabling longer visits and deeper relationships.

episodes.title: Drs Jones & Shannon on Addiction Med Part 1
episodes.speaker: s Jones & Shannon
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Drs. Jones and Shannon provides a practical guide for primary care clinicians on assessing and treating substance use disorders. It covers the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria, severity classification, and recommended screening (USPSTF). Treatment options include various levels of care (inpatient, residential, outpatient), monitoring programs, and 12-step programs, with a focus on Celebrate Recovery as a Christ-centered alternative. The speakers also simulate a Celebrate Recovery meeting to illustrate its structure and principles.
key_points: Start assessment with the least controversial substances (caffeine, nicotine, alcohol) before moving to controlled substances.
USPSTF recommends screening all adults 18 and older for unhealthy drug use.
DSM-5 diagnosis of substance use disorder requires 2 or more of 11 criteria in a 12-month period; severity: mild (2-3), moderate (4-5), severe (6+).
Treatment includes inpatient, residential, outpatient (IOP), detox, and monitoring programs.
Monitoring programs significantly increase the likelihood of abstinence.
Recommend attendance in a 12-step program for anyone with substance use disorder; common practice is 90 meetings in 90 days.
The 12 steps are based on Christian principles but use inclusive language; each step has a corresponding principle (e.g., honesty, hope, faith).
Celebrate Recovery is Christ-centered, emphasizing that identity is in Christ, not in the problem, and includes step studies lasting 9-18 months.
Celebrate Recovery is for anyone struggling with hurts, hang-ups, and habits of any kind.
A typical Celebrate Recovery meeting includes prayer, worship, announcements, step reading, and sharing.
Step one of 12-step programs involves admitting powerlessness and unmanageability.
Refusing to admit powerlessness can lead to losing everything important.

episodes.title: Drs Jones & Shannon on Addiction Med Part 2
episodes.speaker: s Jones & Shannon
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the practical management of alcohol use disorder (AUD) and opioid use disorder (OUD), emphasizing evidence-based medications, screening tools, and the importance of addressing comorbidities. For AUD, first-line options include naltrexone, acamprosate, gabapentin, and topiramate, while disulfiram has fallen out of favor. For OUD, buprenorphine formulations (Suboxone, Sublocade, Brixadi) are the mainstay, with methadone restricted to federally certified clinics. The speakers highlight the need for careful induction to avoid precipitated withdrawal and the importance of reducing cognitive load for patients.
key_points: USPSTF recommends screening adults for alcohol use disorder (Level B evidence); the single-question screen (5+ drinks for men, 4+ for women in the past year) is positive if the answer is 1 or more.
CAGE questionnaire is less sensitive/specific than the single-question screen or AUDIT; use AUDIT for further assessment after a positive screen.
First-line medications for AUD include naltrexone (oral or injectable), acamprosate, gabapentin, and topiramate; disulfiram is no longer recommended due to poor real-world adherence.

Naltrexone is safe in compensated cirrhosis (2024 guidelines) but should be avoided in decompensated liver disease; screen for concurrent opioid use before starting to prevent precipitated withdrawal.
Acamprosate is best for patients already abstinent to prevent relapse; avoid in severe renal dysfunction and adjust dose for CKD.
Gabapentin is safe for patients still drinking and reduces heavy drinking days; topiramate can be started at 25 mg daily and titrated up.
Baclofen and varenicline (Chantix) are alternative options for AUD, especially for patients with severe liver/renal disease or combined alcohol and nicotine use.
Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with a ceiling effect, making overdose risk low; the X-waiver is no longer required—any DEA-registered prescriber can prescribe it.
Buprenorphine induction should begin when the patient is in mild-to-moderate withdrawal to avoid precipitated withdrawal; start with 4 mg and titrate based on symptoms.
Methadone for OUD can only be prescribed in federally certified opioid treatment programs; it cannot be prescribed from a general clinic for addiction.
Sublocade is a depot injection that may require surgical removal if a reaction occurs; Brixadi is a newer IM injection that does not require refrigeration and is less painful.
For patients with OUD, consider long-acting injectable buprenorphine (e.g., Sublocade or Brixadi) to improve adherence and reduce cognitive load.

episodes.title: Female Sexual (Dys)function
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture challenges common misconceptions about female sexual response, emphasizing that arousal is primarily cerebral rather than genital. It critiques the traditional four-phase model for omitting desire and intimacy, and explains why there is no effective female Viagra due to the complex interplay of psychological, relational, and physiological factors. Key concepts include non-concordance, the strong placebo effect in female sexual dysfunction treatments, and the importance of individualized assessment. The talk encourages a biopsychosocial approach and comfort in discussing sexual health with patients.
key_points: Female sexual response is not a physiological drive; it has no essential survival function.
The traditional four-phase model (excitement, plateau, orgasm, resolution) is inadequate; it omits desire, intimacy, and context.
There is no universally accepted model for female sexual response; current models are more complex and include biopsychosocial factors.
There is no effective ‘female Viagra’ because increasing genital arousal alone does not reliably increase desire; psychological and relational factors are paramount.
Arousal concordance (the ability to accurately detect one’s own arousal) is poor in both sexes; men are correct only 50% of the time.
Non-concordance refers to the mismatch between subjective and genital arousal within an individual, not between partners.
Placebo effects in female sexual dysfunction drug trials are substantial (>40%), complicating assessment of true efficacy.
Many common myths about female sexuality are false: women do not respond less to sexual stimuli, and genital response is not a reliable indicator of arousal.
There is more variation in sexual response within genders than between genders, cautioning against overgeneralization.
Clinicians should be comfortable using appropriate terminology and asking about sexual concerns, and should consider collaboration with behavioral health specialists.
Female sexual dysfunction is underdiagnosed due to cultural stigma and patient reluctance.
The three DSM-5 categories are sexual interest/arousal disorder, orgasmic disorder, and genitopelvic pain/penetration disorder.

episodes.title: FMIS August MM
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This FMIS Morbidity and Mortality conference discusses two cases highlighting diagnostic and management pitfalls. The first case involves a patient with ESRD and a TIA who received IVF from an ischemic stroke order set, risking volume overload. The second case describes a patient with atypical heart failure presentation (dyspnea without chest pain) who had a delayed diagnosis of NSTEMI and cardiomyopathy. Key lessons include the importance of verifying all active orders, including IVF, when assuming patient care, and recognizing that dyspnea can be an anginal equivalent for MI, especially in patients with risk factors. The conference emphasizes the need for careful clinical decision-making, thorough handoffs, and appropriate use of order sets tailored to the patient's specific condition.
key_points: Always check the MAR and all running IV fluids when assuming care of a patient, especially those with ESRD or heart failure.
TIA and ischemic stroke are treated differently; TIA does not require IVF, while ischemic stroke may if volume depleted.
Volume overload is a major risk in ESRD patients, especially after missed HD, and can worsen CHF.
Dyspnea on exertion can be an anginal equivalent for MI; one-third of patients with confirmed MI have no chest pain.
If suspicion is high enough to order a troponin in clinic, the patient should be sent to the ER for evaluation.
Acute heart failure requires urgent evaluation and intervention, including possible same-day cardiac catheterization.
Order sets should be reviewed critically; each order must be appropriate for the patient's current diagnosis and comorbidities.
Document all treatments, especially IVF, in the H&P and progress notes under the specific problem being treated.
Consult specialists early for ESRD patients to arrange HD and avoid volume overload.
Atypical presentations of MI (e.g., dyspnea alone) require a high index of suspicion, especially in patients with diabetes or prior heart disease.
Shortness of breath should be nuanced like pain; always consider cardiac causes.
Up to one-third of myocardial infarctions present without chest pain.

episodes.title: Gina Blevins on Healthy Start
episodes.speaker: Gina Blevins
