episodes.abstract: Gina Blevins describes the Healthy Start program, which aims to reduce infant mortality in Tulsa by providing case management and support to pregnant and postpartum women in specific ZIP codes. She offers services including lactation counseling, infant massage education, home visits, and resource referrals, emphasizing early enrollment before the third trimester for optimal data collection. Key teaching points include the importance of wet diapers to gauge feeding adequacy, the normal timeline for milk to come in (3-4 days), and the misconception that hospital-provided formula brands are medically recommended. She also highlights red flags like persistent nipple shield use beyond two weeks and the need to address social determinants of health such as food insecurity and domestic violence.
key_points: Infant mortality is defined as death before age 1; Tulsa's rate dropped from 18 to ~9-10 per 1000 but is trending upward again.
Healthy Start enrolls pregnant women ideally before the third trimester to collect meaningful outcome data for HRSA.
Certified infant massage benefits drug-addicted babies, jaundice, postpartum depression, and failure to thrive.
Breastfeeding education: colostrum is sufficient for a newborn's cherry-pit-sized stomach; milk typically comes in at 3-4 days.
Wet diaper count is the primary gauge of adequate intake; 6 wet diapers per day indicates sufficient feeding.
Return to birth weight within 14 days (21 days for premature infants) is a key milestone.
Hospital-provided formula (e.g., Similac) is chosen by lowest bid, not medical necessity; switching brands is safe.
Similac commonly causes constipation in breastfed infants who supplement; Enfamil is often better tolerated.
Nipple shields should be discontinued by 2 weeks postpartum; persistent use requires evaluation of latch issues.
Healthy Start is not income-based and accepts teens, older moms, and those with complex social needs.
Domestic violence patients can use a code word via text to trigger police response.
Referrals can be made by emailing Gina directly; she also reviews Athena for new OB patients.

episodes.title: Gyn with Dr. Calvert
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews abnormal uterine bleeding, focusing on physiologic causes like menarche, perimenopause, PCOS, and insulin resistance. The speaker explains menstrual cycle physiology, including the roles of estrogen, LH, FSH, and progesterone, and emphasizes the importance of timing when starting low-dose birth control pills. Clinical cases illustrate management of perimenopausal bleeding, hypothalamic amenorrhea from stress, and chronic anovulation. Diagnostic criteria for PCOS are discussed, along with practical pearls for using progesterone-only pills in patients with DVT history and for evaluating irregular periods.
key_points: Abnormal uterine bleeding is categorized as dysfunctional (physiologic) or organic (polyps, cancer, infection).
The menstrual cycle has proliferative (follicular) and secretory (luteal) phases; progesterone withdrawal triggers menstruation.
Low-dose birth control pills (15-25 mcg estrogen) must be started in the first three days of the cycle to prevent ovulation.
Perimenopause onset is defined by irregular periods (interval, flow, or duration), not hot flashes; average onset age is 45.
Menopause is diagnosed after 12 months of amenorrhea; average age is 52, with 90% of women menopausal by age 54.
In perimenopause, low-dose estrogen OCPs can regulate cycles; consider progesterone-only pills if DVT history.
Hypothalamic amenorrhea from stress (e.g., death, divorce, illness) is common; ask about life stressors before extensive labs.
Chronic anovulation has two main causes: PCOS and insulin resistance; check A1c and evaluate for PCOS.
PCOS diagnosis requires two of three: irregular periods, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, elevated testosterone (or clinical hirsutism).
In young girls with irregular periods, observe for up to two years before intervening, as physiology takes time to stabilize.

episodes.title: Heather Bell, DO on the Role of Physician Advisor
episodes.speaker: Heather Bell
episodes.abstract: Physician advisors help residents navigate complex insurance and documentation requirements. Dr. Bell explains how ICD-10 and CMS rules shifted notes from clinical communication to compliance tools, and how her team supports physicians by handling peer-to-peer reviews, denial appeals, and clinical documentation integrity queries. She emphasizes that insurers often deny claims as a strategy, but overturn 92% of denials when challenged. The lecture covers the difference between inpatient, observation, and outpatient-in-a-bed statuses, the importance of documenting severity to justify length of stay, and how good documentation can protect against denials even when patients recover quickly.
key_points: Physician advisors help fight insurance denials (e.g., UHC denies ~70% preemptively; 92% overturned on peer-to-peer review).
Clinical notes must now serve insurance and regulatory language, not just physician-to-physician communication.
Queries are not criticism; they are prompts to document compliantly using required terminology (e.g., CKD stage 3a, acute on chronic kidney injury).
Observation is an outpatient status with observational services; it does not depend on geographic bed location.
CMS two-midnight rule determines inpatient vs. observation; if clinical intent was for longer stay but patient improves quickly, documentation of that intent supports the inpatient designation.
DRG codes link specific diagnoses to expected lengths of stay — detailed documentation directly affects reimbursement and perceived severity.
When a UR nurse says a patient doesn't meet inpatient criteria, it's often a documentation problem, not a clinical error.
Readmissions within 30 days may be bundled for surgical complications or penalized for CHF exacerbations if discharge planning is deemed inadequate.
CMS requires at least three midnights as inpatient for Medicare SNF qualification; status changes can affect that qualifying period.
Good documentation of severity and intent is the strongest defense against retrospective denials.
Physician advisors handle peer-to-peer reviews for insurance denials, freeing hospitalists from disruptive calls.
InterQual criteria are used for most payers; MCG (Milliman) is used by Blue Cross Blue Shield and is more specific.

episodes.title: Inflammatory Breast Cancer - Dr. Jon Calvert
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture reviews inflammatory breast cancer (IBC), a rare but aggressive malignancy that accounts for 1–5% of breast cancers and presents with rapid progression of erythema, swelling, and peau d'orange skin changes over weeks to months. Key diagnostic challenges include distinguishing IBC from mastitis, cellulitis, and other inflammatory conditions; a critical management principle is close follow-up (e.g., 2–3 weeks) because IBC erythema expands quickly whereas infection improves with antibiotics. The lecture emphasizes that IBC often presents without a palpable mass, has a median age of 59, and carries a ten-year survival rate of about 18%, underscoring the need for timely biopsy and referral.
key_points: Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) accounts for 1–5% of breast cancers and is rapidly progressive, often developing from zero to presentation over 3–6 months.
The most common symptom of IBC is unilateral swelling or sensation of heaviness in the breast (79% of cases); the primary presenting sign is erythema.
It is uncommon to palpate a mass in IBC because the pathology involves tumor emboli blocking dermal lymphatics, causing skin thickening and peau d'orange without a discrete tumor.
Large axillary and infraclavicular nodes should be palpated; IBC often presents at stage III or IV (60–70% of cases).
The ten-year survival rate for IBC is approximately 18%, similar to ovarian cancer, but IBC progresses much faster.
A key management pearl: when mastitis is suspected but IBC is possible, start antibiotics and schedule close follow-up (e.g., 2 weeks) because IBC erythema rapidly worsens while infection improves.
The most common finding on ultrasound in IBC is skin thickening.

First-line treatment for IBC involves three stages: neoadjuvant chemotherapy to shrink tumor, then surgical removal (mastectomy), then post-mastectomy radiation — all delivered rapidly due to the aggressive course.

Differential diagnoses for IBC include mastitis (lactational and nonlactational), idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, radiation-induced inflammation, cellulitis, folliculitis, hidradenitis suppurativa, and breast abscess.

Mastitis typically presents with central erythema around the areola spreading outward, whereas IBC erythema is more diffuse and rapidly progresses to involve at least one-third of the breast within weeks.

episodes.title: Injections/Outpatient Procedures
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the principles and techniques of joint and soft-tissue injections commonly performed in outpatient family medicine. Key topics include proper patient selection, adequate NSAID trial duration and dosing, safe use of local anesthetics, and steroid selection. The speaker emphasizes the importance of sterile technique, avoiding common pitfalls like touching the injection site after cleaning, and knowing the contraindications such as joint prosthesis or uncontrolled coagulopathy.
key_points: An adequate NSAID trial should last 10 days to 2 weeks before considering an injection.
The proper anti-inflammatory dose of naproxen is 500 mg twice daily; ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily.
Maximum safe dose of lidocaine is 300 mg for adults, which equals 15 mL of 2% lidocaine or 30 mL of 1% lidocaine.
Always check for contraindications before injection: joint prosthesis, bacteremia, osteomyelitis, impending joint replacement, poorly controlled diabetes, and coagulopathy.
For patients on warfarin, injection is safe if INR is less than 3.0-3.6 and is considered safe.
Never inject into the substance of a tendon; if the syringe plunger does not move, do not force it.
Do not touch the cleaned injection site; if you do, you must re-clean the area.
Always withdraw the plunger before injecting to confirm you are not in a blood vessel.
Common injectable steroids include triamcinolone (Kenalog), methylprednisolone (Depo-Medrol), betamethasone (Celestone), and dexamethasone (Decadron).
A typical knee injection uses 5-6 mL total: 1 mL Kenalog 40 mg, optionally 1 mL dexamethasone, and 4 mL of 2% lidocaine without epinephrine.
Plantar fasciitis hallmark symptom is first-step pain in the morning that improves as the day progresses.
Conservative treatment for plantar fasciitis includes icing, stretching, proper footwear, weight loss, activity modification, night splints, physical therapy, NSAIDs, and orthotic inserts.

episodes.title: Internet Addiction - Rev. Joel Leitch
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: The lecture discusses Internet addiction as a model for process (behavioral) addictions, contrasting it with substance addictions. The speaker notes that Internet addiction is not a formal DSM-5 diagnosis, but gaming disorder is. Key components include excessive use, withdrawal, tolerance, and negative repercussions. The talk highlights the severity of Internet addiction using South Korea data, where 2.1% of children require treatment and up to 24% need hospitalization. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated the problem, with increased screen time and associated mental health issues.
key_points: Process addictions (behavioral) are distinct from substance addictions.
Internet addiction is not a formal DSM-5 diagnosis; gaming disorder is recognized.
Denial is a key defense mechanism that prevents recognition of addiction.
Dependence (e.g., insulin) is not the same as addiction.
Addiction is defined by continued use despite negative consequences, not by amount or frequency.
Withdrawal from process addictions is primarily emotional/psychological, not deadly.
Tolerance develops as need for more time, better equipment, or more intense engagement.
Negative repercussions include arguments, lying, poor achievement, social isolation, and fatigue.
South Korea reports 2.1% of children require treatment, 80% may need psychotropics, 20-24% need hospitalization.
COVID-19 has increased screen time and worsened mental health outcomes, especially in teens.
Internet addiction is classified as an impulse-control disorder with five types: cybersexual, cyber-relational, net gaming, information overload, and computer addiction.
86% of U.S. internet addiction cases have at least one other DSM-5 diagnosis, most commonly insomnia, anxiety, depression, or eating disorders.

episodes.title: Jina Hagen, MS on cfDNA & Carrier Screening 8/28/25
episodes.speaker: Jina Hagen, MS
episodes.abstract: Jina Hagen from Labcorp reviews cell-free DNA (cfDNA) screening using massively parallel sequencing to detect fetal trisomies and subchromosomal abnormalities. She explains that fetal DNA fragments are smaller than maternal fragments, enabling fetal fraction calculation, and discusses ACOG guidelines recommending NIPT for all pregnant women. The presentation also covers the Maternity Genome reflex option for deeper sequencing when later concerns arise and emphasizes the importance of positive predictive value in counseling. Finally, she reviews carrier screening for autosomal recessive conditions, highlighting that CF and SMA screening should be offered to all patients and noting that 1-2% of couples are at risk for an affected child.
key_points: NIPT uses massively parallel sequencing to count DNA fragments from each chromosome and detect overrepresentation indicating trisomy.
Fetal DNA fragments average ~130 bp, maternal ~160 bp, allowing fetal fraction determination by size distribution.
ACOG 2020 practice bulletin 226 recommends offering NIPT to all pregnant women as the most sensitive and specific screening for trisomies.
Positive predictive value (PPV) of NIPT is ~80% overall, compared to ~3.5% for first-trimester serum screening, but PPV depends on population prevalence.
Labcorp retains the blood sample until the due date; if later ultrasound concerns arise, providers can request the Maternity Genome reflex for deeper sequencing to detect subchromosomal events.
Carrier screening for cystic fibrosis (CF) and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) should be offered to all patients regardless of ethnicity per ACOG.
Expanded carrier screening can test many conditions for the same price and is especially useful preconceptually.
Approximately 1-2% of couples are at risk for having a child with an autosomal recessive disorder.
ACOG recommends carrier screening for cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and hemoglobinopathies.
Cell-free DNA (Maternity21) can be initiated at 9 weeks and performed throughout pregnancy, with fetal fraction increasing over time.
Traditional serum screening (quad screen, first trimester screen) uses algorithms and has higher false-positive rates compared to cfDNA.
cfDNA has a screen positive rate of about 1% or less, reducing patient anxiety and unnecessary follow-up.

episodes.title: Joint Injections - Dr. Enis Sakirgil
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Enis Sakirgil lectures on the fundamentals of joint and soft tissue injections for family medicine residents. He covers critical safety principles, including the maximum dose of lidocaine and the importance of knowing milligram doses, not volume. The talk details indications, contraindications, and technique for common injections like trigger points and knees. Emphasis is placed on patient consent, steroid potency equivalencies, and the absolute prohibition of multidose vials to prevent septic arthritis.
key_points: Joint and soft tissue injections are indicated for inflammation (OA, bursitis, tendonitis) after failure of conservative therapy.
The maximum dose of lidocaine is 4.5-5 mg/kg; compute milligram dose, not volume, because concentration varies (1% = 10 mg/mL, 2% = 20 mg/mL).
Never use multidose vials for local anesthetic or steroid due to contamination risk leading to septic arthritis; prepare your own mix from single-use vials.
Absolute contraindications: overlying skin infection, uncontrolled diabetes, allergy to injectate, bacteremia, joint replacement (metal), osteochondral fracture, bleeding disorder with INR >3.
Joint/soft tissue injection with warfarin is safe if INR <3; apixaban does not require monitoring but shared decision-making applies.
Orthopedic guidelines recommend waiting at least 3 months between last corticosteroid injection and joint replacement surgery.
Trigger point injection technique: palpate tender cords, mark spots, inject 1 mL mix (triamcinolone + lidocaine) at 1 cm depth with fine needle (25-27G, 1 inch).
Always aspirate before injecting to confirm no blood return; do not inject against resistance (may be intratendinous).
Corticosteroid equivalency: 40 mg triamcinolone = 4 mg dexamethasone; triamcinolone potency is 5, dexamethasone is 20 relative to hydrocortisone.
Knee injection: patient supine with towel under knee, enter at lateral patellar triangle (45° angle under patella), avoid scraping cartilage.
Plantar fasciitis injection should be performed from the medial side, one fingerbreadth above the sole, avoiding the heel fat pad and the fascia itself to prevent rupture and fat atrophy.
Maximum injectate volume for plantar fasciitis is 3 mL; for the acromioclavicular joint it is 1 mL.

episodes.title: Karen Alley on the Hope Pregnancy Center
episodes.speaker: Karen Alley
episodes.abstract: Karen Alley from Hope Pregnancy Center provides an overview of pregnancy resource center services, including medical services like urine pregnancy testing and limited OB ultrasound, social services such as parenting classes and material support, and spiritual encouragement. She discusses how to compassionately engage with women facing unplanned pregnancies, emphasizing active listening, exploring support systems, and providing accurate fetal development information. The talk covers practical dos and don'ts for healthcare providers, including avoiding assumptions, not overwhelming with facts, and not avoiding hard conversations. She also touches on abortion pill reversal and the legal protections for religious organizations regarding abortion referrals.
key_points: Pregnancy resource centers are nonprofit, faith-based organizations staffed mostly by volunteers, offering medical, social, and spiritual services.
Hope Pregnancy Center provides urine pregnancy testing and limited OB ultrasound to confirm pregnancy, then refers patients to prenatal care.
Centers offer unbiased education on all three options: parenting, adoption, and abortion, but never provide or refer for abortion services.
The Empowered Parenting Program offers weekly classes and a baby store where clients earn points for baby items, supporting them through the first year.
Abortion recovery programs like 'Forgiven and Set Free' help women heal emotionally and spiritually from past abortion experiences.
Half of U.S. pregnancies are unplanned; many women present in crisis with emotions like shock, denial, fear, and confusion.
Providers should use open-ended questions, avoid 'why' questions to prevent defensiveness, and focus on understanding the patient's circumstances.
Fetal development information and ultrasound are powerful tools to help women understand the life within them.
Healthcare providers are not legally obligated to refer for abortion services, especially when part of a religious organization.
Abortion pill reversal is a service some pregnancy centers offer, though Hope Pregnancy Center's nurse manager was unavailable to discuss details.
Mifepristone (the first abortion pill) blocks progesterone, which is essential for maintaining pregnancy.
Abortion pill reversal involves supplementing with bioidentical progesterone within 72 hours of taking mifepristone.

episodes.title: Kelly Dunn, MD on Antipsychotics & Mood Stabilizers
episodes.speaker: Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the pharmacology and side effects of antipsychotic medications, including first-generation (typical) and second-generation (atypical) agents. The speaker explains mechanisms of action, dopamine pathways, and key adverse effects such as extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, metabolic syndrome, QT prolongation, and anticholinergic effects. Clinical pearls include dosing considerations, monitoring recommendations, and identification of subtle signs of movement disorders. The lecture emphasizes the importance of balancing efficacy and safety in psychiatric prescribing.
key_points: First-generation antipsychotics primarily block dopamine D2 receptors; low-potency agents have more histamine and muscarinic blockade.
Second-generation antipsychotics also block D2 but have additional 5-HT2A antagonism, reducing EPS risk; aripiprazole and brexpiprazole are partial agonists.
Dopamine pathways: mesolimbic (positive symptoms), mesocortical (negative symptoms), nigrostriatal (EPS), tuberoinfundibular (hyperprolactinemia).
EPS include akathisia (restlessness, suicide risk), dystonia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia (often irreversible, catch early).
NMS is a psychiatric emergency with fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, and rhabdomyolysis.
Second-generation antipsychotics are associated with metabolic syndrome; monitor BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, A1c, lipids at baseline and follow-up.
QT prolongation risk: baseline ECG for pimozide, IV haloperidol, and others; avoid starting if QTc >450, reduce dose if >500 or increase >60.
Anticholinergic effects are prominent with clozapine, leading to severe constipation; also risk of neutropenia, myocarditis, seizures.
Black box warning: increased risk of death in elderly with dementia-related psychosis; use only when benefits outweigh risks.
Dosing considerations: aripiprazole in morning (activating), lurasidone with food (~300 calories), quetiapine often at night but may need divided doses.
Lithium target levels are 0.6–1.5 mEq/L; for outpatients, 0.6–1.0 is typical; levels >1.0 are used cautiously in acute mania.
Lithium toxicity is dose-dependent and fatal; check levels after 5 days (steady state) and every 3–6 months when stable.

episodes.title: Kelly Dunn, MD on Benzodiazepines
episodes.speaker: Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A receptor activity, producing anxiolytic, sedative, and muscle-relaxant effects. Tolerance develops rapidly—sedative effects within 1–2 weeks, anxiolytic effects within months—and chronic use can increase baseline anxiety through receptor downregulation. Most benzodiazepine prescriptions are diverted; only about 20% of users obtain them through appropriate medical channels. Short-term use (4–6 weeks for anxiety, 1–2 weeks for insomnia) is appropriate, but long-term prescribing should generally be avoided due to tolerance, dependence, and withdrawal risks.
key_points: Benzodiazepines bind to the alpha-gamma subunit of the GABA-A receptor, increasing chloride ion conductance and neuronal inhibition.
Tolerance to the sedative effect develops in 1–2 weeks; tolerance to the anxiolytic effect develops within a few months.
Chronic benzodiazepine use decreases endogenous GABA and downregulates GABA-A receptors, potentially increasing baseline anxiety.
About 80% of benzodiazepine users obtain the drug from a friend or relative, indicating high diversion rates.
Benzodiazepines are first-line for alcohol withdrawal, seizures, acute movement disorders, and catatonia (e.g., lorazepam challenge).
For panic disorder, the time to peak plasma level (1–2 hours for alprazolam) often exceeds the duration of a typical panic attack (5–10 minutes).
Oxazepam, lorazepam, and temazepam undergo phase 3 conjugation (glucuronidation) and are preferred in patients with liver impairment.
Standard benzodiazepine urine drug screens detect oxazepam metabolites; clonazepam and alprazolam often require separate confirmatory testing.
Benzodiazepines are not first-line for generalized anxiety disorder; SSRIs are preferred, with benzodiazepines used only short-term (4–6 weeks) if needed.
Benzodiazepine prescribing peaked around 2013–2014 and has since declined, partly due to recognition of overdose risks when co-prescribed with opioids.
Benzodiazepines should be used short-term (≤4 weeks) due to rapid tolerance and decreasing clinical benefits.
Concurrent use with opioids significantly increases overdose risk; prescribe naloxone and document rationale.

episodes.title: Kelly Dunn, MD on Pharmacotherapy for Depressive Disorders 12/11/25
episodes.speaker: Kelly Dunn
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kelly Dunn presents a case-based lecture on pharmacotherapy for depressive disorders. She reviews the differential diagnosis for depression, including bipolar disorder, thyroid dysfunction, and substance use. She emphasizes the importance of suicide risk assessment and laboratory workup. She discusses how to choose an antidepressant based on symptom profiles (serotonin, norepinephrine, dopamine) and side effect profiles, and highlights specific considerations for atypical, melancholic, and psychotic depression.
key_points: Differential for depression includes bipolar disorder, thyroid disorders, perimenopause, substance use, and iatrogenic causes.
Always perform a suicide risk assessment; most patients who complete suicide saw a physician in the prior 30 days.
DSM-5 criteria for major depressive disorder require 5 of 9 SIGECAPS symptoms for 2 weeks causing distress/impairment.
Rule out mania/hypomania to distinguish unipolar from bipolar depression.
Antidepressant classes have similar efficacy; SSRIs are first-line due to tolerability.
Choose antidepressant based on symptom profile: serotonin-responsive (anxiety, insomnia), norepinephrine-responsive (fatigue, hypersomnia), dopamine-responsive (anhedonia, poor concentration).
Atypical depression (mood reactivity + overeating, oversleeping, leaden paralysis, rejection sensitivity) may respond better to MAOIs or SSRI + aripiprazole.
Melancholic depression (anhedonia, early morning awakening, anorexia) may require ECT or ketamine sooner.
Psychotic depression: ECT is first-line; if not available, combination antidepressant + antipsychotic.
Avoid anticholinergic agents (e.g., paroxetine, mirtazapine, TCAs) in elderly or dementia patients.
SSRIs cause initial GI side effects and insomnia due to serotonergic 'dump' before central efficacy develops over weeks.
Mirtazapine is more sedating at lower doses (due to histamine blockade) and more activating at higher doses.

episodes.title: L’Dogg’s Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: A 31-year-old female with type 1 diabetes presents with DKA, not on insulin. Labs show severe metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap, and superimposed respiratory acidosis. EKG shows sinus tachycardia and prolonged QT. The discussion emphasizes acid-base interpretation using Winters' formula, anion gap and delta gap calculation, and the importance of correcting hypokalemia before insulin therapy. Fluid choice between normal saline and lactated Ringer's is debated, with normal saline preferred for better potassium control.
key_points: DKA presents with hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis; typical labs show elevated BHB, low bicarbonate, and high anion gap.
Use Winters' formula (expected pCO2 = 1.5 × [HCO3] + 8 ± 2) to assess appropriate respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis.
In this case, actual pCO2 was 19, higher than expected 12–16, indicating superimposed respiratory acidosis.
Calculate anion gap (Na − Cl − HCO3) and delta gap ((AG − 12) + HCO3) to identify mixed acid-base disorders.
EKG interpretation should follow systematic steps: rate, rhythm, intervals (PR, QRS, QT), axis, waves (P, Q, QRS morphology, ST segment, T waves).
In DKA, hypokalemia must be corrected before insulin administration to prevent fatal arrhythmias, especially if QT is prolonged.
Normal saline is preferred over lactated Ringer's in DKA due to better control of potassium and avoidance of lactate.
The patient's prolonged QT interval (QTc 468) is a significant risk factor for arrhythmia in DKA.
Serial monitoring of potassium, glucose, and acid-base status is critical in DKA management.
In DKA with severe hypokalemia, hold insulin until potassium is above 4 mEq/L to prevent life-threatening arrhythmias from intracellular potassium shift.
Severe acidosis (pH <7.0) is dangerous to the brain and may warrant starting insulin despite hypokalemia, balancing the risk of arrhythmia against neurologic injury.
Bicarbonate therapy in DKA is controversial; it can drive potassium into cells and worsen hypokalemia, so it is generally avoided unless acidosis is extreme.

episodes.title: L'Dogg's Morning Report
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: A 61-year-old with COPD, bipolar disorder, and home oxygen presents with progressive dyspnea and fatigue. Initial labs reveal anemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated creatinine with a metabolic alkalosis and respiratory acidosis on VBG. Chest X-ray shows no acute infiltrate but elevated right hemidiaphragm. The case evolves to highlight hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on smear, leading to a differential of TTP, HUS, DIC, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and drug-induced causes. The lecture emphasizes systematic problem representation, prioritizing the primary problem with differential diagnosis, and avoiding floating plans in documentation.
key_points: Differential for dyspnea with COPD includes heart failure, pneumonia, PE, asthma, ACS, pleural effusion, anemia, and arrhythmia.
Anion gap metabolic alkalosis with respiratory acidosis (pH normal) suggests chronic compensation, likely from COPD.
Negative hemoccult does not rule out GI bleed; always interpret in clinical context.
Hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on smear suggests microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (TTP, HUS, DIC).
For suspected TTP, order ADAMTS13 activity; for DIC, order fibrinogen, D-dimer, and INR.
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and haptoglobin are key initial labs for hemolysis workup.
Winters' formula is not required when HCO3 > 20; instead assess PCO2 directly.
Always frame orders as name, dose, route, frequency; avoid floating plans (data without linked assessment).
Transfusion for symptomatic severe anemia (Hgb 5-6) is appropriate while investigating cause.
Third years demonstrating critical thinking aloud is a core teaching method; juniors learn by listening and analyzing.
TTP is a medical emergency requiring immediate recognition and treatment.
Classic pentad: thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, fever, renal dysfunction, and neurologic symptoms (not all present in every case).

episodes.title: Lifestyle/Anemia
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This learner-driven session covers four common types of uncommon anemia encountered in family medicine, focusing on diagnoses beyond iron deficiency, B12, or folate deficiency. Each group presents a case with history, exam, and lab findings for others to diagnose, followed by a teaching pearl. Topics include anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, and anemia of chronic kidney disease. The session emphasizes the importance of a thorough history, peripheral smear, and appropriate workup before jumping to treatment, with pearls on avoiding unnecessary iron supplementation and recognizing red flags like hemoglobin below 9 in chronic disease.
key_points: Anemia of chronic disease typically does not drop hemoglobin below 9 g/dL; if lower, consider concomitant iron deficiency or another cause.
In anemia of chronic disease, do not give iron unless there is proven concomitant iron deficiency.
Thalassemia requires hemoglobin electrophoresis to differentiate major/minor and alpha/beta; avoid iron supplementation unless iron deficiency is confirmed.
Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) can present with macrocytic anemia and normal B12/folate/TSH; a peripheral smear is essential for diagnosis.
MDS can transform to acute myeloid leukemia (AML), requiring hematology referral.
Anemia of chronic kidney disease (CKD) typically presents with hemoglobin <10 g/dL; consider erythropoietin (EPO) therapy in conjunction with nephrology.
When giving EPO for CKD anemia, iron stores are rapidly depleted, so iron supplementation is often needed even without iron deficiency.
Elevated BUN in CKD shortens RBC lifespan, contributing to anemia beyond erythropoietin deficiency.
For initial anemia workup, obtain a reticulocyte count and direct Coombs test to guide further evaluation.
If MCV is high and B12/folate/TSH are normal, consider MDS or hemolysis; a high reticulocyte count suggests hemolysis.

episodes.title: Man - Theology Thursday with Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Ledbetter teaches that man was created in God's image, which distinguishes humans from the rest of creation, but that through sin mankind is now lost and powerless to save themselves. He explains three aspects of being made in God's image—substantive, relational, and functional—and emphasizes that sin affects actions, attitudes, and our very nature. The lecture highlights that because of inherited guilt and corruption, no one can earn salvation; only Jesus Christ provides the remedy for this hopeless state.
key_points: Man was created in the image of God (Genesis 1:26–27), which gives humans unique value and distinction from all other creation.
Being in God's image includes substantive qualities (reason), relational aspects (interaction with others), and functional duties (taking dominion over the earth).
Image-bearing means every way in which man is like God reflects His likeness, as Wayne Grudem describes.
Sin is failure to meet God's moral standard in action, attitude, and inherent nature (Psalm 51:5, Ephesians 2:3, Romans 5:12).
The first sin in Genesis 3 involved questioning God's truth, His moral standard, and man's rightful place under God.
The consequence of sin is death—spiritual and physical separation from God (James 1:15, Romans 6:23).
All humanity inherits guilt and corruption from Adam's sin, making everyone legally guilty before God (Romans 5:12, 18; 3:23).
Sinners are unable to do any spiritual good that pleases God; even outwardly good deeds done without faith are not acceptable (Hebrews 11:6, Romans 8:8).
Man is enslaved to sin and cannot choose to please God on his own; freedom is limited by this bondage (John 8:34).
The gospel's power is magnified by understanding that man is utterly lost and powerless to save himself, making salvation by grace through faith truly great news.
Good works are defined by God's standards, not human judgment; actions done apart from faith are not truly good.
The 'why' behind an action determines its spiritual value—doing for God's glory vs. self-glorification.

episodes.title: Medical Education as Missions, Part 1 - Mark Crouch MD in PNG
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Mark Crouch, a US-trained family physician serving in Papua New Guinea, describes the evolution of medical education at Nazarene Hospital. He emphasizes the importance of integrating clinical work with spiritual ministry and adapting training to local realities. Key challenges include balancing overwhelming clinical loads with teaching, and moving from a Western training template to one suited for resource-limited settings. Successes include growing a residency program (Master of Medicine in Rural Health) and seeing a graduate join the faculty. Dr. Crouch advises new missionary educators to first immerse themselves in clinical work and local culture before attempting to lead training.
key_points: Medical education in mission settings must blend clinical competency with spiritual ministry, seeing both as expressions of the gospel.
Western training templates often do not fit resource-limited settings; adapt teaching to available tools and local disease patterns.
Clinical overload can make deliberate teaching difficult; trainees often learn by osmosis in high-volume settings.
Absorbing local culture, language, disease patterns, and faith perspectives is essential before leading educational initiatives.
Successful programs leverage existing national training structures while adding a ministry focus.
Getting promising candidates can be a challenge if the mission hospital's spiritual emphasis deters some applicants.
Having a local graduate join the teaching faculty provides culturally relevant insight and continuity for the program.
Leadership buy-in for training national doctors may take years to develop; momentum builds gradually.
Formalizing training helps ensure ministry and clinical skills are both caught and taught, not left to chance.
Medical educators in cross-cultural settings must be willing to learn from their trainees, who may have valuable local knowledge.
A collaborative, non-authoritarian approach to teaching builds trust and improves the educational experience.
The primary goal of training should not be limited to clinical excellence, which can be achieved elsewhere, but should include navigating the human and spiritual dimensions of patient care.

episodes.title: Medical Education as Missions, part 4, Drs. Sasha and Irina
episodes.speaker: Unknown

episodes.title: Moral Injury
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Moral injury occurs when one commits, participates in, or fails to prevent an act that violates deeply held moral values, leading to guilt, shame, and spiritual alienation. It is distinct from PTSD, which is fear-based and follows a life-threatening event. Cross-cultural medicine is a particular high-risk setting for moral injury, as differing cultural values can create unavoidable ethical conflicts. The injury can be cumulative but can be prevented by identifying mistaken deeply held values and metabolized through questioning.
key_points: Moral injury is defined as committing, participating in, or failing to prevent an act that violates one's deeply held moral values.
Moral injury is distinct from PTSD; PTSD is fear-based and tied to life-threatening events, while moral injury involves guilt, shame, and spiritual distance.
Moral injury is strongly associated with increased suicidality.
Standard secular psychotherapy is not effective for moral injury, unlike PTSD which often responds to such treatment.
Cross-cultural medicine inevitably produces moral injury because different cultures have conflicting deeply held values about life, birth, death, and decision-making.
Moral injury tends to be cumulative unless actively metabolized.
Prevention of moral injury involves identifying and examining whether one's deeply held moral values are based on biblical principles or have been mutated into non-biblical versions.
Questions are a powerful tool for metabolizing moral injury.
Moral injury exists on a spectrum from moral distress (which does not leave a lasting mark) to full moral injury.
Burnout is multifactorial and not simply overwork, but can overlap with moral injury.
Moral injury arises from a delusional belief that we are ultimately responsible for patient life and death, ignoring God's sovereignty.
Biblical teaching affirms both human responsibility (free will) and God's sovereignty; embracing both prevents unnecessary moral injury.

episodes.title: Morning report (SBP and HRS management) - Dr. Lee
episodes.speaker: Unknown
key_points: SBP is defined as infection of ascitic fluid without a clear source, typically due to bacterial translocation from the gut.
Diagnosis requires paracentesis with cell count demonstrating >250 polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs).
First-line antibiotic for SBP is cefotaxime; ceftriaxone is used only if cefotaxime is unavailable.
Albumin should be administered within 6 hours of SBP diagnosis to reduce mortality.
In SBP, hold diuretics and give IV fluids if needed; avoid diuretics.
HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion; consider prerenal, intrinsic renal, and other causes of AKI before diagnosing HRS.
HRS treatment includes midodrine and octreotide.
Systematic EKG interpretation: step zero is the standardization, then rate/rhythm, axis, intervals, and waves.
Tall tented T waves on EKG indicate hyperkalemia.
In liver patients, BUN may be elevated due to hepatic dysfunction, skewing BUN-to-creatinine ratio.

episodes.title: Morning Report with Dr. Lee
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This morning report discusses a 42-year-old woman presenting with respiratory arrest and shock. The instructor emphasizes the importance of immediate stabilization (ABCs, post-ROSC care) before forming a differential. Key teaching points include the OVVVVVVV mnemonic for post-ROSC management, fluid resuscitation with 30 mL/kg bolus in adults, and vasopressor selection with norepinephrine as first line. The case illustrates the need to go see the patient, gather collateral information, and use a status-plan approach.
key_points: Always go see the patient first before any other action.
Stabilize the patient before forming a differential in unstable cases; there is nothing to think about if the patient is dead.
Post-ROSC care includes oxygenation, volume status, vasopressors, glucose, acid-base, nutrition, DVT/stress ulcer prophylaxis (OVVVVVVV).
Intubate if GCS is less than 8.
Initial vent settings: rate 16, tidal volume based on height (500-600 mL), FiO2 100%, PEEP 5, obtain ABG after 30 minutes.
Use straight leg raise test to assess volume responsiveness: raise leg 45 degrees for 30 seconds; a 20 mmHg rise in BP suggests fluid responsiveness.
For adults, give 30 mL/kg fluid bolus; if MAP remains below 65, start pressors.
Norepinephrine is first-line vasopressor for most shock; vasopressin is second line; epinephrine is last resort due to arrhythmogenicity.
Phenylephrine is preferred in tachyarrhythmia (alpha-only); dobutamine is for cardiogenic shock (beta-only).
Use a status-plan approach: articulate the patient's status (e.g., hypotensive refractory to fluids) before stating the plan.
Acidemia refers to the blood pH; acidosis is the process causing it.
Use Winters Formula (1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ± 2) to compute expected pCO2 in metabolic acidosis; compare actual pCO2 to assess compensation.

episodes.title: Pediatric Development with Dr. Bennett
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture emphasizes the critical role of developmental surveillance and screening in well-child checks to identify children at risk for delays or medical conditions. Dr. Bennett illustrates this through a case of a 10-month-old with decreased crawling and weight loss, where careful history and exam revealed truncal ataxia and a full fontanelle, leading to diagnosis of a cerebellar tumor. The talk covers the dual approach of surveillance (at every well visit) and standardized screening (at 9, 18, and 30 months for development; 18 and 24 months for autism). Key domains assessed include behavioral/emotional, language/communication, cognitive, and movement/physical development.
key_points: Developmental surveillance occurs at every well-child visit (2, 4, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 24, 30, 36 months) using milestone checklists that are not standardized or validated.
Standardized screening is recommended at 9, 18, and 30 months for general development, and at 18 and 24 months specifically for autism.
Surveillance and screening are complementary; surveillance can identify risk factors (e.g., maternal depression) while screening can detect cognitive issues not apparent on observation.
Always ask parents open-ended questions about worries or concerns regarding growth, development, or behavior, as they may reveal subtle regression.
Regression of motor skills (e.g., crawling) is a red flag that warrants thorough evaluation, including observation of the child's movement.
Truncal ataxia and a full fontanelle in an infant with motor regression point toward a cerebellar mass until proven otherwise.
Only 63% of pediatricians perform recommended developmental screening, citing lack of time and inadequate compensation, but this is a core responsibility.
Developmental milestones are assessed across four domains: behavioral/emotional, language/communication, cognitive, and movement/physical.
Risk factors identified during surveillance (e.g., maternal depression, lack of verbal interaction) should be documented in a prominent, forward-facing location in the chart.
Early diagnosis of conditions like spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is critical because gene therapy cannot reverse damage that has already occurred.
Ask parents about concerns at every visit; parental denial can delay diagnosis.
Observe the child directly for developmental red flags like not pointing or not responding to name.

episodes.title: Pediatrics Spiritual Care - Roundtable
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This roundtable discussion focuses on providing spiritual care to pediatric patients, using a case of a 13-year-old female with a suicide attempt and severe trauma as a framework. The panel emphasizes the importance of creating a safe space, seeing the patient as a person rather than a diagnosis, and partnering with God rather than trying to carry the patient's pain alone. Practical strategies include asking open-ended questions, allowing the patient to lead the conversation, and offering resources like scripture that reframe God as a good father. The discussion highlights the need for interdisciplinary collaboration with chaplains and social work, and the importance of documenting spiritual history and follow-up.
key_points: Creating a sacred space by allowing the patient to open up is a critical first step in spiritual care.
Ask open-ended questions like 'Tell me about yourself' rather than jumping into diagnostic or problem-solving mode.
When possible, ask parents to step out of the room to allow the adolescent to speak freely.
Residents should recognize their own emotional limits and give the patient's pain to God rather than trying to carry it themselves.
Look for what God is already doing in the situation and partner with Him, rather than trying to fix everything.
Be open to the Holy Spirit giving you a specific word or insight for the patient that can counter lies like 'I'm messed up.'
Document spiritual history and ensure follow-up with social work, chaplaincy, and mental health resources.
Offer tangible resources such as a Bible or specific scriptures that address the patient's spiritual needs (e.g., God as Father).
Always verify the patient's story and guardianship, as the male figure may not be the biological father.
Chaplaincy can provide extended time for the patient to process trauma, making chaplain consultation a valuable resource.
Spiritual care requires respect, sensitivity, and permission; consent should be obtained from both the child and parent.
The degree of consent needed varies by intervention: taking a spiritual history is routine, while praying or sharing the gospel requires explicit permission.

episodes.title: Pelvic Pain Cases - Dr. Calvert
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture presents five cases of pelvic pain, emphasizing a systematic approach using seven historical features: onset, location, quality, cyclicity, duration, radiation, and aggravating/relieving factors. The speaker highlights how patterns in these features can diagnose conditions like endometriosis and adenomyosis without labs or imaging, relying on clinical reasoning. Key points include differentiating primary from secondary dysmenorrhea, recognizing that endometriosis often improves with pregnancy due to progesterone dominance, and diagnosing adenomyosis by cyclic midline pain with a boggy, tender premenstrual uterus. Physical exam findings like decreased uterine mobility suggest adhesive disease from endometriosis.
key_points: Use seven historical features (onset, location, quality, cyclicity, duration, radiation, aggravators/relievers) to define patterns in pelvic pain.
Cyclic pain associated with menstruation or ovulation points to a gynecologic cause like endometriosis or adenomyosis.
Pregnancy suppresses endometriosis via progesterone dominance, reducing endometrial proliferation and pain.
Birth control pills (progesterone-dominant) are first-line treatment for progestin-responsive endometriosis.
Secondary dysmenorrhea changes over time (worsens) and affects daily activities, unlike primary dysmenorrhea.
Decreased uterine mobility on pelvic exam suggests adhesive disease, commonly from endometriosis or prior PID.
Adenomyosis presents with cyclic midline pain, heavy menses, and a boggy, tender uterus premenstrually; history alone suffices for diagnosis.
Deep dyspareunia that is constant and non-cyclic suggests anatomic issues like scarring from endometriosis.
Bowel or bladder symptoms (e.g., pain with defecation, urinary frequency) may indicate uterine pathology impacting adjacent organs.
Endometriosis can be diagnosed 85% of the time by history alone without labs or imaging, relying on pattern recognition.

episodes.title: Petrochemical Exposures and Health Impacts - Dr. Ella Kuchmiy
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Kuchmiy presents research on health impacts of the Tulsa West Refinery, focusing on pollutants such as VOCs, HAPs, and specific chemicals including acrolein, ammonia, benzene, and hydrogen sulfide. She discusses health effects ranging from respiratory irritation to cancer and notes the lack of community monitoring standards. A study of Texas Medicare recipients showed increased cancer risk near refineries. She encourages clinicians to broaden their differential to include environmental exposures.
key_points: The Tulsa West Refinery has been in violation of the Clean Air Act for 12 consecutive quarters (3 years) with penalties of $67,500.
Refinery emissions include hazardous air pollutants (HAPs) such as acrolein, ammonia, benzene, cadmium, carbon disulfide, and hydrogen sulfide.
Community exposure standards for ambient air near refineries are lacking; only workplace exposure limits (ACGIH, OSHA) exist.
Hydrogen sulfide can cause rapid loss of consciousness and death at high levels; its characteristic rotten egg smell is unreliable due to anosmia.
Acrolein has a ceiling limit of 0.1 ppm; exceeding this can cause upper respiratory irritation, pulmonary edema, and emphysema.
Ammonia has a TWA of 25 ppm and STEL of 35 ppm; exceeding these can cause eye damage and upper respiratory irritation.
A study of Medicare recipients in Texas found a relative risk of 1.3 for lymphoma within 0-10 miles of a refinery (95% CI 1.07-1.9).
Clinicians should consider occupational and environmental exposures when patients present with unexplained respiratory, neurological, or hematologic symptoms.
Studies on petrochemical exposure often use ZIP code-level socioeconomic data and only include Medicare beneficiaries, lacking individual exposure measurements.
Worker studies show increased risks for mesothelioma, melanoma, multiple myeloma, prostate, and bladder cancer, but these findings cannot be generalized to the general public.
A meta-analysis found higher lung cancer mortality risk among residents living near petrochemical sites, but the result was not statistically significant.
A Swedish study with community air monitoring found no association between petrochemical exposure and lung cancer, possibly due to stricter regulations.

episodes.title: Physician Assisted Suicide - Ledbetter
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: The lecture examines physician-assisted suicide from a Christian worldview, contrasting naturalistic, pantheistic, and biblical perspectives. The speaker argues that biblical ethics (life as sacred, given by God) prohibit active killing, while relativist systems (autonomy, situationalism) tend to justify it. Practical concerns include the slippery slope seen in the Netherlands, insurance incentives that favor death over treatment, and the need to address underlying depression and pain. The law of double effect is introduced as a key principle for managing pain without intending death.
key_points: Worldviews (naturalistic, pantheistic, biblical) fundamentally shape ethical reasoning about physician-assisted suicide.
Biblical ethics view life as sacred and not ours to take, citing the commandment against murder and the story of Saul.
Relative ethical systems (subjectivism, conventionalism, situationalism, utilitarianism) often lead to acceptance of assisted suicide.
The Netherlands shows a slippery slope from strict criteria to euthanizing children, even without parental consent.
Insurance companies may deny life-saving treatment but cover the cost of euthanasia, creating a perverse incentive.
There is a morally significant distinction between active killing (euthanasia) and withdrawal of care or refusal of treatment.
When patients request assisted suicide, clinicians should address underlying causes such as depression, pain, and social isolation.
The law of double effect allows giving opioids to relieve pain even if it may hasten death, as long as the intention is not to kill.
Palliative care training should be enhanced to better alleviate suffering without resorting to euthanasia.
In states where physician-assisted suicide is illegal, a physician can decline to participate and note that patients may travel to states like Colorado where it is legal.
Clinicians should determine their personal ethical stance on physician-assisted suicide and be able to discuss the opposing viewpoint.
CMDA's 'Standards for Life' PDF addresses physician-assisted suicide, abortion, and other bioethical topics.

episodes.title: POCUS with Dr. Ledbetter
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This interactive POCUS lecture uses case-based learning to teach residents how to interpret ultrasound findings in emergency presentations. Cases include a pediatric bladder rupture after trauma, a massive pulmonary embolism presenting with hypotension, and a patient with heart failure and pulmonary pathology. The session emphasizes integrating ultrasound into clinical decision-making, recognizing abnormal anatomy, and building confidence through practice.
key_points: The FAST exam can identify free intra-abdominal fluid and abnormal bladder morphology, as in bladder rupture after trauma.
A dilated right ventricle (larger than two-thirds of the left) and a D-sign on short-axis view indicate acute right heart strain, classically from pulmonary embolism.
Hypotension and tachycardia are key vital sign triggers for performing cardiac POCUS to differentiate shock etiologies.
In the parasternal long-axis view, mitral valve leaflet separation from the septum >1 cm suggests reduced left ventricular ejection fraction.
Left atrial enlargement (3-4 times aortic root diameter) is a marker of chronic diastolic dysfunction or volume overload.
Lung ultrasound can detect B-lines (interstitial syndrome) and consolidations, complementing chest X-ray findings.
Recording and comparing POCUS clips with confirmatory imaging (e.g., CT) reinforces learning and builds diagnostic confidence.
POCUS findings can expedite diagnosis and management while awaiting definitive imaging, especially in unstable patients.
Teaching point: even without prior experience, residents can identify significant abnormalities by systematically naming the view, three anatomic structures, and normal vs. abnormal findings.
Documentation of POCUS clips with correlating imaging supports future billing and credentialing.
B-lines on lung ultrasound are nonspecific for fluid but when present in three or more zones bilaterally have high sensitivity and specificity for pulmonary edema from decompensated heart failure.
The IVC is identified by its connection to the right atrium and hepatic veins; pulsatility alone is unreliable because it can be transmitted from the adjacent aorta and heart.

episodes.title: Pressors - Engstrom
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture covers the spectrum of vasopressors, focusing on alpha- and beta-adrenergic receptor agonists and their clinical applications. The speaker emphasizes using physical exam findings—specifically skin temperature—to distinguish warm shock (vasodilation, need alpha) from cold shock (poor pump, need beta). Key drugs discussed include phenylephrine (pure alpha), dobutamine (beta with inotropy and vasodilation), and epinephrine (mixed alpha/beta, used in codes and anaphylaxis). Practical dosing, common pitfalls, and the evolving evidence on epinephrine in cardiac arrest are also reviewed.
key_points: Warm shock (vasodilated, warm skin) requires alpha agonism for vasoconstriction; cold shock (poor perfusion, cold skin) requires beta agonism for inotropy.
Phenylephrine (Neo-Synephrine) is a pure alpha agonist rarely used except in MAP push scenarios like spinal cord injury or stroke where the heart is fine.
Dobutamine is a beta agonist used for inotropic support in cardiogenic shock; it causes systemic vasodilation and may lower blood pressure.
Epinephrine is the primary vasopressor in cardiac arrest; the code dose is 1 mg IV push every 3-5 minutes.
Epinephrine for anaphylaxis is given IM at 0.3-0.5 mg (0.3 mg for EpiPen); IV epinephrine in a living patient can cause ventricular arrhythmias.
There is no true maximum dose of vasopressors in a dying patient; escalating beyond typical doses may not add benefit but is not harmful if the patient is profoundly hypotensive.
Epinephrine infusion dosing is 2-200 mcg/min; 200 mcg/min equals 0.2 mg/min, compared to 1 mg push in a code.
Recent data suggest more than 5 doses of epinephrine in cardiac arrest may worsen neurologic outcomes, possibly due to cerebral vasoconstriction.
In atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, dobutamine can worsen tachycardia; alternative agents should be considered.
Isoproterenol is a pure chronotrope rarely used; dobutamine is preferred for inotropy.
For a patient about to code, give 50 mcg (0.5 cc) epinephrine boluses every minute as a bridge to an epi drip.
Dilute code-cart epinephrine (1 mg/10 mL) by drawing it into 9 mL of saline to obtain 50 mcg per 0.5 mL.

episodes.title: Radiation Oncology Primer for Primary Care - Gabriel S. Vidal, MD, FACP
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture introduces primary care physicians to the principles of radiation oncology, covering the types of radiation (photons, electrons, protons), delivery techniques (3D conformal, IMRT, SBRT, brachytherapy), and clinical settings (curative, palliative). The speaker emphasizes the multidisciplinary approach and the importance of immobilization for reproducible targeting. It also highlights that 40% of radiation treatments are palliative, with a focus on symptom control using short, low-toxicity regimens. The fundamental goal of radiation is DNA damage, and dose is measured in Gray (Gy).
key_points: Radiation oncology works alongside medical and surgical oncology in a multidisciplinary approach to cancer treatment.
Four types of radiation are used: photons (with skin sparing at high energies), electrons (superficial), and protons (Bragg peak with no exit dose).
Treatment techniques include 3D conformal, IMRT (intensity modulated), SBRT (stereotactic), and brachytherapy (implanted sources).
Radiation can be delivered in neoadjuvant, definitive, adjuvant, consolidation, or palliative settings.
Approximately 40% of radiation treatments are palliative, aiming for symptom control with short, low-side-effect regimens.
Patient immobilization (e.g., masks, frames) ensures sub‑millimeter reproducibility, critical for accuracy.
A CT simulation is performed for treatment planning; urgent cases can be simulated and treated the same day.
Dose volume histograms (DVH) are used to limit radiation exposure to organs at risk.
Radiation dose is measured in Gray (Gy); 1 Gy = 1 J/kg, and the goal is to cause DNA damage directly or indirectly.
When comparing proton versus photon therapy, two treatment plans can be created to demonstrate the relative advantages.
One in five cancer patients will develop a vertebral metastasis; presentation varies by spinal level.
The NOMS framework (Neurologic, Oncologic, Mechanical, Systemic) helps decide between radiation, surgery, or other treatments for spinal cord compression.

episodes.title: Rev Joel S. Leitch on Suicide Prevention 5/14/26
episodes.speaker: Rev Joel S. Leitch
episodes.abstract: Rev Joel S. Leitch's lecture on suicide prevention teaches family medicine residents to recognize early warning signs, evaluate risk, and make effective referrals. He emphasizes that 95% of suicidal people do not truly want to die but seek escape from unbearable pain, and that most are ambivalent and highly suggestible. Residents are advised to take charge compassionately, ask directly about self-harm, and build hope by reorienting patients to the future. The talk also covers the three H's (helpless, hopeless, hapless), the episodic nature of suicidal feelings, and the risks of institutionalization for the small minority who are truly determined to die.
key_points: Most suicidal people (≈95%) do not want to die; they want relief from unbearable suffering.
Hopelessness is a stronger predictor of suicide risk than depression alone.
Suicidal feelings are episodic, not constant; acute danger often lasts only seconds to minutes.
The three H's—helpless, hopeless, hapless—are key warning signs to listen for.
If you suspect self-harm, ask directly; do not wait for the patient to bring it up.
Do not ask a suicidal person what they want to do; they don't know. Kindly and compassionately tell them what they must do.
Assure the patient you will get them the help they need; take charge of the situation.
Most suicidal people experience only one episode; successful rescue during the first episode greatly reduces future risk.
Family history of suicide and high ACE scores are significant risk factors.
Only about 5% of suicidal individuals are truly determined to die; institutionalization can paradoxically increase risk for this group.

episodes.title: Rev. Leitch on How Continue to Burn Without Getting Burnt Out 1/8/26
episodes.speaker: Rev. Leitch
episodes.abstract: Rev. Leitch addresses burnout and compassion fatigue among medical residents, drawing on Viktor Frankl's concept of meaning to emphasize that loss of purpose exacerbates emotional exhaustion. He defines compassion fatigue as a state of tension with preoccupation with traumatized patients, and burnout as perceived demands exceeding resources. The talk highlights warning signs such as acting like one cares without genuine empathy, the silencing response that prevents help-seeking, and the importance of honest sharing with trusted colleagues. Practical advice includes intentionally managing countertransference and recognizing that medication alone cannot restore meaning.
key_points: Loss of meaning in one's work is a core driver of burnout and self-doubt.
Compassion fatigue involves tension and reexperiencing of a patient's trauma.
Burnout occurs when perceived demands outweigh perceived resources.
Acting like you care does not necessarily mean you genuinely care; this can mask emotional depletion.
Empathy can become overtaxed and exhausted even with diligent self-care.
Secondary traumatization and burnout are the two components of compassion fatigue.
The silencing response—fear of judgment, omnipotence illusions, and distrust—prevents caregivers from seeking help.
Countertransference is normal and must be intentionally managed to keep the focus on the patient.
Medication (e.g., hydroxyzine) addresses symptoms but does not provide a sense of purpose.
Daily honest sharing with one trusted person can counteract isolation and build resilience.

Compassion fatigue symptoms include increased negative arousal, intrusive thoughts, difficulty separating work from personal life, lower frustration tolerance, anger, dread, depression, self-destructive behaviors, hypervigilance, decreased work competence, and loss of hope.
Anger is a control measure used when feeling helpless or overwhelmed.

episodes.title: Rev. Leitch on Suicide Intervention
episodes.speaker: Rev. Leitch
episodes.abstract: Rev. Leitch discusses suicide intervention, emphasizing that most suicidal patients do not truly want to die but seek relief from unbearable suffering. He highlights three key warning signs—helplessness, hopelessness, and haplessness—and notes that acute suicidal episodes are typically brief (seconds to minutes), providing a critical window for intervention. Clinicians should directly ask about suicidal thoughts in every initial interview and avoid asking open-ended questions about what the patient wants; instead, they must compassionately direct the patient toward specific actions and provide immediate assurance of help. The lecture underscores that successfully intervening during a first suicidal episode dramatically reduces the risk of future attempts.
key_points: Key warning signs to listen for are helplessness, hopelessness, and haplessness; hopelessness is a stronger predictor of suicide than depression.
About 95% of suicidal people do not want to die; they want relief from a situation they perceive as intolerable.
Most acute suicidal episodes last only seconds to minutes, making rapid intervention crucial.
Clinicians should routinely ask about any history of suicidal thinking or acting out during initial patient interviews.
When a patient is suicidal, do not ask 'What do you want to do?'—they are unable to problem-solve; instead, compassionately tell them what they must do.
Quickly assure the suicidal person that you will get them the help they need, even if you are unsure of the next steps.
Suicidal patients are often ambivalent and suggestible; use this to offer a structured plan and hope.
Patients may give indirect clues rather than stating they are planning suicide; learn to hear what they are not saying.
If you can prevent suicide during the first episode, the likelihood of a future attempt is low.
Building hope and reorienting the patient toward the future is a key therapeutic goal.
Hardcore suicidal individuals (about 5% of suicidal population) are difficult to identify, often give no clues, and institutionalization may not stop them.
Suicide is a gradual process called suicidal erosion, often spanning 10–20 years, not a spontaneous act.

episodes.title: Rheumatology with Dr. Lucashu
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture presents a framework for evaluating musculoskeletal pain in primary care, categorizing it into four types: inflammatory, tissue injury, nerve injury, and central pain syndromes. Using a case of a 52-year-old woman with widespread pain and fatigue, the speaker discusses appropriate lab testing, emphasizing the limited utility of ANA and the importance of ESR and CRP stratification. Referral to rheumatology is recommended for chronic widespread pain with elevated inflammatory markers, but starting DMARDs is generally outside primary care scope. The talk also covers managing symptoms while awaiting specialist consultation.
key_points: Musculoskeletal pain is classified into four types: inflammatory (e.g., gout, RA, lupus), tissue injury (somatic), nerve injury (e.g., sciatica, carpal tunnel), and central pain syndromes (e.g., fibromyalgia).
Central pain syndromes involve pain lasting >3 months with altered neurotransmitter function; only about 3% of patients need formal diagnostic criteria.
For widespread pain, imaging is unlikely to be beneficial; instead, focus on labs: CBC, ESR, CRP, CK, TSH, uric acid, and possibly RF/CCP if hand-predominant.

ANA should not be ordered routinely for pain evaluation due to high false-positive rate (30% of normal individuals); reserve for cases with lupus-specific symptoms like malar rash or photosensitivity.
ESR can be stratified: 30-50 low-grade, 50-100 moderate, >100 severe inflammation; CRP elevation lacks similar stratification for clinical severity.
Rheumatoid factor is helpful if positive (especially in younger patients) but not helpful if negative; negative ANA can rule out lupus but not other autoimmune conditions.
HLA-B27 is marginally useful for early ankylosing spondylitis; a negative result does not rule it out (e.g., speaker has HLA-B27-negative ankylosing spondylitis).
Uric acid requires trending; a single normal level does not exclude gout, and a single elevated level does not confirm it.
Refer to rheumatology for chronic widespread pain (>3 months) involving more than one joint, especially with elevated ESR; fibromyalgia may overlap but some rheumatologists prefer not to manage it.
Starting DMARDs (e.g., methotrexate, biologics) is generally outside primary care scope unless the physician has additional training; focus on symptomatic management while awaiting specialist.
Symptomatic management options include NSAIDs, duloxetine, lacosamide, CBT, and turmeric; early referral with specific labs (RF, CCP) may expedite rheumatology appointments.
Distinguish between four types of pain (inflammatory vs. centralized) before pursuing a specific diagnosis.

episodes.title: Sarah Janssen on Anemia Outpatient 12/4/25
episodes.speaker: Sarah Janssen
episodes.abstract: This lecture by Dr. Sarah Janssen covers the outpatient evaluation and management of non-urgent anemia, with a primary focus on microcytic anemia and iron deficiency. She discusses when to screen for anemia, initial lab workup including CBC and ferritin, and how to use MCV and reticulocyte count to narrow the differential. Key management pearls include optimal ferritin targets (above 30 ng/mL for general health, above 50 for symptoms, and above 100 for hair loss), practical oral iron dosing (every other day or daily, not BID/TID), and the importance of identifying the underlying cause of iron deficiency. She also briefly touches on macrocytic and normocytic anemias, and when to refer to hematology.
key_points: Iron deficiency is the most common cause of microcytic anemia worldwide; always consider thalassemia and combined disorders in the differential.
Initial lab workup for suspected anemia should include CBC and ferritin; add reticulocyte count and peripheral smear if diagnosis is unclear.
Ferritin <30 ng/mL indicates iron deficiency; for symptomatic patients, target ferritin >50 ng/mL, and for hair loss or restless legs, consider >100 ng/mL.
Oral iron supplementation should be dosed once daily or every other day; BID/TID dosing increases side effects without improving absorption.
Taking oral iron with meat (or a meal containing meat) significantly improves absorption; avoid taking with calcium-rich foods or drinks like orange juice.
Always investigate the underlying cause of iron deficiency—consider menorrhagia, GI blood loss, celiac disease, and dietary insufficiency.
In elderly patients (>60), add B12, folate, and GFR to initial workup due to higher prevalence of deficiencies and chronic kidney disease.
For patients with chronic disease (CKD, autoimmune), order a full iron panel rather than ferritin alone to avoid misleading results.
Diet alone is insufficient to correct established iron deficiency; oral supplementation is needed for treatment.
Refer to hematology if anemia is severe, refractory to treatment, or if there is concern for hematologic malignancy or unexplained cytopenias.
Avoid tea or coffee within one hour of taking oral iron supplements to prevent absorption interference.
Recheck hemoglobin 2-4 weeks after starting oral iron; a rise of 1 g/dL confirms response and supports iron deficiency diagnosis.

episodes.title: Security Training
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: This lecture by a Tulsa law enforcement officer covers current trends in active shooter events, emphasizing the necessity of mindset, proximity-based decision-making (run, hide, fight), and the critical role of pre-incident indicators. The speaker reviews national statistics showing most hostages are resolved by negotiation, but active shooters are 100% committed to mass murder and typically have a prior relationship with the target site. He highlights that these individuals plan extensively—often over months—and that reporting unusual behaviors or social media posts is the most effective way to foil attacks.
key_points: Mindset is foundational to survival in an active shooter event; without a decision to run, barricade, or fight, survival chances decrease significantly.
National average law enforcement response time is three to five minutes, during which the shooter intends to commit mass murder.
95% of hostage situations are resolved through negotiation, but only 4% of active shooter incidents are; active shooters are fully detached from victims as human beings.
55% of active shooters have some relationship with the work site, often a disgruntled employee or client.
Most active shooter plans are foiled by someone reporting bizarre behavior or social media posts; intervention through simple conversation can prevent attacks.
Active shooters are highly calculated; Columbine's planning lasted the entire senior year and involved 95 IEDs.
Common pre-incident indicators include depression, obsession with violence, domestic violence, mental health issues, and dramatic changes in appearance or hygiene.
No negotiation is possible with an active shooter; law enforcement’s role is to go to the threat, not contain it.
Modern active shooters often fight to the death rather than surrender or commit suicide, and body count is the primary goal.
Social media allows like-minded individuals to connect and shorten planning time, as seen in the Buffalo shooter's two-week preparation.
Normalcy bias causes people to interpret dangerous events as normal, delaying response.
Denial is a common initial reaction; quick recognition of a threat improves survival odds.

episodes.title: Spiritual Warfare
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: The lecture explores spiritual warfare through the lens of 2 Corinthians 10:3-6, emphasizing that the battle is primarily for the mind. Fortresses (strongholds) are false beliefs that distort our view of God, self, and others, often built from life experiences and cultural lies. The speaker uses Paul's example of self-image and comparison to illustrate how measuring ourselves by worldly standards leads to pride or depression, both of which are spiritual attacks. The remedy is to tear down these lies with divine truth and take every thought captive to Christ.
key_points: Spiritual warfare is ongoing for Christians and includes a subtle mental battle beyond overt demonic encounters.
Fortresses are protective arguments or beliefs constructed in the mind by the enemy, preventing true knowledge of God.
Speculations (Greek: logismos) are reasoning and imaginations that explain life without God's revelation.
Lofty things are barriers raised against the knowledge of God, such as false views of His character.
Paul's context in 2 Corinthians 10 addresses the Corinthians' judgment of him by outward appearance and eloquence.
Self-assessment through comparison with others is a common stronghold that leads to pride (if better) or depression (if worse).
This kind of comparison is not humility; it is wounded pride or thwarted ego.
The enemy uses self-image attacks to distort our relationship with God and sideline us from ministry.
The correct response is to reject the worldly scale of measurement entirely and adopt God's perspective.
Taking every thought captive means actively submitting our reasoning to the obedience of Christ.
Comparing ourselves with others or with a theoretical ideal self leads to pride, worthlessness, or despondency.
Paul says those who measure themselves by themselves are 'without understanding'—they don't know who they are, don't know God's values, and don't understand others.

episodes.title: The Condies on Surgery
episodes.speaker: The Condies
episodes.abstract: Drs. Angela and John Condie, who served in Pakistan, present a lecture on infectious diseases encountered in South Asia, organized by clinical presentation. They cover hematologic presentations (dengue, malaria, chikungunya), neurologic presentations (measles, neonatal tetanus, polio, rabies, herpes encephalitis), and key diagnostic and management pearls. The talk emphasizes recognizing danger signs like capillary leak in dengue, the importance of presumptive malaria treatment in endemic areas, and vaccination strategies for travelers and local populations.
key_points: Dengue, Zika, and chikungunya present similarly; key distinguishing features include conjunctivitis (Zika) and arthralgias (chikungunya), but lab testing is needed for confirmation.
Dengue danger occurs as fever resolves: watch for sudden abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, capillary leak, and hypovolemic shock.
Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs in children with dengue due to Reye's syndrome risk.
Malaria (falciparum) is chloroquine-resistant; treat with artemether-lumefantrine, which is inexpensive in Pakistan.
Presumptive antimalarial treatment for fever is standard of care in endemic areas because uncomplicated malaria can progress to severe illness in nonimmune individuals within hours.
Measles presents with Koplik spots (white lacy spots on buccal mucosa) followed by rash, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis.
Measles causes T-cell lymphopenia and increased infection-related mortality risk for up to 3 years.
MMR vaccine can be given as early as 6 months for travel to endemic areas, then repeated on the standard schedule.
Neonatal tetanus presents with poor suck, increased tone, and risus sardonicus; prevention requires maternal vaccination and clean cord care.
Polio causes acute flaccid paralysis that is asymmetric, proximal > distal, with normal sensation; differentiate from Guillain-Barre which is symmetric and often painful.
Oral polio vaccine (OPV) provides mucosal immunity and is used in endemic areas; inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) does not prevent transmission.
Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: vaccinated individuals need vaccine on days 0 and 3; unvaccinated need vaccine plus rabies immune globulin.

episodes.title: The Ethics of Contraception - Dr. Lisa Gilbert
episodes.speaker: Unknown
episodes.abstract: Dr. Lisa Gilbert presents an ethics lecture on contraception, beginning with historical perspectives from Christian tradition. She outlines premises that fertility and pregnancy are not diseases, that human life begins at fertilization, and that sexual relations are designed for union and procreation within marriage. The talk traces early church teachings, the 1930 Anglican shift allowing contraception under moral obligation, and the Catholic response in Humanae Vitae. The lecture aims to help clinicians integrate faith with ethical practice in reproductive health.
key_points: The Hippocratic Oath forbids giving abortive remedies and deadly drugs, establishing a foundational ethical standard.
Fertility and pregnancy are not diseases but functions of a healthy reproductive system, challenging the view that contraception is always medically indicated.
Human life begins at fertilization or conception, a premise that shapes ethical positions on contraception and abortion.
Early Christian tradition (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant) universally rejected contraception until 1930.
The 1930 Anglican Lambeth Conference first allowed contraception under 'clearly felt moral obligation' while condemning selfish motives.
