pearls.verbatim: I view this more as, like, guide rails rather than black and white. You have to do it this way because I... Every patient is different. And even if physically they're able to handle the transition, anytime psychologically, they just need, like, an extra two weeks.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering

pearls.text: Remember that as total daily dose decreases, the same milligram cut becomes a higher percentage cut, so smaller absolute cuts may be needed.
pearls.verbatim: Do remember that the lower your total daily dosage go, higher percentage of a cut you're going to be making even if the milligram that you're cutting is the same.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering

pearls.text: Microtapering with a compounded liquid benzo allows daily cuts of 0.1 mg, which may be easier to tolerate than larger weekly cuts.
pearls.verbatim: You can compound benzos into a solution form, and it's called microtapering. So instead of making a big percentage cut every week or two, you make these micro, like, point one mg cut every day.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering

pearls.text: If a patient cannot tolerate a 2 mg cut, have them halve or quarter the 2 mg tablet; the exact fraction is close enough.
pearls.verbatim: I did have one patient who liked to quarter it. It's just like, okay. You're you're making cuts. You're just doing it smaller. And while it might not be exactly exactly exactly half a milligram, it's close enough that I'm not really concerned.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering

pearls.text: When a patient refuses to taper and you decide to stop prescribing, give a one-month supply and clearly document that no further refills will be provided.
pearls.verbatim: I will say I will give you a month's supply. That's plenty of time for you to find a new doctor and establish with them and talk to them about it. But I will not be refilling that.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering

pearls.text: Patients on benzodiazepines who are not in counseling should be referred to therapy as part of the tapering process.
pearls.verbatim: Well, you obviously need to be in counseling or therapy.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering

pearls.text: Offer an SSRI as a controller medication for patients on benzodiazepines who are not on an antidepressant.
pearls.verbatim: if you want to, we can try an SSRI
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Benzo Tapering

pearls.text: Bilateral B-lines in a single zone are highly diagnostic for pulmonary edema.
pearls.verbatim: See or more B lines in a single zone on both sides, that is highly diagnostic for pulmonary edema, again, in the right clinical setting.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: An anechoic triangle on lung ultrasound is fluid (pleural effusion), and it's more sensitive than X-ray.
pearls.verbatim: What is this anechoic triangle, which is fluid. Very sensitive and specific. It's better than X-ray.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: E-point septal separation >8 mm predicts LVEF ≤40%.
pearls.verbatim: if it's greater than eight millimeters, that's good for predicting an EF of 40% or less.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: If the mitral valve does not come within 1 cm of the septum, it suggests reduced EF.
pearls.verbatim: that mitral valve is not coming in within a centimeter of the septum.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: Use the papillary muscle level of the short-axis view to assess LV contractility.
pearls.verbatim: So we're at the papillary view of the short axis, which is where you wanna look for contractility of the left ventricle.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: Only give tPA for PE if the patient is hemodynamically unstable (massive PE).
pearls.verbatim: Unless the vital signs are unstable, ICU won't give tPA.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: A flat septum with a crescent-shaped RV in short axis indicates right heart strain (D-sign).
pearls.verbatim: So the septum's very flat rather than coming out this way into the right atrium. So the right ventricle looks more like half a circle than it does a crescent.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: A plethoric IVC indicates increased right atrial pressure.
pearls.verbatim: We've got a pyloric IVC, increased right atrial pressure.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac POCUS 10/9/25

pearls.text: The left ventricular chamber size should shrink by at least 30% during systole.
pearls.verbatim: the size of it will shrink at least 30%.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: Change the level of the short axis view by fanning: up toward the base to see the aortic valve, down toward the apex to see the papillary muscles.
pearls.verbatim: So you're just fanning up towards the base to see the base, down towards the apex to get to the papillary muscles.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: If the anterior mitral leaflet does not come within 1 cm of the septum visually, that indicates reduced ejection fraction.
pearls.verbatim: if it's visually outside of a centimeter, if it's not hitting within a centimeter of the septum visually, and remember, your markers will generally be on the right side of the screen, that is an indication that the EF is reduced.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: E-point septal separation is considered less reliable than wall thickening and cavity reduction for estimating ejection fraction.
pearls.verbatim: the E-point septal separation is considered less reliable.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: Look for at least 30% change in left ventricular area between systole and diastole as a marker of normal systolic function.
pearls.verbatim: We're looking for 50... Sorry, 30% change in the area.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: In parasternal long axis, the anterior mitral leaflet should approach the septum within 1 cm in diastole; failure to do so suggests reduced left ventricular function.
pearls.verbatim: Mitral valve's hitting the septum here. Great. Not getting even close to within a centimeter here. Not so good.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: Combine cardiac ultrasound with lung ultrasound for B-lines and clinical signs like JVD to assess for heart failure.
pearls.verbatim: You've got the patient that you're wondering if they're in heart failure where you can put this together with they've got rails. You did a focus on their lung, and you saw there's fluid there.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: Before performing a focused cardiac ultrasound, define a binary clinical question: Does this patient have a reduced EF? Pericardial effusion? Wall motion abnormality?
pearls.verbatim: What is your question in that patient? Does this patient have a reduced EF? Yes or no? Does this patient have a pericardial effusion? Yes or no? Does this patient have a wall motion abnormality? Yes or no?
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Cardiac Ultrasound

pearls.text: If you see a hypoechoic disruption in a tendon, change the probe angle; if it normalizes, it was anisotropy, not a tear.
pearls.verbatim: If you see a disruption where it's more hypoechoic, you think, oh, maybe there's a tendon rupture there. But if you change the angle of your probe, that makes it all look normal. Well, then there wasn't a tear there. Your angle was just off.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Ultrasound can rule in a medial meniscus tear if you see it, but cannot rule one out because most of the meniscus is internal.
pearls.verbatim: You can't rule out a medial meniscus tear with ultrasound because a lot of the meniscus is internal, but you can rule one in if you see it.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: For focused knee ultrasound, just answer the clinical question: is there fluid? Ultrasound is better than physical exam and takes two seconds.
pearls.verbatim: I do not do this entire exam every time I'm looking at a knee. Usually, the clinical question I'm trying to answer is, is there fluid in here or not? Because as much as we like physical exam, ultrasound is better at identifying fluid. So just put an ultrasound on there. It takes two seconds to see if there's fluid in there or not.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Always identify the tendon in long axis first, then rotate to short axis so you know where to look.
pearls.verbatim: I always look long axis first to identify where it is. In that way, when I rotate short axis, I know where it is.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Only attempt ultrasound-guided injection when the needle path is clearly visible; if the patient has an effusion, the target is obvious.
pearls.verbatim: I generally will only do this if it's really clear where the needle needs to go. So, generally, they'll have an effusion. Or in Drew's case, he's got a clear enough point there where I I could see my needle in a little bit, spray a little bit of juice in there, open it up, stick my needle in a little bit more. And I don't have to worry about where my needle is because I can see it.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: Standard knee injection volume is 5 mL: 1 mL of 40 mg/mL Kenalog plus 4 mL of 1% lidocaine.
pearls.verbatim: So what I do is one mil of forty mgs per mole of Kenalog and then four mils of one percent lidocaine. Three. Four. Four. So it's still 5,000,000.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Musculoskeletal Ultrasound (Knee Specific)

pearls.text: To detect a pleural effusion, position the patient at least partially upright so gravity pulls the fluid down to the diaphragm.
pearls.verbatim: If you're looking for something that's gravity dependent, like fluid, pleural effusion, having them at least angled up a bit gonna be helpful to pull that fluid down to the diaphragm rather than if they're completely flat or if they're on their head.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Always orient the probe marker toward the patient's head when scanning the lung to obtain the best landmarks.
pearls.verbatim: when you're scanning lung, you want probe marker to the patient's head because that will give you the best landmarks.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: A thickened, irregular, or 'muddled' pleural line on ultrasound is a common finding in pneumonia and should raise suspicion.
pearls.verbatim: In pneumonia, frequently, that that line will be thick or just really sort of muddled up. It's not gonna be a nice clear line.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: A dynamic air bronchogram—visible fluid moving back and forth within bronchioles—is essentially pathognomonic for pneumonia on ultrasound.
pearls.verbatim: a dynamic air bronchogram, which is essentially pathognomonic for pneumonia on ultrasound.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Bilateral B-lines in multiple areas can be multifocal pneumonia, but also pulmonary edema, interstitial lung disease, ARDS, or atelectasis.
pearls.verbatim: Bilateral bee... Bee lines, bee lines in multiple areas could be a multifocal pneumonia, but could be pulmonary edema, could be interstitial lung disease.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Three or more B-lines in a single zone is considered pathologic.
pearls.verbatim: To be considered pathologic, you need three or more B-lines in a single zone.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Dynamic air bronchograms are seen as hyperechoic lines with bubbles moving upward, indicating patent airways within consolidated lung.
pearls.verbatim: the hyperechoic line, and you see, like, little bubbles of the hyperechoic line floating upwards.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: A subpleural consolidation appears as a focal defect in the normally smooth pleural line; that finding is not normal.
pearls.verbatim: normally, that line should be nice and smooth straight across. No disconnection. Here you see disconnection. That's not normal. That's a subpleural consolidation.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: If you see vertebrae above the diaphragm, it indicates pathology in the pleural space (effusion or consolidation).
pearls.verbatim: If we are seeing vertebrae back here, we know there's something going on in this space.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Ultrasound is better than chest X-ray for assessing complications of a pleural effusion.
pearls.verbatim: Ultrasound is better than chest X-ray for assessing complications of an effusion.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: Mirror artifact of the liver above the diaphragm can be mistaken for consolidation; if spine does not extend beyond the diaphragm, it is artifact.
pearls.verbatim: what you're seeing is a mirror image of the liver on the cephalad side of the diaphragm.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on Pneumonia & POCUS

pearls.text: For physical exam alone, the failure rate (no pus when cut) was 17%; with point-of-care ultrasound plus physical exam, it dropped to 3.7%.
pearls.verbatim: So for physical exam alone, it was seventeen percent. And for point of ultrasound with physical exam, it went down to three point seven percent.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Cobblestoning (anechoic lines splitting fat globules) indicates fluid in subcutaneous tissue but cannot differentiate cellulitis from edema without clinical context.
pearls.verbatim: All the anechoic sort of lines and wakes going through the subcutaneous layer is what's creating the cobblestoning. So it's like fluid splitting up the fat globules into more individual spots. ...ultrasound, just like X-ray, just like CT, just like MRI, can't really tell the difference between infected and noninfected fluid.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Doppler shows hyperemia in cellulitis (more blood flow) but not in simple volume overload edema.
pearls.verbatim: Doppler can also be useful when looking at cobblestoning. Again, cellulitis is inflammatory, so you would expect more or less blood flow. More. More. Right? Whereas in just volume overload causing lower extremity edema, not necessarily gonna have hyperemic tissue.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: If an abscess has septations (hyperechoic lines inside), you likely need to open and drain it with hemostats rather than just needle aspiration.
pearls.verbatim: Do you see septations? So hyperechoate lines sort of going through the abscess. If you do, you probably don't wanna just stick a needle in it. You probably have to open that one up and drain it, and you're gonna have to use the hemostats to open things up.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS for Abscess

pearls.text: Nerves in short axis have a honeycomb pattern (hypoechoic circles with hyperechoic borders); tendons in short axis look like a paintbrush end, tightly packed hyperechoic dots.
pearls.verbatim: It's got heterogeneous heterogenous echogenicity. So you're gonna have some hypoechoic circles surrounded by hyperechoic borders. Okay? And so it creates this honeycomb pattern that you can kinda see in this median nerve.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Patient positioning for knee ultrasound: have the patient sit against a wall with the leg straight and a pillow under the knee for comfort and optimal probe access.
pearls.verbatim: So what I would recommend for whoever's having their knee scans, I would have you sit, like, against the wall with your leg straight out with a pillow propping your knee.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For static guidance of an anterior knee injection, find the infrapatellar patellar tendon view, then slide the probe laterally until you lose the tendon—that is a safe needle entry zone.
pearls.verbatim: If you take the probe and you find this view, infrapatellar, and you just... While you're looking at your screen, come off to the side a little bit. And when you lose the tendon, that's a safe place for you to stick your needle.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: The medial meniscus appears as a triangular structure between the femur and tibia on the medial joint line; its echogenicity varies with gain and probe angle.
pearls.verbatim: This triangular structure here, here, and here, and here, this is all meniscus. Okay? So you're just looking. Find the femur, find the tibia, and then find that triangular structure going in between.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: The MCL is visualized in the same ultrasound view as the medial meniscus, attaching femur to tibia; the LCL requires a more lateral and inferior view, attaching femur to fibula.
pearls.verbatim: MCL is gonna be in the same view as the meniscus. Right? MCL attaches femur to tibia. K? The LCL is a little bit different. You have to come more laterally and usually more inferiorly because it's attaching femur to fibula.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: For a therapeutic knee injection, mix 40 mg of Kenalog (1 mL) with 4–5 mL of 1% lidocaine without epinephrine.
pearls.verbatim: Generally, what I do is forty milligrams of Kenalog, which is one mil, and then four to five mils of one percent lidocaine, no epi.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: When loading a syringe, invert the vial and keep the needle tip visible in the fluid at all times; if the tip comes up through the meniscus you will aspirate air.
pearls.verbatim: if you don't know about surface tension, you should use it to your benefit when you're loading your syringe... you can see the tip of your needle. You pick it all the way through, you're gonna be sucking air. Just keep it down there. Keep your eye on it.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Center the probe over the suprapatellar recess at about 2 cm above the patella; anything above that is quadriceps tendon.
pearls.verbatim: So right about two centimeters is what I'm looking at. Anything above that is tendon.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: When applying iodine, start in the middle and go outward—do not touch the same place twice with the same swab—and repeat three times, allowing it to dry between applications.
pearls.verbatim: you start in the middle and you go out. Right? Throw that away, and you do that three times. Wait for it to dry.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: Ethyl chloride spray can be used for topical anesthesia before joint injection; although it is not sterile, studies show it does not affect infection rates.
pearls.verbatim: This is not sterile. And, yes, you are spraying the spot that's supposed to be sterile. The studies show it doesn't make a difference. So your patients might really appreciate this.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS of the Knee

pearls.text: In zones 4 and 6, use the abdominal preset because it provides a much nicer image.
pearls.verbatim: If you're in zone four or six, which I will show you in a minute, use the abdominal preset because it'll look a lot nicer.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Dynamic air bronchograms, seen as hyperechoic dots moving with respiration, are super highly specific for pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: One of the findings you're looking for is called dynamic air bronchograms. So if you see right here, you've got a hyperechoic dot coming down and going back up. ... So this is a dynamic air bronchogram, super highly specific for pneumonia.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Focal B-lines, especially three or more in a single zone, are 96% specific for pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: And, again, 96% specific. Specifically, if there's three or more in a single zone.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Lung consolidation (hepatization) appears as liver-like tissue; if you see organ where only artifact should be, something is wrong.
pearls.verbatim: So if you actually see organ that looks like lung or liver, something's wrong. K? This is called hepatization because this is what liver looks like as well on ultrasound.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Shred sign, a hyperechoic irregular line between consolidated and aerated lung, is very highly specific for pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: This is shred sign. So shred sign is the interaction between the consolidated lung and the aerated lung. It produces this shredded appearance. It's hyperechoic. Can see it here as well. Shredded appearance between consolidation and normal aerated lung.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Pleural effusion allows visualization of the spine above the diaphragm (spine sign), which is not seen with aerated lung.
pearls.verbatim: Notice here, you can see the spine extending above this diaphragm towards the head. Right? Whereas before, we didn't see it because it was just aerated lung. Now we've got an effusion. We've got consolidated lungs. So those sound waves can travel all the way down and show us that there's actually a spine there too.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Bilateral symmetric B-lines with a thin, crisp pleural line suggest pulmonary edema rather than pneumonia.
pearls.verbatim: If you only see B lines and you see it both sides and it's pathologic on both sides, that's highly suspicious for pulmonary edema. ... more symmetrical it is, the more likely it's to be heart failure. Also, if you look at the pleural line, the thinner and crisper it looks, the more likely it is to be heart failure.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS - PNA (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Thyroiditis appears heterogeneous with black-and-white specks due to lymphocytic infiltration.
pearls.verbatim: you get a heterogeneous look because the lymphocyte infiltration.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Be consistent in measurement technique from one exam to the next to ensure reproducible follow-up.
pearls.verbatim: you do the best you can and be consistent from measurement to measurement so that you can get the most reproducible down the line.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Infiltrative margins that extend into the muscle are obviously concerning for malignancy.
pearls.verbatim: This is infiltrative. So this goes on the thyroid gland, starts going into the muscle. That's obviously concerning.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: A halo sign around a nodule is generally benign.
pearls.verbatim: Because if it's got this halo sign, that's generally open.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: A simple cyst is benign and no cause for concern.
pearls.verbatim: So simple cyst, like you were saying, Adam, that's no big deal.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Colloid cysts with a hyperechoic comet-tail artifact are usually benign.
pearls.verbatim: these are usually not a big deal
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: A spongiform nodule is defined as greater than 50% cystic.
pearls.verbatim: So spongiform is greater than 50% cystic, not completely cystic, but greater than 50%.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Microcalcifications (<1 mm) are associated with psammoma bodies and papillary carcinoma, which is malignant.
pearls.verbatim: So microcalcifications are associated with psammoma body... Bodies and papillary carcinoma, which is bad.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: For TIRADS 3 nodules, biopsy if greater than 2.5 cm; follow if less than 1.5 cm.
pearls.verbatim: TIRADS three greater than two and a half centimeters, you're gonna biopsy it. But if it's less than one and a half, you're just gonna watch it.
pearls.speaker: Ledbetter
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Ledbetter on POCUS Thyroid

pearls.text: Confirm unexpectedly low platelets with a repeat sample from a different draw before assuming lab error.
pearls.verbatim: Lab error would be reasonable to do that beforehand. Right? So now we've confirmed it. Right? K? Different lab. Same day.
pearls.speaker: Lee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee on Morning Report

pearls.text: When something unexpected or fishy is going on, explicitly reopen your differential diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: What are you gonna do whenever something is unexpected or if they're... Or if something fishy is going on? Differential.
pearls.speaker: Lee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee on Morning Report

pearls.text: For suspected HIT, order the HIT antibody test.
pearls.verbatim: It's the hit antibody. Yeah. HIT antibody.
pearls.speaker: Lee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Lee on Morning Report

pearls.text: Ensure your assessment and plan are logically connected; avoid non sequiturs in clinical reasoning.
pearls.verbatim: Always, if you write a plan, it should Match the assessment.

pearls.text: For board exam questions, draw a 2x2 table: sensitivity = a/(a+c); specificity = d/(b+d); PPV = a/(a+b); NPV = d/(c+d); relative risk = [a/(a+c)]/[d/(d+c)]; absolute risk reduction = [a/(a+c)] - [d/(d+c)]; NNT = 1/ARR.
pearls.verbatim: you draw a right arrow, that is your positive predictive value. A over a plus b. Opposite arrow, negative predictive value, d over d plus c. And relative risk is just a over a plus c divided by d over d plus c. Flip it and put a subtraction sign. That's your absolute risk reduction. pearls.text: For chronic post-thrombotic syndrome with skin changes (pigmentation, eczema, ulcers), if the lesion is in the SFV (superficial femoral vein) balloon it; if in the iliacs, place a stent.

pearls.text: Only remove clot from deep veins, not superficial ones, because deep veins contain the valves that prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: Only take the deep vein because these are where the valves are. The valves are what we care about. We just want the valves to be both.
pearls.speaker: Megaly
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Megaly on Intro to Peripheral Arterial & Venous Disease

pearls.text: Only two emergencies in pediatric urology: testicular torsion and posterior urethral valves—both occur only in boys.
pearls.verbatim: Emergencies are only... This is great. Only two emergencies in pediatric urology. Only two.

pearls.text: When testicular torsion is found intraoperatively and the testicle is nonviable, anchor the opposite side to prevent future torsion.
pearls.verbatim: What we worry about there is that the other side can do it. So a lot of times, we may not save this testicle if it's black and whatnot, but what we can do is save the other side by anchoring it.
pearls.speaker: Miller
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Miller on Pediatric Urology

pearls.text: Posterior urethral valves cause high pressure that damages kidneys; men cannot leak to relieve pressure, so they are at greater renal risk than women.
pearls.verbatim: Women leak urine. Women can say, darn it. I leaked. And men can say, great. I don't leak. No. The men are worse off because as you get older, that's good. That pressure, whether it's a dilated, you know, prostate, will cause pressure back to the kidneys and the bladder. You, men, are gonna hurt your kidneys with time. Women will not. They leak. It's a pressure relief valve. Men don't have that.
pearls.speaker: Miller
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Miller on Pediatric Urology

pearls.text: Recognize that hospitalized children in this age group are likely to be severe, requiring ICU, BiPAP, CPAP, or ventilator.

pearls.text: Febrile seizures are a rare side effect; only one case occurred in the studies.

pearls.text: Reassure parents that no cases of myocarditis were observed in the pediatric vaccine trials.

pearls.text: Inform parents of vaccine efficacy: Moderna 46% for ages 2–5 years and 31% for ages 6–23 months; Pfizer similar.

pearls.text: Be honest with parents about what you know and don't know, and let them make the final choice.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Morgan on Covid Pediatric Vaccines

pearls.text: If growth measurements look inconsistent, ask the MA to remeasure; if still off, remeasure yourself to ensure accuracy.
pearls.verbatim: When their measurements look wonky and inconsistent, you're asking for them to be remeasured. Then they're remeasured twice and they still don't make sense, you're remeasuring them yourself.

pearls.text: A baby born at third percentile who stays there is not failure to thrive; failure to thrive requires a change from a prior higher percentile.
pearls.verbatim: Failure to thrive inherently usually is a change. Okay? Right? Because that's failure to thrive. Right? That's not something they were born with.
pearls.speaker: Morgan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Morgan on Failure to Thrive

pearls.text: A baby born SGA is not failure to thrive unless it drops from a higher percentile after birth; being small at birth is not a change.
pearls.verbatim: A baby that is born, for example, Doctor. Baby, but it's tiny. Right? That baby's SGA. It's not failure to thrive. It never thrived above whatever percentile it was born, so I'm not gonna say it's not thriving now.
pearls.speaker: Morgan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Morgan on Failure to Thrive

pearls.text: If head circumference drops early in the course of weight loss, it suggests a genetic or organic problem rather than simple undernutrition.
pearls.verbatim: God designed the brain to hold on as long as possible. This kid's brain is not holding on as long as possible. It's probably some genetic programming that's not following it the way that God designed it.
pearls.speaker: Morgan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Morgan on Failure to Thrive

pearls.text: Symmetric growth failure (weight, length, head circumference all declining at the same rate) is a red flag for growth hormone deficiency or a genetic syndrome.
pearls.verbatim: If everything's going all at once, okay. Like, something's probably, like, programming wise, like, not right.
pearls.speaker: Morgan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Morgan on Failure to Thrive

pearls.text: Once a preterm infant reaches a normal growth trajectory on the Fenton curve, you can swap to the CDC/WHO curve.

pearls.text: Without the diagnosis of failure to thrive, families cannot access government-funded resources, so diagnose early.
pearls.verbatim: Without that diagnosis, they're not gonna get those resources.
pearls.speaker: Morgan
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Morgan on Failure to Thrive

pearls.text: If you intervene early (at two months), you can often get the child to eat more without needing complex caloric calculations.

pearls.text: To differentiate acne papules from molluscum contagiosum, look for absence of central dimpling and location around pores.

pearls.text: To improve tolerance of tretinoin, mix a pea-sized amount of tretinoin with a pea-sized amount of moisturizer and apply together.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne

pearls.text: For females with moderate acne, spironolactone is preferred (especially with PCOS); doxycycline is an alternative; birth control can be combined if also desired.
pearls.verbatim: If I had to do my order of preference, I do spironolactone, doxycycline, then birth control unless they're like, hey. I was just gonna be on birth control anyways. I'm like, okay. Then just two birds, one stone this thing, and do it all at once.
pearls.speaker: Nakashima
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne

pearls.text: Severe or scarring acne with ice-pick scars warrants early dermatology referral for isotretinoin and scar treatments (laser, dermaplaning, silicone sheets).
pearls.verbatim: If it's scarring... They do lasering and dermaplaning and things to help with some of the scarring, specifically in acne patients. Also, like, silicone gel sheets that you can get get on Amazon, I think, even with acne scars. So, yeah, referral to derm early for those that are having having scarring that you're noticing. You need ice pick scarring.
pearls.speaker: Nakashima
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne

pearls.text: Prefer ointment over cream or lotion for topical steroids because ointments have no preservatives or alcohol.
pearls.verbatim: Ointment is actually, like, the best of the best, but patients don't like the ointment. I have used triamcinolone ointment for two weeks straight because I have really bad rash. And it's like Vaseline consistency. That's no preservatives, no alcohol. There's nothing in that except for, like, just the good stuff and Vaseline. So always do ointment over all the rest.
pearls.speaker: Nakashima
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne

pearls.text: For severe flares, apply Vaseline liberally and wrap with ACE bandages or gloves overnight (wet-wrap therapy).
pearls.verbatim: you can get, especially in your kids, rattle them up with Vaseline. I mean, just donk them as a Vaseline, and then wrap them in ACE wrap or acrylics, whatever you can find. And we'll put them in their jammies, like, little footy and zip them up to where they can't get out of it, and it traps all of that in. Same thing for the hands for adults. Like, if they get really bad, put gloves on to go to sleep.
pearls.speaker: Nakashima
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne

pearls.text: During steroid breaks, use plain Vaseline (petroleum jelly) as a moisturizer; it is cheap and effective.
pearls.verbatim: Vaseline is, like, so underappreciated. It's cheap. It's petroleum jelly. I mean, it's so cheap, and it does really good with these patients.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Eczema and Acne

pearls.text: Ask patients about their current products; if they use Johnson & Johnson baby products, advise them to stop because these are alcohol-based and drying.

pearls.text: Only 7% of family physicians now practice obstetrics, down from 45% thirty years ago, contributing to obstetric deserts.

pearls.text: The NIDA-4 asks: have you smoked tobacco/vaped, had >4 drinks of alcohol in a day or >10 in a week, used a prescription other than prescribed, or used any illicit drugs (including marijuana).
pearls.verbatim: Have you smoked tobacco or vaped? More than four drinks of alcohol on a day? More than 10 in a week? And then use prescription for something other than prescribed or use any illicit drugs.

pearls.text: If any NIDA-4 question is positive, perform screening, brief intervention, and referral to treatment (SBIRT).
pearls.verbatim: If any of these is positive on this one, then it's considered a recommendation to do what's called screening, brief intervention, and then referral to treatment.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: The 5 Ps (Parents, Partner, Past, Prescriptions, Personal) use indirect questioning to assess substance use, which may be easier for patients to answer.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: Fetal growth restriction is defined as estimated fetal weight less than 10th percentile for gestational age based on abdominal circumference.
pearls.verbatim: By definition, fetal growth restriction is estimated fetal weight of less than 10% of age or based on abdominal circumference through the same.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: The Hadlock formula is superior to NICHD and WHO for detection of fetal growth restriction or small for gestational age.
pearls.verbatim: They discussed the Hadlock formula, which is superior to NICHD and WHO for detection of fetal growth restriction or for small for gestational age.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.verbatim: If you do have a patient that you're worried about that may have had history of SGA in a prior pregnancy or has size-date discrepancies greater than two centimeters, hypertension, kidney disease, there's a bunch a bunch that you have concern for SGA, and then you're gonna get a growth ultrasound. pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: For hypothyroidism in pregnancy, the TSH goal is less than 2.5 mIU/L.
pearls.verbatim: your goal for these patients is 2.5, less than 2.5 for TSH.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.text: Thyroid disease symptoms can mimic pregnancy symptoms, making diagnosis challenging.
pearls.verbatim: It's gonna be hard to determine symptoms from pregnancy versus actual thyroid problems. And that's why thyroid problems are so often missed in pregnancy because they mimic pregnancy symptoms.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nakashima on Updates in Pregnancy Care From: AAFP FCPC 10/2/25

pearls.verbatim: The theory is you're... Overstimulate the nerve, and that makes it reset. Kinda so if they're having aching pain, you overstimulate. You push on it, freaks it out, and it resets back to normal.

pearls.speaker: Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on OMT

pearls.text: If nausea/vomiting persists after 16–20 weeks with abdominal pain, that is abnormal and warrants further evaluation.

pearls.text: Pain that is localized or abrupt in the first or second trimester is a warning sign for non-pregnancy-related causes.

pearls.speaker: Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: Pain associated with nausea and vomiting, fever, or vaginal bleeding is concerning for non-obstetric pathology.
pearls.verbatim: pain is associated with nausea and vomiting, fever, or vaginal bleeding.
pearls.speaker: Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: The most common cause of early pregnancy pain that is most concerning is ectopic pregnancy.
pearls.verbatim: What is the most common cause of early pregnancy pain that would be most concerning? Exopic.
pearls.speaker: Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: A pregnant woman can have one CT abdomen/pelvis without enough radiation to harm the baby.
pearls.verbatim: A pregnant woman is, quote, unquote, allowed to have one c... CT abdomen pelvis in the pregnancy, and it won't be enough radiation to cause harm to the baby.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.speaker: Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.verbatim: Appendicitis remains the most common cause of acute surgical apnea in pregnancy, and delay of diagnosis causes increased harm to breathe.
pearls.speaker: Newborn
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Newborn on Pregnancy Pain

pearls.text: If baseline creatinine is unknown, assume a baseline GFR of 75 to apply the RIFLE criteria for severity assessment.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: Do not perform a fluid challenge if obstruction is present; pushing more fluids into an obstruction will worsen the condition.

pearls.text: Consult nephrology when the diagnosis is unclear, especially for intrarenal causes, or when there is a poor response to treatment.

pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nichols on Acute Kidney Injury (9/11/25)

pearls.text: In trauma resuscitation, after undressing and procedures, it's often forgotten to cover the patient back up, leading to iatrogenic hypothermia, coagulopathy, and other complications.
pearls.verbatim: So what's the first thing that we do when they come in? Right? Undress And then we're worried about them, you know, breathing and putting in chest tubes, and sometimes it's forgotten to cover them back up. And so even though we keep... Probably they're hot, like, they're supposed to be that way to avoid the hypothermia, but they are still very at risk, which can cause coagulopathies and other issues down the road.

pearls.text: The hallmark of Stage III hypothermia (28–24°C) is that the patient is no longer shivering.

pearls.text: The height of the Osborn wave (J wave) on ECG correlates with the degree of hypothermia — more prominent in Stage III than early Stage II.
