pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: First-line management of hypothermia is removing all wet clothes; leave wet clothes on and your rewarming efforts will be negated.
pearls.verbatim: If their their wet clothes just sit on them, they're going to continue to lose body heat, and your your rewarming efforts are going to be negated by that.
pearls.speaker: Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: When rapidly undressing a patient (especially from the homeless population), tell them what is happening and offer replacement clothes if available to reduce distress over loss of their belongings.
pearls.verbatim: I always try to tell people, like, hey. Cutting your clothes off. I will say homeless population, when you do that, sometimes they become very distressed about their clothes, which is reasonable because they have very little. This may be their only set of clothes, or they're they're one of two. Right? And so most people who are, like, denied, right, have a million changes of clothes at home. Right? I need to cut my clothes off. Okay. Cut my... Like, it's fine. But the good thing in the emergency department at John's, not everywhere is like this, but we have a clothing closet. You guys probably utilize it too for people who don't think something happens. If you can tell them that, one, you can tell them that they can keep their clothes even if it's... If they're being cut off. We had that happen in the Trauma Bay the other day. This guy's... We we shredded everything. He was like, I have to keep all of that. Okay. They're yours. Like, I'm not gonna take them from you. And then you just say, hey. I will get you other clothes, right, if you have that available to you. Please don't promise it if you don't.
pearls.speaker: Nicole Tipton
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Nicole Tipton on Environmental Exposures 11/20/25

pearls.text: Differentiate lethargic from stuporous patients: stuporous patients spend more time with eyes closed, interaction is brief and nonsensical, and protective reflexes diminish, making this transition dangerous.
pearls.verbatim: So then comes the stuporous patient. And what defines a stuporous patient from the lethargic patient is they spend more of their time with their eyes closed not interacting with you than they do. And when they do interact with you, it's brief. It's nonsensical. It's in and unintelligible more than likely.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Cortical dysfunction causing coma is most often due to metabolic disturbances (hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia), intoxications (benzos, alcohol), generalized seizures, global hypoperfusion, or anoxic injury.
pearls.verbatim: So often, it's nonanatomical injuries injuries, but things you see all the time. Metabolic disturbances, hyperglycemia, hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia, all of the hyper... Being the biggest one, you're done. Right? Intoxications. Oops. Generalized seizures, toxic metabolic syndromes, and delirium.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Slow roving eye movements (ping-pong balls) are often a sign of delirium or metabolic derangement.
pearls.verbatim: Slow roving eye movements. So I don't know. You probably have seen one of those where the eyes are just going back, back slowly, like ping pong balls. That's what we call them. It's an often sign of a delirium or metabolically deranged patient.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Pinpoint pupils in a comatose patient suggest pontine catastrophe or opiate effect; remember 'ps' for pinpoint leads to the pons.
pearls.verbatim: And then pinpoint pupils, which should be in the other slide. Usually, medication affects opiates specifically. And then pontine catastrophes if they're in a coma. So the ps meaning pinpoint pupils leads to the pons.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: When testing motor response in a comatose patient, pinch once and right to avoid repeated trauma; score as localize (crosses midline), flexion (does not cross), decorticate, or decerebrate.
pearls.verbatim: do it once and right. So you can actually tell a lot about a motor or a person's neurological status from their motor response. So you can't score at zero to five. That infers that that person can comply with exam and show you different forms and powers of strength. All you have to score is localized, flexion, deep corticate, or decerebrate.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: A localizing motor response means the patient crosses midline to the stimulus; flexion means they flex but don't cross midline, indicating blunted cortical function.
pearls.verbatim: A localized means if I pinch you here, you're gonna cross midline with your other side, probably slap me. K? In a person, cross midline to the source of the stimulus. Reflexion means that you don't quite get across midline. So I pinch you here. You flex your arm, but you don't get across.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: If one side flexes and the other does not move, it indicates a unilateral injury; if arms do not move but legs do, consider spinal cord injury.
pearls.verbatim: If you see one side flex and the other side not move, it tells you that it had a unilateral injury. If you see both sides or the arms not doing and legs doing, they might have a spinal cord injury.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus is rare but has >50% mortality because it is poorly recognized; EEG is marginally helpful as it only captures the moment.
pearls.verbatim: Nonconvulsive status is more than half of the people. Why? Because it's so poorly recognized, and it goes on for longer than it should, meaning that there's injury to the brain and complications.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Triphasic waves on EEG are pathognomonic for metabolic derangements, especially renal failure; PLEDs are pathognomonic for HSV encephalitis.
pearls.verbatim: So this is a common triphasic pattern. Triphasic because there's three phases, one two three, which is very, very common with metabolic derangements, specifically renal failure.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Delirium precautions: lights on during day, off at night; patient out of bed; glasses and hearing aids on; TV off at night; advocate with nursing via smart phrases.
pearls.verbatim: Life's long during the day, off at night. That's a nursing issue. I'll tell you, our nurses right now are really, really, really stretched there. So it's up to you to go in and enforce that. Two, make rounds to make sure that lights are on yourself.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: In aphasia, the eyes deviate opposite the side of the lesion; this helps localize the lesion.
pearls.verbatim: the eyes will point opposite of the aphasia.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: After a seizure, a focal deficit (Todd's paralysis) occurs contralateral to the seizure focus.
pearls.verbatim: After a seizure, what can you have? Like, a focal deficit. It's called a something paralysis. Right? Contralateral.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Upward eye rolling (Bell's phenomenon) has no localizing value; it is a normal response in syncope and coma.
pearls.verbatim: this eye rolling in the back of the head thing, that has no localization potential. It happens with it happens with syncope. And, actually, what you're seeing is what is actually called Bell's phenomenon.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Clinical assessment begins as soon as you enter the room; observe the patient before any formal interaction.
pearls.verbatim: your assessment starts as soon as you enter the room. Even before I enter the room, I'm already observing what's going on
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Flushing in a man is abnormal and should prompt evaluation for carcinoid syndrome or other causes.
pearls.verbatim: His face was super red, like, redder than I would expect it to be. So I I asked him, do you feel flushed or, like, are you just really hot? What's going on? And he said, yeah. I just have these, like, random hot flash type of symptoms. But then he's a man who's 52 years old, not a woman who's 52 years old.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: CHF is a clinical diagnosis; Framingham criteria (edema, orthopnea, cardiomegaly) can be met even with a normal echocardiogram.
pearls.verbatim: He has the edema. He has the orthopnea, and he has cardiomegaly. So that's two major and one minor criteria.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Do not order additional imaging based solely on a radiologist's incidental finding; pursue it only if it will change management.
pearls.verbatim: do things that you think will change your management. Don't just do it because the radiologist said it.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Ki-67 index is a marker of mitotic activity and is specific for neuroendocrine tumors; high index indicates aggressive disease.
pearls.verbatim: k I 67 index is either low or high, and it's generally very specific for neuroendocrine tumors. What it's telling us is the rate of mitotic activity in a specimen.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: If a patient needs a PET scan for therapeutic decisions, stabilize and discharge them because inpatient PET scans are not covered.
pearls.verbatim: So if you have a patient that you're like, man, this person really needs a PET scan, and their their therapeutic options depend on the results of a PET scan, please do them a favor and just do your best to stabilize them and discharge them.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Before discussing biopsy results with a patient, look up survival statistics for that cancer to prepare for the inevitable question.
pearls.verbatim: I always have to look it up before I get in that room. If I get a biopsy that's back for some kind of cancer, I stop and I look up because I know they're going to ask me the minute I tell them the results.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Only about 10% of patients with neuroendocrine tumors develop carcinoid syndrome symptoms; most are associated with midgut tumors.
pearls.verbatim: Only ten percent of these patients who have neuroendocrine tumors will actually have these carcinoid syndrome type of visitations, and most are associated with midgut tumors.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Be aware that 17% of patients with neuroendocrine tumors develop a second primary malignancy, which is not a metastasis but a new primary tumor.
pearls.verbatim: Seventeen percent of people with neuroendocrine tumors have a second primary malignancy, not a secondary lesion from a primary malignancy, but a second primary malignancy.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: For carcinoid heart disease, manage with octreotide and diuretics; valve replacement is rarely indicated.
pearls.verbatim: If they have heart disease, put them on octreotide, put them on diuretics
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: For carcinoid-associated wheezing, consider bronchodilators.
pearls.verbatim: Think about bronchodilators for your wheezing patients.
pearls.speaker: Okeefe
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Okeefe on Coma for the non-Neurologist

pearls.text: Pallor of the conjunctiva can predict whether a child with malaria will need a blood transfusion.
pearls.verbatim: I can tell depending on how pale the conjunctiva is, I know whether I'm gonna need to end up giving blood or not.
pearls.speaker: Papp speaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: In Togo, the first thought for fever and abdominal pain should be typhoid fever.
pearls.verbatim: In Togo, your... The very first thing that you're thinking is that this is typhoid.
pearls.speaker: Papp speaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: A neonate with heart rate 60 is in crisis; immediately grab the child, ambu bag, suction, and crash cart.
pearls.verbatim: Heartbeat's 60 in a neonate. Mhmm. So grab that child. You know, I'm asking for ambu bag, suction, crash cart.
pearls.speaker: Papp speaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: Bilateral hydronephrosis on ultrasound in an infant with abdominal distension suggests bladder outlet obstruction.
pearls.verbatim: I see hydro bilaterally, so that also supports my diagnosis.
pearls.speaker: Papp speaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: If unable to place a Foley catheter after multiple attempts, consider placing a suprapubic catheter to relieve obstruction.
pearls.verbatim: We tried to place that Foley three three four attempts. Couldn't get it through. So surgery paste... Placed a suprapubic cath, and we saved her life.
pearls.speaker: Papp speaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: When titrating labetalol, make slower adjustments due to its longer acting nature; nicardipine (Cardene) is fast-acting and allows more rapid titration.
pearls.verbatim: You have to make slower adjustments. The reason why we like Cardene Gript is because it is fast acting, and so you can titrate more rapidly. Watch out with your Lavella. It's a little longer acting, so you wanna make slower titrations.
pearls.speaker: Papp speaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: In a Muslim culture, a female physician must navigate gender norms, such as avoiding eye contact with men and being cautious about physical touch during exams.
pearls.verbatim: And how do I navigate that as a woman in a Muslim culture, I'm not supposed to look at men in the eyes? And they... You know, touching a man for an exam, like, you know, Muslim culture.
pearls.speaker: Papp speaks
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Papp speaks on Medicine and Missions

pearls.text: When examining a patient with possible liver cancer, auscultate for a hepatic rub — only cancer of the liver produces this sound when the capsule is breached.
pearls.verbatim: When cancer comes through the outer lining of the liver, so to speak, the capsule, it rubs up against the peritoneum. You can hear the rub. The only thing that does that is cancer of the liver.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Rather than making statements or imposing an agenda, train yourself to ask sophisticated, sensitive, and kind questions — especially about death and serious illness.
pearls.verbatim: Your job then becomes how to become a sophisticated and sensitive and kind questioner. And if people who are sick will open up where the boss, if... Particularly if you've got some of the more woke varieties around, will go after your guts.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Biblical literacy is essential for understanding English literature, poetry, and cultural references in medicine; test it with tools like those on johnpatrick.ca.
pearls.verbatim: You can test yourself on my website, which is johnpatrick.ca, and you will find there a test of biblical literacy.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The telegram 'But if not' from Dunkirk alludes to Daniel 3:18 — a statement of faith that God can save, but even if not, one will not bend the knee.
pearls.verbatim: The last telegram he sent from the from the beach to London was three words, but if not.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Jonathan Haidt's book 'The Anxious Generation' demonstrates that rising anxiety in young people (women >30%, men ~15-20%) correlates temporally with the introduction of the iPhone.
pearls.verbatim: He'd went... The boy... And the men were somewhat under 10, and the women were somewhat over 10% for years. Then in 2011, it started to change. Now the women are three times higher than they used to be, over thirty percent. The men have roughly doubled. ... And it was realizing that it correlated with the iPhone that start him off.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: In 12th-century England, Archbishop Anselm persuaded all his bishops that slavery was wrong based on the theological idea that the image of God cannot be treated as property, effectively stopping the slave trade in England.
pearls.verbatim: It's the twelfth century. ... And it was Anselm, the great saint, who did it. ... He persuaded all his bishops that slavery was wrong. Paul, in effect, said it when there's neither male nor feed... Female, neither bond nor free. The image of God cannot be treated that way, and they did it.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Patients who understand their diagnosis can organize a good death; the modern approach of trying to make people die without awareness leaves damage behind and will overwhelm psychiatry.
pearls.verbatim: The reason those Jamaicans would say thank you is now they knew what they had to do. They had to straighten out their lives and reconcile it, etcetera, etcetera. They could begin to organize a good death. What we want to do now is get people to die without knowing they've done it and leaving all the the the the damage behind. We won't have enough psychiatrists to cope.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Complicity in administrative assisted suicide will cause guilt that haunts the physician; the only escape is repentance and confession.
pearls.verbatim: If you are, what shall I say, complicit in administrative death, what's that gonna do to your psyche? You cannot avoid feeling guilty about that over time, can you? It's gonna haunt you. ... And the only escape actually is repentance confession.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: In the United States, the founding documents emerged from a moral consensus built on Christianity; referring to the Bible once settled arguments in public discourse, but that authority is now lost.
pearls.verbatim: In the generation before mine, for certain, if there was an argument in a bar in America about how you should behave in a certain situation and somebody said, well, the Bible says, what would that do to the argument? Finish. Over. Now you have no authority.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The Lord's Prayer is entirely about God; the only human requests are for daily food and forgiveness—there is no prosperity gospel in it.
pearls.verbatim: I suddenly noticed that the Lord's prayer is all about God. And when it gets to us, it's just, well, you can ask for your food, and you can ask for the gift of forgiveness. That's it. Now a prosperity gospel in that. This is quite the opposite.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The Hippocratic tradition requires that physicians be granted conscientious rights (freedom to make decisions according to their own judgment), which the profession needs to maintain its respect.
pearls.verbatim: If you want us to behave like this, we require that you give us the right to make the decisions as we see them right, and you respect that. That's Hippocratic medicine in four principles.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The foundational ethical principle for physicians is non-maleficence (do no harm), not beneficence; you can work that out from the Bible where the law begins with prohibitions (the 'ten divine intolerances').
pearls.verbatim: It's nonmaleficence, and you can work that out very well easily from the Bible itself. Because when Moses talks about the future of Israel in Deuteronomy, he says, if you will keep this law, it will go well with you and your children, and you will flourish.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: A culture's stability depends more on what it will not do than what it will; once you have clear negatives (prohibitions), you can extrapolate to positive duties.
pearls.verbatim: A nation and a culture is... Its stability is much more dependent upon what it will not do than what it will.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The moral world does not enlarge; it always goes from truth to falsehood, justice to injustice, love to hatred. Patients live in the middle trying to make sense of the world through a story, which is where religion comes in.
pearls.verbatim: Our moral world is not enlarging. It has always gone from truth to falsehood, from justice to injustice, love to hatred. You see how it works. And we live in the middle trying to make sense of the world, and that's where religion comes in.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Induction (starting from the particular and working to the general) is the method of science, not deduction; it was developed when Christian scholars assumed God's creation is orderly and knowable.
pearls.verbatim: Induction is starting from the particular and working to the general. What they've been trying to do before that was deduction from God to the particularities, and they always got lost on the way.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Reductionism—separating measurable phenomena (weight, distance) from unmeasurable ones (love, justice)—began with William of Ockham and narrowed science to only what can be weighed and measured.
pearls.verbatim: What he did was pull apart the idea of things that we could measure and things that we couldn't. So love, joy, peace, justice, they were left in God's province because we we can't measure them, but we can weigh, and we can measure that area.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: In pagan Africa, malnutrition programs failed not from lack of technical knowledge but because nurses believed an evil spirit took the child's appetite, making it rational to spend money on a witch doctor rather than on feeding.
pearls.verbatim: He said he believed that an evil spirit took the child's appetite away, so he had spent his money on the witch doctor. The child had died. Now that's rational. That is rational.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: In cultures where men eat first, a simple change—giving a slow-eating child his own plate—can prevent malnutrition.
pearls.verbatim: I noticed one of my children was a slow eater, so I gave him his own plate to eat from a common pot. That's malnutrition gone.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: When considering technologies like transhumanism, distinguish between repairing something wrong and redesigning human nature—the latter presumes God's design is wrong.
pearls.verbatim: The distinction, I think, is whether you are looking to repair something that's gone wrong or whether you're proposing that the way human beings are made was wrong in principle.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Seek knowledge to edify others, which is love; avoid seeking knowledge for curiosity, vanity, or profit.
pearls.verbatim: there are some who seek knowledge in order to edify others, and that is love.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The intention of IVF was to cure infertility, to bring lives, which is good.
pearls.verbatim: the intention of IV was to cure infertility. To bring lives?
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: The cardinal problem of human life is to conform your soul to objective reality (God) through wisdom and virtue, not to conform reality to your desires.
pearls.verbatim: For the wise men of old, the cardinal problem of human life is how to conform your soul to objective reality. That's God. And the solution was wisdom, self discipline, and virtue. For the modern person, the cardinal problem of human life is to conform reality to your desires, and the solution is technique.
pearls.speaker: Patrick
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Patrick on Ethics and Morals

pearls.text: Men over 50 should be proactively asked about urinary symptoms, as they rarely volunteer this information.
pearls.verbatim: If you just began querying your male patients over age 50, are you having any urinary complaints at all? You will start it seeing it come out of the woodwork, really. So be sure you're asking that question. It is not usually volunteered by men, I have found, and so it's worth asking.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Constipation worsens BPH symptoms because the full rectum presses on the prostate in the limited pelvic space.
pearls.verbatim: And if the rectum is full, then you're gonna have a lot of pressure against against that that prostate. And so often just having them make sure that they're having normal bowel movements and that things are moving through well will help a lot with with BPH.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Selective alpha-1 antagonists still carry some risk of orthostatic hypotension, like nonsedating antihistamines can cause some sedation.
pearls.verbatim: You will have a little bit of blockage of those peripheral alpha ones even with the selectives. Just like an antihistamine, that's a nonsedating antihistamine. There's a certain percentage of folks that might a little drop in their blood pressure. So just make sure they know that.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Patients on tamsulosin should be warned about floppy iris syndrome; ophthalmologists need this history before cataract surgery.
pearls.verbatim: Floppy iris syndrome is also fairly common with tamsulosin, and so your your eye doctors would like you to tell your patients that. Get their cataract surgery, that they may have a more complicated problem.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Double the measured PSA when a patient is on a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor; a PSA of 4 may actually represent 8–9.
pearls.verbatim: And so we often say at least double the PSA when you're checking it for for prostate cancer if they're on a five alpha reductase inhibitor. K? So don't get fooled into into that that four... A PSA of four that you're sort of watching. If they're on a five alpha reductase, that's a PSA of eight or nine. That's significant.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Use the correct terminology: call them 'lower urinary symptoms' (LUTS) rather than 'BPH symptoms' to avoid diagnostic anchoring and because other conditions cause similar symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: please use the correct terminology. Call them lower urinary symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Straining to urinate involves a Valsalva maneuver that assists the detrusor muscle in emptying the bladder.
pearls.verbatim: This sort of Valsalva having to bear down and to help the bladder, the detrusor muscle, do its job to empty the bladder.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Nocturia is the most common reason patients present; ask how many times they typically get up at night to urinate.
pearls.verbatim: How many times do you typically get up at night to urinate? This is probably the most common reason that a a patient will come in and talk to you.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia

pearls.text: Controlling blood pressure and smoking cessation are the two most impactful interventions in family medicine.
pearls.verbatim: If you spent your career controlling people's blood pressure and getting them to quit smoking, you would help more people, I think, than just about everything else that we do in family medicine.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Cardiovascular disease kills about 18 million people annually; hypertension is the number one risk factor.
pearls.verbatim: Cardiovascular disease kills about eighteen million. All six top cancers, what are they? Lung, breast, colon, prostate, pancreatic, stomach, liver. If you add up the deaths from all of those cancers combined, it comes up to about ten million. About half of the death rate is happening from heart attack and stroke.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: The RAAS system is central to hypertension; angiotensin II is the key molecule causing vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and aldosterone release.
pearls.verbatim: Angiotensin two is where where it all happens.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: At the first visit, check both arms and use the higher reading for diagnosis.
pearls.verbatim: The first visit for anyone is you check both arms, and you take the higher of the two.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Normal blood pressure is <120/80; explain to patients that their organs are designed to function at that pressure.
pearls.verbatim: Your body was designed to function at this pressure. Your heart, your kidneys, your brain, your retina, your tissues, their operating parameter is less than a 120 over less than 80.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: In resistant hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic, first assess adherence before pursuing secondary causes.
pearls.verbatim: But I talk with them about adherence. Start asking your patients when do you take your blood pressure pill. It's almost always adherence.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: If you are managing a patient's blood pressure with a beta blocker alone, you are wrong; it is not an appropriate first-line agent for hypertension.
pearls.verbatim: If you're managing their blood pressure with a beta blocker, you're wrong.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Home blood pressure logs are essential; do not rely solely on clinic readings.
pearls.verbatim: You have to work off the log.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Instruct patients to measure BP twice in the morning after voiding and before coffee, and twice at night before bed.
pearls.verbatim: I like them to do it two times in the morning when they very first wake up after they empty their bladder before their coffee, and then I like two numbers at night before bed.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Measure BP before the morning medication to see the trough effect.
pearls.verbatim: I like to see it before medication first thing in the morning.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hyperextension

pearls.text: Pheochromocytoma is extremely rare (0.6 per 100,000 patient-years); most hypertension is essential, and searching for rare secondary causes is usually not warranted.
pearls.verbatim: About point six per 100,000 patient years. So super interesting. I mean, it's... That's a really cool, interesting thing. Not very important. Not always gonna be what we find as the cause of hypertension.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: If you had to pick one diagnosis to manage for population health impact, hypertension is the most important because it is the number one risk factor for ischemic heart disease—more than cholesterol, diabetes, or smoking.
pearls.verbatim: hypertension is the number one most important risk factor for developing ischemic heart disease. So it's not cholesterol. It's not diabetes. It's not sedentary lifestyle. It's not even smoking.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Patients cannot reliably sense when their blood pressure is high; symptoms like headache or vision changes only occur at extreme levels (e.g., >180/110). Tell patients there is no evidence they can tell.
pearls.verbatim: there's really no evidence that you have the ability to tell. And I'm gonna show you why that is because, definitely, they they may have symptoms when their pressure is one eighty over one ten or 200 over one twenty. Right? But they're not against prehypertension, stage one hypertension, but not all, even stage two.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Angiotensin II is the master molecule of hypertension: it causes arteriolar vasoconstriction, increases sodium reabsorption in the kidney, stimulates aldosterone and ADH secretion, and activates the sympathetic nervous system.
pearls.verbatim: The absolute master molecule of hypertension is angiotensin two. Look at everything that angio does. Again, decrease perfusion. Angiotensin says, we need we need the volume turned up. We need some sympathetic activity. You know, we're bleeding to death. Angiotensin two tells the tubular sodium to start coming back in, increases volume. Right? Angiotensin two tells the adrenal glands to secrete aldo, which is gonna do the same thing, hold on to sodium, get rid of potassium. Angiotensin two causes direct arteriolar vasoconstriction. Direct constriction. That's kind of its name, angiotensin. And then it also acts on the pituitary gland to increase ADH secretion, again, holding onto water that you're not diuresing.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Using a blood pressure cuff that is too small will give a falsely high reading because the artery is not fully occluded.
pearls.verbatim: What happens if you use too small of a cuff? It's gonna be high. Right. Because you're not fully occluding the the artery.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Proper blood pressure measurement requires the patient to be seated for at least five minutes with feet on the floor, back supported, arm at heart level, bare arm, no talking, and no caffeine, exercise, or smoking within 30 minutes.
pearls.verbatim: Properly prepare the patient. Relax. Sitting in a chair with feet on the floor, back supported for more than five minutes. No caffeine, exercise, or smoking.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Encourage medical assistants to obtain a second blood pressure reading in the clinic; it is audited for quality metrics and improves accuracy.
pearls.verbatim: I do wanna encourage you. Make sure that when you have that first one and that little heart is on the door, that you encourage your MA to do that second blood pressure, not just for you and for the patient, but because they're actually being audited for the second blood pressure. And when they don't get it in the chart, that ends up on their, like, evaluation.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Communicate the blood pressure target as 'I would like you to be in the 120s over 70s' to help patients understand the goal.
pearls.verbatim: I would like you to be in the one twenties over seventies.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Resistant hypertension is defined as uncontrolled blood pressure on three medications including a diuretic, with good adherence and no secondary cause.
pearls.verbatim: uncontrolled hypertension with good adherence and no evidence of secondary hypertension on three meds, and one of them has to be a diuretic.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Obstructive sleep apnea is the most common secondary cause of resistant hypertension; work it up before referring.
pearls.verbatim: obstructive sleep apnea is probably the lowest hanging fruit.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Spironolactone is the recommended fourth-line agent for resistant hypertension.
pearls.verbatim: spironolactone is the fourth drug to start.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Do not acutely lower asymptomatic elevated blood pressure in the clinic; it can cause ischemic events. Instead, start or resume medications and follow up in a week.
pearls.verbatim: If a patient comes in with an asymptomatic elevated blood pressure even into what we would consider the danger range, the the data is not there for you acutely lowering that blood pressure. And if something goes wrong and they do have an MI or or a stroke, it is your, I mean, it's your fault.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Do not make management decisions based on a single clinic blood pressure; use home blood pressure logs to see trends.
pearls.verbatim: don't make decisions based on the blood pressure in the in the clinic. Can't do that. You're you're doing some... You're you're flying without a map. You're flying in the fog. You have to have your patients engaged. You have to have the log in front of you. You have to be able to see the trends of what's happening
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Losing 2.5 pounds can drop blood pressure by 5 mmHg.
pearls.verbatim: If you can lose, you know, two and a half pounds, you're gonna drop your pressure by five millimeters of mercury.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: The DASH diet can lower blood pressure by about 10 mmHg.
pearls.verbatim: If you start eating a DASH diet, you're gonna drop another 10... About 10 is what I tell them.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Reducing dietary sodium to about 2500 mg per day (one teaspoon of salt) can lower blood pressure.
pearls.verbatim: About twenty five hundred milligrams of salt is what's in a teaspoon. It's very easy to do that in a day. You're gonna drop your amount of sodium. In some patients, this is very dramatic.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: Using salt substitute (half sodium, half potassium chloride) can lower blood pressure by about 5 mmHg.
pearls.verbatim: just going through a salt lite, which is half sodium, half potassium chloride, or plain old salt substitute will drop their pressure by about five millimeters mercury.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: For prehypertension or stage 1 hypertension, lifestyle changes can often prevent the need for medication.
pearls.verbatim: If you lose five pounds, start eating a little bit better, exercise like what we're telling them anyway, we don't need medicine. I mean, often, if we're in pre or stage one hypertension, we can often keep them from having to be on medication
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: When testing for primary hyperaldosteronism, certain medications (like RAS inhibitors and beta blockers) can be continued, as most patients will have low ratios even on meds.
pearls.verbatim: The endocrinologists have liberalized the testing for hyperaldosteronism by saying you don't necessarily have to stop all of these. There is a list of, you know, certainly the RAS inhibition, and I think beta blockers are on there as well. But there's several that you can actually continue, and you get good enough data.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: In primary hyperaldosteronism, spironolactone is often effective; unilateral disease may be cured by adrenalectomy, though this is rare.
pearls.verbatim: I grew up in a time where it was like, why do I care? Just put them on spironolactone. And if the blood pressure gets better, that's all we're gonna do anyway. So why do I even do all this? Endocrinologists are quick to sort of fuss at you about that. So they really do need to be evaluated. And the reason is because they have unilateral hyperaldosteronism, then they end up with an adrenalectomy, and it's... And they're cured.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: ACE inhibitors are best avoided due to high incidence of cough and risk of burning the entire RAS system.
pearls.verbatim: Why why is the ACE not a good idea to start with with a cough, edema? And it's not a small incidence. Right? The problem that I see is that you all... You almost burn the whole RAS system.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypertension 2.12.26

pearls.text: When asking about libido, compare current sex drive to a couple of years ago, not to when the patient was 20, to distinguish age-related decline from pathologic change.
pearls.verbatim: How's your sex drive? Compare it. What... What's your sex drive like today? And I also make sure they're not comparing it to when they were 20. Right? So if you're seeing a 60 year old guy, ask them, what's your sex drive life like compared to couple years ago?
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: If a patient presents with ED and you check T and it's low, you may create an expectation that T will help; but if the problem is vascular, they won't improve, so be careful with the ED question.
pearls.verbatim: So a lot of patients will come in, they'll say, I'm having ED problems. And if you mistakenly say, well, let's check your T, and it's low, and now you've created an expectation, now you give T, and they're no better because their problem is vascular. So be careful with the ED question.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: Testosterone levels must be drawn fasting; a non-fasting draw can lower the result by 30-50 points, potentially misclassifying a patient as low T.
pearls.verbatim: Testosterone levels need to be fasting. If it's not fasting, it can be a difference of 30 to 50 points. So that can take you from telling somebody they have a low T to normal T.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: If a healthy patient has a total T of 100, you may not need to repeat it; the chance of it being normal is very low.
pearls.verbatim: So if I'm really screening them from... You know, and they're just a healthy guy or whatever, I I do the Total T, and I repeat it. And then there's some nuance there. I mean, it depends on the level. You know, if it's if it's a 100, then I don't necessarily need to repeat that.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: The LCMS total testosterone is the gold standard; the older total testosterone test and the 'testosterone free total SHBG' panel are both outdated and less accurate.
pearls.verbatim: So this is the total LC-MS. So see, if you just do total testosterone, it's the old one. K? So you don't want that top one that's not the one that's as accurate. The LCMS is the one that I'm recommending.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: The 'testosterone free total SHBG' panel in Cerner is the old, inaccurate version; the speaker himself was ordering it incorrectly until preparing this lecture.
pearls.verbatim: And the one that says testosterone free total SHBG is old? The old one. That's what I ordered just recently. That's why I'm doing this lecture. I was doing this wrong.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: In primary hypogonadism, FSH and LH are high because the pituitary is trying to stimulate a failing testis; this is a 'sick testis' pattern.
pearls.verbatim: This is primary. This is a sick testis. The pituitary is trying to make the testis do its job. That's why FSH and LH are high.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: For functional hypogonadism due to obesity, the answer is weight loss and exercise, not testosterone; losing weight can raise total T from 250 to 380.
pearls.verbatim: But the answer for you, sir, is not testosterone. The answer is the gym. The answer is losing weight. The answer is getting rid of your adipose tissue as much as you can. And if they do that, if they will take that seriously, seriously, the next time you check their T, it'll be 380.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: In secondary hypogonadism (low FSH/LH), testicles are small; this pattern suggests a central cause like prolactinoma.
pearls.verbatim: This is secondary. This is true secondary. Right? So this is probably a prolactinoma or whatever. And so in this case, you would... You'd order those extra things. You'd test the other pituitary hormones.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: Only 40% of patients started on testosterone for functional hypogonadism are still on it a year later because the benefit wanes and they remain obese and depressed.
pearls.verbatim: only forty percent of patients that are started in that case will still be on T a year later. Why? Because it runs out of benefit, and they're still fat, and they're still miserable, and they get depressed, and it's not helping.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: The TRAVERSE trial definitively showed no increased risk of major adverse cardiac events or prostate cancer with physiologic testosterone therapy, contrary to FDA labeling.
pearls.verbatim: there was no significant increase in cardiovascular So there was no increase in MACE in patients that received testosterone therapy.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: Testosterone therapy causes erythrocytosis; average hematocrit rise is about 4-5 points. Keep hematocrit below 54% by adjusting dose.
pearls.verbatim: when you put a person on testosterone, if they're gonna have a side effect of they're gonna gain about four or five points in the hematocrit. That's the average. Okay? So if you start at forty eight, and I'm gonna... I'm fixing to tell you that fifty four is the cutoff, so you don't go above fifty four, stop, and adjust the dose.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: Include symptom language in the note (e.g., 'patient is still improving') to support insurance coverage for continued testosterone therapy.
pearls.verbatim: You do need to have some kind of symptom language in in a note that we often will send to them and say the patient is still improving or he's still great on this dose, something that says that this is worthwhile.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Hypogonadism 10/16/25

pearls.text: Bariatric surgery can lead to phrenic nerve injury, causing diaphragm paralysis and chronic hiccups.
pearls.verbatim: They got his phrenic nerve over here on the left side, and he has paralysis of his diaphragm, and he has chronic hiccups.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: ASCVD kills 20 million people per year globally, which is double the combined deaths from all cancers.
pearls.verbatim: Twenty million people died of ASCVD last year.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: If you are managing diabetes and ASCVD without addressing obesity, you are not doing good medicine.
pearls.verbatim: If you're just putting them on a statin and causing their diabetes or you're or you're watching their diabetes and you're struggling with that diabetes and you're not addressing the metabolic and not getting their weight down and not getting them healthy, you're not you're not doing a good job.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Always ask permission before discussing weight: 'Can we talk about your weight today?' Patients expect it and rarely refuse.
pearls.verbatim: Is today a good day? Can I? Can we talk about your weight today?
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: When setting goals, ask for heaviest weight, lightest weight, and goal weight; do not assume current weight is heaviest.
pearls.verbatim: What's your heaviest weight? Don't assume that their heaviest weight is today when they're in your office.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Use the wagon wheel analogy to explain set point: the body wants to stay in its rut; turning out takes sustained effort until new ruts form.
pearls.verbatim: you know how a wagon is going down the muddy road and the wheels get down in the rut. And, you know, that's kinda like how your body wants to stay.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Aim for 5-10% weight loss over a year; rapid loss triggers the thrifty gene and leads to yo-yo rebound with worse body composition.
pearls.verbatim: if you can get 18 pounds every year, that is a win. You win the lottery if you do that.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Know two diets well: DASH and Mediterranean; Weight Watchers is the best commercial diet.
pearls.verbatim: You should know two diets, DASH and Mediterranean. That's it.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Sleeve gastrectomy is a 2-hour procedure, 2-day hospital stay, 2-week recovery; it alters GI physiology, not just stomach volume.
pearls.verbatim: It's a two hour procedure. You're in the hospital for two days, and you recover for two weeks on average.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Metformin causes weight loss primarily through GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea); better options exist for non-diabetic patients.
pearls.verbatim: Why do you lose weight on metformin? You feel terrible. Makes you feel like you wanna vomit all the time.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Phentermine is safe and similar to Adderall; it is an appetite suppressant and can be used long-term with appropriate monitoring.
pearls.verbatim: think of phentermine as kind of like Adderall for the for the gut.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: To prevent constipation from GLP-1 agonists, recommend one tablespoon of Metamucil (fermentable fiber) and two tablespoons of Citrucel (non-fermentable fiber) once daily.
pearls.verbatim: one tablespoon Metamucil, two tablespoons of Citrucel once a day.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Loss of lean muscle mass is the biggest long-term risk of GLP-1 agonists; patients need a high protein intake of 1 gram per pound of body weight and resistance training targeting large muscles like butt and thighs (squats and deadlifts).
pearls.verbatim: they lose lean mass, lean muscle mass. This is the biggest risk, I think, long term. People get feeling really good, and they're losing weight, and they're losing muscle. That's just part of the deal. And so one of the things we talk about, this is a very high level of protein intake. One gram a pound is a ton of protein. If they're normal, they have normal kidneys, they can do it. You gotta get there. They're... They are gonna start wasting away. So cut servings in half, start fiber, start resistance training. That's what I tell them all. What do I mean by resistance training? Your butt and your thighs is the big muscles in your body. I'm not talking about the little... Right? That's what all the guys wanna do is the biceps. Right? Know it's squats and deadlift and, like, big muscles because that's what you... That's where you need the mass.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Topiramate (Topamax) increases the risk of kidney stones. It is useful for patients who eat at night and can cause a taste disturbance that reduces desire for sweets.
pearls.verbatim: Topamax can increase your risk of kidney stones. We know that Wellbutrin lowers the seizure threshold just a bit. Remember? And the GLP ones, and this one is true, history of pancreatitis or multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome, and then thyroid cancer. So those are all kind of warnings. ... CopaMax, I like at nighttime. This is really good for people who get up and eat at night, and and it gives you a little taste disturbance. And so a lot of those... A lot of my patients actually like that because they don't wanna eat sweets.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Recommend Metamucil over Citrucel for additional cholesterol benefit, as it works slightly better.
pearls.verbatim: Metamucil, you get a little bit of the benefit of the cholesterol, and it works a little bit better than just Citrucel by itself. Okay. Try it, sir.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Obesity

pearls.text: Schedule a face-to-face visit for preoperative assessment rather than relying on chart review or email, as this is one of the best reasons to bring a patient in.
pearls.verbatim: Do you do this by just reviewing the chart and sending an email to the surgeon that it's okay to proceed? No. Absolutely not. This is one of the best reasons to bring a patient in to see you.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Procedures under one hour duration pose lower physiologic stress; longer surgeries increase risk.
pearls.verbatim: Minutes, somebody mentioned the duration of time. Right? So is this less than an hour? That's kinda where the data sits. If it's a procedure that's less than an hour or over an hour, there's a little bit higher stress at an hour plus.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Many patients enter elective surgery in a suboptimal nutritional state; address malnutrition before surgery to improve recovery.
pearls.verbatim: Most of our patients are going into surgery, even elective surgery, in a sub optimized nutritional state. Either they're big, they're skinny, skinny. Right? So they're little people that are living in a nursing home. They have a hip or something. They're nutritionally depressed. They go into surgery, and then we wonder why struggle with their recovery.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Assess social support—family, caregivers, socioeconomic status—because patients without a strong support system have worse postoperative outcomes.
pearls.verbatim: What's the social support structure around the patient? Does the patient have family that's gonna be involved? We have lots of institutional support, but they show that when families... When patients come from either a depressed socioeconomic situation where they don't have family, they don't have caregivers, they might be... They have really bad outcomes.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: New chest pain or dyspnea on climbing stairs is a red flag that requires a medical workup for angina or dyspnea, not just pre-op clearance; pause the surgical process.
pearls.verbatim: The other thing to remember is that if if any of this kind of stuff comes back positive in the sense that you're picking up something... Like somebody who's got chest pain or is short of breath when they go up a flight of stairs or whatever, Now they need a workup not for the surgery. They need an evaluation for their dyspnea or for their angina. And, yes, you pause and stop process of surgery to evaluate that problem.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Identify nutritional risk: BMI less than 21, age over 65, and nursing home residence are markers for protein malnutrition, the most predictive bad outcome.
pearls.verbatim: BMI less than twenty one, age over 65, that's every hip fracture that you have seen in the ER. Right? So that's really important. If you're in a nursing home, these are these are people who are, by definition, usually nutritionally depressed. So they're gonna be protein malnourished, which is the most predictive bad outcome.
pearls.speaker: Place
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Place on Pre-Operative Assessment

pearls.text: Target an A1c below 8% before elective surgery; poorly controlled diabetes worsens surgical outcomes.

pearls.text: A key clinical clue for OCD is asking how much time per day is lost to rituals; patients may report hours spent on tasks like redoing makeup or hair.
pearls.verbatim: One of the big markers for OCD that you can ask clinically that often is missed is do you lose... How much time in a day do you lose? Because things have to be a certain way. And you can name it that broadly. Like, how much time? And sometimes it'll be like, well, it takes me four hours to get out the door if I have to redo my makeup four times or if I have to, like, redo my hair four times or whatever it is.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: True panic attacks last minutes, not hours; if a patient reports panic lasting three hours, it's elevated anxiety, not panic.
pearls.verbatim: What lasts three hours? That's stopping. You'd be dead. Your body won't let you be in a true state of panic for three hours. Now you can have elevated states of anxiety for three hours, but that's not panic.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Ask about the first physical symptom of anxiety (GI, respiratory, cardiac, tension) to understand symptom progression and guide intervention.
pearls.verbatim: The other thing I would really wanna know is if it starts in your body, where does it start? What's the first symptom you notice? Is it GI distress? Is it changes in respiration? Is it a feeling of, like, elevated heart rate or, like, pumping? Is it tension?
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Anxiety is rooted in avoidance; if avoidance grows, life shrinks, and adding back avoided activities becomes harder over time.
pearls.verbatim: if they've started avoiding many things and then that immediately makes them feel better, life is getting smaller quickly. And the the longer they... Longer it takes them to find other tools, the longer the list of avoidance gets.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: If anxiety is described broadly and diffusely, screen for childhood adversity (ACEs) because it may underlie the presentation and make treatment more resistant.
pearls.verbatim: the broader they die... They describe it, more broadly they describe it, the more diffuse they describe it, then you you probably wanna start getting some information about, like, their childhood exposure.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: In Cerner, behavioral health screeners are split between ambulatory and behavioral med folders; check both to find tools like the eating disorder screener or adult ADHD screener.
pearls.verbatim: the behavioral med screeners in Cerner are split really oddly. Actually, you just wanna open the ambulatory folder for most of them. If you open the behavioral med folder, your same list, you end up with a different set of screeners.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Benzodiazepines like Xanax or clonidine can shortcut trauma processing in the brain, so therapy work done while on them may need to be redone; propranolol only controls physiological response.
pearls.verbatim: those, for example, who have been prescribed Xanax, all that work that they do in therapy while taking Xanax has to be redone. And same in some ways with clonidine. So just know that. When those come on board, like, the processing in the brain that helps us process trauma, that kinda gets shortcutted or, like, the circuit gets thrown.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: SSRIs are first-line for panic to lower baseline arousal, similar to reducing salt for blood pressure; benzodiazepines and clonidine can impair trauma processing.
pearls.verbatim: for panic, one of the frontline medications is still the SSRI because you're trying to pull that baseline down and trying to build in some things that'll keep it lower. It's like reducing salt for blood pressure.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Propranolol can address physical symptoms of anxiety but may not improve overall anxiety; if a patient stops it despite benefit, explore why—it may not be helping their overall state.
pearls.verbatim: Could it be he finds it not helpful? Why might it not be helpful from an anxiety perspective? I think it's helping his palpitations, but it's not making him feel better overall.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Irritability is a symptom of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), not just a personality trait.
pearls.verbatim: By the way, irritability is a symptom of GAD.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: The main physical risk of panic is head injury from fainting, not the panic itself. Reassure patients that panic is not life-threatening unless they are driving or operating machinery.
pearls.verbatim: What is the biggest risk? If you... Like, physically speaking. Stop breathing. Yeah. You stop breathing, you pass out, and you start breathing. But what could happen when you stop breathing? Get your head. Get your head. Head injury is actually kind of an... Actually, the main physical risk.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: If a patient starts feeling panic, have them do brief high-intensity exercise like burpees or jumping jacks for two minutes to give their body a logical explanation for the symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: Another option is if they start feeling panic is to give their body an explanation for those symptoms. So start doing burpees. Start doing ball push ups. Start doing jumping jacks. Do that for two minutes like a HIIT training.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Panic attacks typically last no more than 15-20 minutes; reassure patients that their body will not allow it to continue longer than that.
pearls.verbatim: Your body will not allow it to last more than fifteen, twenty minutes at the most. It just won't. Not if it's true panic.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: When coaching patients on breathing during panic, emphasize that the exhale should be longer than the inhale to prevent hyperventilation.
pearls.verbatim: the biggest deal is, like, that the exhale is longer than the inhale because that's why people hyperventilate.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Adjustment, Anxiety, and Panic Differentials 10/9/25

pearls.text: Depressed patients will grossly overestimate distance, weight, time, and pain—a key red flag for comorbid depression in chronic pain.
pearls.verbatim: If they're depressed. They will grossly, like, significantly overestimate those very tangible things. Right? Distance, weight, beca... And even time.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Assume patients are doing the best they can in the moment; without that assumption, the therapeutic relationship can feel one-sided and frustrating.
pearls.verbatim: You kinda have to make this assumption. They're doing the best they can in that moment. And if you're... If you don't have that going in, like, we're working together, it can feel like they're not.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Radiculopathy that worsens with exertion is classic for spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication).
pearls.verbatim: So that's how spinal stenosis is is expressed. So it is neurogenic claudication. It is from spinal stenosis.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Post-traumatic arachnoiditis should be considered in patients with spinal trauma who present with radicular pain and adhesive/inflammatory disease.
pearls.verbatim: The other thing is post traumatic arachnoiditis. So she got enough trauma in her spine. She's got adhesive disease and inflammatory disease in her arachnoid.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Be alert that a caregiver may seek more medication to give to their care recipient or for their own escape needs.
pearls.verbatim: It's not unheard of that a caregiver wants to get more medicine to be able to give to, you know, their care givee or that they have escape needs to kinda blow off steam when they're not on it.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: For post-traumatic spinal stenosis, you need flexion-extension X-rays in addition to MRI to assess spinal laxity and instability.
pearls.verbatim: So what else do you have to have besides an MRI? X rays with flexion and extension views.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Frame the independent workup as a collaborative step: 'I want to make sure I know exactly what's going on so we can develop the best game plan moving forward.'
pearls.verbatim: I'm gonna ask to go ahead and do some things so that I am very clear about what the picture is so that we can develop the best game plan moving forward.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Set expectation that opioids are for increasing physical activity and quality of life, not for eliminating pain.
pearls.verbatim: narcotics are going to allow them to increase their physical activities, increase their quality of life, increase their ability to interact with their family.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Use performance-based logs (time out of bed, activities attended) rather than pain scores to monitor opioid effectiveness.
pearls.verbatim: The logs that I'm gonna want you to keep are gonna be much more performance based. How much time are you laying in the bed? How much time are you sitting in a chair? How much time are you out doing those things with your families and friends?
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: A multimodal pain approach requires patients to fill and take all prescribed medications, not just the opioid.
pearls.verbatim: I don't wanna your pharmacy and find out the only medication you filled was the narcotic, and you left all the other ones go.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Include complementary modalities like chiropractic care as part of a multimodal pain approach.
pearls.verbatim: All of the complementary alternative things have ways of making people feel better. So I think chiropractic and or all of those have to be part of your multimodality approach.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: When providing work restrictions for chronic pain, put an initial time limit and then reevaluate.
pearls.verbatim: You put an initial time on it and then reevaluate.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Clarify for patients that acceptance in chronic pain is an active, daily process of acknowledgment, not passive resignation.
pearls.verbatim: chronic pain acceptance does not equal accepting chronic pain
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Be vigilant about secondary gain (e.g., lawsuits, work avoidance) without assuming all patients are malingering; acknowledge the dynamic without negating it.
pearls.verbatim: you don't wanna forget about it. You don't wanna think that they're all in that dynamic, but you don't want to negate that dynamic.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Use the phrase 'hurt doesn't equal harm, sore but safe' to help patients differentiate pain from actual damage, enabling them to engage in meaningful activities without fear.
pearls.verbatim: hurt doesn't equal harm, sore but safe
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Use the 'rules about pain' exercise to challenge automatic thoughts: 'If my pain is this, that means what?'
pearls.verbatim: There's a kind of, like, little exercise called the rules about pain. So if if my pain is this, that means what? If my pain is this, that means what?
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Agree to monitor outcomes specifically for what matters to the patient.
pearls.verbatim: agree to monitor, but very specifically, for what matters to them.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Chronic Pain

pearls.text: Perilymph fistula often follows a combination of fever and head injury occurring close together; surgical repair can dramatically resolve symptoms.
pearls.verbatim: this onset is triggered by, like, a combination of factors. Typically, a fever and a head injury that happen close together. Mhmm. And no one knows why.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: A diagnosis of functional neurological symptom disorder on a chart can persist across systems and lead to undertreatment of future medical conditions.
pearls.verbatim: once that's on her chart as, you know, she goes to the hospital for what feels like seems like stroke symptoms, she has a history of stroke. They can't find a list of evidence that she's had a stroke, so now she has this functional neurological symptom disorder on her chart.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Neurodivergent individuals may have either increased or decreased body awareness; this complicates the differentiation of somatic symptom disorder from normal variation.
pearls.verbatim: those who fall into, like, neurodivergent spectrums often have very low body awareness. ...Do you see that on both sides of neurodivergent people? Hyper and hyper?
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Patients with illness anxiety disorder have minimal or no somatic symptoms but are preoccupied with the fear of acquiring a serious illness.
pearls.verbatim: It's not like actual back pain, or it's not like actual migraines, or it's not like actual GI distress. It's like, oh, my tummy rumbled. Oh, the cancer.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Functional neurological symptom disorder requires that lab/imaging results are incompatible with the loss of function, not just that the cause is unknown.
pearls.verbatim: the lab test, the imaging, whatever is conducted is incompatible with that particular loss of function. Nerve conduction tests are fine, but they can't move their leg.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Factitious disorder involves clear deceit without obvious external benefit like money; patients may self-harm to maintain the sick role.
pearls.verbatim: it's actually, in this case, in the absence of it. So even if there doesn't seem to be any big benefit, I'm not suing anyone. I'm not like... But I still keep having symptoms, and I might even cause my symptoms.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Inconsistent medical history over time, where details change with retelling, is a common feature in somatic symptom disorder.
pearls.verbatim: they tend to be inconsistent historians, though, because so much of their perception of their illness is based on the experience in the moment. ...as I tell the story over the years, it becomes something else.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: A history of multiple hospital systems or extensive diagnostic testing should prompt consideration of somatic symptom disorder.
pearls.verbatim: If you open a chart and it's like, you're the third hospital system they've been to, there's a reason it raises questions.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Illness anxiety disorder is a fear of getting something, not distress from what you already have. The key is the fear of finding out you have a disease.
pearls.verbatim: the critical key point with this, remembering the difference with this one is that it's a fear of getting something. The fear I'll find out I have something. Not that I'm ex... So bothered by what I do have, but the fear that I might have something.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Maladaptive avoidance in illness anxiety can be care-seeking or care-avoiding because the patient may not want to know they have a disease.
pearls.verbatim: maladaptive avoidance. And, again, this can be a care seeking or care avoiding pattern because I might not wanna know that I have a brain.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Illness anxiety disorder appears equally in males and females, unlike some other somatic disorders.
pearls.verbatim: This is the one that's actually most equal in terms of appearing with males and females.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Functional neurological symptom disorder requires loss of function (e.g., limb not working, vomiting) with evidence that it is incompatible with every diagnostic assessment used.
pearls.verbatim: functional neurological symptom disorder. Again, the key here is loss of function. So like a limb that doesn't work or vomiting frequently because... So unable to eat, but no clear evidence of why that would be. But there has to be some kind of loss of that. And then there has to be evidence that it's incompatible with every diagnostic assessment used.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Prognosis for functional neurological disorder is often better than for other somatic disorders, with potential for significant improvement.
pearls.verbatim: the prognosis for this in some ways, even though it may have more impact on daily life when it occurs, the prognosis for improving is a little bit better than some of the others, which tend to just keep coming back.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Integrated treatment includes both physical therapy and addressing underlying anxiety or stress, often in mixed groups with neurological patients.
pearls.verbatim: So they will treat the underlying anxiety that may make this or the stress that's making this occur, but they also are doing the same physical therapy and rehab they would do with them.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: When communicating the diagnosis, avoid saying symptoms are caused by psychological issues; instead say the mind and body are connected and you will treat both.
pearls.verbatim: the standard of care is to have a conversation and to not attribute... To not say, like, these are caused by sight concerns, but to say our bodies and our minds are connected at levels we don't fully understand. And so we wanna come at this with everything we have.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder

pearls.text: Functional neurological disorder is almost always diagnosed by a neurologist, with multiple specialists involved.
pearls.verbatim: it's almost always gonna be a neuro. Right? Like, it's a neuro kind of cluster diagnosis in terms of, like, there probably will be multiple specialists involved.
pearls.speaker: Satterlee
pearls.episode_title: Dr. Satterlee on Conversion Disorder
